William Brayton Ogden
Grand Master 1939-1940

William Brayton Ogden was born of Am'erican parentage in Picton,
Canada, August 26, 1876. He received his primary education in the public
schools of Chicago and in the Colorado State Preparatory School, then
entered the University of Colorado, graduating in 1896 with the degree
of LL.B. On June 18, 1911, he was married to Alta May Swartwout and
they have one son, Robert Ogden. He came to Hollywood, California, in
1910, and has resided ·there continuously since that date, carrying on the
practice of the law and specializing in mining, water and corporation law.
Initiated March 14, 1918, passed April 18, 1918, and raised May 23,
1918, in Hollywood Lodge No. 355, F. & A. M., Grand Master Ogden
served as its Master in 1925 and was appointed Inspector of the 77th Masonic District in 1926, serving in that capacity until 1936. In 1936 he was
a member of the Committee on Grievances of Grand Lodge and was also
appointed Grand Orator and delivered the annual address at the communication of 1937.
In 1937 he was elected Junior Grand Warden; in 1938 Senior Grand
Warden, and in 1939 he was elected Grand Master of Masons in California, being the 73rd Grand Master in this jurisdiction.
Our seventy-third Grand Master is a member of Hollywood Chapter
No. 120, R. A. M., Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine, Hollywood Chapter
No. 209 of the Eastern Star, and holds the rank of Knight Commander of
the Court of Honor, Scottish Rite, Los Angeles. In 1929 he was appointed
Grand Representative of the National Grand Lodge of Egypt near the
Grand Lodge of California, and is still serving in that capacity. . ·
For many years he has served the Masons of Los Angeles as Trustee
of the Los Angeles Board of Relief, Inc., better known as the Bush Estate.
He organized the Masters of Los Angeles Lodges during the year 1925
into the Quarter Century Club and has acted as its president since that
time. During his year as Grand Master he established an unique record
for service by traveling over 40,000 miles, visiting every Masonic District
under his jurisdiction. During his travels he spoke to over 30,000 Masons
and to over 10,000 members of the Eastern Star.
In · addition to his Masonic activities he was president of the Alumni
Association of Delta Tau Delta in 1916; he is a member of the University
Club in Los Angeles, the State Bar of California and the American Bar
Association. He is an active member of the St. Thomas Episcopal Church
in Hollywood, where he has served as vestryman and treasurer. He is a
member of the Republican party.

WILLIAM BRAYTON OGDEN
Grand Master

My brethren of Grand Lodge:

Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free. These words
were spoken by the great Nazarene, and again he said "I am the way, the truth
and the life." In Masonic ritual we say "truth is a divine attribute and the
foundation of every virtue." To be good and true is the first lesson taught
in Masonry. "Magna est veritas et prevablit" (Mighty is the truth and it
will prevail). What the world needs today is the realization of truth as
a permanent factor in life that no dictator or unbeliever can destroy. Where
shall we look for the truth? It is not found from the noisy radio or the
controlled press or the propaganda manufactories, but it is found in religion and in Masonry, in the hearts of honest men and in that wonderful
book opened in the center of every Lodge of Freemasons. Here upon this
book, which is the word of truth and God, our most solemn obligations are
made. The Holy Bible is to Masonr'y what conscience is to man, the guide
of life for, as the psalmist says, "Thy word is truth." In an age where the
Bible has been almost forgotten and its teachings disregarded or lost, as
in some countries in darkest Europe, we must not be· surprised at recent
developments in the so-called civilized old world. Once we spoke of "Darkest Africa," and I remember as a boy reading "Stanley in Darkest Africa."
And today we can speak of "Darkest Europe," not only because of. the
blackouts in its teeming cities, but because of heinous barbaric methods
of modern warfare, that kill more· imr«Xent .civilians, more men, wome~ and
little children than soldiers, and ,so by comparison are mo.re .savage · and
brutal than any of the horrors of the most uncivilized African tribe met
by Henry M. Stanley.
'"
If we turn to the Holy Bible we will find in the Book of Revelation of
St. John the Divine, some of the most remarkable prophesies that are
strange but true. In the 16th chapter we have a description of the great
battle of Armageddon, and in the events leading up to it we read (Revelaation xvi-13:14) "I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the
mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth
of the false prophet. For they are the spirits of devils, working miracles,
which go forth unto the kings of the earth and of the whole world, to gather
them to the battle of that great day of God Almighty.'' Ultimately the victory
is won only by sacrifice of property, the destruction of homes and loss of
human lives. No wonder that Sherman defi·ned war as "Hell" and he did not
k11ow anything of modern destructive machines like Stukas sent · to destroy
innocent cities, nor of the modern devil-fish that can destroy boats laden
with little children on their way to the New World.
Masonry has, I believe, a definite function of tremendous value to perform
in these days of anxiety, by testifying to the reality of God as the great hope
of mankind. Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free.
Belief in God is not only a fundamental essential in a well-ordered life, but
in the passage of history it should be noted that those nations who believed
in God and followed the Bible rather than force are the ones that have
rendered the greatest contributions to mankind . .
Where there is faith in God as the father of mankind, there develops
a corresponding and supplemental belief in the brotherhood of man. It is
therefore natural and logical that Masonry is one of the best expressions of
fraternal life, for God has made of one blood all nations of men. Masonry
belongs to the people, and within the Lodge distinctions are forgotten when
king and subjects are called by the magic word of "Brother.'' It is said when
General -Washington, during the War of the Revolution, would visit a
Lodge his title was forgotten and he was just a plain brother to all brethren
of the Craft.

Democracy Owes a Great Debt to Masonry
Masonry has been called the cornerstone of democratic government.
Masonry and freedom are almost synonymous terms and so, too, are the
words preparedness and peace. Through all the difficulties of the past
history of the American nation Masonry has been the guardian of the truth,
protecting the rights of the people and standing "for the hig?est ideals of
American citizenship. Many Presidents, from George Washmgton down,
have been worthy members of the Craft.
In that most dignified body that is the judicial fortress of the Constitution, the Supreme Court of the United States, the majority have been
Masons. Go to what is facetiously called "the cave of the winds," where
the Senate sits, and there, as in the House of Representatives, an overwhelming majority are members of the Craft. Masonry belongs to the
people and has become an expression of the people's belief in democratic
government. No wonder that Masonry is outlawed in Italy and Germany,
or wherever dictators hold sway.
The only important countries left in the modern world where Freemasonry is welcomed, honored, and respected, will be found among the
democracies of the English speaking people--in the old motherland, where
the Grand Lodge of England still meets regularly in spite of bombs and
shells and blackouts, but witq the sign up, "business goes on as usual."
Besides the people of England and. its colonies, there is the greatest of
all modern republics, the United States of America, with its Masonic Lodges
in all states and cities, in rural sections and in its far-flung possessions.
England and America are united in Masonic fraternity:
Two empires by the sea,
Two peoples great and free,
One antkem raise.
One race of ancient fame,
One tongue, one faith, we claim
One God, whose glorious name
We love and praise.

tempo of the country was changed. A new conception of life and of man
superseded the old. A new and moral impulse spread through every class.

The Traveling Bible
It is most appropriate, and I believe, a most significa.nt occ_asio~ for
us at this communication of the Grand Lodge of Masons m Cahforma to
publicly pay tribute to the power of the Word of God by receiving the
Sacred Book of the Law and the accompanying brochure in these rededication exercises. At the conclusion of this Grand Lodge, and its stay in
California: it will be sent to Brother Adolph S. Walter, Right Worshipful Deput~ Grand Master of New Mexico, that it may be used .there for
similar services of dedication when the Grand Lodge of New Mexico m.e ets
in Santa Fe.
The Holy Bible is the book of truth, indisputable and eternal. Bob
Ingersoll predicted that it would pass into ob_livion in a. few. years, but
today it is still the most popular book in America. The Bible 1s the wo~d
of God, proclaiming truth, life ~nd liberty for a!l p~ople. J_. 1:1· Green, m
his Shorter History of the English People, says m his description of latter
days in the 16th ce~tury, that "England became the people of a Book,
and the Book was the Bible."
Perhaps it is worthy of note that this was ~he beginni_ng of E~gland's
rise as a great world power, rather than to remam a petty msular kmgdom.
He says further: "The effect of the Bible was simply amazing." The whole

11

Our own Theodore Roosevelt said : "No other book ever written in any
other tongue has ever affected the whole life of a people as the authorized
version of the Scriptures has affected the li,v es of the English-speaking peoples." President Andrew Jackson said: "The Bible is the rock upon which
our republic rests." George Washington said: "It is impossible to govern
the world without the Bible."
We as Masons are the guardians of this Sacred Law and today, when
totalitarian ideas are challenging all that we hold dear, let us remember
that through the ages the Bible has been a lighthouse amid raging storms
that has continued to give her welcome guiding beams to enable men to
escape the dangerous reefs of disaster, and to steer safely to the more tranquil waters of brotherhood and peace.
It is indeed a sorry picture that 'faces us when we look across the seas
and behold the wrecks of free governments. The sun of liberty has set in
many countries, but let us hope that as soon as the dark ·night of oppres"
sion has passed there will be a dawn of a better day for mankind.
"Our world is in its autumn, and apparently destined to pass through
some kind of winter before its Easter comes," says Walter Marshall Horton in his new book, "Can Christianity Save Civilization?"

It is with that objective in view that we as Masons look forward to
the future, for "behind the dim unknown standeth God within the shadow
keeping watch above his own."
'
Masonry in its lifelong struggle to uphold the truth and to protect
the people from oppression has become so closely connected with democratic governments that any defeat of England would not only be a catastrophe for democracy, but would mean the banishment of freedom and of
Freemasonry in the land of the Magna Charta; and further, let us not for- ·
get that a similar fate to that of our brethren in France's once proud republic would face us as Masons if the dictators of Europe could gain a
stronghold in this western hemisphere.
As long as the Holy Bible is the inspiration of our nation and as long
as Freemasons uphold their ideals of justice and freedom for all people,
America is safe and truth and freedom will prevail. Because Europe forgot
the lesson of the Bible and failed in its adherence to the truth, neglecting
the mystic power of religion, what do we find as a result? Its people today
are in serfdom, under the three evil spirits mentioned in Revelations. It
is God's truth that makes men free. Ye shall know the truth and the truth
shall make you free. In these services of rededication let us, my brethren
of Grand Lodge, rededicate ourselves to God and country, testifying to our
unswerving belief in the ultimate victory of religion and democracy, because within our hearts we know our cause is just. We have in every
Lodge our Bible and our national banner. Not a flag of a single color like
the red flag of communism, but we pledge our allegiance to the flag of the
red and the white and the blue of America, united, to which as Masons
may we ever be true, one nation indivisible, with liberty and justice for
all.
In the words of a popular patriotic song sung by all gatherings of
those political parties by which a true democracy functions, let these sentiments ring in every heart:

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

This is my final message to you. The term for which you elected me
the titular head of the Craft in this great jurisdiction draws near to a close;
the Masonic year has ended; we, who have served you since the last annual
communication, come to· you with our reports, our recommendations and our
orders and decisions. I trust you will find that our acts and activities have
been well within the authority with which you entrusted us, and in accordance with Masonic· traditions. and teachings.
It has been a busy, fruitful, interesting and instructive year. The program laid out at the beginning of the year has been completed with gratifying results. To me, personally, it has been a year of pleasant service, a
year whose pathway has been strewn with the blossoms of loving acts of
kindness, courtesy and fraternal regard on the part of the brethren, the
perfume of which will come to me again and again in memory as I travel
down the years to that bourne whence no traveler returns.
The jurisdiction is so large that in traveling the length and breadth of
it, as I have done, one meets with every climatic and social condition; from
the tropics of Hawaii and sub-tropics of Southern California to the High Sierras where snow banks in summer are not an uncommon sight; from the mining
camps and small rural communities to the great cities~ from the interior
tle.sert country to the coastal regions of the Pacific; from the citrus groves
and gardens created and fostered by the hand of man to nature's own
towering forests of sequoias and redwoods; each has its own peculiar beauty
and attractiveness. And in such travels one meets Masons of every class
and distinction but · united by the great tie of Masonry, and the urge for
the spiritual side of life for which it stands.
Necrology
The year has not passed without its sorrows and losses as well as its
pleasures and gains. Our Necrology Committee will in due time report upon
our losses, and Grand Lodge will pause in its deliberations to do honor to
our dead. We cannot, however, leave the subject without at this time mentioning the death of our M.'. W.'. Brother William A. Sherman, P. G. M.,
that of M.'. W.'. Brother William H. Waste, who was, at our last annual
communication, elected Grand Master but who, on account of ill health,
.·was forced to decline the office, and that of W.". Brother Frank G. Hobbs,
Assistant Grand Secretary. Each of these distinguished Brothers had devoted more than a quarter of a century to the work of the Craft and their
absence from their accustomed places in Grand Lodge for the first time in
many years is the occasion for sincere expression of sorrow. We should
also note the passing of M.'. W.'. Brother .Orrin S. Henderson, P. G. M.,
who, owing to illness, has not been with us for many years.
Suspensions
The Lodges throughout the jurisdiction are almost without exception
in a healthy condition. The usual number of petitions are being received,
and in addition many brethren who through adverse circumstances during
the past ten years were forced to take <limits, or who through false pride
suffered themselves to be suspended, have now rehabilitated themselves
financially and are returning. Among this group of more tha·n twenty thou-

15

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sand Masons who have been dropped from the rolls are thousands who need
only the extension of the hand of fellowship to bring them back into the
fold. I have advocated that each Brother make himself a committee of one
to extend that hand of fellowship to any worthy Mason whom he may
know, and that our Lodges make easy their return always remembering
that the intervening dues were accumulated at a time when the Brother
did not enjoy the full privilege of membership.
Such as are added to our rolls in this way, come to us with a full
knowledge of Masonry and what it stands for, and moreover they are
re-elected after having been tested and found worthy of membership by
previous years of attendance and participation in our work and fellowship.
They are returning of their own free will and accord and with a full knowledge of their need of Masonry. They come to us with a memory of what
they have missed during their absence from our meetings and such growth
is worthwhile, substantial and permanent.
Owing to the many suspensions we will again show a small loss of
membership. Many of the brethren permit themselves to be suspended
purely through neglect, knowing that for a period of two years their
restoration is the simple matter of tendering the amount for which they
were suspended. But on the other hand, I am convinced, that hundreds
are suspended every year who should not be suspended at all. This results
from inefficiency on the part of the committees on delinquents in many
cases. No member should be suspended without a personal interview. Too
many Lodges consider the matter closed when the Secretary announces,
"He does not answer my letters," but the Brother perhaps does not relish
the thought of putting in writing his real condition. Many hundreds of
brethren annually could and should be saved to our membership rolls if
the members of these committees· would endeavor to personally interview
each delinquent. We have a Masonic duty to perform if the delinquency
is due to the unfortunate condition of the Brother; we have the duty of
remitting the dues in every case where sickness or inability to pay is the
cause of the neglect. In those cases where there is no particular desire on
the part of the delinquent to remain a member, and the neglect is as much
due to this cause as to his inability to pay, nothing would be gained by his
remaining a member and suspension is the proper remedy.

as a part of the annual programs of our District Officers' Associations, a
study of the Digest sufficient at least to enable the officers to know where to
look for the Masonic law concerning any given subject. Facility in the use
of this important work will lessen not only the labors of the Grand Master
and Inspectors, but also that of the officers themselves.
I was greatly surprised as well as disappointed to find that many of our
Inspectors are not holding District meetings of their officers. These meetings can and should be of great value to the officers in an educational way.
The purpose is not served where the meetings are held for social or ritualistic purposes only. The primary purpose should be the advancement of the
officers Masonically' by means of discussions of Masonic law, customs, traditions, history and teachings.

14

Finances
With two or three exceptions, I am happy to report that the financial
difficulties of our Lodges are gradually being solved. It is reported, one
has resorted to the Bankruptcy Court for relief. I find nothing Masonically
illegal in taking such a step but I question the propriety of such action,
especially, if thereby is expressed the desire or hope to discharge its obligations without payment in full of publicly held indebtedness; and I am of the
further opinion, that Grand Lodge by proper action should discourage such
proceedings in the future unless ample provision be made for the payment
of all indebtedness held by others than Masons.
District Officers Meetings
The year passed with few requests for decisions by the Grand Master.
When requests were made for decisions, almost without exception, a new
factual situation was presented or the interpretation of a new feature of our
law was called for. Thus gradually is demonstrated the real worth of that
monumental work of M.". 'vV." . Brother John Stewart Ross, P . G. M. As
officers of Lodges become more familiar with the use of Ross' Digest, the
work of the Grand Master and his deputies, the Inspectors, will be greatly
lessened. The Inspectors can be of great assistance in this by prescribing

Physical Qualifications
With a single exception, the constituent Lodges of this jurisdiction, so
far as has come to my attention, have complied in. every respect with our
Masonic Law. That single exception was in the case of one which elected a
petitioner who was physically disqualified and thereafter conferred on said
candidate the three degrees of Masonry. The candidate had lost a leg
between the hip and knee and was physically unable to comply without the
aid of artificial means. The Inspector was informed of the facts after the
conferring of the second and before the conferring of the third degree. The
Inspector and some two hundred visiting brethren attended the conferring
of the third degree. I accepted the resignation of the Inspector, reprimanded
the Lodge and suspended the Master from office.
There seemed to be no alternative. Had there been I would gladly have
adopted a less drastic course. As long as our law remains as it is, wilful
disregard of its provisions cannot be ignored. It is argued that it is better
to have wooden legs than wooden heads, but it just won't do to have both.
Wooden legs are easily detected, but unfortunately for the Fraternity,
wooden heads are not as readily discernible.
Masonic Interest
I have traveled in pursuance of my duties a distance of more than
40,000 miles, and have addressed groups exceeding in the aggregate a total
of 30,000. It speaks highly for the Masonic interest of the brethren of the
Lodges that such a large proportion of the total membership should thus
have gathered for Masonic fellowship and instruction . .There were several
instances where brethren traveled more than a hundred miles to be present
and would have a like distance to make on the return journey, in one instance over narrow, crooked mountain roads. Again, I say, it speaks well
for Masonry. I have been received throughout the jurisdiction with every
courtesy and honor due the titular head of the Craft and the year has been
one of pleasing contacts and interesting labors.
Masonic Meetings
It gives me pleasure to report that the Grand Master has visited every

one of the one hundred and nineteen Masonic Districts in the jurisdiction.
In the cities, I have been received in one or more joint meetings of the
several Districts, in the less populated sections in individual Districts, and in
many instances, by individual Lodges. The aggregate number of gatherings
which I have addressed Masonically is 151.
By dispensation, Canby Cross Lodge No. 679 invited Silver Trowel
Lodge No. 28 of Phoenix, Arizona, to confer the third degree upon the
latter's candidate and according to the Arizona ritual, ·at a Special Meeting

of Canby Cross Lodge to be held at Prisoner's Rock in the Modoc Lava

By dispensation Midway Lodge No. 426 of Taft was granted permission to hold a Special Meeting for the purpose of conferring the third degree

Both of these Special Meetings were largely attended and much enjoyed by the brethren who were fortunate enough to be present. It is my
opinion that such convocations are good for the Craft but should not be
permitted to grow in number to a point where they no longer serve a useful
purpose.

Employment Bureaus
I returned from the Islands just in time to participate in the annual
breakfast meeting devoted to the interests of the Los Angeles Masonic
Employment Bureau, a department in the Los Angeles Masonic Board of
Relief. There are seventeen boards of relief in the jurisdiction. Seven of
these have employment bureaus.
The work of these employment bureaus is outstanding. We do well
when we relieve the distress of a Brother by a gift of money, food, clothing,
or housing, but such relief is· temporary, and the need a recurring one, and
while for the time being it may satisfy the needs of the physical man it adds
nothing to his moral stamina or spiritual well being. The future is still dark.
But. give him a job where he can earn the money wherewith to procure for
himself and those dependent upon him those self same things and you not
only make provision for his physical needs but you contribute mightily to his
spiritual needs. You have put him on his feet; you have re-spiritualized
him; you have given him a future to which he may look forward instead of
the blank wall of adversity which theretofore had faced him. While we
have salaried employees in charge of this admirable work, nevertheless, it is
a work in which every Mason can be helpful. These breakfasts in the
several sections of the state are the means of communicating to the brethren
wherein they may be of service, as well as being occasions for the outflowing of much good fellowship and fraternal regard.
It was my good fortune to be able to attend similar breakfast meetings
arranged by the several employment 1>.ureaus at Long Beach, Sacramento,
Berkeley and Fresno: The large attendance at each of these meetings indicated the interest of the brethren in this so worthwhile work of Masonry.

A Militant Masonry
My intercourse with the brethren teaches me that there is an undercur,rent of feeling among the Craft that Masonry as an organization should
be more militant. We find this feeling exists more largely among the less
informed members. Among those who have delved into the history of the
Order, its historical approach to the problems of mankind, and can vision
the effect upon our beloved institution which might follow if such a program
were adopted, there is a hesitancy to depart .from our present method of
approach to world problems.
A Brother wrote me, asking a permit to appear before Lodges to show
a film and deliver an address upon the Townsend Plan. I replied as follows :
"Dear Brother :
" I thoroughly appreciate your honest desire to better the condition of the unfortunates of our country. But for hundreds of years
it has been the unbroken policy never to let any· controversial matter enter our Lodge rooms. I fear I would be sincerely and sharply
criticised were I to permit a discussion of the Townsend Plan to
be presented. Were I merely a member on the side lines, but with
my present knowledge of Masonic law and custom, I would most
certainly object. These are matters to which the individual Mason
should devote himself, just as you are doing, and you are to be
commended for taking the interest you do, in the movement. That
is precisely the way that Masonry accomplishes its purpose of
bettering the condition of mankind. Masonry teaches the fundamentals in the Lodge rooms. Masons practice that teaching in the
high-ways and by-ways, in the churches, the chambers of commerce, in the legislatures and the halls of Congress, the Boy Scouts
and in the service clubs. I am sorry that I cannot accede to your
request for the privilege of lecturing in the Lodge rooms, because
I know you are sincere and want to be helpful in the cause you have
espoused. But such is not the way in Masonry."
It must be remembered that we have within our memQership, men of
every race, sect and opinion, and nothing should be said or done in a
Masonic meeting that would be found offensive or emb'l.rrassing to the
least among us.

· Owing to deaths and resignations, I have had .occasion to make more

Constitution and Ordinances with more completeness than their predecessors. One met with some difficulty. In his report he states:

·
When the fact is noted that at least one of these secretaries to whom

In my opinion an Inspector should inspect the books and records of

Master at the time provided in Section 53. This report should reflect the
financial condition of t):i.e Lodges in a general way; its growth or lack of

attendance and harmony or lack of same; and finally what the Inspector has
done to correct any undesirable condition. The report to the Grand Lecturer provided for in the same section should cover the ritualistic wo:k. of
the Lodges, the proficiency of the officers, and those matters appertammg
thereto.

Masonic Education
Many jurisdictions have ceased to use the term "education" in this connection and now have committees of Masonic "advancement." I like the
term better. The term "education" implies a state of ignora?ce on the part
of the subject, and Masons I believe resent the imputation. The te:m
"advancement" carries with it no such imputation. No matter how well mformed he may be, a Mason may yet be capable, and desirous, of advancement.

Patriotic Programs
In accordance with the standing resolution of Grand Lodge, Constitution Day in September, was observed throughout the jurisdiction with
patriotic ~rograms particularly stressing the value of American Citizenship.
Wherever possible these were held as District meetings and open to
Masons, their families and friends.
I appointed a special committee, the Constitution Day Progra~ committee, composed of M."."W.". Robert B. Gaylord, P. G. M., Chairman;
M.".
Randolph V. Whiting, P. G. M., and M.". W.". Charles M. Wollenberg, P. G. M., to assist Lodges and Districts in preparation of worthwhile programs. A panel of well known speaker~ was arranged and many
notable meetings were held throughout the jurisdiction.
It seemed to me that Masonry could do no more worthwhile work
than to aid and assist those who are striving to arouse in the American
people a proper sense of the value of the right of citizenship as we know
and have it here in America. Because it came down to us from our fathers
with its freedom of speech and press, freedom of conscience, freedom of
assembly, and all those rights which may be grouped under the head of the
Rights of the Individual, and because we are far removed from those days
when they suffered, bled and sacrificed that we mis:ht .have them, we are
prone to think of them as irrevocable. For the thmkmg man, however,
current history teaches that in many nations, rights that they thought and
hoped might be irrevocable, were nevertheless, transitory.
The lapse of time, the ruthless hand of ignorance and the devastations
of war have, indeed, laid wastie and destroyed many valuable monuments
of antiquity on which the utmost ~xertions of human genius were employed not the least of which are the rights of the individual. That ignorance a~d war may not be the means of destroying our hardly gained civil
rights requires the utmost exertions and sacrifice on the part of this generation; a patriotism, in its truest sense, on the part of each of us.
The fraternity owes a deep sense of gratitude to this committee for
their admirable handling of the program and speakers bureau. We are
also indebted to W.". Brother Lee T. Mullen, P. M., who, as an added

Relief
Upon the urgent appeal of Swiss Grand Lodge Alpina, I directed the
Grand Treasurer to transmit to their New York bankers the sum of $2000.
The distress of thousands of our European brethren is dire and their need
urgent. Swiss Grand Lodge Alpina is the only grand body on the continent
that is freely functioning at this time, and Switzerland, itself, is the only
haven of countless refugees, among whom are thousands of our brethren.
The resources of the Swiss people are stretched to the utmost, and of the
Grand Lodge completely exhausted. All able bodied Swiss of the ages
of 20 to 60 are mobilized. The people are unable to give more.
I therefore deemed, that although the assembling of Grand Lodge was
little more than a month away, that the needs of our brethren were so great
and so urgent, that we ought not await the annual communication, and
caused the above mentioned amount to be transmitted as an earnest of our
go.ad. faith and fraternal regard, and I recommend that such further appropriation be made as may be consistent with the state of our finances, and
other calls thereon, present and prospective.
I tendered our assistance to our brethren of Louisiana at the time of
the recent floods in that state but was informed that no assistance was
needed and our offer was declined and their thanks expressed.
Recommendations

I.
In my travels throughout the jurisdiction I have found that in a num. ber of the Lodges, the work and harmony in the Lodge is seriously affected
by the fact that junior officers, such as Wardens or Senior Deacons occupy an office 'in some other order, society or club which takes so much
time that the work of the Lodge is severely hamper~d. The honor and distinction flowing from the fact of holding office in a Masonic Lodge should
be sufficient to enti.tle the Lodge to the undivided effort and attention of
the holder. If it is not, and in some cases such s.eems to be the case I
would recommend that an Inspector be authorized to withhold the · Certlficate of Qualification wh_en, in his judgment, the holding of such outside
office may seem to be in conflict with the duties of the office in the Lodge.

II.
Life Membership Funds seem to be a source of difficulty for many
small Lodges, and for some large ones too. The restrictions attached by
Grand Lodge to the investment of such funds are wise and prudent and
should not be removed, but, _in many cases, the amount of money in the fund
permits of no diversification in its investment even though the Lodge has
among its members those possessing the necessary investment education
and experience, which it usually does not have. This leaves available only
the usual savings bank account returning a maximum of 2% per annum
Which is a totally inadequate return for the purposes of the Lodge.
th~refore recommend that some committee of Grand Lodge, or a committee to be established by proper legislation, be entrusted with the duty
of investing all Life Membership Funds that may be entrusted to Grand
Lo~ge by the c?nstituent Lodges. That the constituent Lodges, at their
?pbon, be perm1.tted to transmit to the Grand Treasurer cash representmg such f,l.lnd~, m any amounts, all of said funds to be placed in a common pool or fund. to be invested from time to time. and as speedily as

i

25

possible, by the aforesaid committee, and the income therefrom apportioned annually or oftener, if it seems advisable, among the Lodges contributing thereto in proportion to the. amounts contributed and the time
of receipt by the Grand Treasurer. Such funds might be made subject to
withdrawal upon six months' notice by the contributing Lodges or any of
them. By such legislation the Lodges, especially the smaller Lodges, would
gain expert and efficient handling of the funds and also a diversification in
the investment so essential to safety. It is possible that a safe alternative
for this plan might be found in the lifting of the ban against Federally Insured Building and Loan Associations some of which pay as much as 4%.

III.
I have found it necessary on several occasions, following the ruling of
Grand Lodge, to deny to officers of other organizations whose membership
is composed of Masons, or in part composed. of Masons, information concerning the present Masonic standing of certain Ma!ions, members of such
other organizations. Inasmuch as continuance of membership in those other
organizations is based upon continuance of good standing in the Masonic
Lodge it would seem that it is to the interest of the Lodge to advise such
other organizations of the failure of a Mason to maintain his good standing in the Lodge. I am credibly informed that there are cases where a
Mason has been suspended in his Lodge yet continues to pay dues and
maintain his standing in such other organizations. If the fact of his suspension could be divulged to the proper officers of such other organization,
I am convinced that it would result in many who stand ·suspended seeking
restoration, with a consequent enrichment of the Lodge treasury. A case
was reported where a Brother quite active in a so-called "higher" body was
surprised to learn that it was necessary to maintain his membership in the
Masonic Lodge, and having accepted office in that body was forced to .pay
several years' back dues to restore himself to good standing. We have
always leaned over backward to protect the privacy of the individual, but
if a Mason is in good standing he should take pride in the fact, and a certificate to that effect issued with or without his knowledge, could do him no
harm, and in fact would reflect honor upon hifll; if he is not in good standing it would seem that the Lodge owes him no duty to withhold that information. I therefore recommend that appropriate legislation be adopted by
this Grand Lodge, authorizing Secretaries of Lodges to issue certificates
stating that a named person i,s or is not a member of such Lodge, and that
for the purpose of said certificate only, that a suspended member be treated
as no longer a member of the Lodge.
IV.
During election years in the past we have found the so-called "Masonic"
magazines and periodicals flooded with articles, cards and pictures of candidates for office. On the front cover of one periodical during a recent campaign year appeared the portrait of one, not a Mason, with none too good a
personal and political record with beneath it the words "Elect So and So to
the office of Such and Such." From all appearances, the non-Mason had
every right to assume from this that M'asonry as an organization was supporting the named candidate. We are again in an election year and we may
expect a repetition of such infractions of our well-known and historical
policy. I recommend that no paper: periodical, magazine or publication
using the words "Masonic," "Freemasonry," "Hiram" or any word implying a connection with Freemasons or Freemasonry, be permitted to publish
the portrait, card, or statement of any candidate for political office, whether
partisan or non-partisan, or of any political party, without printing im-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mediately above or below the same, in a type not smaller than the smallest
type used therein, the words "Paid Political Advertisement. Not intended
as an expression of opinion of this Magazine or of Freemasonry."

to the offense for which the accused was convicted; the Master of the
designated Lodge should preside at the trial.
In filing the charges the Juriior Warden was merely performing a duty
fixed upon him, and upon no other officer by the provisions of Section 192-a,
and the mere fact that he, the Junior \Varden, mistakenly refers to the
Master in the charges as having ~·requested" the filing, should not alter the
situation.

v.
The usual flood of criticism of the so-called "Masonic" magazines and
periodicals has come to the Grand Master during the past year. A new
object of attack by the critics has arisen by reason of a radio program sponsored by one of these magazines. This magazine is one that now, and in
the past, has been among the least offensive of these publications, and
speaking from personal knowledge, its management has at all times expressed a desire to meet the wishes of Grand Lodge as to form, contents
and management. I see no more reason for suppressing a radio program
·sponsored by a "Masonic" magazine than for suppressing the magazine
itself, nor can I conceive that. the form which the advertising matter takes
whether in type or air can alter the rules of ethics applying to the subject.
Each must be kept within proper bounds to be entitled to the patronage of
Masons and Masonic Lodges.
Many of the criticisms directed against these publications were amply
justified by the facts. Other Grand Masters have indicated by their remarks
that they have had similar experiences. It is my opinion that the time has
come when action must be taken by Grand Lodge to remedy an evil that
has long existed in this jurisdiction, and which has long been a discredit
to the Craft. I recommend that legislation be adopted to the end that
whenever facts presented to the Grand Master prove to his satisfaction
that any such paper, periodical, magazine or publication of any kind, or its
editors, managers, agents or employees, have engaged in any unethical,
fraudulent. misleading, or questionable acts or practices, that the Grand
Master be authorized to place an interdiction upori such publication, and
immediately notify all Lodges and Masons in this jurisdii:tion by a communication to be read at the next Stated Meeting in each Lodge, to cease
and desist from giving any aid or support of any kind to such offender.
I further recommend that the foregoing recommendation be considered
by Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in the year 1941, and that
the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint a committee of three
whose duty it shall be to consider said recommendation, and kindred and
associated matters in the broadest sense relating to the subject of "Masonic"
publications, and that said . committee be ordered to report their findings
thereon to the Grand Master not later than ·August 1, 1941, and .that the
Grand Master be requested to include said report in the advance information to be furnished the Lodges of this jurisdiction.
As the executive head of the Fraternity, it is the duty of Grand Master to interpret Masonic law and enforce its provisions in the jurisdiction
in the interval between communications of Grand Lodge. In performance of
that duty I have made certain decisions and orders which are herewith
submitted for approval by Grand Lodge. I have omitted such decisions
as were clearly within the purview of previous rulings of Grand Lodge.
Decisions

I.
I ruled that where pursuant to Section 333 of our Ordinances, the
Grand Secretary has procured the record; the accused has been notified;
he has demanded a Masonic trial; the Grand Master has designated the
place of trial; the Junior Warden of the Lodge designated by the Grand

27

II.
Two towns, Whitetown and Blacktown, are situated less than ten miles
apart. . Whitetown has one Masonic Lodge and charges $30.00 for the three
degrees; Blacktown has two lodges and each charges $50.00 for the degrees. The normal jurisdiction of each Lodge is within the enlarged jurisdiction of the others under Section 218. Naturally, the first mentioned
Lodge having the lower fees, all other things being equal, will receive a
majority of the petitions from both ·towns. Whitetown had been requesting
waivers but claimed a right to receive the petitions without such waivers
being granted.
I was asked if Whitetown Lodge could be compelled to raise its fees,
or if not, was it required to secure a waiver from one of the Lodges in
Blacktown before receiving a petition from a candidate residing within the
normal jurisdiction of Blacktown Lodges, but within the enlarged jurisdiction of Whitetown Lodge. I decided as follows:
Section 218 after making provision for concurrent jurisdiction of
Lodges within a ten-mile radius of the Lodge room further provides: "then
the procedure to be followed in acting upon that petition shall be that
prescribed in cases of concurrent jurisdiction." The provisions relating to
concurrent jurisdiction are found in Section 82.
Section 214 among other things, provides: "If two or more Lodges are
located within the corporate limits of any city, town, or place, they shall
have concurrent jurisdiction therein, and none of them shall confer the
degrees for a smaller sum than fifty dollars without the consent of all."
It is my opinion that in enlarging the normal jurisdiction of the Lodge
under Section 218, it was not the intention of Grand Lodge to permit a
Lodge located as is Whitetown Lodge to invade the normal jurisdiction of
the Blacktown· Lodges, without also complying· with Section 82 relative to
minimum fees, and it is therefore my decision that before Whitetown Lodge
can take advantage of the enlarged jurisdiction so as to invade the normal
jurisdiction of Blacktown Lodges it must establish a minimum fee of $50
for the degrees, and until it shall do so, it must continue to apply for and
obtain, in every case, a waiver from one of the Blacktown Lodges, when
the petitioner resides within the normal jurisdiction of the l.atter.
(Note: Whitetown and Blacktown are substituted names).

III.
I was asked: 1. Can a Junior Warden, who, by direction of the Master,
or as a part of his official duties as Junior Warden, has preferred charges
of un-Masonic conduct, act as stenographic reporter at the trial of such
charges? I ruled he could not. While there is nothing apparently in the
law of this jurisdiction covering such a situation, yet there might be some
question raised as to the fairness of the trial under such conditions, a situation that we ought to avoid in every case.
In connection with the same matter, I was asked if a non-Mason might

act as such stenographic reporter, to which I also answered "No." Under
no circumstances can a non-Mason act as the reporter or be present as a
spectator.

VI.

I was presented the following question: The members of a Lodge
maintain a charity box which is placed on a pedestal in the Lodge room
during recess. The members put voluntary contr!but.ions in the box. Th.e
purpose of the box is to create a Charity Fund whtch 1s not to be used until
a specified time, after which the interest only will be used for Lodge
charity. Money received in the Charity Box is kept separate from Lodge
funds. Transaction of business as to investments, etc., is carried on during
recess with the Master presiding and no record is made in the minutes of
the Lodge. In response to questions they stated the purpose in as~ing
whether Grand Lodge had jurisdiction of the fund was to have determined
if the investment of the fund is restricted the same as Lodge funds, and
also in event the Lodge should be "dissolved" what would be the disposition
of this special fund.
I replied: It seems to me that we cannot divorce any of the monies
raised from our members from their character of Masonic funds. They
may be impressed with a trust for certain purposes, and I therefore hold
that the raising of such funds in the manner described in your letter of
inquiry is a legitimate endeavor on the part of the Lodge and monies so
raised could not be diverted to any other purpose, nor could any part of
the principal sum be used for any purpose, the income only, after a specified time, being available for the sok purpose of Lodge charities.
I am reluctant to place any additional restrictions on Lodge activities
or increase the burden of Grand Lodge in supervising or controlling the
affairs of a Lodge, nevertheless, I am constrained to hold that such funds
solicited from members for a Maso,nic purpose such as you propose would
be subject to the provisions of Section 152 of the . Constitution and Ordinances of Grand Lodge (Ed. 1940) and in the event of the dissolution of
the Lodge such funds, impressed with the trust, would pass to Grand Lodge
under Section 160.

A Brother was raised April 28, 1888. He dimitted January 13, 1897 and
was not restored until September, 1901. I was asked when the Brother
would be entitled to rec.e ive a SO-year button. To which I replied: the resolutions providing for the SO-year button require no more than that he shall
have been a Master Mason in good standing for a period of fifty years, and
a member of a recognized Lodge of Masons. While he was dimitted he was
not a member of a Lodge in good standing. As he was dimitted for a
period of four years and eight months, this length of time would have to be
added to time within which he would normally have been eligible for the
button, which would make the date of eligibility, December 28, 1942.

VII.
The following situation arose in one of our Lodges: On the second
ballot upon an application, the Junior Warden declared the ballot "fair,"
the Senior Warden "dark" and when it was brought to the east it was
declared "black." There was one cube. The application was declared rejected. As the Senior Deacon was about to place the ballot box on the
Senior Warden's pedestal he accidentally hit it with i:onsiderable force and
several brethren thought the cube might accidentally have been bounced
into the voting compartment. The Master did not hear the Junior Warden' s declaration of "fair," and being informed took a third ballot which
came to the east "bright." No one had entered or retired from the Lodge
room, there had been no intermission, and all members voted each time.
The situation was presented with the question as to whether the application had been accepted or rejected. I held, that the application having been
declared rejected it must stand but under the circumstances I would consider
favorably an application for a dispensation to receive and act on the petition
of this rejected candidate within twelve months.

VIII.
A Brother joined .the Lodge before a Home fee was charged and later
was suspended for non-payment of dues. He now applies for restoration.
Will he have to pay the Home feet before he can be restored? I held, the
Brother should not be required fo pay the Home fee. He has never ceased
to be a member of the Lodge, having never taken a <limit or been expelled.
He merely stands suspended which implies the continuation of his membership and therefore upon lifting the suspension his membership to all
intents would be continuous from its inception.

IX.
A Lodge elected an applicant to take the degrees of Masonry who had
suffered the loss of a leg at the thigh, and thereafter conferred upon him
the three degrees of Masonry. The Inspector was informd of the facts
after he had been passed and before being raised. He advised the Master
concerning the law. Nevertheless, the Master conferred the Third Degree
and · the Inspector attended the meeting of the Lodge and witnessed the
ceremony.
Much as I disliked to do so, I felt constrained to punish all concerned
for a breach of our Masonic law in a particular so well known as is our law
relating to the physical qualifications of an applicant for the degrees.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

I asked for and received the resignation of the Inspector; I reprimanded
the Lodge; and I suspended the Master from the exercise of the powers
and duties of his office.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

30 .

Grand Secretary and Officers
To our Grand Secretary whose long years of experience and wisdom
ripened by age, makes his advice in moments of perplexity of incalculable
value, I extend my thanks for his ever ready rendition of service when
sought. The appointive officers of Grand Lodge have added much to the
pleasure and satisfaction of the year by their presence on numerous
occasions. The ready acquiescence and cooperation of the Masters and
Wardens in all matters and on every occasion was very gratifying.
And I am sincerely grateful to the Craft throughout the jurisdiction for
the kindness and friendliness everywhere displayed, grateful for the harmony and peace and brotherly love that have prevailed throughout the year,
grateful for the honor conferred upon me, grateful for the opportunity to
have served Masonry during a year of pleasant associations and interesting
activities.
May I close with an ancient Masonic benediction:
"!vfay no· strife disturb thy days, nor sorrow disturb thy nights, and
the pillow of peace kiss thy cheek, and the pleasures of imagination attend
thy dreams; and when length of years hath made thee tired of earthly joys,
and the curtains of death gently close around the scene of thy existence,
may the angels of God attend thy bed and take care that the expiring lamp
of life shall not receive one rude blast to hasten its extinction; and finally
may the blessing of God wash thee free from all impurities and prepare thee
to enter into the land of everlasting felicity."
WM.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I present herewith my thirty-third annual report:
Death of Frank G. Hobbs
On the morning of the 14th of June, 1940, this office particularly and
the fraternity generally suffered a severe shock in the sudden and unexpected death of Worshipful Brother Frank G. Hobbs, Assistant Grand
Secretary. He died as any of us would wish, at his desk and at his usual
labors, without previous warning.
Brother Hobbs was appointed Assistant Grand Secretary after the
death of Harry S. Johnson in 1922, and for nearly eighteen years served in
that capacity loyally, faithfully, industriously and always with a fine courtesy alike to rich and poor, high and low, with whom he came in contact.
He was born in San Francisco, April I, 1877, and received his schooling
in his native city. For many years he was engaged in the lumber business
in northern California and in merchandising in Nevada. He married Miss
Helen Williams at Sisson on June 25, 1903, who with a son; Frank Wilson,
survives him.
His Masonic record begins with his degrees in Montezuma Lodge No.
31, at Goldfield, Nevada, in 1906, from which he withdrew at the formation of Alexandria Lodge No. 531 of San Francisco, of which Lodge he was
the first Master. His Chapter degrees were conferred on him by Goldfield
Chapter No. 10, Nevada, subsequently affiliating with San Francisco Chapter No. 1 His Scottish Rite degrees were received in Reno Consistory
No. 1 at Goldfield, from which he withdrew to become a member and active
worker in San Francisco Consistory No. 1. His memberships also included
Islam Temple of the Mystic Shrine; and San Francisco Past Masters
Associatiqn.
The funeral of our brother was conducted under the auspices of Alexandria Lodge, Deputy Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson conducting the services
in the presence of a large gathering of brethren and friends.
The vacancy occasioned by the loss of Brother Hobbs was filled July
1st by the appointment of Henry D. Oliphant, Past Master of San Francisco Lodge No. 360.

Unfinished Business
Past Grand Master Adams presented the following resolution on the
third day of the last Annual Communication (p. 602 of Proceedings) and
it was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and Committee on Policy
and General Purposes with instruction to report thereon at the next Annual
Communication:
Resolved, that unless otherwise ordered by unanimous consent,
every resolution proposing to amend the Constitution, Regulations,
or the Uniform Code of By-Laws, shall be presented in writing at a
regular annual communication and be immediately referred to the
appropriate committee, which shall report thereon in writing at the
next annual communication; and that the proposed resolution shall
appear in full in fhe printed Proceedings of the communication at
which it was presented.
JoHN WHTCHER, Grand Secretary.

To the Finance Committee, Grand Lodge:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Grand Lodge F. &
A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1940 and present herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's accounts, statement of cash receipts and
disbursements-general fund.for t_he fiscal year ended July 31, 1940.
Exhibit B-1: Statement of per capita dues collected during 1939-40 for
Grand Lodge from 1939 annual returns.
Exhibit B-2: Statement of per capita dues and Home tax collected during 1939-40 for Masonic Homes of California from 1939 annual returns and
$25.00 Home tax for three quarters of 1939-40.
Exhibit C: Grand Treasurer's accounts,_ statement of cash receipts and
disbursements-fiscal year ended July 31, 1940.
Exhibit D: Statement of assets and capital account, as at July 31, 1940.
Comments-As shown at the bottom of our Exhibit D, the revenue from
per capita dues and other sources exceeded the total of expenses and appropriations by $12,864.63.
All dues payable during the current year, as reported on the 1939 annual
returns have been paid in full. Our Exhibit B-1 and B-2 shows proof of
revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1939 annual returns
and the $25.00 Home tax reports for the first three quarters of the fiscal
year 1939-40. The total revenue due, as shown, agrees with the total cash
received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary. Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries. Disbursements were
made by checks and supported by properly approved vouchers.
All bank balances were verified by correspondence. Certified lists of
stocks and bonds belonging to all funds were received from the Anglo
California National Bank which holds the securities in trust.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
P~rsuant to the requirements of Section 50 of the Constitution and
Regulations I submit to you a report of my services as Grand Lecturer
during the past year. First, may I say that I am deeply grateful for having had the privilege of serving you in this high'office. It has been a year
of pleasant experiences, yet of some regrets. Regrets for not having been
able to answer all of the calls made upon me, but I have responded to every
case where time and circumstances would permit. I have handled all matters that have come before me for my attention, to the very best of my
ability and I hope, to the satisfaction of this Grand Lodge.

Traveling Expenses of Inspectors
Agreeable to the recommendations of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes and the Committee on Finance, and in accordance with
their suggestions, I drafted a set of regulations governing claims for reimbursement of Inspectors for traveling expenses incurred in the discharge
of their official duties, and after submitting the same to the Grand Master
for his approval I forwarded a copy to each of the Inspectors in the jurisdiction. They read as follows:
January 1, 1940.
Regulations governing reimbursement of Inspectors for traveling expenses in performance of official duties for the period beginning October
13, 1939, and ending October 8, 1940.
In accordance with recommendation of the Committee on Finance the
following regulations will be observed by Inspectors in filing claims for
reimbursement:
1. No claim shall be made if Inspector receives money from the Lodge
visited.
2. No claim shall be made when distance traveled is less than twenty
miles for the round trip.
3.(a) When trip is made by public conveyance, claim shall be for actual fare paid.
(b) When trip is made by privately owned car, claim shall be on basis
of five cents per mile for actual mileage traveled.
(c) When two or mor~ Inspectors travel in same car claim shall be
made QY one Inspector only.
(d) When overnight stop is necessary, claim shall be for actual
amount paid for hotel and meals.
4. Claims shall be limited to two visitations to each Lodge for the
purpose of instruction or the performance of other official duties;
attending two schools of instruction with Assistant Grand Lecturer; and such other trips as may be made at the request of
the Grand Master or the Grand Lecturer.
In response to the request that a survey be made to determine the
probable cost, I addressed a letter to the Inspectors asking for information
relative to expenses incurred by them in visiting the Lodges of their respective districts, holding district meetings and schools of instruction, meeting with the Assistant Grand Lecturers and all other p'e rtinent information. After all replies had been received I compiled a detailed statement and
submitted a report to the Grand Master reading as follows :

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

45

August 6, 1940.
William B. Ogden, Grand Master,
1301 No. Flores Street,
Los Angeles, Calif.
Most Worshipful Sir:
H~ving completed a survey m~-de at ~he direction of Grand Lodge to
determ1.ne the .Probable cost. of re1.mburs~ng Inspec~ors for traveling expenses m the discharge of their official duties, I submit the following report:
While it was the intent of the Committee of Inspectors and the Committee on Finance that no reimbursement should be made to those Inspectors serving in metropolitan areas, reports received indicate that there are
a number of Inspectors without, whose expenses are no greater than those
within, such areas. These Inspectors, together with those in metropolitan
areas, fifty-nine in number out of a total of 119 Inspectors have expressed
themselv:es as having. no desire for reimbursement and, the~efore, they have
been om!tted from this repc_>rt and only those Inspect<;>rs, 60 in number, who
are required to travel 20 miles or more on any one trip, have been included.
The minimum of 20 miles has been used because that is the minimum
prescribed in the regulations issued for the period October 1939 to October
1940, a copy of which is attached hereto.
'

Condition of Lodges
Section SO of the Constitution and Ordinances requires that the Grand
Lecturer shall make a report "setting forth the condition of the Lodges
throughout the jurisdiction." Section 53 requires the Inspectors to report
to .the Grand Lecturer "the working condition of each Lodge in his district," and to the Grand Master regarding other matters. From reports
sent to me I find a question rests in the minds of many of the Inspectors as
to what is meant by the phrase "working condition." I have construed it
to have particular reference to the ritual and degree work, inasmuch as other
matters are covered in the reports to the ·Grand Master, and I am confining myself t-0 that subject in this report.
Judging from reports received from the Inspectors, and from my own
observation, the ritual as taught by the Ritual Committee is being adhered
to, and in the vast majority of cases the work is being done in a satisfactory manner. In a few instances, in Lodges where there is little or no
degree work, the Inspectors report that it requires constant effort on
their part to maintain interest in the work. This situation no doubt will
adjust itself as conditions improve. About seven per cent of the Lodges
have had no degree work during the past year. Twelve per cent raised
only one candidate; forty-four per cent raised from two to five candidates;
twenty-five per cent raised from six to ten; twelve per cent raised more than
ten, the average in the latter group being fifteen and the greatest number
being twenty-eight.
Masters of Lodges should be particularly careful in conferring degrees
to see that there is no infraction of the law. In one instance this year the
degrees were conferred upon a candidate who could not meet the prescribed
physical qualifications. This matter is covered more fully in the message
of the Grand Master. There is another infraction to which I would call
the attention of Masters and Masons in general : That is the occasional
publication of the names of candidates for the degrees in Lodge bulletins,
and also at times in announcements sent out by degree teams to members
of their organizations. In fact, there recently appeared in one of our daily
newspapers an announcement that the degree team of a local bank was
to confer the third degree upon a candidate, giving his name. These things
are done inadvertently, of course, and I mention them as a reminder that
not only Lodge officers but all Masons are amenable to our laws.
I would also call to the attention of officers-elect for the coming year
the necessity of their having a: copy of the 1940 edition of the Constitution
and Ross Digest, as the questions on · law this year will be predicated upon
this book.
In conclusion, I wish to express my great pleasure in having had the
opportunity of working with our Most Worshipful Grand Master. I had
met Brother Ogden at Grand Lodge for many years when we were both
Inspectors, but it is only during the past year, through frequent contacts
with him that I have come really to know him, and I am indebted to him
for his kindly advice and counsel. I wish also to express my appreciation to
the Very Worshipful John Whicher, Grand Secretary, and to the members
of his staff, for the many courtesies extended to me throughout the year.
Respectfully submitted,
WALTER LEONARD,

Grand Lecturer.

REPORTS OF THE COMMITTEE ON SEGREGATION
Grand Master's Message

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The committee to which was referred the report of the Most Worshipful Grand Master begs leave to make its report.
The Grand Master has rendered to this Grand Lodge a report of his
stewardship and will ~oon surrender the power and authority given hm
a year ago. His report is an account of a year's work; hard work, work
both day and night. It is amazing that one man could crowd into a year's
time all that our Grand Master has accomplished; 40,000 miles of travel,
an official visit to each of the 119 lnspectorial Districts, 151 meetings, over
30,000 Masons in his audience. This, in addition to officially visiting the
Grand Lodges of Nevada and Arizona and attending the Grand Masters'
conference at Washington, D. C.
It is apparent that the Masons of this jurisdiction desire that the
Grand Master visit with them and are not satisfied with lesser lights, but
we must remember, my brethren, that the Grand Master is only human
and we should not tax him beyond his physical endurance and should so
arrange these meetings by grouping them through the Inspector and Inspectorial Districts that this load may be made as light as possible.
This committee believes that this load may be further lightened by
· requesting the Masters of the several Lodges to route all requests for decisions through their Inspectors. We have no doubt that many of the
questions presented to the Grand Master for decision might be answered
satisfactorily by the Inspector.
This jurisdiction rejoices that our Grand Master was so singularly
recognized at the Grand Masters' conference in being selected to give the
eulogy at the tomb of Brother George Washington. This address was
printed for distribution to all the Lodges. We commend it to you. We
urge you to read it again in your Lodge. It truly is a classic.

ANNUAL ORATION
(by LEO E. ANDERSON, Grand Orator)
OCTOBER

8, 1940

Civic Responsibilities of Masons
Mingled with the pleasure of speaking to you today is a sense of responsibility, and genuine concern, not only as to what I should say on
this occasion that might be of value to you, but also what I must say if
Masonry is to be a living force. Upon reflection, it has seemed to me that
I could not better employ this opportunity than to bring home to you
with such emphasis as I can, the truth of a conviction that has more and
more gained upon me as the years have gone by. That conviction, briefly
put, amounts to this: That upon the members of the Masonic fraternity,
whose predecessors were largely responsible for our form of government,
and the situation under which we live, and more especially upon the Masters and Wardens of the various Lodges, there evolve public duties and
civic responsibilities which they may not any longer ignore or evade without neglecting the trust imposed in them.
These are perilous times in which we are living. Our ritual, in a lecture of the second degree, expresses the present international situation
better than I could when it say~:
"The lapse of time, the ruthless hands of ignorance, · and
the devastations of war, have laid waste and destroyed many
valuable monuments of antiquity on which the utmost exertions of human genius were employed."
Nothing could portray more graphically the picture of today, except
to add that those same forces also have destroyed, and are destroying,
the rights and privileges of free men and of citizens, as known to Americans. Those rights and privileges are "valuable mon.uments of antiquity
on which the utmost exertions of human genius were employed" and,
U!]less guarded, bid fair to disappear from the world.
You brethren know that our forefathers and predecessors in Freemasonry here in America fought, bled and died to secure the blessings of
liberty to themselves and to their posterity. You brethren know that the
ilrmy, under that great Mason, George Washington, was officered almost
entirely by Masons. You brethren know that the Constitutional Convention, which gave us the basic law of the land, was largely composed of
Masons and that that Constitution clearlr e!Tibodies those three great
principles for which Masonry has stood. thro_u gh ·the centuries, .religious
freedom, political freedom and education. You brethren will recall that
when Benjamin Franklin, the venerable. Grand Master of. Masons in Pennsylvania, emerged from the Convention hall and was 'a~ICed, "What kind
of a government have _you given us?" he r_e plie_d , "A .:Reiiublic~ ' if you can
keep it." In the light of this knowledge I propose to discuss the public
duties and civic responsibilities of Masons and particularly Masons as
citizens. I ask ydu to consider what kind ·of citizens should we Masons be
and what are a Mason's· duties as a citizen.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The fundamental premise upon which the Constitution was based was
that the government was the servant of the people, not that the people
were the servants of the government. The Constitution grants to the government certain powers and all others are reserved to the several states
and to the people. It seems clear to me and history has demonstrated that
unless the people seriously assume their duties and responsibilities as
citizens, the government assumes more and more power and soon becomes
the master rather than the servant of the people.
In proportion as public opinion is wise and enlightened, . the . government will be enlightened and wise. In other words, the people will always
have as good a government as their intelligence and patriotism deserve and
no better. In the long run, government can be made better only by the
improvement of the public opinion upon which it rests. From time immemorial history shows that the brightest Jewels in the Diadem of Wisdom
and Integrity have been members of our great Fraternity. The need of our
day in America requires that Masonry again furnish to our nation men of
wisdom, men of integrity, men of ability, men capable of molding public
opihion in their several communities away from the radicalism to which
we have fallen and back to sanity and Americanistic tradition.

and our posterity, do ordain and establish this Constitution
for the UNITED States of America."
Thus, in the first part of the first degree, we find the first element of
citizenship, namely, unity.
Let us explore further. The charge of the first degree tells us to regard
the volume of the sacred law as the great light of our profession and "in
it you will learn the important duties which you owe to God, your country,
your neighbor and yourself." Then we are told, and I quote:
"As a citizen you are enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of your civil duties by never proposing or countenancing any act which may have a tendency to subvert the
peace and good order of society, by paying due obedience to
the laws under whose protection you live, and by never losing
sight of the allegiance due to your country."

52

It is for you as individuals to examine all proposals of political change
in a light of knowledge and under the guidance of judgment and to appraise
each at its true value. It is for you as individuals to recognize and expose
the fallacies which too often lie in novelty and pretension; to caution and
restrain those who would rush blindly into a field of political expel"imentation; to instruct the uninformed and the thoughtless that our Constitution
affords in itself the best and surest means of constructive and wholesome
change. In brief, it is for you to guard our system against the proposals
and reckless innovations which would cheapen it to a scheme of inconsistencies.
Now you brethren may properly ask why I have chosen to discuss this
subject so seriously. Let me tell you. All of us here are Masters, Wardens,
or Past Masters of our Lodges. You are familiar with the ritual and ceremonies of our Fraternity. Therefore, in a11swer to your question, I shall
quote of few portions of the ritual and of our ceremonies. You will find
that citizenship should be one of your particular interests and you may be
surprised to find how closely it is woven into the fabric of Freemasonry.
The reason for the great stress laid upon citizenship in our ritual is obvious.
No individual a·nd no organization can shut itself away from the life of the
community in which it lives. No individual is so self sufficient that he can
go through life disregarding that community life and not affected by its
changes. No individual is so unimportant that he should not add his voice
to the composite voice of the community. Every man, whether he knows it
or not, is a citizen. Let us see what our ritual has to say about citizenship.

In the first !legree, while the candidate makes his first trip around the
Lodge, he hears the Chaplain say: "Behold how good and pleasant it is
for brethren to dwell together in unity." "Unity," the word alone brings
me a feeling of pleasure. It is the foundation of citizenship and of society.
It was uppermost in the minds of those great Masons who did so much
to give us our Constitution. You will recall the preamble of that Constitution:
"WE, the people of the UNITED States, in order to form
a more perfect UNION, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the COMMON defense, promote the GENERAL welfare and secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves

53

We are then told :
"As an individual you are charged to practice the domestic
and public virtues."
There, in the first degree, plainly and forcibly, emphasis is laid upon
our duties as citizens, but our ritual does not stop there. From the reference in the ritual to the beehive, I take a clear description of man's re.latio~ship to man and a Mason's duty to his community, and I quote:
"When we take a survey of nature, we view man in his infancy-more helpless and indigent than the brute creation. He
lies languishing for days, months, and years, totally incapable
of providing sustenance for himself, of guarding against the
attack of the wild beast of the fi.eld, or sheltering himself from
the inclemencies of the weather. It might have pleased the
Great Creator of heaven and earth to have made man independent of all other things, but his dependence is one of the
strongest bonds of society. Mankind were made dependent on
each other for protection and security as they thereby enjoy
better opportunities of fulfilling the duties of reciprocal love
and friendship. Thus was man formed for social and active
life, the noblest part of the work of God, and he that will so
demean himself as not to be endeavoring to add to the common
stock of knowledge and understanding may be deemed a drone
in the hive of nature, a useless member of society, and unworthy of our protection as Masons."
And finally in our ceremonies of the installation of officers we find the
charges given to each incoming Master of his Lodge in this jurisdiction.
Those charges include the following:
"You agree to be a peacable citizen and cheerfully to conform to the laws of the country in which you reside.
"You promise not to be concerned in plots and conspiracies
against government, but patiently to submit to the decision of
the supreme legislature.
"You agree to pay a proper respect to the civil magistrate, to
work diligently, live creditably and act honorably by all men."
Following these charges, the installing Master states to the incoming
Master with reference to the brethren of his Lodge:
"Charge them to practice out of the Lodge those duties
which they have been taught in it."
