GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

And in his closing statement to the members of the Lodg~, the installing Master says :
·
"Within your peaceful walls may your children's children
celebrate with joy and gratitude the annual recurrence of this
auspicious solemnity."

privilege which can be conferred upon a citizen. It is his privilege of self. e)!:pression in the selection of those who shall stand over him in authority
in the administration of the affairs of the nation, the state and the community and it is a privilege which too many of us do not take advantage of.
George Washington in his first inaugural address stated our responsibility in these words:
"The preservation of the sacred fire of liberty and the destiny
of the republican model of government are justly considered,
perhaps, as DEEPLY, as FINALLY, staked on the experiment entrusted to the hands of the American people."

54

I could quote many other portions of our ritual and ceremonies to
illustrate the great stress placed upon om: -citizenship as Masons, but the
quotations I have given you should suffice. ·
You prethren know that you .o.nly get out of anything, and . particularly
Masonry, that which you put into it. The Mason who joins a Lodge and
never attends a meeting gets very little ..in return for his investment in
Masonry. The Mason who attends meetings, studies the ritual and joins in
. Masonic fellowships gains much from Masonry, . carries Masonry onward
and continually finds new philosophy unnoticed before. So it is with citizenship. The man who practices citizenship and engages in civic activities
gains much from his citizenship, contribut~ to better government and
hands down to posterity the rights and privileges he enjoys. As our Most
Worshipful Grand Master has said many times during his travels in the
past year, the standing of the Masonic Fraternity depends upon the standing of its members. Where it is active and in good repute we find the memo
hers of the local Lodge active in civic affairs, honest in business and giving
freely of their time in the discharge of their duties as citizens. Where
Masonry is inactive and the community uninterested in it, we find the
members of the local Lodge inactive· in civic affairs . and lax in the discharge of their duties as citizens. That is a practical illustration of the necessity that we Masons be good, active citizens. It also shows that we must
educate and encourage our members to be good citizens, but above all we
must practice citizenship. I do not advocate that our Lodges as organizations participate in politics, but I do .a dvocate that Masons as citizens
must take a real interest in government and community life.
. Since we learn by doing, we shall never become good citizens simply
by studying civic relations and problems. Nothing was ever solved or
accomplished by shifting our problems and our duties to others. We all
know that our individual requirements are so various and our system of
living so complicated that no individual actually provides for himself more
than a few of the things necessary to his existence and comfort. The house
in which you live h·a s b'e en built by one set of men, painted by another,
and provided with plumbing by a third. Your carpets have probably come
from one state, your furniture from another and your pictures from a
third. Your everyday needs and wants have been supplied by the exertions
of a multitude of workers, some of whom live in America, but , many of
whom reside in foreign lands. Each of you must of necessity do the work
for which you are particularly fitted, depending at all times upon the assurance that the other fellow will do the work for which he is particularly
fitted, conscientiously and dependably. 'If it were otherwise, you ·could not
exist and live as you now exist and live. Thus we see that the fact that you
are a citizen gives you many rights that every member of the group enjoys.
No person may claim all of the advantages of citizenship ani1 then' live in
seclusion and do no work with his fellows. If he is to associate with his
fellows, he must not only be a fit fellow with whom to associate,. but he
should be such a citizen that others will gain advantage from acquaintance
and friendship with him. If he needs, as all of us do, the cooperation of
those with whom he lives and works, he must expect to contribute what
he can. Some people think that the right to vote' is the right otcitizenship.
The .rig ht to vote is merely a privilege of'citizenship but it is tl-!'e'··h ighest

SS

Whether 't hat experiment which has succeeded so marvelously in the
last 150 years ' will continue to succeed depends upon the citizens of this
country. It' depends upon their use of the priviieges which they enjoy.
It depends· upon their interest in government. It depends upon whether
· or not they will, by their intelligence and interest, select proper men and
women to· carry on the affairs ·of our government. Longfellow said: "For
some must follow and some command, though · all are made of clay."
It behooves us as citizens to see that those who command are made of
the finest kind of clay. That means interest in government-not just voting
for someone ahd then forgetting that he needs help to carry out the job
you have given him. It means interest in politics, a word that has been
much misunderstood. Politics means government and interest in politics
· means interest in government. That is one of our real duties as citizens.
To what does this discussion lead us? I believe it brings us to the
· question, for what does Masonry exist?
You are all familiar with the globe, which we are told is for improving
the mind and for giving it the most distinct ide.a of any problem or proposition as well as enabling it to solve the same. What is the end and purpose
. of our Order?· I believe it is to diffuse light, that is, to spread knowledge
among men.
You might agree with the historian Krause that the ultimate purpose
is to perfect men, to make them better, wiser and consequently happier,
but the means' of achieving this perfection is general diffusion of knowledge.
Hence, above: all things, Masonry exists to promote knowledge. The Mason
ought first of all to cultivate his mind. He ought to study the liberal arts
_a nd sciences, he ought to be become a learned man.
The state seeks to make men better and happier by preserving order.
The church seeks this end by cultivating the moral person and by holding
in the background supernatural ~anctions. Masonry endeavors to make men
better and happier by teaching them and by diffusing knowledge among
them. This, bear in mind, was true before education of the masses had become a function of the state.
Society is divided sharply into classes that unde~stand each other
none too well and hence are getting wholly out of sympathy. What nobler
Masonic lecture could there be than one which took up the fundamentals
of social science and undertook to spread a sound knowledge of it among
all nations? Suppose such a lecture on citizenship were prepared, delivered
in Lodge after Lodge, and after criticism and recasting as a result of years
of labor, was taught to all our Masters, would not our Lodges diffuse
a real light in the community and take a great step forward in their work
of making for human perfection?
We are taught that the roof of the Mason's workshop is nothing less
than the "clouded canopy or star-decked heavens" and that nothing that
goes on beneath th~t spacious covering can be wholly alien to us. The needs

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

56

57

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of no one time and of no one people can circumscribe our objects. If the
Craft is to be perpetual, it must appeal to each time as well as to all times.
It must have in its traditions something that Today can use, although
Yesterday could not use and Tomorrow need not. Hence we may properly
inquire: what can we make of this wonderful tradition of which we are
the custodians that will serve the world of today?
Our task as members of society is to advance civilization by asserting
ourselves consciously and intelligently to that end. Every man may do this
in some measure in his time and place. So every man may retard or obstruct
civilization in some degree in his time and place.
What will serve civilization in the world of today? I believe the great
need of today to be the practice of citizenship, interest in our form of government and the protection of those inalienable rights of free men which
are under attack all over the world and without which civilization will
falter and fall back toward the dark ages. We Americans of today were
born to those rights, we did not have to fight, bleed or die to secure them,
but we may yet have to fight, bleed and die to keep them.
Few can really appreciate what we have here in America until they
have seen the immigrants from foreign lands entering New York harbor
and coming off the boats to set foot on our soil. They have lived under the
systems of government in Europe-they know what those systems are.
They know what living conditions are there. They come to America because they want to. They are not here simply because an accident of birth
made them Americans. They appreciate what America has to offer, and to
see them fall upon their knees and kiss the soil of this great free country
would make you realize what this country offers as nothing else could. It
would make you dedicate yourself to the task of working and fighting to
keep those things. And finally, may I leave you with this thought.
I believe in America as I believe in God and I know that as Freemasonry did a great work in the past of America, so it can do a still greater
work in the future of our country. With the utmost respect and regard for
other lands and peoples, our care and our energy is for America, our
America, God's America, to keep it true to its high heroic tradition.

The Homes are our greatest care. They require constant thought an<l
attention. ·The Trustees, as your representatives, not only direcli the operation of our two Homes but assist mothers to care for their children in theii
own homes, Masons and widows in their homes or help them in securing
Old Age Aid.
We do not believe there exists anywhere a finer expression of Masonic
charity than is represented by our Masonic Homes and we should never
permit any lowering of the standards there established.
It is not the intent of your Trustees in this report to take up the details
of the Homes' operation. You will find this in detail in the splendid reports
of Superintendent · Hartman of Decoto and Superintendent Downen of
Covina. It is hoped you will carefully read them.
Responsibility of Lodges
Few Lodges realize or understand their responsibility with reference to
payments for maintenance of wards at the Masonic Homes where the applicant is admitted to the Home, whether a child or adult, and it is ordered or
agreed that legally responsible relatives shall contribute toward their maintenance. The Lodge and not the legally responsible relative is charged with
the amount to be paid and it is therefore incumbent upon the Lodge to collect from the legally responsible relative and remit to the office of the
Masonic Homes, Masonic Temple, San Francisco. In other words, the
Masonic Homes deal directly with the Lodge rather than with the individual, therefore, the Lodge is required to pay whether the legally responsible relative reimburses the Lodge or not. Instances have occurred whereby ·
legally responsible relatives pave had a change in their financial status and
could no longer contribute, in which case the Lodge found it necessary to
appeal to the Trustees for a reco.nsideration of the case. The Field Worker
then reinvestigates the case where it is deemed advisable, especially on behalf of children, State Aid may be secured.
In May, 1940, due notice was sent to all Lodges that from and after that
date all remittances with respect to payments for account of legally respon-

sible relatives and excess quota items were to be made direct to the office
of the Masonic Homes instead of to Covina and Decoto as theretofore. At
that time it was found that a number of Lodges had failed to make the
agreed collections from the legally responsible relatives and therefore had
not remi~ted to the Masonic Homes, and it was likewise found that Lodges
were delinquent under the excess quota rule. At this writing all but two
Lodges have liquidated or adjusted the arrearages above referred to.
Attention is also brought before the Lodges in consideration of children accepted into the Masonic Home where an estate or trust fund has
been left to the child. Upon admission to the Home it is the ·Lodge's responsibility to conserve these funds .for the benefit of the child until his
dismissal from the Home.

Scholarships
. With funds generously donated for the purpose, we · are enabled to
assist graduates from the Covina Home to secure vocational training or
university education, thus fitting them for self-support. In the last fiscal
!ear we received for the benefit of the Scholarship Fund in dividends and
in~erest the sum of $1571.92, and from loans returned by beneficiaries now
gainfully employed the sum of $482.50, a total income of $2,054.42. Out
of this we disbursed to worthy children $1,510.87.
In connection with the Scholarship Fund, we· may mention here the
good work of three former beneficiaries and graduates of the Home who on
several occasions appeared before Lodges and spoke of their experiences.
One is Fred Prewitt, who was admitted to the Home in 1919 from Sisson
Lodge No. 310 and graduated from the high school at Covina. in 1924.
Fred is now in business for himself at Woodland. Another is Byron Athan,
admitted from Petaluma Lodge No. 180 in 1927, graduated in 1936 and is
now in his second year in law school. . .The third one is Anna May' Miller,
who was admitted to the Home in 1925 from Durant Lodge No. 268 and
was graduated from high school and dismissed in 1937. She 'is now in her
senior year at the University of California at Berkeley. These children were
chaperoned by Elsie Schulte, Hermann Lodge No. 127, who was graduated
from the Home in 1929 and later took a course in pedagogy at the San
Francisco State Teachers College and is now an accomplished and efficient
Investigator for the Masonic Homes.
.
The talks of these Home. graduates to the brethren were enthusiastically
received and did much to bring home to their hearers just what the Masonic
!fome is doing for children.
Labor by Residents
Under the rules and regulations established by the Board, all residents
are required to perform such duties in or about the Home as may be required . by any authorized representative of the Trustees, unless in the
opinion of a licensed physician they are physically unable to do so. This
rule is .necessary and its cheerful acceptance by residents goes far to enhance their happiness and contentment and in maintaining a real homelike
atmosphere.
'·.
Unfortunately, some-and happily they are few in number-do. not
seem to adjust themselves to their environment and are therefore unhappy
in their idleness. But in general the residents do adjust their lives to their
new condition, thus tending largely to make our Masonic Home what it is
intended to be-a real home.
It would take too much time to name all the men and women who
assist in the physical conduct of the Home, but to all who volunteer cheer-

Christmas Entertainment
tEach November a Christma~ c~!":d is sent to all. Lodg~s i.n the jurisdiction suggesting a donation to. the Christmas and Entertainment Fund. The
response is generous but ·not .sufficient to meet the activities usually charged
against it. From it we provide: a gift and cash allofment for each member
of the Honie at Christmas and meet the expenses of the camp at Balboa
maintained for the children in the summer, as well as other recreation not
ch~rgeable to the General Fund.
A more generous response would enable us to give each resid~nt of the
Home at Decoto $1.00 ·a month as pin money. Many Lodges see that their
members receive spending money on occasions, but there are others too
proud to ask, with empty pockets. We believe such an allowance will be of
value to the discipline of "the Home as well as to· the morale of the resident.
Recommendation
We recommend that the per capita tax for the coming year remain at
40 cents.

Securities, Notes, Contracts, Real Estate, etc.:
All of the securities listed under Schedule B-1 have been received by
clonation. The stated or book value represents the value placed upon the
securities at the time of donation. Where the value of the security is unknown it is recorded at a nominal value of $1.00 solely for purpose of record.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as on
July 31, 1940. Insurance policies, received mainly from residents of the
Home have been recorded at the amount recoverable at the death of the
insured except in certain cases where the value has not been determined, in
which case entry is at a nominal value of $1.00.
Real estate has been recorded at the assessed value as taken from the
tax bills. Although a number of parcels were sold during the year, there
still remains on hand real estate at an assessed value of $14,710.00.
Trust and Annuity Funds:
Under Schedules B-4, B-5, B-6, B-7, and B-8 are shown the details of
the various trust and annuity funds. Payments due from these funds according to the contracts and agreements were made from the general fund
of the Homes which should be reimbursed as sufficient cash is available
in the various funds.
General:
All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
The securities and notes were verified by certification from the Anglo California National Bank which holds certificates and notes in trust. All life
insurance policies are at the office of the secretary and were checked to the
subsidiary ledger accounts.
Sufficient examination and tests were made of the detailed revenue and
expense accounts to satisfy ourselves as to the general correctness of the
accounting. Detailed distribution of the operating expenses of the Homes
were made by Decoto and Covina offices and were accepted as correct after
we had verified amounts by totals.

GRA N D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

10,145.50

To the Board of Trustees :
In presenting my thirty-first annual report as Superintendent of the
Decoto Home, I am pleased to say that conditions in general are very good,
and with few exceptions the morale of the Home has been satisfactory
during the year.
It has been our endeavor to operate the several departments as economically and efficiently as possible, and to provide every possible care for
the well-being of the members of our family, and to have the buildings and
grounds present a neat and attractive appearance.
In the operation of the several departments of the Home, there are
many phases to be taken into consideration; the most important among
them being the comfort of those who are entrusted to our care.
yve have endeavored to .maintain a social atmosphere in keeping with
the ideals of our Fraternity and bring as large a measure of contentment
as possible into the daily life of all who are enjoying the many benefits
of the Home.
At the beginning of the fi scal year, there were enrolled 348 ; 200 men,
148 women. There were admitted from September 1, 1939, to August 31,
1940, 18 men and 14 women, making a total of 380. Passed away during the
year, 34 men and 18 women. Voluntary departures, 4. There are now 324
residents at the Home. There are 23 married couples. The average age of
the residents of the Home is 75 years for men and 73 years for women.
The general health of the Home has been good with the exception of
those who are infirm and feeble, owing to advancing years. There are now
42 of our members being cared for in our hospital department, where they
are receiving every care and comfort our physician and nurses are able to
give them. The members requiring hospital care are gradually increasing.
Additional room, when needed, can be provided by the completion of the
interior of the second floor of the two wings of the hospital building.
I am pleased to report that many of our men who are physically able,
assist in many light duties in the several departments of the Home, which

78

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

are of material benefit. Many of the women residents assist in the dining
room, sewing and linen rooms, reception rooms, library, office work, etc. A
number of the men residents render service in th_e kitchen, pantry, grounds,
carpenter and paint shops, store room, engine room, garage, mail, express,
and passenger service, and many other duties in a general way.
As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been leased on
shares or cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of fruit for table use.
The returns from the hay crop have been fair. The garden has supplied
vegetables, berries, and plenty of greens. The chicken ranch has supplied
eggs for table use.
It was necessary to overhaul and repair our deep well pump. Part of
the casing was renewed. The cylinder had to be rebored. The pump was
put in serviceable condition. Our three reservoirs, with a capacity of 500,000
gallons, are at all times nearly full, which furnishes a plentiful supply for
household, garden, irrigating and fire protection.
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The specials are those which were held on New Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's and Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day, Fourth of July,
Thanksgiving, and Christmas.
Many splendid programs, stage plays, band and orchestra concerts
have been provided during the year by visiting Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, and friends, for the entertainment of the members of the Home; the
evening often closing with dancing. From time to time, entertainments are
prepared entirely by members of the Home, consisting of vocal and instrumental music, community singing, cards, games, · dancing, etc. Tuesday
evenings are devoted t<;> cards, and Friday evenings to chorus practice. A
religious service is held in the Assembly Hall every Sunday afternoon and
Sunday . evening. The Association of Ministers of Washington township
' have arranged to send one of their members to conduct our services. They
are often accompanied by their church choirs. Our Home choir often furnish the music for these services.
The entertainment fund, comprising gifts and donations by Lodges and
individuals, enables the management to provide various forms of entertainment for the enjoyment of the members of our family. Vocal and instrumental concerts, lectures, picnics, birthday parties, have added much to the
comfort and pleasure of all, in the social life of the Home.
Moving picture programs are presented every Thursday evening. These
films are furnished by the San Francisco Film Distributing Companies,
without charge, for which we tender our heart-felt thanks and appreciation.
During the past year, the following repairs and improvements have
been made. N early all of the outside door and window frames, and a large
number of rooms and halls in the several buildings have been painted.
A retaining wall of rock has been built in the rear of the East wing
building, the Hospital, Kitchen, Dormitory and Temple buildings. The
entire length of the wall is about 1705 feet. The average height is about
four feet. This rock was salvaged from the foundation of the old buildings
which were removed to furnish the site of the present Administration building. Climbing roses, vines and shrubs have been planted along the entire
length of the rock walls. Many small garden spots around -the buildings
are beautified and made attractive by the planting of shrubs, flowers, building walks and concrete curbing. The care and work performed is entirely
done by the members of the Home.
The new sewer system of the Decoto Sanitary District of Alameda
County was completed the early part of this year. We have discontinued the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

79

use of our septiC tanks, and connected the Home sewage with the main
sewer system of Decoto. It was necessary to abandon the old sewer line
from the building to the septie tank, and a new line of sewer pipe was laid
from the old connections to the new line of pipe and connections made
with the main line of the Decoto highway, at a point in front of the Home
property. The new sewer system has been of great benefit to this community; the service has been very satisfactory. In opening the line for the
new pipe, a large part of the new macadamized road laid down last year was
damaged, and for a time the road was impassable. The roads have been
repaired, and are again in good condition.
Many donations of books have been received and placed on the shelves
of our main library and branches, located in the several departments of
the Home. The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda County Free Library
enables our family to obtain many of the latest books, and an opportunity
for special ones.
In addition, we are the recipients, through friends and members of the
Fraternity, of daily papers, magazines and periodicals, which are placed on
the tables of the library, club rooms, and social halls, where the members of
the Home can enjoy them.
Arrangements have been made whereby members of the family,· a few
at a time, can keep dental, optical and hospital appointments, and to enjoy
an outing to nearby places of interest. Also, an occasional visit to nearby
Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters. During the year, weekly trips are made
to San Francisco, Oakland, and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Last year, the Home Trustees made it possible for members of the
Home to visit the <;;olden Gate International Exposition on Treasure
Island. One hundred and eighty-five residents of the Home enjoyed their
visit there.
This year, similar arrangements were made, and all who were able
and cared to go, had the opportunity to do so.
From time to time, officers and members of Lodges from San Francisco and East Bay cities, visit the Home for the purpose of conferring
degrees on their candidates. On these occasions the brethren of the Home
have the opportunity of being present at the meeting in our Temple. Many
of the brethren of the Home are unable to visit their own Lodges, and all
greatly appreciate the opportunity given them to meet with the officers and
members of visiting Lodges.
We have been favored during the year by visits of officers of the Grand
Lodge, members of the Board of Trustees, and members of various Lodges,
and friends of the Home.
The Matron joins me in expressing our appreciation of the efficient
and conscientious work on the part of the officers and employees, whose
earnest efforts have been a factor in maintaining a high standard of service
throughout the several departments of the Home, and to thank the Board
of Trustees for their kindly assistance, and for the many acts of courtesy
received.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

· 'Reuort of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Herewith I am presenting my fourteenth annual report as Superintendent of the Covina Home. During the past year there were 26 admissions
(17 boys. and 9 girls) ; and 34 discharges (19 boys and 15 girls). Boys in
the Home outnumber the girls approximately two to one.
In June 13 of our children (6 boys and 7 girls) graduated from the
Covina High School and were discharged, and these are now distributed
as follows :
Working in manufacturing plants........................................2
Working in clerical and clerking .jobs.........- .......................5
Attending agricultural college..................-............................1
Attending junior eollege..........................................................1
Attending business eollege...........................................•..........2
Attending cosmetology school........................_......................2
John Morgan, the boy who last year won a national scholarship at
Harvard University, finished his first year's work with three A's and one B
has been reappointed for the scholarship for the coming year. During the
past summer he acted as supervisor of older boys at our summer camp; in
this work proved very efficient.
Notable Donation&--There has been an increasing amount of interest
by Lodges in the work of the Home and in the welfare of their particular
wards therein. Visitations at the Home during the past year have been
more numerous, the list of gifts from Lodges and individuals greater than
ever befcre.
Among the donations particularly to be noted are :
By Hollenbeck Lodge, a very large lot of canned peaches and other
fruit, following a custom of t his Lodge for many years.
By Lodges of the 87th Masonic District, numerous items of furnishings
for the living room in the Intermediate Boys' Building. This room is to
be maintained by them in memory of Frank M. Wise.
By Sam L. Warner Square Club, completion of refurnishing of living
room, Intermediate Girls' Department. This is now a beautiful home-like
room.

The Christmas and Entertainment Fund-At Christmas time particularly the thoughts of Masons turn generously toward t~e children at Covii;ia.
Contributions made at that time are put into "The Christmas and Entertamment Fund," which enables us not only to make a Christmas for the children, but to carry on with an entertainment program through~ut the yea~.
All expenses incident to maintaining the summer ca~p are paid from this
fund. This year contributions to this fund were received from 31? Lodges,
82 other Masonic organizations and 20 individuals. These are hsted elsewhere in this report.
Awards for Good Citizenship-Again for the third time we were able
this year to make awards of gold watches to the boy and the girl who were
adjudged to have made the best per~onal c~mtribution to .t~e life. of the
Home community in the way of public service and good c1t1zensh1p. The
prizes w ere donated by Albert J. Robbins, Jr., and Joseph Hartman.
Scholarship Loan . Fund-The Southern California Past Commander s'
Association has made available .to Masonic Hom.e graduates a student loan
fund which assists worthy young people who are ambitious for vo~ational
or c~llege courses and · who may be in a position to accept such aid on .a
loan basis. This will make educational opportunities on a. self-help basis
available for a number of our boys and girls from time to time.
.
Health-The past year has been marked by unusually good health
among the children. The number in hospital has a".eraged on!?' l.7o/o of
those enrolled. Epidemic conditions were not experienced. ~h~s may be
attributed to a considerable preventive medical program admm1~tered by
competent physicians, to good nursing service, abundant recreational and
play facilities, and a varied and plentiful diet of good food. Our cost for
foodstuffs served at the Home averaged 10.6 cents per meal ; on school days
our children have an allowance at the school cafeterias of ~O cents for
lunch. Children coming to the Home almost always show durmg the first

99

few months a marked gain in weight, and in general appearance of good
health.
The Summer Camp-A summer camp experience is valuable to any
child, and particularly to institutional children, whose lives are necessarily
more subject to routine than is the case with other children. In the report
of the Homes for 1913 we find Brother Hartman, who was then superintendent of both Homes, saying: "The camping trip for the children at
Balboa Beach in Orange county was positively the event of the year, not
even excepting Christmas." For twenty-eight years this camp has been
maintained on Balboa Island. In the meantime the character of the surroundings there has greatly changed. Then the camp was in an isolated
place with plenty of room ; now it is in the midst of a thickly settled summer resort city, no longer a desirable camp location. The property has
greatly increased in value, could probably be sold for $25,000.
We are in search of a new camp location which we can recommend to
the Board. It .should have twenty-five or more acres of groun d, should be
away from civilization and commercialized amusements, thus removing from
the children all resources except camp activities. It should have woods for
woodcraft, mountains for hiking, some level space for playground, a lake
or pool for swimming.
Mode of Life in the Home-There has been no important change in
policy or plan of handling children during the past year. The well-conducted private home is the model which we aim to imitate; every procedure
is measured by the test : "How does this compare with the way they would
do it in a real family?" While in some respects we cannot r eproduce private
home ways of doing, we come as near it as we can.
The grouping of children as must be done in our Home has both its
advantages and disadvantages. The noise and hurly-burly generated in a
crowd tend to rub off the fine edge of gentle manners. Quiet and restraint
can be insisted upon, but only at the cost of undue repression.
On the other hand ours is a highly competitive society, which puts our
children on their mettle. Again, co-operation and team work are certainly
bett er learned by children in group living. Our children learn to lend and
give and share and help.
Visitors often ask whether our children suffer from homesickness.
They do not, except in some cases briefly upon· first arrival. When they go
to visit relatives, sometimes they are unwisely treated to a round of entertainment which causes temporary discontent after their return. On the
whole, however, the children · in the Home are a very happy group.
Individual children, like adults, have their problems, which may look
'v ery serious to them. Our children live in groups, but must be dealt with as
individuals. The measure of our service to a child is the amount of individual attention which we can give to his needs. We can never do enough
along this line.
Community Contacts--We endeavor to make available for our older
children community contacts, not only in the Home community, but also in
the Covina community. They have of course the public schools, and their
affiliated organizations, such as athletic teams, musical organizations, etc.
During the past year we have required children of high school age to attend
some Sunday school or church in Covina. Our boys are encouraged to
belong to local Boy Scout troops; several girls are members of the local
Bethel of Job's Daughters. Through these contacts our children make
acquaintances with children outside their own . group, exchange visits with
them for meals or overnights. All of this is a part of a valuable social
education.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Our Alumni-We maintain contacts with a large number of our old
boys _a nd girls, tho~e who grew up in the Home and are now out in . the
world. During the year we have had three considerable reunion meetings
of these alumni· in addition to this many of them visit the Home from time
to time or co~municate with us by letter. We give weight to their appraisals' of their experience in the Home, their estimates of what it did or
failed to do for them.
They do not think the Home was too strict or too severe with them;
often they express the opinion that they were held with too gentle a hand.
We would rather hear this criticism than its opposite; we think it is better
to be too easy than too institutional.
Our graduates have shown a remarkable ability to win their way in the
outside world, to make a living, to keep off of relief rolls, to marry and
stay married, to raise nice families of their own. A gathering of our alumni,
with their families, is an inspiring occasion ; they are a fine-looking lot of
representative American people.
JoHN M. DowNEN, Superintendent.
Report of Field W.orker-Covina
During my nine years as field worker for the Masonic Homes my tasks
have been many and varied, and have afforded a rich experience in human
relationships. In fulfilling them it has been my constant endeavor to render
a sincere service to the organization and the recipients of its philanthropy.
The following is a summary of my work for the past ye;ir:

Aged Program:
a. Investigation of applications for admission to the Home for the
Aged; or for outside relief.
b. Periodic visitations to recipients of outside relief to determine
any change in status.
Children's Program:
a. Investigation of applications for admission to the Children's
Home; or for outside relief for children in the homes of their
mothers.
b. Periodic visitations to outside aid families to determine change
in status; and to aid mothers in problems which arise in the care
of their children.
c. Investigation, placement, and supervision of children in foster
homes.
·
d. Investigation of applications for State Aid for those children in
the Covina Home who are eligible for same.
e. Visits to children's parents, relatives, Lodges, and other interested persons regarding children "in the Covina Home.
f. Vocational counselling with children about to graduate from
the Covina Home.
g. Follow-up prog~am of children discharged from the Covina
Home.
Assistance to Lodges: ,
a. In establishing Old Age Assistance.
b. Preliminary investigations, either for children or aged, to determine need for making applications.

101

During the past year 840 visits were made in the Southern District,
requiring 13,726 miles of travel. Seventeen applications were investigated for
admission to the Home for the Aged; and sixteen applications investigated
for admission to the Children's Home.

Aged R ecipients of Outside Aid: Periodic visitations were made to
twenty-six aged persons residing in their own homes. These visits had a
two-fold purpose: ( 1) to secure information concerning financial status; and
(2) to render any service which might make these aged men and women
more comfortable physically, mentally, or emotionally. · Through our efforts
five aged persons were transferred to State Old Age Assistance. One
recipient was admitted to the Veterans' Home, while continuing to accept
Masonic Aid. If it had not been for periodic visitation he would still be
benefiting from both sources; Masonic aid has been stopped.
Outside Aid to Children : We have twenty-five children receiving aid
in the homes of their mothers. The amount of aid varies according to the
circumstances in each family. We have used the budgetary standard set up
by the State Department of Social Welfare, which is adequate to provide
basic necessities. As the public program for aid to dependent children has
become more liberal, it is quite possible that our outside aid program for
children will be further decreased. Masonic relief can no longer be used
to supplement public aid to children, because rulings of the State Department forbid it.
A number of the children on outside aid have participated in a few of
the activities of the children in the Covina Home. At Christmas each child
received . Christmas gifts equal with those in the Home. During the summer
twelve outside aid children had an opportunity to spend two or three weeks
vacation at Camp Tucker, at Balboa. To most of the boys and girls this
summer outing has become a treat eagerly anticipated from one year to
the next.
'
While our relationship to outside aid families has its origin in their
economic need, considerable part of our work with them has been in helping in their personal difficulties ; to build more desirable emotional and social
adjustments so that they can get along more happily and successfully in the
_c ommunity in which they live.
·
·

a

Foster Home Care : We have at present six children in carefully selected
private homes. Occasionally it becomes necessary to remove a child from
the Covina Home because he finds himself in conflict with his environment,
thus becoming a detriment not only to himself but to the group. To help
that child solve his problem we seek a suitable private home where by individual care his twisted thinking and behavior will be turned into healthier
expression. A year ago we had occasion to remove a girl who presented a
serious problem, complicated by the parent's very bad relationship to her.
Twelve homes were investigated before one was selected for that child.
We work closely with foster mothers, visit them and the children under
their care frequently, and put forth every effort to help these children attain
their fullest development.
State Aid Program: The investigation of applications for Children's.
State Aid is a part of the field worker's · job. Preparation of an application
before submitting it to the State Department of Social Welfare requires
much time. Renewal applications must be submitted annually. The Covina
Home is receiving from the State at present $15.00 a month for each of 38
children, a total of $6840 a year. Recent changes in legislation affecting
this type of public aid will result in our filing applications for a number of
children not heretofore entitled. to such aid.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Childreii in the Covfoa FI ome: In investigating an application for. admission of a child to the Covina Home, it is the field worker's duty to find
out the facts, including the child's family background, his cultural and
social setting, relationships within the immediate family, relatives, the
family's purpose in placing the child, his health, intelligence, school record,
personality anq emotional adjustment. This information is important to
the Home as an aid in adjusting the child in his new environment, and in
helping the Home to meet his individual needs. The field worker, having
knowledge of the child's background; is often called into conference with
the superintendent and the houseparent when difficulties arise.
Graduates and Vocational Guidance : It is a serious responsibility in our
rapidly changing world to counsel young people preparing to enter the
world. For several years our graduates have been benefited by a vocational
guidance program under the leadership of Professor J . Gustav White. Following up· Professor White's work, the field worker has assisted many of
the outgoing graduates in making their. first steps in the outside world, and
in some instances she has gone with them through their difficulties for a
year or longer after they leave the Home, until they are definitely established upon a self-help basis.
CATHERINE NOEL, Field Worker.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the M.". W:. Grand Lod,ge of California:

Your board herewith presents its eighth annual report, being for the
period between July 31, 1939, and July 31, 1940.
The board is now constituted as follows:
1940
1941
Ernest G. Bashor
Reynold E. Blight
Arthur S. Crites
Jos. L. Shell
Louis C. Drapeau
Harry F. White
J. T. Fraser
John F. Pullen
Ira D. Wheeler
Rollie W. Miller

1942
Wm. Rhodes Hervey
Edmund A. Lockett
Robert B. Gaylord
T. M. Wright
Frank M. Smith

The officers of the board are:
Frank M. Smith, Chairman
Wm. Rhodes Hervey, Vice Chairman
Robert B. Gaylord, Vice Chairman Wm. P. Filmer, Treasurer
Reynold E. Blight, Secretary
Our report, this year, covers the period between July 31, 1939, and July
31, 1940-dates that in themselves mean little, other than that of a calendared
series of days bearing upon a cycle of benevolence extended by members
of a free and accepted organization.
Yet in the history of the world, the period covered by this report will
be reco;ded as the most stirring and important of all time. In the interim
since our last report, time-honored institutions have fallen; rights and privileges recognized as the birthrights of individuals throughout the ~orld have
been denied; free speech and free press have been abrogated by ammal force
and power · the common assemblage of persons dedicating their efforts toward prog~ams of human betterment have been broken up, and in their
place councils of destruction h~ve met. ~ife, through?u.t. the_ lands formerly
possessing culture and the higher attainments of c1v1hzat10n, are forces,
which, paradoxically, are using the products of modern progress to destroy
the things for which men have consistently fought and sacrificed.
The pitiable spectacle of men, women, and children, harried and agonized by organized arrogance is a thing which shocks men's souls! Homeless,
abandoned hungry of body and soul, bewildered by events over which they
had no co~trol countless thousands, at this moment, are praying for the
blessings of no;mality, which we, here, are enjoying as a priceless privilege.
Old men and women innocent babes, eager and inquiring youth, alt
have felt the imprint of b;utality's heel and have questioned, wi~hou~ coh_erent answer. Devoid of hope, bereft of home and loved ones, brmsed m mmd
and body, these refugees from lust and assumption "".ill remain f_or all time
in the pages of history as evidence of the ghastly and mhuman pnce exacted
by the enemies of democratic governments.
Program for Year
Here in our own fair land, free of the compulsions of dictatorship, 01;r
work of humanity has gone forward; gone forward on a scale not wh?lly ~n
keeping with the need and the aspirations of the program, but which,, m
contrast with other · countries and sections, has been most heartwarming
and encouraging to the members of the board.

119

Realizing the many calls made upon the brethren by other meritorious
programs, which demanded their consideration and openhandedness, the
board, during the period just closed, made no excessive demands nor importuned a single member to make other than a purely free-will contribution
to the program. Continued belief and confidence in the educational program
instituted several ·years past, caused the board to limit its efforts to this
method and, despite the decrease which this year will show, our assurance
in such a program has not been impaired nor shaken in the slightest. We
believe, rather, that the value of such educational procedure has been reaffirmed in the face of continued unemployment, in the uncertainty of the
times, and in view of other worthwhile and bona fide demands made upon
our brethren, wl:io are also, it must be remembered, members and .affiliates
of other fraternal and charitable groups, each exacting its deserved quota of
attention and care.
At the outset of the year, the board, in keeping with established precedent, again requested the reappointment, wherever possible, of former Endowment Fund chairmen. Where this was done each constituent Lodge
gained the experience of past years, and the results obtained offer evidence
of the wisdom of such reappointments.
Masonry makes no man perfect. It merely indicates one road by which
a man may travel toward the goal of spiritual perfection more easily and
with more help than by other roads. It has no motive power to drive men
over that road; it but smoothes the path and points the way. The travel
thereon is strictly up to the individual brother and, in the opinion of the
board, the roadmarks to charity are better seen and observed under the
guidance of competent roadmasters, who have served their novitiate and
are qualified to show the way.
Correspondence and Literature
The board makes no exclusive claim to the achievements of the Endowment Fund program for the year. Serving merely as a clearing house for
Masters, Secretaries, Endowment chairmen and individual brethren, the board
boasts simply of its interest in, and coordination with the various Lodges
participating in the program. In evidence of the widespread interest in the
welfare of our homes 1500 pieces of correspondence were received by the
board, and 17,518 letters were forwarded to Lodges and individuals concerning home matters. Included in the year's board correspondence were Christmas letters to all Lodges, announcements of the homes endowment program
for the year to new Masters, regular monthly correspondence with secretaries; special letters to individuals regarding bequests, and other matters
concerning the program, and general information imparted to Lodge officials, Home guests and interested brethren.
Bearing in mind the need for economy for the year, the board curtailed
the preparation and printing of new pamphlets and other printed material,
and urged the Secretaries and Endowment chairmen to assist in distributing
the printed material already on hand. The extent of this distribution
amounted to 109,812 pieces of literature, divided into 28 different subjects
dealing with the Homes at Decoto and Covina. They covered every phase
of the program and offered to the brethren the Masonic fact that happiness
to others costs so little and pays such great dividends in contentment and
security for our elders, and promise and advantages for our youngsters.
The board especially requests. all Lodge officials to seek a wider and
more complete distribution of these informative pamphlets among the brethren, in order that· the message of the Homes be carried to every craftsman

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in the jurisdiction. \Ve sincerely believe such coverage will result in a new,
or renewed, interest in the work of the homes, with a corresponding surge
of awakened concern in the lives and welfare of our Home guests.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In good times or bad, these same brethren have offered their share

:vhet~er it be large or small, to the major charity of the jurisdiction, and
m domg so have clearly shown the way for others to follow. Can it be
said that they possess more heart than others? Can it be said that to them
is given a broader vision and appreciation of the program than is accorded
the average member? Or can it be said simply that they remembered
where others, with equally good intentions, postponed and delayed until
too late? The board likes to think this is so, and offers as a remedy for
such forgetfulness a visit to the Homes, where the work being accom~lished will bring a new spirit of response from those not now participating
m the program.
The board sincerely believes that the vast majority of those contributing regularly are also regular visitors at the Homes at Decoto and Covina.
There they see our Home guests, young and old, in an environment as
closely resembling a home as it is possible for the jurisdiction to provide.
There, they may mingle with our elder guests, watch them at work
and at play, and observe the care, the kindliness and the deep concern
with which they are encompassed. A cheerful word of greeting a firm and
friendly hand-clasp, and inquiry regarding their lives and outl~ok are the
keys which open the locks of neighborly contact, and are not only ~egarded
as acts of signal importance by our Home guests at Decoto but are the
friendly and cordial deeds demanded of conscious Masonry.
A vi1;it to the Home at Covina is a visit to a large family circle, where
foster-fathers and mothers serve in a capacity approximating as nearly as
humanly possible the real parentage denied our young wards by the will of
Divine Providence; The love and care shown our youngsters; the total lack
of strict and forbidding institutionalism, the open affection exhibited by
the children for their foster-parents, the cheerfulness with which they
perform their allotted chores; the ed~cational and money system in effect
at the Home ; the shouts of childish glee at games and at play; these and
a hundred other details strike the visitor with .singular force, and make
him feel proud of the fact that he is a part-a necessary and vital partof this magnificent and heart-warming enterprise.
Yes, if your board members could have dictatorial powers delegated
to them, their first (and only) act of power would be to cause every craftsman in California, whatever his standing or calling, to pay a visit to our
Homes .at Decoto and Covina. Our dictum would be : "See for yourselve.s,
and seemg, know our Homes for what they are; a haven of security and
peace for the aged; a shelter and a pledge for the future for our children;
an institution American in concept and principle. See your Homes and
realize with pride that Freemasons are Builders, and that our generation
has not been bankrupt of accomplishment. Become a part of this work,
help build better boys and girls, and assist in the care and protection which
your Grand Lodge is desirous of extending to those in the sunset of their
liv&S."

These gifts go into the Permanent Endowment Fund and will accomplish much good now and in the years to come. The name of each donor
w~ll rema~n permanently on the rolls of the jurisdiction, and the proceeds
will be wisely and economically expended in carrying out the wishes of
the benefactor.
Each year attorney members of the craft have interested themselves
in supplying information regarding the Homes to clients preparing wills
and bequests, and the results of such interest is becoming more and more
apparent. The board is most grateful to members of the legal profession
for their cooperation with the program and urges their continued and active
support.
Now here in the field of charity does a more extensive, noble, and
worth-while venture offer itself, than the Homes Endowment Fund of
California. It is the hope of the board that brethren throughout the jurisdiction will continue to regard this phase of Masonry as a road to practical
and spiritual charity, and to .remember the lasting good which emanates
from a testamentary gift.
Work of Grand Master and Officials
It is the happy privilege of the board to record the fact that the most
indefatigable worker for the Homes Endowment program this year was
our Grand Master. Brother Wm. B. Ogden, through long association with
the program and with a heart attuned to the need and the worth of our
program of benevolence, worked in harness throughout the year and rendered Trojan service to the work closest to his heart. Practically every
talk he made to constituent Lodges contained a stirring and sincere appeal
to craftsmen to remember and to cherish the great work being carried out
by the Grand Lodge for the betterment and security of our Home guests.
His work of education will be long remembered, and your board considers
it a privilege to record officially his efforts and his unquestioned contribution to the program for the year.
As usual the Masters, Secretaries, and Home Endowment chairmen
took the lead in their respective Lodges, and much value to the program
came through their joint efforts. Secretaries were in constant touch with
the board and assisted the Home Endowment chairmen in distributing
pamphlets and keeping the program before the brethren. The board is duly
appreciative of all Lodge officials' efforts, and urges a continuation of the
unselfish devotion shown the program during the past year.
The board would like again to suggest to incoming Masters the need
of reappointing, if possible, the old Home Endowment chairmen, who
have functioned so ably and efficiently in the past. Their work is of educational character, and both the Lodges a!!d its members will gain in the program by continuing their services. The Board again offers its whole-hearted
cooperation with Lodge officials and chairmen in carrying out the necessary
details for the coming year and expresses its sincere appreciation for past
efforts and accomplishments.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Coming Year
· What of the future?
Today, and during many years past, men have spoken often of changing and even abolishing the Constitution. But which Mason would think
of changing so much as a single comma in the great Bill of Human Rights
and Faith? Who, among us, would add or detract one syllable from such
inspiring words as, " ... we hold these truths to be self-evident, that all
men are created equal."
Some listen to the alluring voice of the foreign agitator, with his
promises of Utopian conditions that have long ago proven visionary and
impossible of realization. These foreign in heart know little of our own
history and nothing at all of our ideals. They look upon government as a
thing to be feared, as a thing to be hated, as an instrumentality in the
hands of rulers and privileged <;:lasses that takes men and money from the
people, giving them nothing in return. These things may be true of other
governments of the world, BUT NOT OF OURS!
The founders of our Constitution believed in a living God, as we do.
The founders of our country believed in compassion to the weak and the
ill, as we do. The fathers of our country believed in freedom and equality
of all men, as we do. The founders of our nation believed in truth, in
decency, and in humanity, as we do.
Therefore, we as Masons realize that in paying the duty we owe to
our God, to our country, and to our neighbors, we also pay the duty we
owe to ourselves as citizens ·a nd as Masons with heads up and eyes forward,
and with re-awakened courage and fortitude for the days to come.
Realizing this there can be no question as to the outcome of our dedicated services to our country, to Masonry, and to those dependent upon
our care and protection, because THIS IS AMERICANISM.
Fraternally submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD,
WM. RHODES HERVEY

Report of Auditors

To· the Endowment Fut1d Committee, Masonic Homes of California:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes of California fo~ the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1940 and present herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of cash receipts .and disbursements, (other than
Luckenbach Fund-Exhibit C) for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1940.
Exhibit B: Summary statement of Endowment Fund assets, as at
July 31, 1940.
·
Schedule B-1 : List of regular Endowment Fund securities on hand-'acquired prior to July 31, 1940.
Schedule B-2 : List of regular Endowment Fund securities on handadditions to fund fiscal year 1939-40.
Schedule B-3 : Statement of securities redeemed and sold.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach fund as at July
31, 1940.
Exhibit D : Statements of Endowment Fund income and capital accounts.

Securities (Schedules B-1 and B-2) :
All of the corporation · stocks and the irrigation district bonds were
received by donation or bequest; other bonds so received are designated
by the letter "D." All donated securities are listed at market value at the
time of donation, with the exception that where the value is uncertain because of its being an unlisted or a closely held security, then in that case
a nominal value of $1.00 is listed for the purpose of record. Insurance policies are listed at a nominal value of $1.00 for conservative purposes.
Bonds purchased ~re recorded at cost. As most bonds carry a heavy
premium, an amortization schedule has been put into effect in order to reduce to a minimum any loss to the endowment fund when the bonds are ·
redeemed. ·
·

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
When last year we referred to the observance as "bigger and better"
than those which had preceded it, we could not of course know that that
description would have been better reserved for this year.
The phrase is a hackneyed one and smacks of "Main Street"; but in
no other way could the Twenty-first Annual Observance of Public Schools
Week be more aptly described. There have been in the past individual
local observances as successful as any reported this year.· But considered
as an entirety, and throughout the State generally, our latest observance
was bigger and better than the most successful of past years-bigger and
better in every way and from every point of view-in attendance at public
meetings, in .the number of visitors to the schools, in the types of. pro~r~ms
presented, in the generous support of the newspapers and the broadcastmg
stations and in the effective ·cooperation given by the groups which join
with us in the annual observance.
The following excerpt from a newspaper clipping accompanying a
report from one of our Lodges fairly indicates the situation throughout the
State generally:
"Last evening at the High School Auditorium another chapter
was written in the history of Public Schools Week when all records
of attendance at the combined school program were shattered. Not
only did the att~ndance record fall, but all records for quality and
balance of program tumbled also."
The frequent reference in the reports to the increase in attendance is
no doubt due to the fact that it continues to be the measuring stick of a
successful observance, and of public interest. In this connection it is to be
noted that in the early years there appeared to be greater public interest
manifested in the smaller communities than in the large centers of population; and it was believed that it was not only because there were fewer
distractions but also because the people generally were probably closer to
the institurlons they maintain and with a correspondingly greater interest
in them.
It later developed however that what seemed a lack of interest in tho
. large centers of population was probably due to the difficulty of a~tracting
the attention of any considerable proportion of the large population of a
city. With the growth and development of the observance, and by reason
of the publicity obtained through the newspapers and broadcasting stations,
this disparity disappeared; and for a long time now it has been practically
impossible to determine whether the most successful observances are in
the large centers of population or in the smaller communities.
The only thing about the matter that is fairly certain is that now, as it
always has been, the success of any observance, either with respect to
attendance or otherwise, is fairly proportionate to the zeal, industry and
intelligenc~ with which the arrangements are made and carried out. An
instance of this is furnished by the report this year from a large city in
which the public meetings constitute the dominant feature of the observance; although visits to the schools with exhibits of school work are by no
means neglected.

146

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We purpose referring briefly to the preliminary arrangements there
made, not merely because they resulted in an especially successful observance but also because similar arrangements, and more or less along the
sam~ lines, are now very generally pursued wherever warranted by the size
of the population.
..
In this instance the arrangements were made by a Committee appointed
through the Masters and Wardens Association under a very efficient chairman, acting in conjunction with committees representing the school department, and the Junior Chamber of Commerce.
Speakers from the Speakers Bureau of the Chamber of Commerce and
from the Speakers Bureau of the Masters and Wardens Association appeared at meetings of civic, fraternal and service organizations explaining
the purpose of Public Schools Week and seeking cooperation. Letters w~re
sent to 165 service civic women's and improvement clubs, and commercial,
patriotic and frate'rnal ~rganizations; there were also letters sent to Ministers of the Gospel suggesting how they might cooperate; 40,000 printed
invitations to the week's activities were sent to the parents through the
children in the elementary schools; letters were sent to all the Masonic
Lodges and to the Chapters of the Order of Ea~tern Star ~sking the
inclusion in their bulletins of announcements relative to Pubhc Schools
Week; attractive posters were prepared and through the courtesy of the
management displayed in all street cars; one hundred quarter cards were
placed in the retail stores and school exhibits were displayed in the st?re
windows; and in addition there was obtained the very generous cooperation
of the local newspapers and broadcasting stations, which was undoubtedly
largely responsible for the public interest aroused.
In connection with the mention of the assistance rendered by the Junior
Chamber of Commerce in the community to which reference has just been
made, it may be here noted that this year .the California Junior State
Chamber of Commerce joined with' those other state organizations which so
enthusiastically cooperate with us in the annual observance by the issuance
of proclamations and announcements to their units, and which include California Congress of Parents and Teachers, California Teachers Association,
California Department of the American Legion, Cal~fornia Federation of
Women's Clubs, California League .o f Women Voters and State Farm
Bureau Federation.
·
The service clubs seemed to be especially helpful this year. In one
community the Rotary Club, which always observes "International Boys
Week" (which ordinarily follows our observance) moved that event up one
week so that the activities might be ·coincident with, and ·made a part of,
the observance of Public Schools Week. This made possible a huge "father
and son's banquet," with more than 500 present as a part of one of the
programs presented at a high school.
Many of the service clubs made their luncheon meetings occurring
during the week a. part of the observance. In some instances the programs
presented consisted of addresses by school men or student speakers and in
others of an entertainment presented by pupils from the schools, usually of
instrumental or vocal numbers.
At one of the most interesting meetings reported a representative of
the school department answered a list of questions which had been prepared
in advance covering the details of the school system df that community,
and particularly with respect to the criticism of the curriculum of the
modern school now so often encountered. There was also another meeting in a service club· of somewhat the same sort in which the address given

GRAND LODGE OF GALIFORNIA

147

by the President of the Board of Education gave d~tails of the school system of that city from what might be termed the business point of view.
In several communities this year a service club held its luncheon meeting in a school cafeteria instead of at the usual place;• and at the conclusion
of the luncheon, at which there was usually a program of some sort presented, a large proportion of the members present remained to spend an
hour or more in personally inspecting the school and its facilities.
As has been intimated, the large increase in the number of people in
attendance at the public meetings and visiting the schools was not the only
factor contributing to the success of this year's observance. Each year now
for several years past· there has been an increase in the number of programs
evidently designed for the dissemination of information as to the aims and
purposes of modern education rather than merely for entertainment; and
as a result of the suggestions and directions contained in our bulletins and
in those issued by the State Department of Education, there is now considerable similarity everywhere in the general nature of the programs
presented.
·
Speaking generally it may be said that visits to the schools continue to
grow in popularity and seem to be preferred to the public meeting. In some
communiti'es there is what would seem to be a very happy combination of
the two features. Visits to the school are arranged for each day throughout
the week, with a public meeting on the last night and at which the program is presented by pupils from the different schools.
Each year more attention seems to be given to the detail with which
arrangements for the visits are made. There were attached to one of the
reports this year two bulletins consisting of seven pages intended for both
teachers and pupils. They included not only the outline of the plan for the
"Open House" activities. with information for the students and teachers, but
also suggestions for student discussions which were not without educational
value.
The following "heads" will give some idea of the purpose evide~tly intended to be served: I: Class discussions of the purpose, nature and
procedure of the "open house"; II: Class consideration of students' responsibility; III : Class practice or dramatization of (a) introductions; (b) assisting a guest in need of a host; (c) dealing with noisy or out-of-order groups
with a friendly reminder; (d) leave taking of friends graciously; and as
evidence of the practical value of certain suggestions made it may be noted
that under III(a) there were reminders of the way introductions should be
made, and of the desirability of pronouncing nanies carefully and giving
every syllable in the name its full value, and pointing out that a child
should always be presented to an adult and a gentleman to a lady. Included
with the other directions there were forms to be used, and others to be
avoided.
The care with which these directions were prepared must have contributed to the comfort and convenience of the visitors; and there can be
no doubt that they likewise inured to the benefit of the pupils. But there
was not always even advance notice of visits to be made, to say nothing of
directions for the reception of the visitors.
An interesting visit reported this year was by members of one of our
Lodges to the twelve district schools located in a territory fifty miles long
and twenty miles wide. At the request of the County Superintendent and
Rural Supervisor no advance notice was sent to the schools; it being the
opinion of the school people that a school should always be ready to receive
visitors. Twenty-four visits were made by members of the Lodge, and at
each school visited the pupils explained the work they were doing and the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

principal subject to which they were giving attention-such as conservation,
transportation and irrigation.
While the programs are now basically similar throughout the State
there are some features extremely popular in certain communities which
would be hardly practicable in large metropolitan areas. Of this sort is a
parade of school children with floats and school bands which mark the
opening of an observance which is concluded with an interschool track meet
and field day.
It should be remembered, too, that even what might be termed a typical
program is subject to modification and variation. "Fashion shows" in which
the girls "model" dresses they have made in school are no longer a novelty
on a school prog·ram. But one of the presentations this year was a fashion
show in which each model, after describing the material, gave in detail the
complete cost of the dress, and told how much time had been spent in
making and just what assistance, if any, she had received.
Among other very interesting programs reported this year were several
arranged to carry out selected "themes" such as "America in the Making,"
"Building America," and "California the Golden." These took several forms,
including elaborate plays and pageants illustrating episodes of American
history.
.Akin to those built around themes, there were programs publicized by
slogans designed to attract attention to the observance. At least two of
these slogans, "The 4 R's in the Forties" and "The 3 R's and the 3 C's,"
not . only apparently admirably served their primary purpose, but brought
forcefully to the attention of the patrons of the schools the fact that public
education today means far. more than the "readin' 'ritin', and 'rithmetic,
taught to the tune of a hickory stick" of our pioneer days. In all the
publicity, and through the programs and school exhibits, and wherever the
opportunity offered, it. was explained that the fourth "R" signified "Richer
Educational Opportunities," and the broadened educational methods which
distinguish the modern school; and the 3 C's were explained as "Character,
Culture and Citizenship," which it is sought to inculcate in every boy and
girl.
There would seem to be no better way to illustrate the value of such
programs than to here set forth excerpts from an extremely interesting
newspaper article (too long to· quote in its entirety as we should like to do),
written by a well known columnist.
·
After a very witty introduction in which he confesses that he is one
of those fathers who leave to the mothers the duties and responsibilities of
"parent-teachering," and explains that he was finally induced to "go back to
school" during Public Schools Week, not merely because of his wife's
determination and insistence, but also because of his interest in recent discussions of the kind of schools we have, continues:

riched its curriculum, a step made necessary by the growing complexity of civilization itself and stepping up in the minimum demand
made upon the schools by the public. It has reorganized certain old
subjects to make them appeal more strongly to the natural interests
of the child, correlating overlapping subjects both to save time and
give richness and body to the subject matter . .
'
"I was hunting the answers to certain questions which the educational discussion has raised: 'Do students now spell as well as
they used to? Is their composition and understanding and their
grammar up to par?' One paper was a girl's theme on English
literature. She had gone all the way back to Chaucer to get the
background for her work. I was surprised at .its range and grasp.
As a newspaper man with a gimlet eye for spelling I noted not one
misspelled word . . .
"There were several other papers likewise free of this defect.
One was a boy's theme on the background and origins of the first
World war . . . I wish we could get cub reporters who could
turn out jobs like that. It would save many an old city editor and
copy desk man from the nuthouse. I even wish the people who
write letters denouncing the schools would spell as well and write
as grammatically as do those students."
Now the conclusions of this honest seeker for information are not
quoted as an encomium of our public schools; but rather as evidence of
the fact that it was through Public Schools Week that he was afforded th'e
opportunity to find out just "what sort of a job the schools are doing with
all the students.''
While a visit to a school is undoubtedly the best way to ascertain the
facts, it is not the only way afforded during Public Schools Week; and of
only little less value are the panel and forum discussions which each year
seem to be growing in popularity.
The panels and forums this year· were of all sorts and kinds with subjects no less varied. What must have been an extremely interesting one
was developed under the title "Youth Looks at the Schools," and in which
the participants were all students representing, respectively, a high school,
a continuation school, a trade school, a junior college, and a state college.
It is significant that one of these young men deprecated the fact that so
much attention is being given to games in which the great mass of students ·
do not participate; and that received with evident approval was the expression of an opinion that for the large majority of the youth of our land there
was today greater need than in the past for industrial and technical education as a part of the training for good citizenship.
Again this year there was a large amount of informative literature
distributed to those in attendance at the meetings or visiting the schools.
Especially noteworthy was a little booklet with the title "Do You Know"
containing material assembled by the teachers of an elementary school system giving information in the words of the booklet, "concerning odd and
little known facts about the school system and explaining the reading program in the grades."
The items of information were set forth in nine pages of very short
paragraphs of two or three lines each with perhaps ten or twelve on a page,
with the heading on each page "Do You Know?" With other information
there were given names of books enjoyed by the children in the different
classes. This information of itself should be valuable to those who have
occasion to make gifts of books to children.
Many of the items in the booklet concern only that particular school
system. There is however considerable information of a general nature.
Incidentally, the 3 Rs and the 3 Cs receive attention in this form:

148

"Now despite my avoidance of parent-teacher doings, I have a
very real interest in education. It has manifested itself in reading
a good deal of the professional literature on the subject, including
John Dewey and the dull but encyclopedic Cubberly, the Gibbon
of the educational historians. On my visit to
Junior High,
where our son attends, I wanted not only to find out the worst
about him but what sort of a job the schools are doing with all
the students . . .
"My visit was too brief for any such an ambitious inquiry but I
did get some reassuring impressions. . . . From what I saw _I
do not think that
has gone off the deep end on what ts
called 'progressive education.' At least not if one means educational
faddism-'lollypops instead of learning.' It has broadened and en-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Do You Know":
"That the 3Rs still receive from 95% in first and second
grades to 75% in seventh and eighth grades of school time?"
"That the 3Cs-Character, Citizenship and Culture are
taught by definite lessons as well as woven through all other
subjects?"
"That these 3Cs are more 'caught than taught' so great care
is taken to surround children with the best training obtainable?"
It would thus appear that in every way possible those to whom we
entrust the administration of our schools, and the education of our children,
seek to have us know just what they are doing and why it is being done.
And if there is one thing to which more than to any other the success of
our latest observance may be attributed (no reference now being had to
the individuals and organizations actually responsible therefor) it is the
fact that never before apparently was there so much intelligent questioning
and so little captious criticism on the part of the public.
·
Of course our public schools are not completely fulfilling the hopes of
the layman. They never have done so and in all probability they never will.
There is however nothing strange about this. Indeed it would be extraordinary if it were otherwise; because there is no problem with which we are
confronted-social, economic, industrial or political-domestic or foreignfor the solution of which we do not look to public education.
There will therefore probably never come a time when there will not
be some criticism of what our schools are doing or leaving undone ; and
the answer to the question "What the School Should Teach?" will not be
found until we first find the answer to that other question asked by Herbert
Spencer "What Knowledge Is of Most Worth?"
There can be no doubt, of course, that our public schools should teach
what the people who support them want taught; but what the people want
taught should be determined by an informed opinion based on knowledge
and experience and not by one which results from the hysteria occasioned
by criticism more likely to be well intended than well informed. On one
thing at least it would seem there should be general agreement. And that is
that there should result from what is taught and the way it is taught a belief
in, and an adequate preparation for, the democratic way of life where no one
will claim for himself a right or privilege he would deny another, and where
with every right and privilege there go corresponding. duties and responsibilities.
All of which is respectfully submitted,
