REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCING
BUILDING PROJECTS
To the M.' . W.'. Grand Lodge of California :
During the year ending September 30, 1940, your committee has reviewed the following projects in accordance with the provisions contained
in Section 152 of the Ordinances:
Salinas Lodge No. 204, F. & A. M., situated at Salinas:
Your committee approved the request of this Lodge for perm1ss1on
to purchase capital stock in the Masonic Hall Association of Salinas with
Lodge funds, not to exceed $1,000.00 in amount, for the purpose of purchasing a new carpet and making necessary repairs to the Lodgeroom.
Caledonia Lodge No. 486, F. & A. M., situated in Bakersfield:
The Caledonia Building Association has recently completed the construction of a Masonic Temple at East Bakersfield, which cost approximately $30,000.00. An additional $6,000.00 is needed to fully complete the
project, and to provide the necessary funds for this purpose the Association proposed to negotiate a loan of $3,000.00 from the Bank of America,
and to borrow $3,000.00 from the Lodge for one year, unsecured, at three
per cent interest.
The Lodge requested your committee to approve this latter proposed
loan. After carefully considering the matter your committee was of the
opinion that such a: loan could not be approved for the reason that Section
87 of the Constitution specifically sets forth the classes of investments in
which Lodg~ . funds may be invested, and this proposed loan does not fall ·
within any of the classes contained in this section.
An alternative plan was presented to your committee, whereby the
Lodge sought permission to purchase $3,000.00 of capital stock in the
Caledonia Building Association with Lodge funds, the Lodge having heretofore invested $4,000.00 in the Association's stock. The financial statement
furnished your committee reflects that the Lodge has in excess of $5,000.00
cash on hand. The Lodge herein having complied with the constitutional
requirements and suggestions · of your committee, approval was accordingly given.
Laurel Lodge No. 245, F. & A. M., situated in Willows:
Your committee approved a request from this Lodge to purchase not
to exceed fifteen shares of the outstanding stock in the Willows Masonic
Temple Association at $100.00 per share with funds of the Lodge. The
assets of the Temple Association exceed $40,000.00, all the common stock
being owned by the Lodge, and more than 60 per cent of the preferred
stock, valued at $20,000.00, being .also owned by the Lodge. Your committee
noted the fact that in addition to the foregoing, the Lodge is free from
debt, with $2,548.00 cash on hand.
Mission Lodge No. 169, F. & A. M., and Mission Lodge Masonic Hall
Association, situated in San Francisco:
The Hall Association owns 54 feet frontage on Mission street upon
which is erected a two-story building (stores on the lower floor, and Lodgeroom, banquet hall, etc., on the upper floor) entirely free of all encumbrance.

The Association also owns 54 feet adjoining, upon which it desires to erect

to the present structure, ~t an estimated cost of $75,000.00.

East Bay Lodge No. 489; .F . & A. M., situated in Berkeley:
This Lodge was desirous of acquiring all the outstanding stock of the
East Bay Masonic Building Association, which is its meeting place. Your
committee was requested to approve "as broad a permit as it is possible
to grant, and for as long a term period as the Grand Lodge regulations
will permit." The past history of the Association, and financial statements
submitted were found to be entirely satisfactory.
Your committee approved the request in principle, but due to the
human equation on the part of the Lodge, as well as on the part of your
committee, we feel that no permit of this nature for an unlimited duration
should be granted, for the reason that those charged with the administration
of the financial problems of the Lodge and Building Association, as well
as the members of the Grand Lodge Committee on Financing Building
Projects may retire, thus leaving matters of this nature in the hands of
those uninformed of the present situation. Your committee therefore
granted permission to East Bay Lodge to purchase a reasonable amount
of stock from time to time with the understanding that the approval of
your Committee be obtained whenever such purchase is deemed advisable
to be made.
Warren G. Harding Lodge No. 579, F. & A. M., situated in Sacramento:

·

the State of California . . . Under. no circumstances shall life membership· funds be invested other than in sec~rities as above set forth."

practicable.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Califo,.nia:
Unexpected word has ~eached· us o( the serious illness of the chairman
of this committee, Brother A. Heber Winder. He was unable to attend
this communication and was also prevented, by the orders of his physician, from preparing the report of the committee. Therefore the report
will be brief and lacking in details with which only the chairman of · tlie
committee is. familiar.
The work of the committee during the past year has been along two
general lines. First, we have been engaged in a revision of the pamphlets
previously published on Masonic education; secondly, ·w e have continued
our endeavors to obtain a more general use of the Lodge system of Masonic
education.
The pamphlet entitled "Masonic Law and Custom" has been revised
by us and is now in the hands of the printer. This pamphlet was originally
composed several years ago by the :g-ducational Committee of Grand Lodge.
Three editions have been printed and distributed. As the supply of the
third edition was about exhausted we were requested to revise and prepare
a fourth edition. We have tried to make as few changes as possible, but
we did bring the text of the manuscript down to date. We have endeavored
to make it conform with alterations in the Constitution and other changes
in law and custom. The revised manuscript was submitted to Most Worshipful Past Grand Master John Stewart Ross for his approval as to statements of Masonic law. Two thousand copies have been ordered from the
printer; they will be paid for out of funds in the hands of the Grand Secretary, received from the sale of previous copies; and they will be ready
for distribution on or before November 1st. This booklet has been one of
the "best sellers" . issued by Grand Lodge, and it ·is anticipated that its
popularity will continue. It sells for five cents a copy and is one of the
most concise and readable things that has ever been published on the subject. We suggest that all Lodges will do well to keep a supply on hand
and to distribute them gratis to all members who are interested. Many
Lodges follow the practice of presenting a copy to each candidate immedi:ftely after the conferring of his third degree, aqd we commend this practice.
The pamphlet entitled "Manual on Masonic Education" is also being
revised by the committee. The revised manuscript will be ready for printing prior to the time that the present supply is exhausted. Over seventysix hundred copies have already been distributed to the Craft throughout
the state. It is expected that the first edition of ten thousand copies will
be exhausted during the year and it will then be necessary to order the
printing of a new supply. They will be paid for out of funds which have
been received by the Grand Secretary through previous sales. In other
words the work is self-supporting now, as the money received from previous sales will take care of the expenses for the next publication.
Substantial progress has been made, we consider, in putting the Lodge
system of Masonic education into practical operation. The committee feels
that it has had the active cooperation of the officers of Grand Lodge and
the officers of constituent Lodges. We earnestly urge your continued interest and activity.
The committee has met and will continue to meet the needs of Masonic

156

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

education in this jurisdiction. We therefore make the following recommendations:

(~) That the Committee on Masonic Education be continued next
year, its members to be appointed by the incoming Grand Master.
. (2) That the use of the Lodge system of Masonic education be continued.
·
(3) That the sum of $300 be appropriated from the funds of Grand
Lodge for the incidental expenses of this committee.
Respectfully submitted",

To the M: . W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
At the annual communication of 1939 the Grand Master directed the
attention of this Grand Lodge to the fact that some grand jurisdictions
have established research lodges for the purpose of engaging in Masonic
research and giving to the Craft the results of their reports in printed form,
and stated that he felt that this Grand Lodge could materially contribute to
the cause of Masonic research by authorizing the establishment of one or
more such lodges in this jurisdiction. He recommended that the incoming
Grand Master be empowered to appoint a committee of three to investigate
the advisability of the establishment of such lodges and to report at this
annual communication. The Grand Master appointed your committee to ·
make such examination and report .
It is common knowledge that the Lodge Quatuor Coronati No. 2076
of London, England, is the outstanding research lodge in the Masonic
world. It has forty-two regular members and about six thousand five hundred · contributing members. Its revenues are sufficient to enable it to publish a quarterly journal, which furnishes to thousands of Masons the results
of the research and activities of this particular group of scholars. Undoubtedly the inspiration far the formation of research lodges in the American grand jurisdictions was drawn from this old and highly respected
Lodge, which devotes itself to Masonic archaeology, literature and research.
It is not acting under any special conditions or privileges, but is a regularly chartered and constituted Lodge, with the same privileges, and subject to the same rules, as that of any other duly constituted subordinate
Lodge of the . United Grand Lodge of England.
The Grand Lodges of New York, North Carolina, Oregon and Georgia have authorized the formation of a special type of lodge to engage in·
research.
That organized in New York is proceeding along the same general

158

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

lines as the Quatuor Coronati and has three classes of memberships, active,
correspondence and fellowship.
·
The research lodge in Oregon arranges for the presentation of addresses and papers before Lodges throughout the State, and in addition
to the forty-five members they have memberships known as contributing
Lodges and also corresponding members.
In Georgia the Grand Lodge authorized the Masonic Educational
Commission to organize lodges of research and the establishment of a
Grand Lodge library. This commission publishes the Masonic Messenger
as a medium for presenting the work of the commission and formed a
mother lodge of research to assist the commission in the promulgation of
regulations to . govern local research lodges and courses of study. The
mother lodge appears to be composed of the four members of the commission and three Grand Lodge officers. The vested power and authority
over the mother lodge and the local research lodges are in the Masonic
Educational and Historical Commission, which causes the mother lodge
to issue charters for local research lodge's. It further appears that the purpose of the lodges of research is solely of an educational and instructive
nature, and that they have none of the prerogatives or characteristics of
a chartered Lodge of the Grand Lodge. Charters have been issued by the
commission to twenty-six local research lodges.
Our information is vague relative to the activities of the research
lodge of North Carolina, but we are informed that it is largely devoted 10
Masonic history.
From its studies your committee is of the opinion that the work of
research lodges, with the exception of the one in New York, is fully covered by our Committee on Masonic History, the Committee on Education,
and the District Inspectors meetings. The field we do not cover is that of
extended archaeological and literary examination o.f original sources and
the publication of the findings presented in papers and reports. Masonry is
young in California and our Committee on Ma.s onic History can cover that
field in this state. We are far distant from original sources of an archaeological and literary interest and of necessity our research therein must be
by the reading and studying of the results of those who have done the
real research work.
Notwithstanding these facts, it is entirely possible that a research
lodge or lodges could do interesting and effective work in the study of
Masonic lore, but until a group or groups of Masons are banded together
and undertake the work of research, or the study of Masonry, and find it
expedient or desirable that the group be clothed in the form of a Lodge,
it is not possible for your committee to recommend the particular type of
lodge and the incidental legislation that would be appropriate. We are
not opposed to the formation of a research lodge when a real demand
arises therefor, but we think this Grand Lodge is not justified in setting
. up a system which may never be put into ·operation. We should not change
our Lodge system in the hope that at some time some one may be interested
in taking .advantage of the changes in our law. We therefore recommend
that no action be taken at this time in the matter of establishing research
lodges.
WM. RHODES HERVEY, .
LEON 0. WHITSELL,
G. ELLSWORTH MEYER,

Committee.

The report was adopted.

We are still endeavoring to fully identify all members of the "Mormon

160

l'ROCEEDI!liGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Batallion," who came to California with General Kearny in 1847, and who
wer_e members. of th~ I;odge at Nauvoo, Illinois. Also to identify all those
having. Masonic affiliations who took part in the San Francisco Vigilante
Comm1!tees of 1851 and 1856 ; the Jay Hawker's Party, which crossed Death
Valley m 1849, and members of the Constitutional Committee of 1879.
We expect to complete our studies of the life history of Abel Stearns
by a. careful perusal a?d analy~is of the private papers of Stearns recently
ac_qu1red by the Huntington Library and now made available to the committee. We trust that these ~rivate a_nd official papers may solve and fully
:inswer the many controversial questions surrounding the activities of this
important personage in ~he pre-American days of California when Abel
Stearns, alth?ugh a Mexican ~itizen, was reputed to be the' secret agent
o~ th~ American . government m Southern California, working under the
direction of Thomas 0. Larkin, the American consul, who was stationed
at Monterey.

The cabin he occupied was the cabin used by the Peter Breen family
during their enforced stay at the lake two years later.
Josiah Belden, afterward a member of San Jose Lodge No. 10, came
to California in 1841, and by hard work and unusual ability, became one
of Central California's most prosperous and influential businessmen-so
much so that he was able to retire in 1851, having amassed a very substantial fortune.
We find that W. H. Eddy, a member of the Donner party, who played
a rather heroic part in the rescuing of several members of that party, was
a Mason, afterward affiliated with San Jose Lodge No. 10.
We have recently ascertained that Quila Glover, who was a member
of the first relief party which left Sutter's Fort and rescued members of
the Donner party, was a Mason. He was made a Mason in .a so-called
"Mormon Lodge" at Nauvoo, under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of Illinois.
In 1853 two members of our Fraternity, P. H. Poindexter and W . C.
Orr, embarked in the cattle business in Siskiyou county and they selected
as their brand the square and compass. Afterward they settled near Dillon,
Montana, and there the square and compass is still registered in the name
of the Poindexter & Orr Livestock Company.
We find a rather peculiar coincidence in the name and number of
Western Star Lodge No. 2, and we have searched through the blue book
containing •the list of all regular Lodges recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California, and we find no other similar parallel of name and number.
There are three Western Star Lodges with the No. 2, and they are as
follows:
Western Star No. 2 at Shasta, California;
Western Star No. 2 at Little Rock, Arkansas;
Western Star No. 2 at Nebraska City, Nebraska.
The Western Star Lodge No. 2 at Little Rock was the Lodge in which
Albert Pike received his degrees.
On May 21, 1940, there passed away at Tres Pinos the oldest Mason
in California, bo.th in point of years of life, and of membership: Daniel
McDonald, 102 years, 4 months, and 21 days old at the time of his death.
Brother McDonald had the distinction of being the only California Mason
to receive a seventy-five year pin, emblematic of his seventy-five years of
membership in the Fraternity. He was born in Nova Scotia and there
made a Mason. He lived an active life in several states, most notably in
Utah, Nevada and California. He was a member of San Benito Lodge
No. 211.
On September 12th our Most Worshipful Grand Master presented a
fifty-year button to Brother John Larrabee of McKinley Lodge No. 347
at Richmond. Seven of the Lodge stations were filled by members who
wore fifty-year buttons. The senior brother had been a Mason for sixtythree years. Other stations were filled by brothers with twenty-five or
more years of service to Masonry. A rather unique and unusual meeting.
We again respectfully urge the constituent Lodges to keep scrap books
in which may be pasted newspaper clippings, Lodge programs, and other
printed matter rel<!ting to the activities of the members, the Lodge, and the
community. In the future these printed records of Lodge and membership
activities and the biographies of local Masons, etc., will be particularly
interesting to newly-made Masons and will greatly assist in the future
compilation of historical data.
In view of the fact that there is still additional work to be perfected

Amon~ the i~teresting _items collected by your committee during the
year we might briefly mention the following:
The ~uthentic history.of Dr. Benjamin Cory, who arrived in California
.
in 1847 with the Hawes party and who subsequently became a charter member of San Jose Lodge No. 10. Brother Cory was for many years San
Jose's most useful and honored citizen.
We have perfected the history of James F. Reed, a member of the
Donner party, who played a leading role in the development and history
of Santa Clara county.
After t~o years of painstaking research we have at last secured a
comprehensive story of the Masonic and professional life of Dr. John
Tov.:nsend.' In 1844 Brother Townsend headed an immigrant party to Califorma w~1ch was known as the Townsend party. He practiced medicine
~t Sutter s Fort and served as Captain Sutter's aide during the revolution
~n 1845: He served as alcalde in San Francisco and was actively engaged
·in pubhc school work. He invested heavily and profitably in San Francisco
real es~ate. Subsequently he moved to San Jose and there practiced his
pro~ession and was one of the fifteen petitioners for dispensation to orgamze San Jose Lodge No. 10.
A similar fate to that of the Donner party in the winter of 1S46-47 was
faced by another immigrant party at the same spot, Donner take, in 1844,
?r t"'.o yea~s before the Donner tragedy. The Elisha Stevens party, formed
. m Missouri ea.rly i? 1844, arrived at the lake the middle of November. Bad
weather was immi?ent. T.heir safety from the deep snow depended upon
the u~most speed in crossing the mountains. They hurriedly constructed
a cabin and stored the greater portion of their goods therein. The party
then h~stened westward, leaving three boys who volunteered to stay in
the cabin and look after the goods. One of the three was Morris Shallenberger, a boy of seventeen.
·
A short . time after the departure of the party the food in the cabin

b~came practically exhausted. The three boys attempted to cross the moun-

t~ins. Young Shallenberger became violently ill and his companions helped
him back to the cabin. He insisted that they leave him in the cabin and
attempt to reach Sutter's Fort. Several days after they left young Shallenberger recovered sufficiently to find, among the things left in the cabin
some steel traps and, although there was fourteen feet of snow on th~
ground, he managed to trap fox, which constituted his only food until
he was rescued, exhausted and near starvation, by a party early in the
spring.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws reports that during the past year thirtyfive Lodges submitted changes in their By-Laws to the Grand Master for
approval. We are pleased. to report that all amendments submitted were
in proper form and approved.
Five Lodges changed their place of meeting.
Six Lodges amended their By-Laws to except holidays.
Eleven Lodges decreased the amount of the fees for the degrees.
Four Lodges eliminated the fee for affiliation entirely and t~o Lodges
rtduced the amount of the affiliation fee.
One Lodge raised its dues from $9.00 to $10.00.
One Lodge raised its dues from $12.00 to $32.00.
Ten Lodges changed the time of meetings, one of which advanced
the time of its stated meeting from 7 :30 to 6 :00 P. M. Many of their stated
meetings will probably be dinner meetings (it calls to mind the meetings
of the English Lodges). It will be interesting to see the effect of this
change as to the possible increased activities of this Lodge.
Names of Lodges follow: Menlo Park N.o. 6Sl, Fruitvale No. 336,
Oakland No. 188, Wilshire No. 44S, Petaluma No. 180, Eden No. 113, All
States No. S93, La Jolla No. S18, Alta Vista No. 464, San Dimas No. 428,
Unity No. 368, South Pasadena No. 367, Buckeye No. 19S, Alexander Hamilton No. S3S, Oxnard No. 341, Alameda No. 167, Nevada City No. 13, lone
No. 80, Evening Star No. 186, Santa Barbara No. 192, Sunset No. 3S2,
Waucoba No. 413, Sunrise No. S22, Fairview No. 629, Plymouth No. S60,
Henry S. Orme No. 4S8, Jewel No. 374, San Fernando No. 343, Lankershim No. S42, Covina No. 334, Riverside No. 63S, Brawley No. 402, Paul
Revere No. 462, Triangle No. S48, Colusa No. 240.
We move the adoption of this report approving all of said amendmen ts.

Under the authority of Section 333 of our Constitution (formerly Section 192) there . was filed with the Lodge a duly certified copy of the final
judgment of conviction of accused in the Superior Court of Sacramento,
of the crime of grand theft, a felony; the regular notice ·provided by our
Masonic law was attempted to be served. However, the certificate of service states· that the notice was forwarded, by registered mail, to accused
at a .certain address on Twenty-fourth street, Sacramento, when the c0urt
record filed in this matter shows that the address of accused was, at the

language of Masonic law in matters of this character makes i~ necessary for
this committee to recommend to Grand Lodge that proceedings be remanded because jurisdiction to act was never acquired by the Lodge.

:!\o. 980, concerning 0. A. W., a member of Multnomah Lodge No. 1,
A. F. & A. M., of Oregon City, Oregon, is of the opinion that the trial
commissioners were evidently confused by an argument of counsel, which
would have been sound in a court of law, but was not sound under our
Masonic law; as further proof of the confusion into which the trial commissioners evidently fell, we note that at the conclusion of the trial a
ballot was taken on the question of guilty or not guilty on the specification, and the vote thereon was: guilty, none; not guilty, seven; a vote of
guilty or not guilty was then taken by ballot upon the charge of unmasonic
conduct, and the vote thereon was: guilty, three; not guilty, four. In view
of the fact counsel for the accused apparently succeeded in convincing the
trial commissioners that no disciplinary action could be taken against the
accused under the provisions of Section 192a of our Constitution, and offered no evidence in support of his contention and a plea of not guilty,
your committee is of the opinion that such record should be remanded to
San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214, the trial" Lodge, for a new trial, and
your committee therefore offers the following resolution and moves its
adoption:

Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and moves

Your committee to which was referred trial record No. 977, of San
Joaquin Lodge No'. 19, beg leave to report as follows :
On April 8, 1940, accused, a member in good standing of said Lodge,
pleaded guilty to the charge governed by Sections 501 and 480 of Vehicle
Code of the State of California, felonies. Probation was granted on condition that defendant serve six months in the county jail and thereafter
to pay a fine of $300.00 or serve an additional four months in jail; and to
refrain from using alcoholic liquors, etc., the violation of any of which
terms of probation would result in an immediate revocation of the probation. If at the end of five years the terms of probation are kept, the court
was to permit the defendant to withdraw his plea of guilty and the accusation would be dismissed.
Thereafter the Secretary of defendant's Lodge procured two certified
copies of an order granting probation, and filed one of said copies in the
records of the Lodge, and gave sixty days notice in writing to the defendant, by registered mail, forwarded to his last known place of address. This
notice to the defendant recited that the certified copy of the final judgment
oi conviction for the crime of violation of Paragraph 4 of Section 1302
of the Pen.a l Code of the State of California had been filed in the records
of the Lodge.
Your committee feels that the terms of Section 332, formerly 192, of ·
the Constitution were not complied with in this case. No certified copy of
the judgment of conviction was filed in the records of the Lodge, but only
a certified copy of a court order. granting probation. Moreover, the notice
sent to the defendant by his Lodge, and also the said order granting probation referred to Paragraph 4, Section 1302, of the Penal Code, which
section of the Penal Code relates to the surrender of bail money before a
forfeiture thereof, and does not prescribe a crime. Since the notice· to defendant and the certified record filed with the Lodge were both erroneous,
we therefore believe that this conviction should be reversed.

In the matter of trial record No. 979, being that of E. H . B., expelled
by All States Lodge No. 593, your committee reports as follows:
The accused pleaded guilty to a felony, the possession of a firearms
silencer. He was granted probation and fined, but was not imprisoned.
Charges of un-Masonic conduct were preferred against him, and at a
regular meeting of the Lodge the Master announced that a certified copy
of the judgment of the Superior Court had been filed in the records of the
Lodge, that the accused had been notified of the charges against him, and
having failed to appear within sixty days, pursuant to the provision of
Section 332 of our Constitution and Ordinances (formerly Section 192), he
was expelled.
Before a member of a Lodge may be expelled pursuant to Section 332
he must have been convicted of a felony and have been "imprisoned in
pursuance thereof." Inasmuch as the accused in this case did not suffer
imprisonment he may not be expelled in the manner above outlined.
Your committee therefore recommends the adoption of the following
resolution:
Resolved, That the action of All States Lodge No. 593, in expelling

Your committee to which was referred trial record No. 978, of Brother
K. R. S., a member of Las Palmas Lodge No. 366, respectfully reports
as follows:
Brother K. R. S. suffered a final judgment of conviction of a crime
classified as a felony, to wit: the crime of forgery, and was imprisoned in
the state prison at San Quentin in pursuance thereof. The Secretary of
his Lodge attempted to proceed against him pursuant to the provisions
of Section 192 of the Constitution. Although the provisions of said section
clearly state that the notice to the accused must be mailed to him at his
last known place of address, which in this case could only be the state
prison at San Quentin, the record shows that the Secretary mailed the
notice to 423 Courtland street, Fresno, California, which was probably
the address of the accused prior to the time he took up residence at San
Quentin.
Grand Lodge has many times called attention of its subordinate Lodges
and their officers to the necessity of mailing notice to the accused at the
place of his incarceration and not to an address at which he may have
r esided prior to his imprisonment in a penal institution.
The failure of the Secretary to follow the procedure clearly set out
in Section 192 compels us to recommend the reversal of the action of the
Lodge in expelling K. R. S. The fact that an accused brother has proper
notice of the intention of his Lodge to expell him, unless within sixty days
he demands a Masonic trial,' is of vital importance, othei;-wise one might
b e deprived of membership in the Fraternity without the opportunity of
presenting a defense. Because there can be no certainty that a notice mailed
to the accused at a place other th.a n where he actually is present, will be
delivered to him, the requirement that he b e notified at his "last known
place of address" was incorporated in Section 192.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption:
, .. .. (.,
Resolved, That the action of Las Palmas Lodge No. 366, in expelling
K. R. S. J.n>m all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is
hereby rc;versed, and that the case be remanded for new .pr.o ceedings.

REPORT OF. COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Vocal solo: "The Souls of the Righteous" (Pears) ........Gwynfy Jones
Invocation: Grand Chaplain.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Another year has passed since we last met and we find many .familiar
faces missing. Two hundred and twenty-seven of our brethren of Grand
Lodge have been called. from time to eternity. We do not meet today to
mourn their departure, but to pay tribute .\ o. their memory, and to rejoice
with them since they are now in our Father's house, where there is "no
more death, neither sorrow nor crying." Whate~er our creed or Ol.\r faith,
we must sound . a note of gladness, not because they havi; passed from
among us, but because they are now living in the presence of the great
triune God, the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe.
We learn from the Great Light of Masonry that "it is appointed unto
man once to die," but we also learn .from the same sacred source that
"Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea saith
the spirit that they may rest from th~ir labors and their works do follow
them." Also, "He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he
live and he that liveth and believeth in me shall never die." Our brethren
are not dead but are translated to that undiscovered country where "eye
hath not seen, ear hath n,0.t heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of
man the things that are _prepare<! for those who fove the L ord." We shall
miss them, but could they speak .to u:; today I am sure they would convey
to us their experience in those [natcbless words:
"And so for me there is no sting· to death
And so for me the grave has lost its victory.
. It is but crossing with abated breath
· And with set face a !itt1e. strip of sea,
To find the loved ones waiting on the shore,
More beautifu), 111ore precious toon before."
Freemasonry has been define'd as ·a progressive moral science, taught
by degrees only. It is this, and it is mor.e than this. I would even dare. say
to you, my brethren, that it is a way 6f life, of living. It· points out to
us clearly our many duties' ·while here. It goes farther than this. It leads

182

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

l'ROCEEDINGS OF THE

us into ways of useful and helpful thinking and living and teaches us symbolically the "Way Everlasting."
A general eulogy has been prepared and will be given as a part of
this program, but I feel that I must call your attention to some startling
facts.
First, there never has been as great a loss from the membership of
this Grand Lodge in any one year as this past year, 227 of the brethren
of Grand Lodge having been called from time into eternity.
Secondly, no year in the history of this Grand Lodge has ev~r been
called upon to record the passing of so many Grand and Past Grand officers.
Two Past Grand Masters and our Assistant Grand Secretary were called
to their eternal reward. Also, our Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master
of last year who, because of failing health, could not serve this Grand
Lodge as Most Worshipful Grand Master, was called to his final reward.
Thirdly, death has claimed as its victims four of the Inspectors of this
Grand Lodge during the interim of communications.
The members of this Grand Lodge of California were grieved and their
hearts were saddened when on June 26, 1940, our Past Grand Master, Orrin
Staples Henderson, was called from this earthly Grand Lodge to the Supreme Grand Lodge above. He had the distinction of being the senior
living Past Grand Master of this Grand Lodge. He was born in San Andreas, Calaveras County, California, June 2, 1863. His Masonic history
is as follows: Initiated October 2, 1884; passed November 6, 1884; and
raised November 20, 1884, in Morning Star Lodge No. 68. Served as
Master of Morning Star Lodge 1890- 1891. Served as Gran(;! Master of the
Grand Lodge of California beginning October, 1902. He received the
Royal Arch degrees in Stockton Chapter No. 28 in 1891, and served as
High Priest in 1895. He received the Cryptic degrees in Stockton Council
No. 10, Royal and Select Masters, in 1892. Served as Illustrious Master
1915-1916. He received the Templar degrees in Stockton Commandery
No. 8, Knights Templar (Orders of Red Cross October 20, 1899, Knight
of Malta and the Temple November 3, 1899).
These are the stepping stones to Masonic usefulness in the life of our
Brother Henderson. This seems lifeless, especially when compared with
the greatness of his soul. Having read most of his address at the annual
communication of Grand Lodge in 1903, I bow in humility in the presence
of the memory of one who was great in his simplicity, one whose faith
in divine guidan.c e was as unshaken as Eternity itself. May I quote briefly
from him : "Soon I will lay aside the pleasures as well as the cares of this
time-honored station, and another will assume them. My best wishes go
out to him. May his heart, as is mine, be always filled with the greatest
of gratitude to our beneficent Heavenly Father for His bountiful blessings
and watchful care." His message and his service were characterized by
a childlike faith and trust in that beneficent Being who orders all things
wisely. May we say in bidding farewell to our brother: "God bless, hallow, .and sanctify the memory of this great soul in its influence upon each
one of us."
·
The grim messenger of death called another of our Past Grand Masters, William Albert Sherman, who passed to his reward February 19, 1940.
He was born September 17, 1880, in San Francisco. He r eceived his early
education in the historic old town of Sonoma in the Valley of the Moon.
He was made a Master Mason in Presidio Lodge No. 354 in San Francisco
in 1904. He was a member and Past High Priest of California Chapter
No. 5, Royal Arch Masons; a member of ·California Commandery No. 1,
Knights Templar ; California Council No. 2, Royal and Select Masters;

183

San Francisco Bodies of Scottish Rite, and Islam Temple of the Mystic
Shrine. He served this Grand Lodge as Grand Master October, 1922._ to
October 1923. My first recollection of our Brother Sherman was seeing
him at Big Bear Lake in July, 1923. My impression of that meeting was :
"Here is a man with a real vision." This was verified in a summary of his
year's activities. May I quote from his own words, showing the largeness
of the vision that motivated his every thought :
"My closing. admonition to this great body of California Masonry is 'To
watch at all times; watch all political and economic problems and act upon
them with the sole ideal of benefiting our land and humanity, always remembering that like produces like is the eternal law of the universe, and
that in the end right will prevail.'" Thank God for this Past Grand Master, whose ideals, then as now, fit into the thinking of men and Masons
everywhere as a measure of soundness and safety.

Not entirely unexpected was the call which came to our beloved
Brother William Harrison Waste June 6, 1940. He was born near Chico,
Butte County, California, October 31, 1868. He died at his home in Berkeley, California. He was the son of John Jack.son Waste. and Mary. Catherine Mcintosh. His early training and education fitted him very eminently
for his future career as a jurist. For 37 years he devoted his time and talent
to public service. For this devotion he was awarded the f~llowing positions of responsibility: 1903-1905, Assembly of the State Legislature; !9051919, Judge of .Superior Court in Alameda County; 1919 he was apJ?Olnt~d
Presiding Justice of the District Court of Appeal of the State of Cahforma,
First Appellate District, and the following year elected to that court . for
a full term. He resigned in 1921 to accept an appointment as Associate
Justice of the Supreme Court of California. The year following .he was
elected to fill the unexpired term. In 1926 he was elevated by appoint,,ment
to the office of Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of California. Following that appointment he was twice elected to the same office, in the years
1928 and 1938. He occupied the highest judicial office in the State of California at the time of his death. The outstanding characteristic in the life
of our brother, Judge Waste, was "service." We often quote, "he also
serves who only stands and waits." 'this was not true of our brother. In
all the years of his life as a public servant, but mor~ espe~ially .in his lon.g
and active Masonic career, Judge Waste served actively, intelligently and
aggressively with the full measure of his abil~ty. He was raised a Ma.ster
Mason in Durant Lodge No. 268, F . & A. M ., in August, 1895. He received
the degrees in Berkeley Chapter No. 92, Royal Arch Masons, Berkeley,
California. He received the degrees in Oakland Council No. 11, Royal and
Select Masters in 1905. He was knighted in Oakland Commandery No. 11,
Knights Tem~lar, in November, 1905. He retai.ned his _membership in all
these bodies until his death. He was elected Right Eminent Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of California in April, 1922. In Octobe~,
1936 he was elected Junior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of Cahfornla, and in October, 1939, he was exalted to the highest office i!1 this
grand body, being elected to the office of Grand Master, fro.m which he
at once resigned, on account of failing health. If there w~re ~1me I would
like to review for you his more than twenty years of service in .the Grand
Lodge of California. His outstanding achievement .was the planm~g, supervising and final completion of our beautiful Masomc Club House in Berkeley This will always be a monument to his untiring efforts. He has heard
the. welcome plaudit, "Well done, good and faithful servant. Ent.er t~ou
into the joy of thy Lord." May God bless his memory to our sanctification
and inspire each one of us to emulate him.

One of our best loved and most valuable workers in the Grand Lodge

If a Man Die, Shall He Live?

By REYNOLD E. BLIGHT

M:. W:. Grand Master and Brethren:
We are becoming too familiar with death. Death, which should always
be a serene benediction, a splendid tragedy or a shattering horror, has become commonplace. Time was when no reputable magazine would show
the picture of a dead body, but now hideous grotesqueries are splashed
across whole pages, and there is no protest. Berlin · calmly announces that
30,000 people were killed in Rotterdam in the air raid after the city had
surrendered and casually regrets that it had not been possible to call back
the bombers, although the army had surrendered. Artists graphically portray machine guns spraying the roads crowded with helpless refugees.
The newspapers publish a picture of a liner torpedoed in niid-ocean. The
water is filled with black dots and the caption explains that each dot rep·resents the bobbing head of a drowning man and that twenty minutes after
the picture was taken, not a survivor remained. We glance at the picture
light-heartedly and, stifling a yawn, turn the page to read the box score
of yesterday's game. We joyfully acclaim the news that a hundred Nazi
air raiders have been shot down. Merciful Christ, two hundred men died
in that flaming hell in the blue skies over the English coast, and we do
not flutter an eyelash.
Perhaps it is just as well that we .ar,e tqo callous-too dumb, if you
li~e-to fully realize the appalling drama qf death being enacted before
our eyes: If we took it literally the mind would snap under its unrelieved
frightfulness and the human heart would break under the impact of the
world's agony. Just as the camera lens can take in only the limit~d range
of its focus, so the human mind can regist'et . only that sorrow that touches
it sensitively.
.
.
,'
Death means little to us until the shadow that we fear and hate falls
across the threshold of our home and ravishes the loved ones from our
arms. Then
come fac·e to face with the grimmest, the most implacable
fact of human existence; and usually we ~read the via dolorosa alone.
Have you ever thought upon the ·lonelin.e ss of the human soul? Men
march and play and make war and run ,political campaigns in mobs, in
thronging crowds; but they suffer and pray ·a nd die alone.
Have you ever seen a strong man pass through a great agony ? It is
a ner ve-shattering sight. Wrapped within the seclusion of supreme tragedy,
l;ie walks the way of sorrows alone and no one may catch step with him
and no one may comfort him. The friend, even though bound to him
by ties of closest intimacy and sympathy, is stricken into silence. Gethsemane is the most lonely spot in the world. Jesus was never more intensely
human, never touched our pitiful, broken humanity more tenderly than
in that tragic moment when he cried from the Cross : "My God, my God,
why hast thou forsaken me?"l
Have you ever watched a man die? It is an experience that plumbs
the profoundest dep.ths of the human spirit. You have not sounded the
deeps of human emotion until you have held a loved one in your arms,
and watched him or her slip away into the shadows, watched while the
men:iless clock ticked off the fleeting seconds, watched while the pulse
beat slower and slower until at last it was but a flutter, watched the color
fade from the face as the tide of life receded.

we,

PROCEEDINGS Oi' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

How desperately you wanted to break through that impalpable but
impenetrable wall that separated you. How you reached with impotent
fingers into the invisible to touch once more the loved hand. How you
choked back the cry that rose involuntarily to .the lips, seeking to call
back the beloved spirit that was going out into the darkness. And when
the droop of the head and the last shuddering gasp told you the end had
come-how utterly alone you felt, how utterly bereft.
Death is such a shattering experience it must hold some supreme significance.
As we meet today in this beautiful association .of brotherhood, we
look sadly upon the vacant places, reminding us of beloved brethren who
met with us last year but will never meet with us again. We recall their
names. We recount their virtues. We tell of their good deeds and we
remind one another of happy experiences had together.

No, no--man has not been content to bow the head of hopeless
despair in the face of the great mystery. Rather does he say, in the words
of the famous agnostic: "From the voiceless lips of the unreplying dead
there comes no word; but in the night of death hope sees a star and listening love can hear the flutter of a wing."9 And it is not wholly wishful
thinking, not merely the upsweep of quickened imagination, that causes
that star to become " some white, tremendous daybreak"lO and that fluttering wing become the Te Deum of a heaven\,Y host. The deepest intuitions
of the soul confirm the exultant declaration of Longfellow in the familiar
poem:

196

Lo, some we loved, the loveliest and the best
That time and fate from all their vintage prest,
Have drunk their cup a round or two before,
And one by one crept silently to rest.2
It is eminently fitting that we should, at the order of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, pause in our deliberations not only to pay tribute
to those who have gone, but to ponder upon the meaning of this experience we call death.
Nor should we resent the call to such a meditation, although most of
us can sympathize with that good man who, when a persistent friend
demanded his opinion about life after death, replied testily: "Of course
I believe we shall all enter into bliss, but I wish you wouldn' t talk about
such unpleasant subjects."
'
Let us once and for all get over the foolish notion that death is a
morbid subject. Wise men have always pondered upon the meaning of
death. Plato once defined philosophy as a meditation on death. One can
and should take a sane, healthful attitude toward the subject. Charles
Frohman, on the shuddering deck of the sinking Titanic, smiled and said:
"Why fear death? It is the most beautiful adventure in life." Tennyson,
the great-hearted, when told that he was dying, exclaimed : "Death! Ah,
that is well." Clemenceau, the old tiger, declared, as he approached the
end: "Death is a magnificent purification of life."3 And Admiral Sigsbee,
after a life crowded with adventure and achievement, peered expectantly
at the· distant horizon and cried : "It seems I am once more putting out to
sea."
The seers and poets have all given an affirmative answer to the challenge: if a man die, shall he live ? Seldom is heard the pathetic plaint of
Theodore Dreiser: " As I see it, the utterly infinitesimal individual weaves,
among the mysteries, a flosslike and wholly meaningless course, if course
it be. I catch no meaning from all I have seen, and pass quite as I came,
confused and dismayed."4 Or the hopeless cry of Maurice Maeterlinck:
"Since humanity began to exist it has not advanced a sing le step on the
road of the mystery of immortality."5 Or the troubled lament of Prospero :
We are such stuff as dreams are made on,
And our little life is rounded with a sleep.ft
Perhaps the saddest line in all literature is the heart-breaking cry of
Hamlet just as the curtain descends upon that "supreme tragedy 0£ the
. human dream."7 The noble prince exclaims with his last . breath: "The
rest is silence."8

197

Life is real! Life is earnest I
And the· grave is not its goal;
Dust thou art, to dust returnest,
Was not spoken of the soul.11
Rising to the glad assurance of Tennyson, poet and mystic:
My own dim life should teach me this,
That life shall live forevermore,
•Else earth is darkness at the core,
And dust and ashes all that is ... 12
Thou wilt not leave us in the dust:
Thou madest man, he knows not why,
He thinks he was not made to die ;
And thou hast made him: thou art just.
Thine are these orbs of light and shade ;
Thou madest life in man and brute;
Thou madest death; and lo, thy foot
Is on the skull which thou hast made.13
Man has always believed in life beyond the grave. Even the cave men
of the Neanderthal age left evidence that they buried their dead in the
hope of future existence. At Le Moustier the skeleton of a youth about
sixteen years of age was found ca~efully placed in the attitude of sleep
with the right forearm under the head. A bed of flint chips formed his
pillow and close by his hand was a splendid implement. The men of the
neolithic and bronze ages painted the bones of their dead red. The purpose
of the rite is clear, for red is the color of living health.14
From the very cradle of civilization in pre-historic India, from the
slopes of the Himalayas, come the Vedic hymns attesting how strong was
the belief, even in that early time, in the future life, and also it was given
a spiritual significance. One quatrain especially has been immortalized in
lines of imperishable beauty by that splendid poet and good Mason, Sir
Edwin Arnold, in his translation of the Bhagavadgita:
Never the spirit was born, the spirit shall cease to be, never ;
Never was time it was not, end and beginning are dre;i.ms,
Birthless and deathless and changeless remaineth the spirit forever,
Death hath not touched it at all, dead though the house of it
seems.16
The philosophers of the ancient Mediterranean world held an exalted
thought of immortality. Asserts P lato: "the immortality of the soul has
been established beyond the reach of doubt."16 Aristotle declares : "Whatsoever that be within us that feels and thinks and animates is something
celestial, divine, and consequently imperishable."17 And our ancient brother,
Pythagoras, somewhere has said : "When thou shalt have laid aside thy

198

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

bod)', thou shalt rise, freed from mortality, and become a god of the kindly
skies."
Socrafes, one of the noblest characters of the early days of Greece,
after he had drunk the hemlock and was composing himself for the final
act of the tragedy, good humoredly chaffed his disciple Crito when Crito
asked him : "In what way shall we bury you?" "However you wish," Socrates replied, "only you must catch me first, and see that I don't slip·
away." ' Which was in keeping with the admonition he had addressed to
hiS followers: "Be of good cheer about death and know this of a truththat no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death."18
Judaism had little to say about the future life, but the whole sweep
of the later Christian eschatology or doctrine of last things is implicit in
the vivid and poetic myth of the creation of man: "God breathed into his
nostrils the breath of life and man became a living soul.~'19
So we are brought to Christianity with its jubilant teaching of the
resurrection of the dead centering in the transcendent miracle of the resurrection of Christ. The Christian standing by an empty tomb sees the
mystery and horror stripped away and the future made radiant with hope
and joy.
Perhaps the tenderest passage in a11 the Scriptures of the world is the
story of Jesus gathedng His disciples around Him, when already the baleful
shadow of the cruel Cross was falling across His path, as He comforts
them with the words: "Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God,
believe also in me. In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were
not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I
go and prepare a place for you, I will come ·a gain and receive you unto
myself, that where I am there ye may be also."20
The writings of the Apostle Paul are full of the glad tidings. "Behold,"
he writes to the Corinthian Christians, "I show you a mystery . .. the dead
shall be raised incorruptible and we shall be changed."21
"In another letter to these same Corinthians appears a passage that is
part of our Masonic burial service: " For we hope that if our earthly house
of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not
made with hands, eternal in the heavens."22
So vivid and vital is this truth to Paul that at times the highest flights
of purest eloquence are inadequate to the splendor of his theme. Writing
fo his beloved co-worker and young disciple, Timothy, he speaks of "the
appearing of our Saviour, Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death and
brought life and immortality to light through the gospel."23
In fact it is not too much to say that the hope of the resurrection
was the conquering dynamic of the Christian evangel. Before the proclamation of this Gospel brutal kings trembled, thrones of injustice tottered,
and pagan civilizations crumbled. The liturgy of the church emphasizes and
re-emphasizes the centrality of immortality in the Christian faith. It finds
its most beautiful expression in the prayer that opens the· communion service in the Anglican rite : "we also bless thy Holy Name for all thy servants departed this life in thy faith and fear, beseeching thee to grant them
continual growth in thy love and service."24 Love, service, continual growth,
dominant in the concept of the future life, could anything be more uplifting and inspiring?
•. :
· In the light of this unanimous .testim~ ny through the centuries to the
truth of immortality, it is easily unde.rstood why Freemasonry, enshrining
0

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

199

as it does the winnowed wisdom of the ages, has made belief in immortality a cardinal tenet of its teachings. Says Albert Pike, one of the greatest Masonic scholars of any country, "To every Mason, the soul of man
is immortal. Whether it emanates from and will return to God, and what
its continued mode of existence thereafter, each judges for himself. Masonry was not made to settle that."25
The glorious climax of our sublime ritual proclaims that the soul of
man, faithful to its trust, loyal to principle, does not go down into the
grave, but purified by suffering, it wings its way above the murk and fog
of our mundane life to find its larger fulfilment in the realms of light.
Cecil B. deMille, the famous dramatist, tells us of a startling experience
he had. He says:
"Many years ago I was commissioned by David Belasco to write a
play, "The Return of Peter Grimm." The play was being written for David
Warfield and the story hinged upon the continuation of life after death.
" I got the inspiration for that story from a water beetle.
"I was up on a lake in the Maine woods. The canoe was drifting. I
was reading, resting, searching for an idea. I looked down in the water,
for my little craft had drifted to where the lake was only about four inches
deep. There, in a world 6f mud and wet, were water beetles.
"One crawled up on the gunwale, stuck the talons on his legs into
the woodwork, and died.
"I let it alone and turned to 'my reading.' The sun was hot. In about
three hours I looked at my water beetle again. He was parched. His back
was cracking open. I watched and out .of the back of that dead beetle 1
saw crawling a new form-a moist head-then wings. A most beautiful
dragonfly. It scintillated all the colors of the rainbow.
"As I sat watching, it flew. It Hew farther in a second than the water
beetle had crawled in days. It hovered above the surface, just a few inches
from the water beetles beneath. They did not know it was there.
"I took my fingertip and moved the shriveled water beetle husk from
the canoe's gunwale. It fell back into the lake' and sank down to the mudcovered bottom.
"The other water beetles crawled awkwardly to see what it was.
"It was a dead body.
"They backed away from it.
"If God does that for a water beetle, don't you believe he will do it
for me?"26
So faith reads a profound meaning in the mystery. So faith, springing
from the deepest intuitions of the soul, strikes down the negation, and
even in the agony of a great bereavement, proclaims the everlasting "Yes,"
and in the threnody of woe beats out the mystic music of eternal life and
hope.
As Masons, we believe in God who is Love, and we cannot think He
ever created a soul to be annihilated or lost in the eternal dark. We rely
on the Omnipotent Benevolence, who doeth all things well, from whose
great love sprang the stupendous universe in which law and order and
purpose reign, and He who spake the mighty cosmos into being and holds
the wheeling constellations in their courses, may be trusted to care for
the human souls that He has made. Feeble and foolish though they be,
they are His offspring and the children of his love.
Deep within the profoundest consciousness of man resides the assurance of immortality that tells him:
0

200

The stars shall fade, the sun himself
Grow dim with age, and Nature sink in years,
But thou shalt flourish in immortal youth,
Unhurt amid the war of elements,
The wrecks of matter and the crush of worlds.27

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
· The Board of Control respectfully submits a report of i~s activities
during .the past Masonic year.
We desire again to indicate our appreciation of the information and
assistance ,given to us by our Grand Secretary, and emphasize our recognition of the assistance and cooperation given by Boards of Relief and individual Lodges.
All matters that have come before the Board have received the usual
consideration and analysis, with the objective that no justified relief should
be in any way curtailed.
The continued standardized procedure adopted by the Board of Con·
trol and the Bc;>ards of Relief, developed over the years, coupled with the
intelligent care and watchfulness exercized by the Boards of Relief, is
again reflected in the small amount of reimbursements shown in this report.
Meetings
We held a business meeting of the board on April 28,.1940, at Sacramento. A further conference was held on May 19, 1940, in Oakland. The
principal matters discussed were in connection with the employment service.
On October 7th an all-day meeting was held, the purpose · being a
further clarification of matters in connection with the annual employment
bureau reports.
Reimbursements
We believe that the Boards of Relief have made every endeavor to
secure reimbursements for relief advanced,. which is reflected in the small
amount of reimbursements requested.
We have recommended to the Finance Committee that the following
requests for reimbursements be granted :

Compl!-ratively Inactive Boards of Relief
The· Board of Control finds cert:!.irt.' Boar9s of Relief are doing an exceedingly small amount of work and further consideration will be given as
to the advisability of recommending their discontinuance or continued
recognition by the Grand Lodge.
Employment Service
Placing our Brethren and their dependents in a position to take their
places among their neighbors and fellows as self-supporting, self-respecting
citizens is practicing Masonry in the highest sense of the word. Nothing
destroy's a man's morale so much as being unemployed, and nothing restores and builds his morale as does gainful einploymerit._
Our seven employment services have closed the most helpful and successful year in our history; 12,154 jobs were sect1red for our brethren and
dependents, and this in the face of keen competition.
It is encouraging to note the change in trends as compared with a
year ago. The number of applications received this fiscal year was 17,650,
as compared to 19,066 in the year previous; a reduction of 7.5%. This is
the first time in several years that there has been a reduction in the number of applications received. On the other hand,' there were 12,154 jobs •
secured, as compared with 10,657 during the previous fiscal year; an increase
of 14%, which is a remarkable showing. During this year employer interest
has been greatly increased; 14,836 employers' inquiries for help were received in our offices.
The total expens~ for the year was $29,005.99, of which amount Grand
Lodge appropriated $14,150.00, or 49%, the other 51% being provided by
the Lodges and other Masonic bodies served.
The average cost per job secured was $2.39, as compared with $2.64
last year. Had these jobs been secured through private fee -charging agencies, our distressed brethren would have paid out more than $150,000.00
in fees. We spent $29,000.00, but we saved them mote than five times that
amount. No one ever made a more profitable investment. This employment
service cost the Grand Lodge $1.16 per placement.
Changed business conditions have had something to do with the fine
showing made this year, but much credit is due the thirteen men and women
who operate our seven employment services, the Employment chairmen
and committees in our Lodges., and our brethren generally.
Member interest is of great help and can and should be stimulated.
Let's give our Employment people a hand-a hand for what they have
done and a helping hand in the coming year.
Appropriations
It has been the policy of the Grand Lodge for many y~ars to contribute
various sums of money to the support of the several employment services.
In addition to these appropriations made by the Grand Lodge, the local
Boards of Relief expend money from their own funds to such an extent as
will not curtail or cripple their own work. We have carefully considered
the requests of these Boards and have recommended to the Finance Committee the following appropriations for 1940-41:

REPORT OF U. C. LOS ANGELES CLUBHOUSE
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California.:
As the Clubhouse at the University of California at Los Angeles enters
upon its second decade of service to its young people, we look forward to
a splendid year.
There can be no doubt but what our Clubhouses fill a very definite
and much needed requirement.· Those of you who are or may be in the
vicinity of either of these Clubhouses are urged to visit them and see for
yourselves what is being accomplished. You will be well repaid by such a
visit. Those of you who have a boy or girl attending our University or
know of any with proper Masonic ties should see that they contact the
Masonic Club which was built and is maintained for their comfort, convenience and enjoyment. Participation in its activities will give them a
richer, more interesting University life.
The official visit of the Grand Master is always the highlight of the
year. The dinner and reception given in his honor was a very enjoyable
and inspiring occasion.
During the past year, two members of our Board of Directors have
answered the final summons. Brother Frank X. Pfaffinger was our
Treasurer, and a member of the Bpard from its inception. He assisted in
the selection of the Clubhouse site and was most helpful in the negotiations for its purchase. A great man and Mason. Brother Knowlton R.
Bradley, a Past Master of South Gate Lodge No. 320, was chairman of our
Building Committee and rendered valuable service in that capacity.
The financial condition is reflected by Brother Reynold E. Blight's
report which is attached and made a part hereof.
With respect to the budget for the ensuing year, our estimate is as
follows:

REPORT OF U. C. BERKELEY CLUBHOUSE
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
As Vice-President of the Trustees of the Berkeley Masonic Club, I
desire to make a brief report. The Clubhouse is a credit to the Masonic
fraternity. No finer body of young men and women assemble in any place
within my knowledge. Here life friendships are formed. There is no other
meeting place on the campus that approaches this Club in the upbuilding
of the character . of young men and young women. Between 200 and 300
young men and women pass through its doors daily. No investment made
by our great fra,ternity returns to us better or larger dividends than does
the Masonic Club. That the members of the Clubhouse fully appreciate
these advantages is best evidenced by the letter following from the President of the Masonic Clubhouse Council:
Executive Committee of the Board of Trustees of
The Masonic Clubhouse of the University of California
Dear Sirs:
Our members have at various meetings with the men comprising our
Board of Trustees, endeavored to show our appreciation for this magnificent building and all that it has to offer. I do not know whether or not
our expressions of gratitude have ever been carried formally and presented to the Board as a whole.
With a meeting place such as you have provided, our possibilities
are unlimited to provide a social center for students with mutual affiliations. Our program is continually in operation to promote greater
acquaintance among the members. With this as our goal we cannot follow a single line of entertainment. We must experiment with activities
of every degree. This has led to glee clubs and music appreciation
groups. Our dramatic circles have made various presentations and the
support of our luncheons and picnics is well known. Of course all of
these functions are not in continuous operation but vary with the
interests and spirit of the members.
We who are at present attending the University and belong to the
Masonic Club can realize the true meaning of the club only to a limited
degree. It is when we have graduated and leave our casual camnus
friends that the true and significant meaning -behind the Masonic Club
will appear. Today and every day that I walk in the door of this building my spirit is lifted because it is here that I have made my true
friends, it is here that I have been given the opoortunitv to meet and
talk with other students having the same and varying scholastic interests.
Also, it is here that I can openly discuss everyday problems. I know of
no other body ·on the campus that has the ability to present the broadminded possibilities that are provided here in our Masonic Clubhouse.
I am aware that my opinion is shared by every member and· we only
hope that by our present program we are fulfilling the ideals upon which
this building was established.
WILLIAM G. KIRKHAM,

President, Masonic Cl1tbhottse C011ncil
Within the last year and a half the entire. building has been renovated
and refurnished and is now in perfect condition, the cost of which has been

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

folly paid. The Trustees are happy to acknowledge that the Grand Chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star of California appropriated and paid
to us the sum of five hundred dollars of the cost of these improvements.
The Club budget asks the Grand Lodge to appropriate $8,000 for the
next Masonic year. The budget and the report of a certified public accountant has been placed in the hands of the Finance Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report
covering the Ninety-first Annual Communication of Grand Lodge:
Those entitled to compensation are the duly accredited Representatives
of each Lodge, Inspectors, Past Grand Masters, Officers of Grand Lodge
and the Chairmen and members of Committees enumerated in . Section 27
of the Constitution, who are actually in attendance at Grand Lodge.
Compensation of members is fixed in Section 71 of the Constitution as
being twice the single first-class one-way railway fare, plus sleeper where
necessary. As has been the custom for many wears, no compensation is
allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity, nor
where the prescribed compensation does not exceed $1.00.
We have computed the transportation rates from all points in California and Hawaii to San Francisco. We have checked the pay-roll with the

examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary,
the Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The reports

committee and have had its consideration. These reports are now on file
with the records of Grand Lodge. They indicate that all records are correct
and in proper shape and all receipts properly accounted for and all expenditures properly made.
Your Committee is again mindful of the debt it owes Brother Webb
for the personal interest he has shown in making the various audits. He
has devoted considerable time to the affairs of Grand Lodge for which he
is asking no remuneration, and for which your committee is duly appreciative.

Committee on Finance their reports for the year just past, together with
statements of accounts prepared by certified public accountants. It is evident that the Trustees are continuing to exercise every care in the expenditure of funds for maintenance of the Clubhouses. While doing so, however,

brought into being, that is, to serve in ever-increasing ways the young men
and women from Masonic families, to the end that their University life may
be enriched by Masonic infiuence.

so unstintingly of their time to this worthy enterprise, R. '.W: .\Villiam

Masonic Homes Endowment Board
Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration the report of
the Masonic Homes Endowment Board. In reading this report, and in considering what this Board has accomplished during its existence of eight
years, we feel that the intangible results are perhaps more important than
the amount of some $500,000.00 that has been added to the fund during this
period. While this is no inconsiderable sum, and while it is important, we
feel that the work of the Board in attempting to reach the individual Mason,
and to translate Masonry to him in terms of service, is of far greater importance.
By its policy of publicizing the Homes continuously, and of keeping
before the Masons of California the problem of the Homes and of their
privilege and duty of assisting in increasing the Endowment Fund, the
Boar:d ·has made Masonry very real to many Masons. Of course, the
definite results are not known, and may never be known. We do not know
how much the Endowment Fund has benefited from wills not yet operative,

220

or how many Masons have been in'fluenced so that they, too, may eventually make substantial contributions.
Your committee feels very definitely that this good work that has been
accomplished must not be allowed to lapse, but that the Board should
have every means of assistance and encouragement made available to it
by Grand Lodge.
We commend the zeal and the faithfulness of every member of the
Board, and part~cularly of its chairman, Brother Frank M. Smith, and
~ecommend that its support by Grand Lodge be continued during the coming year,
. We therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:

Portrait of Grand Master
It has, for many years, been the pleasing custom of this Grand Lodge
to request the retiring Grand Master to have his portrait painted so that it
might be included in the gallery of portraits of Past Grand Masters, the
expense thereof to be paid out of Grand Lodge funds.
Your committee is sure that this communication of Grand Lodge will
wish to continue this pl~asing custom and have the portrait of our present
retiring Grand Master included in this gallery. Your committee therefore
recommends that our retiring Grand Master, the M:. W:. William B.
Ogden, have his portrait painted and present the bill therefor, in an amount
not to exceed $250.00, to the Grand Secretary, who is authorized to pay
the same, and when the portrait is painted, to be hung in the gallery of
Past Grand Masters.

Adopted.
Portraits of Preceding Past Grand Masters
For several years now this committee has made the effort by calling
Grand Lodge's attention thereto and making the appropriation therefor,
to have our gallery of portraits completed by securing the portraits of all
living Past Grand Masters not in the gallery. It is pleasing to note that
Past Grand Master Mixter's portrait has been added to the gallery and
also that the M.'. W.'. Leon 0 . Whitsell has had his portrait painted.
There are, however, two living Past Grand Masters whose portraits
are not in the gallery, that of Past Grand Masters Warren and Miller. Your
committee would like to see these portraits added, and therefore again
repeats the request that these two worthy brothers have their portraits
painted, the bill therefor in an amount not to exceed $250.00 for each portrait, to be presented to the Grand Secretary, who is authorized to pay
the same.

Adopted.

seems that this Lodge has operated under some difficulties this past year,
due to the loss of both the Master and the Junior Warden. I~. would seem,
however, that the Lodge is doing reasonably well and that 'the commuriity
in which it is located is prosperous, and there is no reason to believe 'tliat
the Lodge will not continue to carry the banner of Masonry' high.
·

in the payment of its Grand Lodge dues, and therefore offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption:

Rearrangement of the Constitution
At our annual communication a year ago this committee commended
our good brother, Past Grand Master John Stewart Ross, for the monumental work he had done in the rearrangement of the Constitution and.
Ordinances of this Grand Lodge. At that time we called the attention of
Grand Lodge. to the very generous offer which Past Grand Master Ross
had made to donate to this Grand body not only his entire services, but
also the expenses which he had been put to in the preparation of this work,
and it was only with difficulty that the committee persuaded him to accept
pay for the expenses he was actually out.
At that time we we.re advised that $300.00 would approximately cover
these expenses, and that amount was appropriated. InfQrmation now comes
to us that in the additional work it was necessary to do in further editing
and preparing this work for publication that our esteemed Past Grand
Master went to a further expense of $536.00, for which sum we feel he
should be reimbursed. The work which he has done is of very great value
and has required a great deal of his personal time. We are unanimously
of the opinion that in addition to contributing his time he should not be
asked to personally pay for any expenses incurred. We therefore offer the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $536.00 be- appropriated from the funds of
this Grand Lodge and be paid to Past Grand Master Ross to defray further
expenses incurred in the rearranging of the Constitution.
Adop~ed.

Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
At the last annual communication of this Gr;i.nd body there appeared
before this committee a committee selected by the Inspectors for the pur-

225

pose of conveying to this committee a wish that the manner of returning
the expenses of Inspectors in performing their various official duti_es ~~ould
be changed and that, instead of t:eceiving their expenses from the md1v1dual
Lodges of their districts, that the same be paid by Grand Lodge.
This committee was in accord with the suggested change, but as it
was not possible to determine with any degree of accuracy the cost to
Grand Lodge that such a change would entail, and as such a change would
entail amendments to our Constitution and Ordinances, your Finance Committee in its report to Grand Lodge last year, recommended that the
Grand' Lecturer make a study of the problem and report at this session
his conclusions. You have already heard and ·approved his report.
The details furnished this committee by the Grand Lecturer of the
work being done and the expenses incurred by the Inspectors is most complete. We commend our Grand Lecturer and wish to ~xpress our appreciation to him for the manner in which he has done this work.
The estimate given by the Grand Lecturer for the total expenses of
all Inspectors of the jurisdiction is $2627.80. He has also called our attention to his inability to accurately measure all needs. We can fully appreciate the impossibility of accurately determining all contingencies.
The Grand Lecturer's recommendation was that $3000.00 should be
appropriated for these expenses.
It is particularly pleasing to this committee to note the great amount
of work which the Inspectors are doing, all of which entails some expense
to them, and that this work is being done for the pure joy of the services
rendered without the willingness to accept any return for any money out.
Eighty-t~o Inspectors have asked for no return. This is the spirit whi~h
has made Masonry, and which will always keep the banner of Masonry
high. It is our belief that the greatest satisfa.c tion derived in life is the unselfish rendering of service, and so it is particularly gratifying that this
seems to be the spirit which prevails among the entire corps of Inspectors
of this Grand 'jurisdiction. Masonry is indeed fortunate to have such a
body of men.
As was expressed in the report of the Finance Committee last year,
we are in entire accord with the reimbursement of the expenses of Inspectors by Grand Lodge, instead of by the individual Lodges. We are also of
the opinion, as also was formerly expressed, that the Grand Lecturer should
promulgate certain rules governing the reimbursement of these expenses,
such rules to first have the approval of the Grand Master.
We looked over the rules under which reimbursements were made
this. past year, and approve the tenor thereof, and are of the opinion that
the rules for further reimbursements should rather closely correspond to
the rules which were laid down this past year. We are also of the opinion
that the amount that is asked 'to be appropriated this coming year for the
purpose of ca,ring for these expenses, that is the sum of $3000.00, is reasonable. We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resol~ed That the sum of $3000.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodg~ for the purpose of defraying expenses of Inspectors in performing their official duties, such repayment to be made upon bills duly
presented to the Grand Secretary, which said bills shall first be approved
by the (Jrand Lecturer.

Adopted.

Swiss Relief
This committee has had under consideration that portion of the Grand
Master's address reporting the relief sent by him to our needy brethren
in the republic of Switzerland, which portion of his report has been referred
to this committee.
Your Finance Committee is not only in accord with the Grand Master's having sent $2000.00 for the relief of these needy brethren, but commends him for the promptitude displayed in answering this call of distress.
We also note that he recommends "that such further appropriation be
made as may be consistent with the state of the finances and of the calls
thereon, present and prospective." It appears to this committee that it is
not possible at this time to determine just what further needs our brethren
in Switzerland may have, nor is it possible to determine what calls there
may be upon Grand Lodge funds for relief purposes. It therefore seems
best that the determination of what further relief may be accorded should
be left to the discretion of our incoming Grand Master, and we so recommend.

Adopted.
