Grand Lodge Per Capita
The Co~stitution provides for the levying of a per capita of fifty cents
to provide for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various activities. In
addition to the sum provided for by this per capita levy, there is additional
revenue accruing to Grand Lodge from degrees conferred and income on
investments of approximately $20,000.00. There is also some other revenue
derived from the sale of supplies and from surety bonds covering Lodge
officers. This revenue, however, cannot be taken into consideration in the
budget because it. is offset by corresponding items of disbursement, which
are also eliminated from the budget.
The income derived from these sources is not sufficient · to pay the
operating expenses of Grand Lodge during this coming year, and to care for
the various appropriations being recommended in this report. For a number of years in the immediate past, the-expenses of Grand Lodge have exceeded its income, the deficits thereof being cared for out of surpluses
accumulated a number of years ago.
This committee has always taken the position that while there was
no particular need of increasing the surpluses which Grand Lodge had,
yet sufficient funds should be raised each year to -care for all reasonable
expenses. It is particularly pleasing to note that the budget which was
set up a year ago, together with the per capita levy which was made to
care for this budget, has resulted in a surplus for this ·particular year of
approximately $12,000.00, which surplus will help in replacing the deficits
which have been occurring for a number of years now.
This committee has always been mindful of the financial burden the
Lodges are .c arrying, and therefore, for some years, has been disposed to
provide only sufficient funds to be sure that no additional calls shall be
made upon the previously accrued surplus. In niaking our calculations for
this year we are still mindful of this burden. Due, however, to the fact
that the $12,000.00 surplus of this year was largely due to a decrease in
the calls for outside assistance, and that such demands are very uncertain
to determine, and are, in the minds of this committee, likely to increase
this coming year, we have decided to recommend to Grand Lodge the same
per capita levy as last year, that is $1.65. The levy is made up as follows:'

SALE OF MASONIC TEMPLE STOCK
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance has for some time had under consideration
the investment which Grand Lodge has in the capital stock of the Masonic
Temple Association of California, Inc., this being the corporation which
owns the building in which we are now meeting. It believes this holding
to be excessive and, with respect to income, disproportionate to other investments of Grand Lodge. Looking forward to liquidation of some of this
stock, your committee has discussed the matter with the management of
the Temple Association with the result that the Temple Association, having the necessary funds available, will entertain a proposal to buy not
exceeding 25,000 shares at a price not over $4.00 per share.
The ~orporate control of the Temple Association would be retained by
Grand Lodge, the total outstanding stock after retirement of the 25,000
shares being 65,854, with Grand Lodge holding 33,985, or 51.6%.
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge be hereby
authorized to offer up to and not exceeding 25,000 shares of the capital
stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California, Inc. owned by Grand
Lodge at a price not less than $4.00 per share.
'

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON OBSERVANCE OF
CONSTITUTION DAY
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
At the suggestion of a group of Past Grand Ma11ters, Grand Master
Ogden appointed a committee to promote the observance of Constitution
Day by the Lodges of this jurisdiction; such observance to occur at the
most convenient time during the month of September. Unfortunately, the
subject was not presented to the attention of the Grand Master until about
a month before the normal time for observance, making it impossible to
accomplish the results which would have followed a longer time in which
to lay the foundation.
Notwithstanding the limited time available, an extended panel of able
speakers was provided; one panel for the northern portion of the jurisdiction and the other for the southern portion, 'thereby facilitating convenience
for arrangements, and minimizing expense for transportation.
We regret that the committee overlooked requesting specific reports
from all Lodges but sufficient illformation has reached both the Grand
Master and the committee to demonstrate that the suggestion was well
received. · It is also a tribute to the public spirit of our organization that
with very few exceptions brethren who were requested to speak expressed
their willingness to coop'erate; the exceptions being due to special conditions which made participation impractical.
While the meetings were held under the direct sponsorship of the
Lodges, your committee urged that so far as possible the meetings be
open to the public, with the purpose of disseminating as widely as possible
in every community, respect for, and the necessity for perpetuating, those
free American institutions which are declared in the Constitution of the
United States.
Clippings which have reached• the Grand Master demonstrate that
newspaper publicity was freely available and in some instances notices were
inserted in the general advertising columns .. Without derogation of meetings held in other localities and under varying conditions, the ·.interest of
the Craft was demonstrated at one meeting in Southern California, at
which there was · an attendance of over 4,000.
With world conditions whic;h require no emphasis, with institutions
guaranteed by the Constitution which represent an outpost of civilization,
and with the necessity for consecration and sacrifice for their perpetuation,
your committee is of the opinion that no greater work can be continued by
Grand Lodge than to stress the importance of constitutional guarantees
of liberty and the part which may be played by every American citizen in
maintaining them, not only for ourselves and our children, but for generations yet unborn. We therefore recommend:
1. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to continue during the coming year the work of the present committee;
2. That the committee be promptly appointed in order that a proper
foundation may be laid for its work and that there be a proper dissemination of information throughout the jurisdiction;
3. That the committee for the coming year emphasize the importance
of public meetings, but that these meetings be held under the direct supervision of our Masonic Lodges. While efforts have been made in Public
Schools' Week to leave Masonic initiative in the background, we believe that
in this instance the Masonic organization may with propriety and without

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

2:n

imputation of partisan politics, place itself squarely in the foreground of
measures for the defense and perpetuation of constitutional liberty;
4. That an adequate panel of suitable speakers be provided, available
through channels to be indicated, for Lodges which desire that service.
5. That the dignity of the occasion be emphasized by cooperation
where possible among Lodges in districts and localities, rather than limited
·observance by an individual Lodge without cooperation.
In conclusion, your committee suggests for consideration by Grand
Lodge, that constitutional liberty and democratic ideals are the most important issue confronting our country and our civilization, and that if
Masons discharge the' responsibility which we are capable of assuming, we
may contribute substantially to the welfare of the world and achieve results which will compare favorably with those which have followed the
efforts of Grand Lodge to emphasize the importance of our public schools.
Respectfully submitted,
ROBERT B. GAYLORD
RANDOLPH V. WHITING
CHARLES M. WOLLENBERG
LEE T. MULLEN

Report adopted.
REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California.:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
The several irregular clandestine organizations which we have .previously reported as operating in California are still continuing their activities. One however, reported upon last year as being a Masonic organization, Brother Alpers finds on further research not to be such but to have
simply pursued the practice of the various Chinese organizations of using
· the Square and Compass and designation of a "Masonic" body. "The
Chinese Grand Lodge of the World," mentioned in our last report is not in
any respect Masonic.
·
Negro Masonry
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge Ancient Free and Accepted Prince
Hall Masons, formerly known as the Worshipful Sovereign Grand Lodge
of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, held its 86th Grand Communication
in Portland, Oregon, July 15th to 20th, 1940. Roscoe H. Broyles of 1545
Seventh Street, Santa Monica, presided as the Grand Master and he was
reelected to that office. Raymond Hunter, 1421 Stanislaus Street, Fresno,
was elected Senior Grand Warden; S. 0. Sheffield, 49 Kearny Street,
Fresno, was elected Grand Trustee. There are still 36 subordinate Lodges.
A specially enthusiastic Communication was held in Portland. Special
trains were used and drill teams and marching contingents made the trip
to Portland.
·
During the Communication a meeting of the Grand Chapter of the
Eastern Star, Negro, held its sessions, and we are informed was well
attended.

Up to July, 1939 a movement was afoot to consolidate the two Negro
Grand Lodges. This movement was fostered by the then officiating group
,oi Grand Officers in both Grand Lodges.
During the Grand Communications of 1939 the officiating Grand Officers were ousted and new Grand Officers elected who appear to have put
a quietus upon the consolidation efforts. There is considerable rivalry
between the two Negro Grand Bodies and there will probably be no
fraternizatfon for some time to come.

The Sovereign Grand Lodge of the Philippine Archipe1ago:--This Grand
Body has previously been reported as active in California and it now
probably carries the greatest activity among the irregular Philippine bodies
in this State. It seems, however, that a split has occurred in the State
Grand organization. Some three Lodges, Nilad, Neptune, and Solomon,
appear to have revolted against the Grand Lodge under the leadership of
one Aquilino Monsod who was formerly the Grand Delegate of the parent
Grand Lodge in Manila. Monsod is retaining the same name as the larger
irregular Grand Lodge and seems to be conducting quite a racket. He is
selling diplomas up to the 32nd degree for 5.00 and we are informed that
he personally demands a fee of $5.00 for attendance upon the meetings of
subordinate Lodges. Monsod is a janitor in a Pasadena shoe store.
The main body of subordinate Lodges unqer this Sovereign Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Archipelago is led by one Avelino Requeja Villanueva who was deputized on December 9, 1939 by the Manila Grand Body
as the Grand Master for California.
This original main body of the Philippine Archipelago Grand Lodge
informs its . subordinate Lodges that it is a member of the International
Masonic Association of Geneva, Switzerland. The truth however appears
to be that it applied for membership in the I. M. A. but was not accepted.
Mr. Villanueva claims the 33rd degree of Masonry, and he is Master of the
Lodge Jerusalem No. 39 of Berkeley. This Lodge publishes a periodical
known as "Jerusalem Bulletin" several times a year, and it has the appearance of the work of an informed and intelligent element in the Lodge.
We are informed that a new Lodge under this jurisdiction is to be
formed shortly at Long Beach, and another one at Stockton, and a third
one is under way at Reno, Nevada.
On Sunday, April 7, 1940 a new Lodge under this Filipino Grand
Jurisdiction· with the name of "Rising Sun" was instituted at West Los
Angeles, California, in the Sawtelle Masonic Temple. Lodge Master is
Brother Segundo S. Dayrit, who claims the 32nd Degree and whose address
is· 10743 Lindbrook Drive, Westwood Village, Los Angeles. We are informed that there were representatives present from more than fifteen
Lodges from many jurisdictions. The ceremonies were conducted at the
Masonic Temple in Sawtelle and among the guests we are told were alleged
Masons from the jurisdictions of Mexico, Chile, Colombia, Denmark, the
Philippines, Germany, and Br;;tzil. After the installation ceremonies the
first degree of Freemasonry was conferred upon two candidates.
Brother Fred P. Roullard qf our Committee reports that during March,
1940 a Filipino named Julio T. Aquilano died in the Sart Luis Obispo Tubercular Hospital. He was a member of Jerusalem Lodge No. 38 of Berkeley
under the Philippine Archipelago Grand Lodge. The undertaker, a Junior
Warden of King David's Lodge, San Luis Obispo, found upon the body
eight typewritten sheets which are apparently the candidate's lecture of
the first and second degrees minus the obligation. Aquilano's friends requested King David's Lodge for a Masonic funeral but this of course had
to be denied,· but a church service was conducted at the funeral.

Lodge, operating in the northern district of Lower California with headquarters at Tia Juana, had chartered a Lodge in Los Angeles called "Cinco

members joined the Lodge Quo Vadis No. 1, noticed above, and others
joined the Lodge Ignacio Zaragoza of Tia Juana.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Charters submits for your consideration the following report:
Since the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, three
Lodges have been working under dispensation, namely :
Barstow Lodge, Barstow, San .Bernardino County. Dispensation issued
Oct. 1, 1939, by Grand Master Leon 0 . Whitsell.
Redwood Empire Lodge, Garberville, Humboldt County. Dispensation
issued March 26,1940, by Grand Master William B. Ogden.
Trona Lodge, Trona, San BernardinQ, County. Dispensation issued
Sept. 10, 1940, by Grand Master William B. Ogden.
Your committee has examined the records and files of Trona Lodge as
compiled during the brief period of operation under dispensation and we
find the same to be in order and they are approved as submitted. The members of this Lodge do not seek a charter at this communication. They do
ask, however, that their dispensation be continued until the next Annual
Communication, thus affording them ample opportunity to demonstrate
their worth as a Masonic Lodge.
We look with favor upon the request for an extension of the dispensation, and we wish for the group that measure of success which their zeal
and enterprise so fully deserve.
Your committee has had under consideration the r espective petitions
for charters of Barstow Lodge and Redwood Empire Lodge. The period
of the actual operation of these two Lodges has, in each instance, been of
sufficient duration to enable the members of your committee to form an
opinion upon which to base our recommendation.
We have interviewed representatives from the two Lodges and Brother
Ralph Logsden, Inspector, to whom we are indebted for much helpful information concerning the Barstow group. We are pleased to report that all
records submitted are in order and we commend those who are responsible
for the careful observance of our constitutional requirements.
These two Lodges are not only clear of debt, but the financial report
of each reflects a substantial bank balance. Following the established policy
of your committee, satisfactory assurances were obtained from the respective representatives that there will be no assumption of financial obligations
inconsistent with current resources of these Lodges.
The members of your committee are firmly convinced that a Masonic
Lodge, like the public school and the church, is an invaluable asset to any
community in promoting civic, educational, moral and r eligious w elfare and
development. Particularly does this hold true in those small communities
like Barstow and Garberville where there are no Masonic Lodges and
where those who would hold Masonic communication with their brethren ·
must, of necessity, measure their zeal for the fraternity in miles of travel,

REPORT OF ACTIVITIES COMMITTEE

w:.

To the M:.
Grand Lodge of California:
· Your Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities respectfully reports
as follows:
The committee is charged with the duty of making suitable arrangements for the entertainment of the members of Grand Lodge during the
Annual Communication. The experience of all deliberative bodies is that
better results are 'obtained when work is interspersed with recreation and
entertainment, and to that end we have endeavored to provide the entertainment in keeping with the dignity of the Craft. Once again nature
favored us, and San Francisco, so beautifully described by our own poet
laureate, George Sterling, "The cool, gray city of love," gave its sunniest
skies to aid in the program that had been arranged.
· Your committee has kept close to the liberal allotment of funds made by
this Grand Lodge for the purpose, and has tried to diversify its program
so that something was provided which would meet the demands of every
one of the members and the ladies accompanying them.
A committee report at this time is without practical effect and the
verdict as to whether or not it has succeeded in its efforts rests in the
opinions that you have formed. We especially thank the many brethren of

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on· Policy and General Purposes herewith submits
its reports and recommendations with respect to the various matters _contained in the annual message of the Grand Master and the resolutions introduced into this Grand Lodge, which have been referred to it for consideration by Grand Lodge:
Proposed Amendments to go Over One Year
At the last communication of Grand Lodge, Past Grand Master Adams
presented a resolution, which· is unfinished business of this communication.
The resolution was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence ando the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and reads as follows:
"Resolved; That unless otherwise ordered by unanimous consent,
every resolution proposing to amend the Constitution, Regulations,
or the Uniform Code of By-Laws, shall be presented in writing at a
regular annual communication, and be immediately referred to the
appropriate committee, which shall report thereon in writing at the next
annual communication; and that the proposed resolution shall appear
in full in the printed Proceedings of the communication at which it was
presented."
As a matter 'of policy, your committee is of th~ opinion that amendments to the Constitution, or Ordinances, excepting in cases of emergency,
might well be postponed for a period of one year before adopting or rejecting the same. During this period of time a careful examination and a
full discussion could be had. Matters of importance are presented to Grand
Lodge, and, because of the shortness of the session, and the volume of
business to be considered and transacted, it is not always possible to give
a subject matter the careful consideration to which it is entitled. It is true
that our Constitution and Ordinances are so well seasoned that few important changes are necessary or desirable and that action on many of
the resolutions presented at an annual communication may properly be
1ms.tpciried {or a reasonable time.
. sl:i.o.uld the resolution be adopted, the legislation should be ex!ilicit
in its terms, so that amendments and alterations in the original prqp'osar
would not operate to continue the matter for a further ye.ar, and so that·
exceptional matters of an emergency nature should not be postpon.e d. 'because of a: negligible number of dissenters.
· <"i
We recqmmend that the resolution be adopted as a ·matter 6£ p~iicy
and referre'd to the Jurisprudence Committee for the preparation of appropriate legislation to be presented to this Grand Lodge for its adoption by
a five-siXths vote, or its rejection by a vote of more than on'e:s.ixth'. ~:· •·

Report adopted and referred to Committee on Jurisprudence.
· Authorit:y: ·of In11pectors to Withhold Certificates
The Grand Master recommended that an Inspector have authority
to withhold the certificate of qualification of a Warden or Senior Deacon
when, in the judg1;m;nt of th.e. Inspector, the holding of outside offices by ·
such Warden or Senior Deacon may seem to the Inspector to be in con- .
flict with the duties of the office in the Lodge.
Your committee i·s in full sympathy with the thought of the Grand ·
Master that officers .often undertake to perform more duties and fulfill .

239

more obligations than their time and circumstances will permit. He doubtless is of the opinion that no man should accept a high office in his Lodge
unless he is fully able to properly perform his duties.
Notwithstanding all this, however, it would appear that the Lodge,
rather than the Inspector, should be the judge of the question of whether
or not an officer will have the time to properly perform his duties in the
Lodge. An .obligation devolves upon the elected Warden, or appointed
Senior Deacon, to determine this question conscientiously at or before the
time of his election or appointment. Your committee does not feel that
an arbitrary power so far-reaching, and that might be productive of such
sad results, as that proposed to be given to an Inspector should be taken
from the Lodge and the officer concerned.
We therefore respectfully recommend that the recommendation of
the Grand Master be not adopted.

Adopted.
Notice of Membership
The Grand Master recommended that appropriate legislation be adopted
by this Grand Lodge authorizing secretaries of Lodges to issue certificates
that a named person is or is not a member of such Lodge and that for the
purpose of such certificate only a suspended member be treated as no
longer a member of the Lodge.
The Grand Master supports his recommendation with a strong argument in favor of the legislation and your committee is of the opinion that
the secretary of a Lodge should be permitted to make a statement to a
proper officer of any organization, the prerequisite for membership therein
being that a man be a Master Mason, concerning the standing of any Mason
· who is a member both of his Lodge and of such organization.
We therefore recommend that the policy above outlined be adopted by
Grand Lodge.

Adopted.
:i:,ife Membership Funds
The Grand Master in his message directs our attention to a source
of difficulty for many Lodges in the matter of the investment of life membership funds. He calls our attention to the fact that in many cases the
amount of money in the life membership fund permits of no diversification in its investment and, because of the small amount of the fund, that
the usual avenue of investment is in savings bank accounts, returning a
maximum of 2% per annum. For the foregoing reasons he recommends
that some committee of Grand Lodge, or a committee to be established
by Grand Lodge, be intrusted with the duty of investing all life member"ship funds that may be entrusted to the Grand Lodge by the constituent
Lodges; and further recommends that all of said funds be placed in a
common pool to be invested from time to time by the committee, and the
income apportioned among the Lodges contributing in proper proportions.
He further suggests that a possible alternative for this fund might be the
inclusion of federally insured building and loan association certificates in the
class of securities permitted for investment.
Your committee is cognizant of the difficulties existing in many Lodges
in the management of the life membership funds, but is not satisfied that
the Grand Lodge should take over the task of investment and accounting
with respect thereto. When a Lodge passes a resolution setting up a life
membership fund it should do so with a clear understanding of the advantages and disadvantages of such a fund; and with a reasonable belief

240

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

that the fund will attain a magnitude which will enable the Lodge to handle the same to its benefit. It seems to us that it is unwise for a Lodge
to set up a life membership fund for the purpose of providing a life membership for one or more popular members. This is equivalent to remitting the member's dues for the remainder of his life through the medium
of such a fund, and with small consideration. If there is no expectancy that
the fund will attain reasonable proportions, then it should not be established. Moreover, in considering life membership funds the Lodge should
understand that over the near period such a fund would be a burden on
the Lodge, and that only over the long period could it be advantageous.
Investments prudently made cannot be made to yield a return commensurate with the amount of dues lost by the Lodge, but, because the fund
remains the property of the Lodge in perpetuity, in the course of time, by .
reason of the death of life members, the Lodge will receive a continuing
benefit.
In the case of life membership funds in small amounts the investments
of necessity will yield a meager interest, and at the same time be subject
to the usual investment hazards. Even if the fund was turned over to a
Grand Lodge committee for investment it would still yield a low return,
and in addition to that a responsibility which rightfully belongs to the
Lodge would be evaded without a commensurate benefit.
The alternative suggested by the Grand Master meets with the approval of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes. At the annual
communication of 1939 it was proposed to amend Sections 87 and 129 of
the Constitution by adding thereto the following language: " ... and certificates and/ or shares in state chartered institutions to the extent of such
institution's insurance for its deposits in the Federal Savings and Loan
Insurance Corporation."
Your committee reported adversely on the proposed amendment, giving as one of the reasons for its recommendation that the legislation did
not give an investment status to certain associations, and that action by·
the legislature rather than by this Grand Lodge should be taken. Under·
the present status of the law, the certificates of federal building and loan
associations are legal investments for savings banks and are a legal medium for the investment of life membership funds, but the certificates of
state associations, while legal investments for trustees, are not qualified
by the legislature as legal investments for savings banks. This is an anomolous situation because many of the state associations have the full coverage·
of federal insurance and in addition to 1such coverage have a capital invest- .
ment which .provides additional security to the holder of the certificates.
After a more careful study of the matter, your committee is of the ·
opinion that Lodges should be permitted to invest their life membership
funds, if they see fit so to do, in certificates of building and loan associations organized under the laws of the State of California which are insured
by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation. There seems
to be no difference in the safety factor between well managed state asso-.
ciations and well managed federal associations if the insurance protection.
is the same in each case.
Your committee recommends that no committee of this Grand Lodge
be intrusted with the duty of investing the life membership funds held by
the constituent Lodges; and it further recommends that Section 152 of the
Ordinances ·of this Grand Lodge be amended by adding the words "or
trustees" following the word "banks" and preceding the semicolon in the
first sentence of said section.

The report of the committee was adopted, referred to the:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Committee on Jurisprudence, which committee approved the recommendation, and thereupon Section 152 of the Ordinances was
amended by unanimous vote.

Repeal of Fee for Dispensation
Thurman A. Baldwin of Hemet Lodge No. 615, Clarence F. Neuman
of Riverside Lodge No. 635, Raymond P. Kirby of San Gorgonio Lodge
No. 668, Hardus Sorkness of San Jacinto Lodge No. 338, and Oakley R.
Morton and William 0. Mackey of Evergreen Lodge No. 259, have presented a resolution to repeal Subsection 5 of Section 97 of the Ordinances.
Article 7 of the Ordinances provides for the source of revenue of Grand
Lodge and designates certain fees to be charged by Grand Lodge. Subsection 5 of Section 97 provides a fee of $10.00 for a dispensation to receive
and act upon the applications for degrees of a person belonging to the army
or navy of the United States who may not possess the qualification of
residence. The proposers of the repeal of said Subsection 5 direct our attention to the fact that March Field, a United States army aviation post,
is locatecj in the vicinity of the Lodges represented by the proposers, and
that there are officers and men temporarily stationed there who are prospective petitioners for the degrees of Masonry. They further represent
that the $10.00 charge for dispensation falls not upon the petitioner but
upon the Lodge, and that under the circumstances of today it would be
helpful and · beneficial to the Lodges and not detrimental to Grand Lodge
if the dispensation fee should be abrogated.
Your committee is of the opinion that in the face of war preparations
on a large scale and a possibility of a state of hostilities it would be neither
unwise nor unjust to eliminate for the time of emergency the fee now provided for dispensations to receive petitions from men wearing the uniform
of our country who may be stationed in California, and therefore respectfully recommend that Subsection 5 of Section 97 of Article 7 of the Ordinances be repealed.

The Jurisprudence Committee concurring in the report, Subdivision 5 or Section 97 of the Ordinances was repealed by unani;..
mous vote.

Who May Apply for Relief
Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, by resolution, proposes
that Section 263 of the Ordinances be repealed. Section 261 of the Ordinances provides the duties of a Lodge in respect to relief, while Section
263 provides who is entitled to ask for relief. Section 261 fully covers the
subject matter so far as concerns the Lodge, and in addition thereto provides that a Master Mason, his widow or orphan has the right to ask relief
from any Master Mason able to bestow the same. Elsewhere in Masonry
this subject is properly covered and therefore Section 263 of the Ordinances
deals with surplusage, and your committee respeetfully recommends that
the same be repealed.
· .

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which committee approved the resolution as to form, and thereupon Section
263 of the Ordinances was ·repealed by unanimous vote.

Brother C. E. Mallachowitz, Past Master of Caledonia Lodge No. 486,

"Your committee is of the opinion that no persuasive reasons appear
for the abrogation of the Masonic Home fee, charged either for the degrees or for affiliation. It is possible that there are cases where the Masonic Home fee deters a Mason from affiliating with a California Lodge,
but such cases cannot be numerous. Our Homes are so important and the

our orphan children that there would be few indeed who would hesitate to

Militant Masonry
Under the heading "A Militant Masonry" the Grand Master mentions
an undercurrent of feeling among the Craft that Masonry as an organization should be more militant, and correctly, we think, points out the importance of maintaining our traditional declination to introduce controversial matters in our Lodges. He quotes a letter written by him to a brother
who desired to appear before Lodges. showing a film and delivering an
address upon the Townsend Plan, which, of course, falls clearly within
the range of controversial matters.

In concluding thi~ section of his message, the Grand Master says:
"It must be remembered that we have within our membership men
of every race, sect and opinion, and nothing should be said or done in
a Masonic meeting that would be found offensive or embarrassing to
the least among us."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes desires to record its
approval of the policy and position expressed by the Grand Master.

Report approved.

Decisions
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
d.e~isions reported by t~e Grand Master and are of the opinion that de-

c1s1ons Nos. 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, and 8 are in strict accordance with our law and
should be appro'ved.
Y c:iur committee has also considered the · various dispensations issued
by the Grand Master and the life membership resolutions approved by him,

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered Decision No. 2, contained in the Grand Master's message, and repor~ thereon as follows:
Section 82 (now 214 of the Ordinances) provides that two or more
Lodges located within the corporate limits of any city, town or place, shall
have concurrent jurisdiction therein and none of them shall confer the
degrees for a smaller sum than fifty dollars without the consent of all.
Section 82a (now · 218 of. the Ordinances) provides that any person
residing within ten miles of the Lodgeroom of a Lodge may present his
petition to such Lodge, regardless of the fact that he may reside within
the normal jurisdiction of another Lodge.
The Grand Master decided that a Lodge located within ten miles of a
city in which two Lodges. had concurrent jurisdiction, as above specified,
could not receive applications for degrees from persons residing within
the limits of such city without charging the minimum fee of fifty dollars.
Section 82a has been considered before. In 1927 the Grand Master
decided that the purpose of the section was not to enlarge the jurisdiction
of Lodges in every respect, but solely in regard to the reception of a petition for degrees, and its provisions should be limited to that matter alone,
which decision was approved by Grand Lodge.
The decision of the Grand Master, now under consideration, would
have the effect of extending the scope of Section 82 beyond its expressed
terms, which provides only for concurrent jurisdiction within corporate
limits of cities.
It is our opinion that in enacting Section 82a it was not the intention
of Grand Lodge to enlarge the application of Section 82 beyond extending its territorial limits for residential qualification of applicants.
While it may be that the . law should be so amended as to cover such
a situation as here presented, we consider that a matter for future legislation if investigation shall disclose that any amendment be advisable.
We therefore recommend that Decision No. 2 of the Grand Master
be not approved.

The report was adopted.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration decision No. 9 of the M.'. W:. Grand Master, as set forth in his message, and
report as follows:
The action of the Lodge, the Inspector, and the Master, and the resulting ruling of the Grand Master, are concisely stated in the decision
under consideration. This ruling calls for the approval of the Grand Lodge
without hesitancy.
The conferring of the degrees of Masonry on one whose physical disqualification was so evident, was done in the face not only of the law of
the Fraternity, but also of admonitions heretofore given by Grand Lodge
in terms so strong that a failure to heed them demands drastic action
against those who close their eyes to the law and the admonitions. In the
present case, the Lodge may deem itself fortunate that a reprimand only
was meted out to it as its punishment in permitting this violation to have
oc.curred.
Grand Lodge has declared in no uncertain terms that an applicant
maimed as was the applicant here admitted, is ineligible to be made a Mason,

and a reference to the rulings made by Grand Masters of late years, which
rulings were approved by Grand Lodge, and which are set out in the Ross

The effect of the order of the Grand Master as it applies to the Master
of the Lodge : was to suspend him from the exercise of his powers and

REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the M:. W:. Graiid Lodge of California:
Your committee is a continuation of the Special Taxation Committee
originally appointed in November, 1938, by M:. w:. Leon O .. Whitsell,
pursuant to a resolution of the 89th annual communication of Grand Lodg.e.

Members of the committee are:
Henry C. Clausen, chairman, Ingleside Lodge No. 630;
James E. Hammond, Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568;
R. P. Wisecarver, Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478.
Your committee has actively functioned in accordance with a resolu- ·
tion by the said ninetieth annual communication of Grand Lodge.
Numerous meetings have been held. Correspondence has been exchanged with subordinate Lodges. Several interim reports have been rendered, one of which was printed and distributed to the subordinate Lodges.
In proper cases your committee has counselled with subordinate Lodges
and advised applications for refunds in matters affecting their tax problems. Interviews and conferences have been held with Grand Lodge officials. Communications were exchanged with the M:. w:. Joseph Earl
Perry of Massachusetts, chairman of the Grand Masters' Committee on
Social Security Taxes, and with counsel for said committee. The law and
regulations and prospective legislation appertaining to tax problems affecting the Masonic Fraternity have been studied.
The problems of taxation with which your ~ommittee wrestled involved
not only payments of money but also an attendant heavy clerical burden
on the secretaries. Tax legislation has become increasingly complex. There
is a great deal of confusion with respect to these tax problems. We have
not had the benefit of any clear-cut court decisions to follow as a guide.
In 1939 it was thought that a main cause of complaint had been clari- •
fied. But more recent developments have added to the uncertainty and
confusion.
We refer particularly to the re<:ent rulings on the Social Security Act,
as amended. It should be remembered that the original Titles VIII and
IX of the Social Security Act, relating to "old age" and "unemployment"
taxes, have been repealed and re-enacted as Subchapters A and C of the
Internal Revenue Code. Each division has also been amended. The effect
of these amendments has created an _important additional test for exemption as to .Masonic "employees." On this subject one amendment removes
the age limit of 65 years. Another exempts all employees whose remuneration in any calender quarter does not exceed $45.00. Also, one amendment we feel was intended to put into the statute the exemption of ritualistic officers regardless of the amount of their compensation.
Lodges have received letters from their local Federal Tax Collectors,
advising that before their exemption as to old age or unemployment ·taxes
can be determined, it will be necessary for them or their Grand Lodge to
make a formal application for exemption.
This committee, therefore, has caused an application to be made by
the Grand Lodge on behalf of itself and the subordinate Lodges for exemption from federal income tax as a basis for the establishment of exemptions under the Social Security Act. It was the opinion of your committee
that this application should be filed first by the Grand Lodge, rather than
by the subordinate Lodges, so we would not be working at cross purposes.
In the interests of uniformity, clarity and complete presentation of the
facts, this committee has also worked in unison and kept in close toU<;h
with the said Committee of Grand Masters.
The recent developments and present confosing status of. these tax
questions may be stated briefly as follows : The Committee of Grand Masters appeared before the Commissioner of Internal Revenue at Washington,

248

PROCEEDINGS OF TR.I!;
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

D. C., and contended that the Masonic Fraternity came within certain exclusions of the Social Security Act, and that therefore the Fraternity was
wholly exempt. But on July 1, and July 10, 1940, opinions were rendered
by the C?mmissioner to the contrary. Stripped of their technical language,
these rulmgs declare that the Masonic Fraternity is a "fraternal beneficiary
society" which is exempt from income tax, but is not wholly exempt from
the Social Security Act. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue also issued
orders that officers of a Masonic Lodge and even members of committees
should be considered as employees for the purpose of counting employee~
under the said act. This latter conclusion is based on a contention of the
Commissioner that a portion at least of the Lodge activities of these members consists of administrative work.
. !his latter ruling is inconsistent with previous rulings by the Comm1ss10ner of Internal Revenue and by the California Commissioner with
respect to similar taxes. As stated in our 1939 report, the Commissioner
of Internal Revenue ruled that unpaid ritualistic officers were not to be
counted as employees and that incidental administrative duties should be
disregarded. Pursuant to this ruling the California Commissioner held that
unpaid officers were not to be counted as employees. This automatically
exempted most of our Lodges. Refunds of taxes improperly paid were
consequently ordered and made.
·
Your committee has pioneered the contention and concurs with the
Grand Masters Committee in urging that any such recent and contrary
rulings by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue are incorrect; and must
per.force be based upon a mistake of fact as to the nature of our organization.
In our 1939 report to Grand Lodge, we also advised the desirability
of determining these questions by a test case. · It now appears that the
Committee of Grand Masters has reached the same conclusion and has
instituted such a case. It is the recommendation of your committee, therefore, that we now await that decision rather than institute a case ourselves.
From our review of the desirable jurisdictions in which to bring such a
case, it also appears that the Commonwealth of Massachusetts where the
stated test case is being prosecuted, will be a good forum for ~uch a purpose because the Supreme Court of that commonwealth . has at various
times favorably defined the nature of the Masonic Fraternity as a matter
of law.
·
In light of the foregoing, our present recommendation to the subordinate California Lodges as to the taxes assessed upon the grounds we dispute, is to pay those taxes under protest. A claim for refund should then
be fil~d. After filing, ho':'ever, this claim should not be pressed. Thereby,
a period of two years will be available in which an authoritative decision
by a court of competent jurisdiction should be rendered.
. . ~t is our ~op~ that Washington will co-operate in seeking a speedy
Jud1c1al determmat1on of these questions. Your committee intends making
such su.ggestions of fact or law as it feels will be helpful in sustaining the
conclus10ns we have reached and which are in harmony with the contentions of the Grand Masters Committee.
It should be borne in mind that the Commissioner recognizes that under the Social Security Act there are certain instances wherein the Lodges
and their employees may be exempt as matters now stand. For example,
as hereinbefore stated, there· is a provision now in force exempting those
employees. whose remuneration does not exceed $45 per quarter if employed by an organization that is exempt from the payment of an income
tax under Section 101 (3) of the Internal Revenue Code, provided that such

~49

service is in connection with the coflection of dues and is performed away
from the home office, or is ritualistic service.
Recently, several amendments have been proposed to the Social Security Act with respect to the foregoing questions. It is the intention of
your committee to study these amendments and make suggestions to the
Committee of Grand Masters pursuant to a request made by the chairman of that committee in a letter dated September 3, 1940.
Tax laws are being changed annually and rulings and interpretations
are being made continually by the departments in charge of tax collections.
As to these questions, therefore, your committee can serve as a clearing
house and central point of study and information for Grand Lodge and subordinate Lodges.
We, therefore, recommend for your approval:
(1) That this committee be continued.
(2) That a copy of this report be sent each subordinate Lodge
for its information.
Respectfully submitted,
R. P, WISECARVER

J. E. HAMMOND
HENRY

c. CLAUSEN
Committee

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
Special Taxation Committee
The Committee on Special Taxation has made a report to this Grand
Lodge wherein it recommended that the committee be continued for the
period of the coming Grand Lodge year and that a copy of its report be
sent to each subordinate Lodge for its information.
Your committee is advised of the confusion and difficulties facing the
subordinate Lodges with respect to the law and the rulings of the Internal
Revenue Bureau on the subject of Social Security taxes, as related to old
age and unemployment benefits. It is a matter of common knowledge that
the rulings of the Bureau of necessity are being changed from time to time.
We are also advised that other Masonic bodies throughout the United
States are interesting themselves in the matter of these laws and that it is
desirable for all of us that a serious effort be made to secure a clarification
and a uniformity in the tax laws affecting fr·aternal beneficiary societies. To
properly safeguard the interests of this Grand Lodge and its subordinates,
it is definitely beneficial to have the Special Committee remain on guard
and to keep itself advised of the efforts of others and the trends in legislation and rules affecting the taxation of Masonic Lodges.
For the foregoing reasons your committee recommends that the Committee on Special Taxation be continued and that pertinent imformative
matters in said report ~ubmitted at this annual communication be sent to
subordinate Lodges for their information.

Adopted.

ANNUAL ELECTION ·oF OFFICERS
The annual election of officers was now held, with the following result :
The R. ·. W. ·. Lloyd E. Wilson of Ingleside Lodge No. 630
was elected Grand Master.
The R.'. W.". Frank M. Smith of East Gate Lodge No. 290
was elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R.". W.". Leslie E. Wood of Provident Lodge No. fm
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
W.". Claude H. Morrison of San Diego Lodge No. 35 was
elected Junior Grand Warden.
V.". w:. William P. Filmer of King Solomon's Lodge No.
260 was re-elected Grand Treas~rer.
V.". W.". John Whicher of King David's Lodge No. 209 was
re-elected Grand Secretary.
W.". \Valter Leonard of Oriental Lodge No. 144 was reelected Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master-elect caused to be read the names of the
appointive officers as follows:
Grand Chaplain, Morris Goldstein of Fidelity Lodge No. 120.
Grand Orator, Henry C. Clausen of Ingleside Lodge No. 630.

cisco Lodge No. 360.

410.

de l'Oceanie No. 371.

No. 337.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE · .

Grand Organist, Charles E. Anderson of Jewel Lodge No. 374.
Grand Tiler, Ralph K. Marsha~l of Occidental Lodge No. 22.
The Grand Masteri-elect announced the appointment of Samuel E. Burke to be a member of the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes of California, vice self, term expired.
The M.°. W.°. Dana R. Weller was appointed Master of
Ceremonies and the officers elect and appointed were installed
by the retiring Grand Master in due and ancient form.
The newly installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a Past Grand Master's lapel button and also invested
him with the apron of a Past Grand Master.
The Charles Albert Adams insignia was then transferred
from the retiring to the incumbent Grand Master and the other
chair officers exchanged the Arthur S. Crites lapel pins.
Dudley F. Black of Hollywood Lodge No. 355 then, in behalf
of Grand Lodge, presented the retiring Grand Master with a
beautiful grandfather clock.
Henry C. Clausen, in behalf of the members of Ingleside
Lodge No. 630, presented the newly installed Grand Master with
a gavel and gavel block, made from olive wood grown on Mount
Moriah.
·
At 1 :35 P. M., all business being completed, Grand Lodge
was closed in Ample Form.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
For the seventeenth annual period in a service of nineteen years as
Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, herewith is presented its
.Report. As in former years, the same is the work of the Chairman and the
views expressed under the various topics are, of course, his own.
In compiling the same the Proceedings of over 68 Grand Lodges have
been sutnmarized, with a view of giving the reader briefly the thought and
action of the various jurisdictions. There is no dearth of material and the
problem is to select and confine within the pages allotted interest and instructive information.
During the preparation of the report for the last seventeen years the
trend of Masonic activities, discussions, or legislation have generally featured a particular subject and pertinent in all the various Proceedings.
At the present time, with world conditions as they are, we believe an
editorial from "The New York Times" is pertinent to America and Masons.
"What is the love of country for which our Flag stands?
"Maybe it begins with love of the land itself. It is the fog rolling in with
the tide at Eastport or through the Golden Gate and among the towers of
San Francisco. It is the sun coming up behind the White Mountains, over
the Green, throwing a shining glory on Lake Champlain and above the
Adirondacks. It is the storied Mississippi rolling swift and muddy past St.
Louis, pouring down past the levees of New Orleans. It is the lazy noon~
tide in the pines of Carolina, a sea of wheat rippling in western Kansas, the
Grand Canyon, a little trout stream coming down out of a New England
ridge.
"It is men at work. It is the storm-tossed fishermen coming into Gloucester and Provincetown and Astoria. It is the farmer riding his great
machine in the dust of harvest, the dairyman going to the barn before
sunrise, "the lineman mending the broken wire, the miner drilling for the
blast. It is the servants of fire in the murky splendor of Pittsburgh between
the Allegheny and the Monongahela, the trucks rumbling through the night,
the locomotive engineer bringing the train in on time, the pilot in the
clouds, the riveter running along the beam a hundred feet in air. It is the
clerk in the office, the housewife doing the dishes and sending the children
off to school It is the teacher, doctor and parson tending and helping body
and soul for small reward.
"It is the small things remembered, the little corners of the land, the
houses, the people that each one loves. We love our . country because there
was a little tree on a hill, with grass thereon and a sweet valley below;
because the hurdy-gurdy man came along on a sunny morning in a city
street; because a beach or a farm or a lane or a house that might not seem
much to others was once, for each of us, made magic. It is voices that are
remembered only, no longer heard. It is parents, friends, the lazy chat of
street and store and office, the ease of mind that makes life tranquil. It is
summer and winter, rain and sun and storm. These are flesh of our flesh,
bone of our bone, blood of our blood, a lasting part of what we are, each
of us and all of us together.
"It is stories told. It is the Pilgrims dying in their first dreadful winter.
It is the Minute Man standing his ground at Concord Bridge and dying
there. It is the army in rags, sick, freezing, starving at Valley Forge. It is
the wagons and the men on foot going westward over Cumberland Gap,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

319

floating down the great rivers, rolling over the great plains. It is the settler
hacking fiercely at the primeval forest on his new, his own lands. It is
Thoreau at Walden Pond, Lincoln at Cooper Union and Lee riding home
from Appomattox. It is corruption and disgrace, answered always by men
who would not let the Flag lie in the dust, whp have stood up in every
generation to fight for the old ideals and the old rights, at risk of ruin or of
life itself.
"It is a great multitude of people on pilgrimage, common and ordinary
people, charged with the usual human failings yet filled with such a hope
as never caught the imaginations and the hearts of any nation on earth
before. The hope of liberty. The hope of justice. The hope of a land in
which a man can stand straight, without fear, without rancor.
"The land and the people and the Flag-the land a continent, the people
of every race, the Flag a symbol of what humanity may aspire to when
wars are over and the barriers are down. To these each generation must
be dedicated and consecrated anew, to defend with life itself, if need be,
but, above all, in friendliness, in hope, in courage, to live for."
It might be well for the United States and Masonry to consider the
sentiment as expressed in the "New York Herald":·

.T HE GREAT PROOFREADER
When the story of Mammon is printed,
And the binder has laid down his tools;
When none of the facts have been stintedAnd the deeds of the wise and the fools
Have been written by prophets and sagesAnd bound in the rawhide of man;
Then God will blue-pencil its pages,
As only the Almighty can.
He will see the proud kings of the ages
As they rot in their filigreed graves,
And measure their virtue with gauges
That He'll use for both master and slaves;
While princes whose caskets were freighted
With laurel leaves, honors and flags,
May find that their souls have been rated
'Neath beggar-men buried in rags.
So in the long run it is better
To lead our lives humbly contrite;
Find truth, live up to the letter,
With hearts free from rancor and spite;
For the great proofreader is tracing
Man's record straight back to the flood,
And we hope for a merciful placing
In the book that is printed in blood.
Yours sincerely and fraternally,
JESSE M. WHITED, Chairman.

CO-ORDINATE BODIES

Next, a sustained program of charitable, educational and social activity.
Freemasonry will never be a dead institution as long as it does things. As
an individual you may help by withdrawing your support from extraneous
societies which have nothing to offer in a Masonic way and which only
sap the strength and finances of legitimate Masonic organizations. Not
how many degrees have you, but how well you practice those you have.
Finally, there should be more brotherhood. If we are to delay or to
ward off the dangers of class warfare, we must begin to reduce the feeling
of class consciousness. A friend of mine who has attained national prominence recently said to me:
"What this country needs right now is for men such as you and myself
who have attained a certain amount of prominence, to visit their Masonic
Lodges and sit beside their brethren, to speak to them in their own language,
and to make them feel, that after all we are brethren, made of the same
clay, and anxious and trying to do God's will justly and fairly. Man cannot
feel ill will toward their brethren while sitting within the tiled recesses of
a Masonic Lodge."

From a resume of the Proceedings there appears to be very little complaint as far as the activities of the co-ordinate bodies of Masonry are
concerned. There have been complaints in some jurisdictions as to their
operations, but generally speaking there has been little transgression of the
tenets of the Craft. There are, of course, members who at times take advantage in the various co-ordinate Bodies to exercise their personal privileges,
which are not in line with the Blue Lodge teachings.
We believe that discipline of these members should b~ handled through
the Blue Lodge rather than through any co-ordinate body. If the Masonic
authorities in the jurisdiction where these offenses occur will not take a
positive stand they will continue to have the same complaints. In a number
of jurisdictions where such offenses have occurred it will usually be found
that the co-ordinate Bodies, through Grand Lodge officers, are very closely
allied with those that operate what are usually called "the barnacles of Freemasonry." As we remember it, the Grand Master of Illinois corrected the
proposition in a short and summary manner.
Georgia ( 1938):
(Grand Master): There are some 250 organizations, membership in
which is predicated on Masonic membership. Their names are legion, some
of them fantastic, and some ridiculous. Among names we may cite are :
Beggars, Death, Old Souls, Running Footmen, etc. Some have their members parading in gaudy uniforms and indulging in foolishness in public,
which does not tend to increase respect for Masonry. It might be well to
consider prohibiting membership in any organization, except the York
Rite, ·Scottish Rite, the Sojourners (a military organization of Master
Masons), the Shrine, and such other bodies as are recognized to be dignified, until such body is first approved by Grand Lodge. Otherwise Master
Masons may be tempted to spend their money for that which is not liread
and their substance for that which profiteth not.
Missouri (1938):
(Grand Master): Where a few years ago we had only Lodge, Chapter,
Council and Commandery, today we have an auxiliary built upon the foundation of each-and not content with these, our brethren rush about in an
ambitious desire to learn more about co-masonry, adoptive masonry and
the like. Our juniors are urged to join Rainbow, Job's Daughters, Builders,
or the DeMolay; mothers and fathers are pushed into auxiliaries until we
begin to feel that the only field left is that of Infant Masonry, limited to
sons and daughters of milk-and-bottle age. Then we shall all be organized
and wait only for the millenium.
The dang:r is that of divided interest. Hundreds of men are frivoling
their time away with useless organizations when their efforts applied to the
promotion of Masonic ideals and Masonry would advance our interests
materially.
Our needs? Anything which will supply the an'.idote to the above named
evils. First, however, is leadership. The leadership of conservative, dignified and influential men-men who will attract other men and who have
influence in their commun.ity. If you want to do your part in such a constructive work, go out into your community and draft such a one. The fraternity .need not worry as to whether he can repeat the ritual forward or
backward or whether he knows his title to be "Worshipful," as long as he
has something in his heart and in his head.

North Dakota (1938):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Michigan has a law similar to
ours regarding the formation of organizations based on Masonic membership. The state association of "High Twelve" clubs asked for approval but
on recommendation of the jurisprudence committee this was refused, quite
rightly, we believe, on the ground that, while they were supposed to cooperate with the. local Lodges, they would not be in complete subordination
to and an agency of the Lodges. It is easy to see how they could develop
into an actual detriment.

COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
The functions of the Committee on Correspondence can be traced back
to Revolutionary days. In order to maintain contacts between the various
Colonies committees were appointed for this purpose, and afterward this
procedure among Grand Lodges was adopted in order that the members
might be informed of what was transpiring in the different jurisdictions.
The Chairman, or Correspondence Committee of any jurisdiction, after
reviewing the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges, is perhaps in a
better position to give to the Craft what has occurred during the preceding
year. The forewords of the chairmen of a number of jurisdictions, some
of which follow, are perhaps the best index as to what is taking place in
Masonry at the present time.
Florida (1939):
(Grand Lodge) : The Committee on Foreign Correspondence reported having
reviewed all Proceedings received and recommen·d ed that same be published
as usual, etc. However, the Proceedings carry no such reviews. In the
absence of other explanation of such omission, we quote from a "Supplemental Report of Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence" : "We respectfully .recommend that the Foreign Correspondence Report as printed in our
1938 Proceedings be expunged from the record and that the incoming
Grand Master and Grand Secretary promptly notify Grand Jurisdictions
with which the Grand Lodge of Florida sustains fraternal relations of this
action . . .. We further recommend that the compilation and printing of
the usual reviews of foreign Grand Jurisdictions be discontinued for the
present."
Illinois (1939):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The reports of Grand Masters,
Grand Secretaries and various Grand Lodge Committees afford ample proof
that Freemasonry is in a strong and healthy condition throughout the
world except in those countries where it has been wholly suppressed and
practically annihilated by the unreasoning prejudice, stupid ignorance, and

GRAND LODGE OF. CALIFORNIA

325

wicked intolerance of the few men who at present wield autocratic power.
In one of these countries, torn by civil warfare unequalled for cruelty,
destructiveness, and hideous barbarity in the entire history of the world,
large numbers of Freemasons have been forced to face firing squads simply
because they were Masons. In another Godless country still larger numbers
of Freemasons, solely because they were Masons, were arrested, thrown into
concentration camps, ruthlessly stripped of all their possessions and then
exiled to foreign countries, broken and penniless. Many starved or perished
from lack of clothing and shelter and many others would have suffered
similar fates but for the donations from Grand Lodges in this country and
from humanitarians in and outside the fraternity. The dictator in that
unhappy country has assured his deluded followers that the Freemasons
and Jews, few as they are, perhaps not more than one in one hundred of
the total population, are wholly responsible for this second world war
which now threatens to devastate the entire world. Fantastic, absurd, and
false as the suggestion is, doubtless, many believe it. What else can be
·hoped for in a country where freedom of speech and of the press has been
suppressed and where it is a capital offense to listen to radio broadcasts
from other countries?
But we have wandered from the subject on which we wished to speak,
influenced, perhaps, by our futile anger and emotions. Finances, that is
the subject from which we strayed. It is a matter for congratulation that
in only two or three Grand Lodges has the problem of financing the customary Grand Lodge activities assumed major proportions. But even here
the question seems not to be one which need cause serious anxiety. Careful budgeting and sound business management are all that. are needed to
put these Grand Lodges on a sound financial footing.
The steady loss in membership during the last seven or eight years is
a matter of graver concern than some Grand Masters have seemed to
regarcl it. A few Grand Lodges have shown gains, but there are still
heavy losses in most of the Grand Jurisdictions in this country. For the
first year or two of this downward trend Grand Masters appeared not to
be worried, and some even expressed the opinion that it was a healthy
sign as the Grand Lodges were pruning out dead material and this they
thought would leave them in a sounder and healthier condition. The downward tr.end, however, has steadily continued for seven or eight years, and
the loss of seven hundred fifty thousand or a million members in that
short time is not a matter to be ignored, unpleasant though it may be. If
a discussion of the question is to be of any use, we must strive to find the
answers to two questions and these are, what is the cause and what is the
remedy for this apparently abnormal loss in membership? There are probably two main causes, Indifference and Hard Times. Regarding the second
cause, we probably shall not be able to do much about that. It suggests
the observation of Mark Twain abou.J: the weather, "We all talk about it,
but no one seems able to do anything about it." Hard times manifestly
tends to reduce Masonic membership in two ways, it causes indifferent
members to allow their memberships to lapse for nonpayment of dues, and
it .keeps . many good and desirable men from applying for membership. The
remedy which we shall suggest for loss in membership is not to reduce
Lodge and Grand Lodge dues nor to reduce the fees for degrees, these
are probably already too low. No one ever received so much for so little.
Much good has been accomplished by having competent Lodge committees
contact every member, whose membership is endangered by nonpayfnent
of dues, urging him to pay his dues if he is able to do so, and securing
remission of dues for those unable or to<;> poor to pay them. Much has
also been accomplished by having committees c9ntact those already sus-

pended and inducing them to seek restoration, although this suggests the
old adage about locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen. fo
our opinion none of the above ways is adequate, no matter how successful
one or all of them might be in particular instances.
In the long run, the principal and practically the only way, by which
a Lodge can increase its membership is by receiving petitions and conferring degrees. We .would by no means relax the rule forbidding the
soliciting of petitions for degrees. We hope every Mason will always be
able to truthfully say that he was prompted to solicit the privileges of
Freemasonry of his own free will and accord, unbiased by friends and
uninfluenced by mercenary motives, because of a favorable opinion conceived of the institution. In my humble opinion the only legitimate way
to increase Masonic membership is by so living and conducting ourselves
so that good men everywhere shall continue in greater numbers than heretofore to form a favorable opinion of Freemasonry and for that reason
shall in greater numbers seek membership in the fraternity. Let us live
such exemplary and honorable lives as men and Masons and as loyal and
patriotic citizens that the ancient prestige and honorable reputation of the
Institution may be restored and good men shall vie with each other for .
membership. It is only by establishing and maintaining an enviable reputation based on real worth and character that we may hope to acquire such
prestige that good and suitable men will be attracted to our ranks. Fifty
years ago it was a greater honor and distinction to be a Mason than it is
now. Let us reverse this and make it a greater distinction and honor to be
a Mason now than it has ever been. That will end our membership problem and financial worries.

increasing average age of the men making up our membership, due to the

These tendencies and conditions lead your Reviewer to feel that
Masonry's appeal in the future in this country will in the main be heard

Wisconsin (1939):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The symbolism of Masonry is
largely taken from the building trades and in these trades the. trestle-board
is of deep significance, for the beauty, strength and usefulness of a building
depend largely on the designs prepared for its construction by men skilled
in the art. It is no less true that the beauty, strength and usefulness of a
man are largely dependent on the designs which he inscribes on the trestleboard of his soul. No man achieves any great measure of success in life
unless he lives his life in conformity to some preconceived plan. He must
have some definite objective in life; some ideal toward which he is striving.
Just as the architect must spend years in studv and observation before

328

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

he has the requisite skill to design a beautiful building, so must we, as men
and Masons, prepare ourselves for the art of living by careful study of the
designs for living laid down by the great and good men who have lived
before us.
The officers of many Lodges are complaining that. they have no work,
that the brethren are losing interest and no longer attend Lodge. Our
ancient brethren, working in operative Masonry, were wont to draw their
designs upon the trestle-board, and when there were no designs drawn, the
Craftsmen were idle and confusion resulted. It is just as true today in
Speculative Masonry ; unless there are plans made for the Craftsmen there
will be idleness and confusion, a loss of interest and a falling off in membership. It is not enough to hold meetings twice a month, allow bills, confer
an occasional degree, and eat an occasional lunch. Man is essentially
creative in his instincts ; he must be given something to do which will make
him feel that he has a distinctive place in the Fraternity. It is the duty of
the Master to see that there are "designs drawn upon the trestle-board" ;
that "there is work laid out" for as large a part of the membership as possible. It is therefore essential that in choosing the Master of a Lodge, you
choose some one who has a genius for leadership; who is a skilled designer
and has the love of Masonry ingrained into his very soul.
What designs can be drawn upon the trestle-board?
If the Lodge has a great deal of degree work, Degree Teams can be
organized, and those who would otherwise tire of sitting on the side-lines
and watching the same degree conferred time after time would t ake a keen
interest in perfecting their work; a friendly rivalry would grow up to see
which team could reach the highest degree of perfection; and the brethren
could get a line on the best material for future officers.
Study and discussion groups could be arranged and they could present
papers on Masonic History and Symbolism before the Lodge. There is so
much misinformation about Masonic History, it is high time that the
brethren be given some authentic information.
Social gatherings could be encourag ed and some of the brethren
appointed to plan for and carry them out. The wives of Masons should
be included in these social events and they would soon get over the idea
that the Masonic Temple is a place where the husband goes to escape from
his family. Masonry would secure their good will and their husbands would
be urged by them to attend Lodge.
Masonic Play groups can be organized and plays put on in the local
L odge and in the neighboring Lodges, thereby promoting interest in
Mastmry, increasing Lodge attendance and creating a true feeling of
brotherhood between Lodges.
Such are a few of the designs which can be drawn upon the trestleboard; their number is limited only by the resourcefulness, energy and
enthusiasm of the Lodge Officers.

FUNERALS
There are a number of Funeral Rituals which might be brought up
to the present conception of what a Funeral Service should be, not a
replica of the old-time ceremony, which was one of harrowing sorrow.
The main complaint as to Masonic funerals at the present time is that
while the Ritual is sufficient, the Master, or some one else officiating, has
never had experience and, therefore, in a service of this kind, produces an
unfavorable impression on Masons and non-Masons attending.
Louisiana (1940):
(Grand Master): The performing of the last rites over the body of a
deceased Brother is one of the most sacred and solemn duties that any
Masonic Lodge is ever called upon to do. The right of a Masonic burial
has come to be regarded as universal in this country. The burial privilege
should be so dear to every Mason's heart and so conducive to increasing
the harmony and love among members, that the Worshipful Master and
Officers of a Masonic Lodge knowing that death's shafts fall indiscriminately and without warning ·will make every effort toward perfecting themselves in regard to the burial service, that it can, upon all occasions be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

creditably performed. All too little attention has been paid to this most
valuable function of ours. The average member has little conception as to
where his duty lies when the call comes for the Lodge to perform this rite.
The average Masonic burial is performed by officers who give every indication that the undertaking in which they are engaged is something unfamiliar to them and that they are not well grounded in their respective
duties. This coupled with the fact that there are as a rule hardly more
than a handful of brethren present to assist, hardly speaks well for the
esteem that the deceased Brother was held in the eyes of the Fraternity.
This is not a product of the imagination. Time after time I have witnessed the conducting of a Masonic burial when it would have been far
better for all concerned had it been omitted. If we are to continue so, we
are not conducting the burial of a deceased Brother but are in fact conducting the burial of the Masonic Fraternity iri the eyes of the world. I
have placed this matter squarely before the officers of every Lodge in this
district, stressing the necessity for a more diligent attention to this branch
of our service. Where the information is available since we have been
stressing this point, the reports are that the Masonic funerals have been
better attended and the ritualistic deliverance more impressive.
I have encouraged the use of the dispensation that permits a Lodge to
conduct its burial service under the perpetual "Lodge of Sorrow." By
eliminating the time necessary to open and close a Lodge it is found that
more brethren are in a position to leave their work and be in attendance.

"THE FOUNDING FATHERS"
There were two men so far as Masonk History records that were
responsible for changing Masonry from Operative into Speculative; one
was James Anderson, and the other was John D. Desaguliers.
The history of these two men is presented with the thought that we
will realize what these ancient brethren accomplished by their work of the

Queensland (1939):
(Past Grand Master): Who Was Jas. Anderson? History is very
meager and contradictory in relation to this brother, but his father, one
Jas. Anderson, was a substantial Burger of Aberdeen who was also a member of a Lodge in Aberdeen for 50 years, and is recorded as Master of this
Lodge, "by the Grace of God," on two occasions, viz., the years 1688 and
1694.
He had two sons, James and Adam, and although the actual date of
the birth of the elder son, James, is not known, it is recorded that he was
born in Aberdeen in about 1680, and was educated in that town, at the
Marischal College, and took the degree of M. A., and became Pastor in the
Presbyterian Church.
In this capacity he officiated in several parts of Scotland, but between
the years 1705 and 1710 he appeared in London as minister of the Scotch
Church in Swallow Street, St. James, Westminster.
In 1731, the University of Aberdeen conferred upon him a Doctor's
Degree in Divinity: "He being a gentleman well known for his extensive
learning."
He was also Chaplain to the Rt. Hon. David, Earl of Buchan.
