The Grand Lodge of England
The history of the formation of the Grand Lodge of England is well
known to you all, but it is essential to refer to it tonight to enable us to
recognize the tremendous amount of work that was formed by such men
as the Rev. Bro. J. T. Desaqulier and Bro. Geo. Payne, both of whom had
been Grand Masters; the Rev. Bro. Jas. Anderson, Bro. William Cowper,
and others.
·
Prior to 1717 there were a number of Lodges in Great Britain which
were .what is known as professional or Craft Lodges; that is, they ~ere the
remams of the Operative Masons who, owing to the decline of Church
building, found themselves almost in a position of extinction.
Each of these Lodges was an independent body unto itself which
proved added weakness to the whole Masonic body.
Early in 1717, four of these Lodges, for their own protection amalgamated, and this new body was called the Grand Lodge of Engl~nd thus
beco~in~ the 1;1other Grand Lodge of the world. During the first six ~ears,
from its mcepbon, from 1717 to 1723, no records of the proceedings were
kept, but 15 years later, when the Rev. Bro. Jas. Anderson submitted his
second rev~sion of t?e. Constitutions, he was instructed to write the history
of that period, and 1t 1s recorded that the number of Lodges had increased
from the four original Lodges to 30. In the year 1723, "William Cowper,
Esq., a Bro. of the Horn Lodge at vVestminster," became the first Secretary
of Grand Lodge.
From this date Freemasonry advanced very rapidly, and it would appear
that the. idea. in the minds of those men was to establish an International
Brotherhood of Man.
A Grand Lodge was formed in Irela.nd i~ 1729, followed by the Grand

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge ,of Scotland in 1736. France, America, and other parts of the world
Lodges were formed either directly connected with or recognized by the
Granp Lodge of England; and these accepted the Constitutions of Rev. Bro.
J as. Ari Cler son.
Masonry had possessed since the 15th century if not earlier a set of
ordinances of their own as well as a Traditional Hi~tory. These h~ve come
down to us in several forms, and it was with these that Anderson had to
deal.
. If you peruse our Book of Constitutions commencing on page 3, you
will fi.nd "The Charges of a Freemason, etc., etc.," and if you compare these,
and, m fact, the whole Constitution, with the original manuscript as well
as with the revised Constitutions by J as. Anderson, you will find that
although the verbiage is in accord with the times in which they wer~
written, the text, principles and tenets are identical.
There are many items of comparison and interest in the Anderson
Constitutions which could be dealt with tonight, if time permitted but I
propose only to briefly deal with two of these items.
'
(1} "That it is not in the power of any man or body of men to make
any alteration, or innovation in the Body of Masonry."
This has become, with us, one of the landmarks of today's Freemasonry,
and every Master-Elect solemnly accepts it when taking his obligation as
Master of a Lodge. Thus is Freemasonry kept pure.

It established the Craft into a "Fraternity," in . which, Unity of the
whole gave strength and legal right to the individual whilst he continued
a member of the Order. It gave us a democratic form of · government, in
that, all being equal, we elect our rulers annually and all business is determined by the vote of the majority.
It did away with intolerance in any form and introduced the practice
of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
It became influential in diffusing the light of Wisdom, in aiding the
strength of Reason, in illustrating the beauties of Virtue, and in lessening
the aggregate of human misery and distress.
Unfortunately, the ·Church, which, under the old regulations, we, as
Operative Masons, had been associated with for hundreds of years in building cathedrals, monasteries and abbeys, and helping financially to maintain
throughout the world, decided no longer to countenance us as speculative
Masons ; for on the 28th of April, 1738, Pope Clement XU issued a Papal
Bull, which has since been enacted by his successors, condemning Fre4'!masonry.
A Papal Bull is an edict with the seal and signature of the Pope. It
derives its -name from the leaden seal which is attached by a hempen or silk
cord. This, in medieval Latin is called " Bulla." According to these Bulls a
Freemason is excommunicated, and thus deprived of all spiritual privileges,
and rights of burial when dead.
Therefore, all Roman Catholics are enjoined in the name of the Holy
Obedience, neither to enter the Society of Freemasons, or to disseminate
its principles, to defend it, or to admit or to conceal it within their homes
or palaces or elsewhere, under the pain of excommunication, with death and
confiscation of property, without the hope of mercy.
In England, Papal Bulls were forbidden to be printed, but in R. C.
countries such as France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, etc., where there were no
such restrictions, it had tremendous force, particularly at that time.
In France, it proved particularly destructive to Freemasonry, as the
then Grand Lodge of France very largely c·o nsisted of members of the
French aristocracy.
These, rather than face excommunication, withdrew from the Craft,
thus leaving Freemasonry in the hands of men with, perhaps, less religious
scruples, but with more defiant courage.
These, owing to intense persecution, even to torture and death by the
secular arm of the church, dropped out of sight, and thus became, for the
time being, a Secret Society, but they were engaged in active political work
against the Church.
The Grand Lodge of France had disappeared, but in 1771 the Grand
Orient of France took its place, and it is reported that Freemasons of this
Grand Lodge took an active part in the storming of the Bastille in 1789.
In 1787 a Lodge was founded in Rome, in a locality known as Mount
Trinity under the eyes of the Inquisition authorities. The Lodge started
with seven members, viz., five Frenchmen, one Pole and one American.
It was known as the "Lodge of Reunion of True Friends." It existed
for two years and in that time increased its membership to 80.
It was in touch with the Grand Orient of France, the Grand Lodge of
England and several other Lodges. It was raided by the Inquisition
authorities on the 27th day of December, 1789-St. John the Evangelist's
Day.
The Inquisition authorities were spying on one Joseph Balsamo, known

(2) In the year A. D. 926 the old regulation read:
"Every Mason shall cultivate brotherly love and the love of God, and
frequent the Holy Church."
In 1663 this regulation was altered to read: "That ye shall be true men
of God and the Holy Church, and use no error or heresy by your under-.
standing, and by wise men's teaching."
Dr. Anderson, being a Presbyterian minister, could not continue to
accept this, so he submitted that all that was necessary was, "that every
Mason should belong to that religion in which all men agree, leaving their
particular creed to themselves." So we obtained the first great acknowledgment in Freemasonry, "that we put our trust in God."
It was also provided that discussion on politics or religion in the body
of Masonry was to be avoided.
This latter has also become a landmark of the Order of today.
The suggested breaking away from the Holy Church caused much discussion in Grand Lodge, because it appeared to be making an innovation
in ~asonry, but it was eventually approve.d by Grand Lodge, and thus we
obtained, not only our religious freedom, but also a universality we should
not have attained if we had continued our adherence to the one Church.
The first expansion outside the Christian faith was in 1732, when a Jew
was .admitted into Freemasonry. Since then, they have been among our
strongest supporters.
T~e conditions in England at the beginning of the 18th century were
very different to what we are accustomed to in the middle of the twentieth
century. We recognize the leniency of our laws toward offenders and the
freedom of the individual, but in 1717 there were at last -160 crim~s in the
calendar which were punishable by death, whilst the mode of living then
would. be intolerable to us now.
It was in such adverse conditions that speculative Freemasonry was
born: and. it 'taught the individual Mason self-discipline, morality, integrity
and mtelhgence, thereby helping in that great spi,ritual uplift of mankind.

What of Masonry at this period? Today we hear in the lecture of the
second degree these words, "Our Ancient Brethren Wrought in Operative
Masonry." This is literally true. Masonry at the beginning of the 18th
century was limited to Guilds of Operative Masons. It was these early
Guilds that had erected the magnificent cathedrals of England and France,
of Germany and Italy. From these cathedrals came the early fame of
the Guilds that ripened into prosperity, influence, prestige.
Masons, proud of their position, kept the basic principles of building,
the practices of the trade, as closely guarded secrets of the Fraternity known
only to themselves. Revealed to initiates only in their tiled meetings, these
professional secrets and the esoteric nature of their liturgy combined to
weave a spell that later drew all eyes to Freemasonry. ·
In a firmament emblazoned with the figures of kings and nobles, of
stone masons and cathedrals, on the 12th day of March, 1683, in the city
of Rochelle, France, a Star was Born. There were no fanfare of trumpets,
no herald angels singing, "Peace on Earth, Good Will Toward Men." But
there must have been joy in the Celestial Lodge above, as Divine Providence
sent into the world a New Hope. A babe came to the humble home of a
French Huguenot clergyman, a son, who, when he grew to man's estate
was destined to create a force so powerful that its influence carried into
every phase of the lives of all who lived after him, a force which reached
to the very foundation of civilization and changed the destiny of man, a
force which gave to man a liberty he . had never before experienced and
which has been called the Forefather of Democracy.
Two years later Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had
for nearly a century assured to French Protestants a religious liberty and a
legal status. As a result of the Revocation thousands of loyal French were
driven into exile. Among those who were forced to flee was this Huguenot
clergyman, John D. Desaguliers. Escape was difficult and dangerous, but
hiding his two year old son, John Theophilus, in a wine cask which was
loaded on a ship bound for England, Desaguliers managed to find refuge.
It is to be regretted that so little is known of this babe of the wine
cask--0nly the scanty Masonic records and a few contemporary noticesbecause Freemasonry and modern civilization owe more to him than to any
other person of the 18th century. ·
The Rev. John D. Desaguliers became chaplain of a French Huguenot
chur~h in London and there personally guided the training of his son in
the classical languages. Later, with the assistance of the boy, then only in
his teens, he founded a school at Islington. Thus at an early age, this
youth formed the habit of molding other's minds. He never lost that habit.
He became the great pedagogue of Hanoverian England.
After the death of his father, John Theophilus Desaguliers decided to
finish his studies at Oxford, where he attained fame in Experimental
Philosophy, or Science. He was given the chair of Experimental Philosophy
in Christ Church College and acclaimed the great authority of all Europe.
• In )713 he left Oxford for London, taking spacious quarters, and in
them gav~ lectures. Thus he became the first public lecturer on Science in
Europe. Success immediately greeted his audacious enterprise, because the
people of London had never seen anything like this. They crowded his
quarters. He became the fashion. The greatest noblemen of his time
honored his courses wi!h their attendance and him with their friendship.
He became one of the most important personages of all Londop, the intimate of the illustrious Sir Isaac Newton. He was elected "Fellow of the

Washington (19.39):
(Grand Orator): The history of the world is the story of its great men.
They have been the modelers, they have been the patterns of whatsoever
the general mass of men have contrived to do or attain. All things that
we see standing accomplished in the world are the material result, the practical realization and embodiment of the thoughts that dwelt in the great
men sent into the world.
Some men, we are told, have become great :because opportunity has
made them so. Others have attained distinction because they thems.elves
created the vehicles which carried their influence to posterity. Some of these
men have received the plaudits of countless millions. Others, even some of
the greatest of them, have passed all unnoticed, their names unheralded,
their fame unsung. One of these we shall discuss for a moment, one who
lived at the beginning of the 18th century. Inasmuch as present day historians state that we owe much of our modern civilization to the leaders of
that century, first let us prepare for him a brief historical background.
Prior to the early years of the 18th century it was quite generally
accepted throughout Europe that the essential principles upon which established order everywhere rested were the supreme authority of the Church; a
dogmatic Christianity; the divine right of kings; heredity, and its resultant
-inequality. There were wars-much more than there was peace; wars that
sometimes dragged on for generations, struggles not only between nations,
but continuous strife within-strife between the kings and the nobility, the
nobility and the middle classes, often between several of the stronger houses
of the nobility where all sought command of the throne at the same time.
In such a struggle in England, the House of Hanover, which represented protestantism and liberalism, was jus.t emerging victorious over the
Stuarts. Under Hanover the nobility had been granted broader privileges
which made them the envy of the rest of Europe. But in France, under the
reign of Louis XIV and his predecessors, monarchs had governed without
consulting either the princes of the blood or the nobility, never invited them
to the councils and distributed favors as one gives toys to children. For a

336

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Royal Society of London," chosen Curator and Demonstrator of that
august Society, and it was here that Desaguliers took the great doctrines
of Newton and through his experiments made them accessible and understandable to the minds of all. He invented the planetarium. His .~cientific
and philosophical treatises and books were accepted as the standa.·d works
of his day.
The social world was so carried away with enthusiasm for his lectures
that he was invited by royalty to give 'his experiments at court. His patriotic
zeal and the quality of his endeavors won for him one of the most prominent places in Hanoverian England.
If at any time in her history England needed strong leadership it was
at this moment. There had been a continuous political strife and dissension.
Morality was at a low ebb. Religiouswise that nation, as perhaps the rest
of the world, was in a chaotic state. Fads and isms had sprung up. Confusion was the order of the day. Darkness was upon the face of the deep.
On June 24, 1717, as a strategic move in the political game of· chess
between the Houses of Hanover and Stuart, the Hanoverians, just to accomplish their own selfish ends, gathered together four comparatively unimportant Masonic Lodges lying in the outskirts of London to form the
Grand Lodge of London, the·first Gran·d Lodge of Masonry. It was on that
·day that Freemasonry, all unexpectedly, started on its world mission.
For at least two centuries people on all sides had been looking for such
a thing as Freemasonry. Inquiring minds, irritated by the social and intellectual discipline imposed by the Church, had been centers of resistance,
around which formed societies which took issue with the Church. For a
long time those forces had been turning 'expectantly toward Masonry.
Every ism indeed had sought the influence of some one or more of the
Masonic Guilds, and one can well imagine the chaos in that multitude of
loosely organized associations which seemed groping without aim or purpose.
·
For a time it looked as though even this newborn Masonry was to fail,
but in 1719 Desaguliers was elected Grand Master, and he brought to Freemasonry the life it needed. He wrote most of its ritual. He brought to it
his experimental philosophy, and gave to it a touch of Newtonian Christianity, a belief in Newton's God, now and for the first time, "The Great
Artificer and Creator of the Universe." The world had been openly venal
and immoral. It had been attacking religion in self defense, and all the
more easily because religion seemed but an ancient dogma. But here was a
new idea in religion , one appealing to the intelligence instead of offering a
creed, for it was based upon analysis and reality. Here a contemplation of
nature produced certain logical facts . It taught men to think.
Desaguliers brought back into Masonry many of those who had been
in the habit of neglecting it. Further he introduced into the Fraternity a
group of the greatest noblemen of E .n gland. He it was who inaugurated
the idea of making speeches at the end of Masonic banquets. Again, he
restored the ancient custom of presenting at the conclusion of banquets
those emphatic toasts which played such an important role in the formal
life of England. These took the place of our contemporary political discussions and created the political atmosphere of the day.
Fashion is one of the most powerful of social forces. Freemasonry
under Desaguliers became the fashion . The very elite of England quickly
rushed to the order. Its Grand Masters were selected from the highest of
the nobility. Powerful indeed became our Brotherhood and one definitely
designed for the temporal influence by reason of the importance of its
leaders.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

337.

Those who developed this new order enjoyed a success that surpassed
their fondest hopes. Their aim had been a strong central Lodge around
which the other ·Lodges in and about London, then working in an incoherent
manner, could be grouped. But around this new movement the nobility, the
clergy, the army, the middle classes, all the forces of the nation gathered
in a single body.
Fifteen years after its formation the Grand Lodge of London had
become the center of all English Freemasonry and after thirty years
dominated the Masonry of the world-thanks to one man I
The latter days of Desaguliers appear to be clouded in mystery, perhaps in sadness. One report has it that misfortune overtook him and that
sorrow and poverty were his fate.
What matter it as to his end? It is what he did while here that is the
measure of the man. He took an old dying order and gave to it a philosophy
which was peculiarly his own. He added a touch of science, and then a
practical concept of the Great Architect and Organizer of the world; into
this he breathed a prayer and Speculative Freemasonry was born. Through
the force of his own personality he brought to this new institution the
important men of England, royalty, the nobility, the elite, the great minds.
Because of the purity of its principles, and because of the importance of its
early leaders brought in by Desaguliers, Freemasonry since his day has
been a living thing, pulsating with the very best that is to be found in man.
His life was a veritable fountain of light, a beacon to show the way
for countless generations. John Theophilus Desaguliers has, even in death,
ruled nations. Was it not as though the Supreme Grand Master spoke to
men's minds through him and said, "What is the cause of this confusion?"
. With all this information before us may anyone question that Freemasonry had a political and religious mission in England during the first
half of the eighteenth century.
By 1750, then, England had found a new equilibrium in both politics
and religion. Freemasonry had played a great part and had become strong'
socially and financially, with a world wide influence. With these assets it
went on triumphantly leading its crusade.
In France-Louis XIV was dead and the crowd in Paris had laugfie°d
and here and there had lighted bonfires to celebrate its joy. English
fashions, which had enchanted the French nobility and had held sway over
the minds of French writers, now made it easy for Freemasonry to establish
itself in France. English Freemasonry, desirous of achieving a triumph,
seized the opportunity to cross the channel. The Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge of London did not disdain to take his colleagues to Paris to encourage the zeal of the Lodges which were established there.
Temperamentally, the French were an entirely different people from the
English. Freemasonry to be acceptable to the French had to be noble, not
professional; mystic rather than scientific. England sought the dignity in
Masonry, France the bizarre. Jn England, it was the trowel; in France, 'the
sabre-in the ·many new degrees added by the French.
Iri spite of ban of King, in · spite of Papal Bull, Freemasonry during
the last quarter of the eighteenth century became soundly entrenched as a
part of the social life of all France, not, however, as a body cooperating
with the State as in England, but more as a personal adventure. Its presence
could be detected everywhere; in Parliament, in the army, in the monasteries, in school and at court. As in England, its leadership generally remained in the hands of the high nobility. Ten of the most influential aristocratic dynasties ·of France were engaged in spreading the Masonic message.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA .

Here, too, as in England, men were called upon to study this new religion
of Freemasonry, which was reported to be older, more beautiful, more·
philosophic than any of the organized churches.
For centuries French classes had been separated by old prejudices and
habits. Every few miles the traveler found himself in a different atmosphere,
"'.here habits, dialects and social customs had changed. Each province, each.
city, had its own measurements, its own justice, its own points of view.
Freemasonry, alone, remain~d everywhere the same and everywhere welcomed its children without prejudice as to country, race or religion. Instead
of the old spirit of class which had formerly bound together all of the noblemen of France, Freemasonry organized and substituted a good-fellowship
which broadened to include all ranks and estates. This it was that made it
the greatest social force of the century.
Loose a great social force like this in a country whose King had said,
"The State-it is I," and the results are likely to be as unforeseen and as
shocking as the new electricity Benjamin Franklin was then demonstrating
to the world.
A political revolution is never the matter of a moment. History has
shown time and again that before political revolutions great intellectual
and moral revolutions must first have been effected.
Certainly, revolution had not been the conscious aim of Freemasonry in
France; no socially minded person likes revolution; no benevolent soul
accepts lightheartedly its miseries. But consider what happened. Masonry
in France preached equality. This is a basic Masonic principle and wherever
Lodges met, members of the privileged classes, of the aristocracy, bowed
solemnly before the symbols of equality. The acceptance by the French
nobility of equality before a common altar turned the influence of Masonry
toward the intellectual and social revolution which preceded the political
one in that country. The very Freemasonry which had so intrigued the
nobility of France that they gladly spread its doctrines saw its teachings
absorbed in the cry of the people, "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity," and eventually helped to destroy that same nobility.
What of Freemasonry in the Americas?
Prior to our own Revolution thirteen small colonies were separated by
such distances that it took a letter three weeks to travel from Boston to
Georgia. There was no uniformity in the administration of those thirteen
separate governments, or in their religious affiliations, or social standards.
There were the merchant class of the North-the great land owners of the
South. There were the Puritans, the Quakers, the Catholics, the Dutch,
English, Scotch-Irish, Germans and French. All rivals and jealous of each
other. There was no unity.
·
Freemasonry alone, undertook to prepare a common foundation. It
spread throughout the Colonies among a prominent class of people. Contact
between American Lodges became closer and closer each year, and any
Mason traveling found a welcome in the Lodges he visited.
Benjamin Franklin had been the first great American apostle of Freemasonry and had busied himself in organizing not only the Society but also
a Colony-wide press with a strong Masonic influence. From 1750 to 1773
all the Masonic newspapers and Lodges were united in resisting the encroachment of the English Government. Americans remained faithful to
English civilization, but they were fast becoming conscious of an inevitable
national unity. Freemasonry, in the meantime, was still the only meeting
ground for the exchange of views of the Colonies.
Boston was the center of discontent in America. Feeling ran high in
the Puritan capital. The merchants were angry with England because of

restrictions imposed on their trade. All were ready to pay the price to get
rid of English custom officials. It took but a spark to produce the conflagration.
St. Andrew's Lodge, while not the wealthiest Lodge of Boston, could
well be termed the most active. It was headed by a famous surgeon, Joseph
Warren, an intimate ·friend of Franklin and a man whose intellectual renown and political influence had spread throughout the Colonies. Here
belonged Paul Revere and John Hancock. St. Andrew's Lodge held its
meetings at a tavern called "The Green Dragon, or the Arms of Freemasonry." The Green Dragon also was the meeting place for others who
damned the English and denounced the new tax which had just been imposed upon tea imported into the Colonies.
On Thursday afternoon, December 16, 1773, the members of St.
Andrew's Lodge proceeded to the Green Dragon for their regular communication, but the minutes show that they must have been busy elsewhere. Suddenly, out of the Tavern appeared a band of redskins strangely
masked and shabbily clad. Rushing to the docks them boarded some sloops,
proceeded to three English merchantmen in the harbor, threw overboard
342 cases of tea; returned to the sloops; regained the docks, marched to the
Green Dragon with song and hurrah, and entered the Tavern. But,
strangely, no redskins were thereafter reported to have left.
Have you ever attempted to picture the assistance given by the Masonic
order to the Colonial army? We scarcely need mention its chronic condition; untrained country lads with short enlistments; a quartermaster corps
that failed to supply clothes, food or guns; a militia that was never dependable. What was it that held this army together, that could turn it around
after a long retreat through the Jerseys and march barefoot men through
ice and snow to a Trenton midnight attack and give our country the best
Christmas present it ever received? Nothing but the spirit of one man, who
had earned the confidence and worship of the entire army-himself a member of the Masonic Order since the age of twenty-one, and acquainted with
its colony-wide influence as "the cement which binds us together."
Into this Colonial Army of Washington came those famous Lodges of
the Line. He visited them personally-in one Lodge, tradition says he
raised LaFayette.
These ten or eleven Lodges of the Line served well in their stations
and places. They kept alive morale, they restored courage, they inspired
hope. The indomitable spirit of Washington found its greatest ally in the
work of militant Masonry. May it not be that when, as President, he accepted the Mastership of Alexandria Lodge, he was making formal acknowledgment before the world of the debt the United States owed to Freemasonry?
When Benjamin Franklin was sent to Europe to seek the aid of France
in the struggle against England, on all sides the American Minister found
a people filled with enthusiasm for his country, and kindly disposed toward
him, but who adhered strictly to the policy of avoiding war.
His cause seemed hopeless. However, the Colonies could not succeed
without the help of France, and Franklin would not be denied. A new,
brilliant and very influential Lodge had but recently been organized, the
"Lodge of the Nine Sisters." Franklin joined this Lodge, and what he now
accomplished was a stroke of genius.
M. de Voltaire was the hero of the French public. He had spent his
whole. life battling error and had won the acclaim of the nation. From
royalty to tavern waiters-they worshipped him. He was the realized idol
of everyone of them; of all Frenchmen, the most French.

It was in this Lodge of the Nine Sisters Voltaire was initiated under
the direction of Franklin.
Is there not a glorious opportunity for the type of Masonic leadership
we have had before? Or is it true instead that all human things have an
end, and that even our institution of Freemasonry has been forced out of its
place in the sun?
The forces which have created havoc in Europe are desperately striving
to accomplish their ends in America and at this moment.
It was but a few weeks ago that American newspapers carried the
story of the trial of the directors of the German-American Settlement
League. One of these directors, while upon the witness stand, was asked
by the prosecuting attorney to salute the Stars and Stripes, and he responded with the stiff gesture of the Hitler salute. When the prosecutor
thundered af him, "Is that the American salute?", he responded, "No.
But it will be!"
Recently hot over the wires came these words spoken by Mussolini of
Italy, "No matter how things go we wish to hear no more about brotherhood, sisterhood and such other bastard relationships, because relationships
between s't ates are relations of force and these relations of force are the
determining elements of their policy."
Let us not laugh at that ,old adage, "The price of liberty is eternal
vigilance." There never was a time when we needed to be more alert and
watchful than now.
The world is in the throes of a struggle between democracy and
totalitarianism; the essence of the former is Justice; that of the latter,
Force. The aggressive brutality of totalitarianism appears to be riding the
crest of a triumph.
Democracy has been the great goal of man for the past two centuries.
It is recognized as that form of society which is inspired above every other
with the feeling and consciousness of the dignity of the individual man. It
is the embodiment of personal liberty.
Totalitarianism teaches contempt for human kind. Its terrorism 'degrades and destroys peoples. It corrupts character, releases every evil impulse, turns men into cowardly hypocrites and shameless informers. That is
why dictators love terrorism. The totalitarian state subordinates every
phrase of public life itself. What we call culture-religion, art, research,
higher morality, free human thought-falls under the crime of treason whenever it pursues truth through to independence. Totalitarianism sacrifices the
individual to the power of the State.
Are we asleep? Is that spirit of Masonry of old just lying dormant, or
has it passed out of existence? Is there not enough of the old fire left to
offer even a word in self _defense?
There was a day when this institution of ours took a definite place in
world affairs. There was a day when it was the meeting place for minds
opposed to tyranny. Have we forgotten?
In the early days of American history man came here to worship as he
pleased. Later, it was oppression, a disregard for right and justice that
produced an American revolution. The great Commander of the Colonial
forces was fighting for personal liberty. It was the belief of Washington
and his army that liberty, democracy, religion walked hand in hand.
During revolutionary and pre-revolutionary days the institution was
not a party; it was not a sect; it was not a school. But it bound men together in a feeling of brotherhood. It led and it guided. It was a society
of ideals, and that society was the power of powers that could make and

unmake kings, direct the course of empire, and give birth to our own
democracy. What has become of that Freemasonry that could be called a
meeting place for minds opposed to tyranny when today a small minority
may work its will upon a nation?
We have been called the most efficient social power on earth. Then
is it trite for us to remind ourselves that the price of greatness is responsibility? Is it disloyal to the Freemasonry of Desaguliers, of Voltaire
Franklin, Washington and Bolivar to urge that Freemasonry again reach
out to take its proper place in world affairs?
The time has come when our members should no longer sit and bask
in the sunshine of a glorious philosophy. There is work to do .. If Freemasonry is worth anything, if personal liberty is the precious thing we
think it is, if the heritage of worshiping as one pleases is still of any value,
then Freemasonry must again assume the responsibility of preparing for
that leadership which is to bring light ~o this generation.

The Reports of the various Grand Lodges reviewed contain the procedure in various jurisdictions. Heretofore, we have expressed our opinion,
that the English system of handling details through a Board of General
Policy and Purposes, who meet quarterly, consider the various questions
that should be submitted to the Grand Lodge at its annual session, would
be a more satisfactory way than the American way of holding Grand Lodge
sessions covering all the way from two to six days.
It would also give the members in attendance at Grand Lodge a
greater opportunity for participating in social activities and becoming better
acquainted with each other.
We think that a Grand Lodge session should be for the promotion of
good fellowship among those in attendance, rather than handling detailed
reports in which the general member is not interested. All of them have
been printed and circulated before the opening of the session so why bore
the members with a repetition?
Missouri (1939):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Did you ever hear of a "Grand
Jurisdiction"? Well, there is nothing grand about jurisdictions. It is an
invention of these people who delight to revel in the sunlight of glowing
titles. How much easier to refer to the Jurisdiction of a Grand Lodge or
a Lodge Jurisdiction? What these people really mean to say is "Gr~nd
Lodge Jurisdiction." And here is a fine opportunity to mention the public
and indiscriminate use of "Most Worshipful," "Right Worshipful" and
"Worshipful Brother." Such words are entirely proper when sparingly used
in Lodge ritual, but extremely out of place in printed publications, newspapers, and elsewhere. We only hope the time will come when it will be a
Masonic offense for one to refer to "MvV's," "RW's" and "W's" outside
a Lodge duly convened.

(Grand Masters' Conferences): The Annual Conferences of Grand Masters, U. S. A., are claimed by most of those who attend them to be what
one called "promotive" of good arising out of the interchange of ideas.
If this be so, one good result should be respect for each other's differing
viewpoints, for what most folks need is the possession of greater tolerance.
No doubt, it was inevitable that the conferences should be viewed with positive dislike, caused not only by the fear that .the deliberations might
threaten Jurisdictional sovereignty, but also by a not unreasonable conviction of their inability as a means of solving problems confronting Grand
Masters. Lately, a new note has been sounded by the Grand Master of an
important Jurisdiction who declared that prepared studies on interesting
and controversial subjects were presented to Conference, but that the time
was too limited to permit of adequate discussion and, perhaps, find a
genuinely adequate solution of the question, if that were at all possible .
"There are," he said, "forty-nine Grand Masters each of whom has his own
ideas as to how things should be done, and I doubt whether any one of them
would concede that the other was right." Doubtless, the Most Worshipful
Brother had no desire to impute intoleran<ie or stiffneckedness to anyone,
but his observations suggest a hopelessness of understanding as striking as
the hopelessness of an attempt to correctly interpret the farcical meanings
of the art of the Surrealist.

MASONRY-ITS OBJECTIVE?
The question as to just what Masonry stands for and what it should
accomplish may be gleaned from the quotations under this heading.
At the present time Masonry appears to have no set program, other
than approve a "Declaration of Principles" and passing Resolutions which
u.s ually are soon forgotten after the adjournment of the Grand Lodge.
Times change and we believe that if Masonry is to accomplish anything it must become a militant body with some objective. This does not
mean engaging in partisan politics, but a program that will demonstrate
to the world that the Craft stands for something more than lip service,
and that its members are a select body of .men ready and willing to sacrifice themselves for the good of their country.
Grand Orators aad others dwell on the part that Masonry played in the
establishment of our Republic. We wonder how many of our present members would go through the trials of Valley Forge, the experiences of Andrew
Jackson, Lewis and Clarke and other members of the Craft who built this
Nation..
When America and Masonry become "soft" we are headed for the fate
of France and some of the other Nations that are now "Provinces" of a
Conqueror and his militant nation.

(Chai,.man Co,.,.espondence Committee): Years ago my neighbor in New
York was Felix Adler, one of the greatest men of hi!\ generation, the founder of the Society of Ethical Culture.
There were Buddhists, Mohammedans, Parsees, Hebrews, Catholics
and Protestants; and all meeting in a Masonic Lodge. I had the honor of
serving as Chaplain that evening. At the close of the Lodge tho.s e men.wearing their native garbs, most of them-joined hands about the Masonic
Altar, and I asked each one to pronounce the benediction of his own religion
in his own language, and then to join with me in the Lord's Prayer all

Charles Beard, the dean of American historians, was asked how long
it would take him to sum up the teachings of American history. He said
he thought it could be done in a week, and as he thought about it longer
he thought he could do it in a day. After considering it further he said:
First-He whom the gods would destroy they first make mad.
Second-The mills of the gods grind slowly, but they grind exceeding
small.
Third-The bee always fertilizes the flower that it robs.
Fourth-When it is dark enough we can see the stars.

So a great living historian summed up the teachings of history. Just
turn those sayings over in your minds.
I remember the first time I was there and tea was brought in, and I
said, "It is a pity that we Americans do not have a tea-time where we can
relax and indulge in chit-chat." The Prime Minister said, "Remember, Doctor, we offered you Americans tea once, and you would not take it."

(G,.and Maste,.): From time to time the United Grand Lodge of England
has deemed it desirable to set forth in precise form the aims of Freemasonry
as consistently practised under its Jurisdiction since it came into being as
an organized body in 1717, and also to define the principles governing its
relations with those other Grand Lodges with which it is in fraternal
accord.
In view of representations which have been received, and of statements
recently issued which have distorted or obscured the true objects of Freemasonry, it is once again considered necessary to emphasize certain fundamental principles of the Order.
The first :ondition of admission into, and membership of, the Order
is a belief in the Supreme Being. This is essential and admits of no compromise.
The Bible referred to by Freemasons as the Volume of the Sacred
Law, is alway~ open in the Lodges. Every candidate is required to take
his obligation on that book or on the Volume which is held by his particular
creed to impart sanctity to an oath or promise taken upon it.
Everyone who enters Freemasonry is, at the outset, strictly forbidden
to countenance any act which may have .a tendency to subvert the peace
and good order of society; he must pay due obedience to the law of any
state in which he resides or which may afford .him protection, and he must
never be remiss in the allegiance due to the Sovereign of his native land.
While English Freemasonry thus inculcates in each of its members the
duties of loyalty and citizenship, it reserves to the individual the right to
hold his own opinion with regard to public affairs. But neither in any
Lodge, nor at any time in his capacity as a Freemason, is he permitted to
discuss or to advance his views on theological or political questions.
The Grand Lodge has always consistently refused to express any
opinion on questions of foreign or domestic state policy either at 'home or
abroad, and it will not allow its name to be associated with any action,
however humanitarian it may appear to be, which infringes its unalterable
policy of standing aloof from every question affecting the relations between
one g-0vernment and another, or between political parties, or questions as to
rival theories of government.
The Grand Lodge is aware that there do exist Bodies, styling themselves Freemasons, which do not adhere to these principles, and while that
attitude exists the Grand Lodge of England refuses absolutely to have any
relations with such Bodies, or to regard them as Freemasons.
The Grand Lodge of England is a Sovereign and independent BC1dy
practising Freemasonry only within the three Degrees and only within tht
limits defined in its Constitution as "pure Antient Masonry." It does not
recognize or admit the existence of any superior Masomc authority, however styled.
On more than one occasion the Grand Lodge has refused, and will continue to refuse, to participate in Conferences with so called International
Associations claiming to represent Freemasonry, which admit to member-

ship Bodies failing to conform strictly to the principles upon which the
Grand Lodge of England is founded. The Grand Lodge does not admit
any such claim, nor can its views be represented by any such Association.
There is no secret with regard to any of the basic principles of Freemasonry, so_me of which h.aye been stated above. The Grand Lodge will
alwa:l'.'s consider the recognition of those Grand Lodges which profess, and
practise, an~ can show that they have consistently professed and practised
those established and unaltered principles, but in no circumstances will it
enter into discussion with a view to any new or varied interpretation. of
the?1. They must be accepted and practised wholeheartedly and in their
entirety by those who desire to be recognized as Freemasons by the United
Grand Lodge of England.

Freemasonry is not to be entered into through mere curiosity, ambition
for honors 1 or in the hope of personal gain or advancement. Admission
must not b e sought for mercenary or other unworthy motives. The aim of
the true Freemason is to cultivate a brotherly feeling among men, and to
help, aid and assist whomsoever he can.
•
The right to petition for the degrees of Ancient Craft Mas~nry is
rarely denied to any man, but this right goes no further than granting t~e
privilege of petitioning, and all who petition are not admitted. The Masonic
Fraternity does not solicit members, but wants and welcomes only men of
high character and integrity, who seek admission entirely of their own free
will and accord. Should a petitioner be accepted, he should understand
that he will get no more out of Masonry than he puts into it, that to receive
benefits from such a society one must devote himself to its interests.
I hereby certify that I have read the foregoing and fully understand the
principles and purposes of the Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons
as explained therein.

When I have been asked, as several times has happened, what attitude
Masonry takes toward some political or semi-political cause or what
Masonry is doing to assist some humanitarian movement which has political
or g~vernmental aspects, my answer has been to hand the questioner a
co~y of the. above statement. The Craft survives, and has through the centur!es survived, only he~ause it avoids the discussion of political and sect:inan problems. Of this we need periodical reminders in stirring times
hke these.

(Grand Master): Copying somewhat from a law lately enacted by the
Grand Lodge of the State of New Jersey, I recommend that the Grand

tha~ . each constituent Lodge may have a supply, one to accompany each

Principles and "Rurposes of Freemasonry
Grand Jurisdiction of the State of New Hampshire
Freemasonry is neither a religion, a political organization nor a social
club. It interferes with none of these, but has for its f~undation the
bas.ic pri~ciple,s of the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man. It
believes m a Supreme Being, the immortality of the soul and that the
~oly _Bible is the i~estima~le gift of God to man as the rul~ and guide for
his. f~1th and practice. It 1s a Fraternity or Brotherhood pledged to the
bm.ldmg o~ character--thoughts, words, motives and deeds being the materials used.
Freemasonry strives to teach man the duty he owes to God his country, his neighbor and himself. It inculcates the practice of ~irtue and
morality in daily conduct, and conveys its teachings through rites and
symbols.
The Masonic Fraternity is in no sense an insurance society · neither
does it pay benefits in case of sickness or death. In a correct a~d broad
sen.se: it i.s ?oth educational and charitable. It extends such assistance only
as 1t 1s w11lmg and able to grant. It knowingly admits none to membership
except those who are able to provide for themselves and those dependent
upon them. It expects and requires that its members contribute to the
support of the Masonic Home and other Masonic charities.
Freemasonry teaches, and gives opportunity to its members to inculcate
morality, honesty and integrity in all walks of life, and renders assistance to
worthy members to a limited extent. It expects its members to obey the
moral law and to practice charity toward all mankind. It believes its members should have a strong desire to aid their fellow creatures. It has its
own laws, rules and regulations, and requires a strict obedience thereto.

New Jersey (1939):
(Grand Master) : Freemasonry is a charitable, benevolent, educational
and religious society. Its principles are proclaimed as widely as men will
hear. Its only secrets are in its methods of recognition and of symbolic
instruction.
'
Believing these things, this Grand Lodge affirms its continued adherence to that ancient and approved rule of Freemasonry which forbids the
discussion in Masonic meetings of creeds, politics, or other topics likely to
excite personal animosities.
It further affirms its conviction that it is 11ot only contrary to the fun.
damental principles of Freemasonry, but dangerous to its unity, strength,
usefulness and welfare, for Masonic Bodies to take action or attempt to
exercise pressure or influence, for or against any legislation, or in any way
to attempt to procure the election or appointment of governmental officials or to influence them, whether or not members of the Fraternity, in
the performance of their official duties. The true Freemason will act in civil
life according to his individual judgment and the dictates of his conscience.

MEMBERSHIP
Delmar E. Darrah, Past Grand Master of Illinois, expresses his opinion
as far as Masonry is concerned in the following quotation:
"If Masonry is going to succeed in the future it will have to change
some of its practices. Heretofore it has been possible to sell a man three
degrees for a stipulated sum of money, but today men are not satisfied
merely to purchase degrees. They want something more; they want enter-.
tainment; fellowship. They want something that will furnish entertainment
for the members of their families. The Masonic Lodge of the future is
going to be that Lodge in which degrees are a means to an end-the end
will have to be fraternal relations--the privileges of which are human
fellowship."
A check of statistics shows that at the present time very few young
men are entering the Masonic Fraternity. It might be well then for the
Craft to hold out some inducement to the "Future Generation."
The following verse may illustrate better than a thousand words what
Masonry must do if it is going to continue as a vital organization.
When we build a house we have a plan;
We start with a boy when we build a man;
A good foundation is a vital thing
If you're building a man or anything.
The longer it lasts, the more care we should take
To follow the plan, and make no mistake;
We can change a house and make repair,
But a man lives forever, so build with care.

Missouri (1939):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Before the period A. I. (Anno
Influx), the average Master of a Lodge was the village doctor, the lawyer,
merchant, minister---conservative, dignified men of reputation and standing
in the community. After the influx, a younger group of men, many of whom
were seeking only the glamour of office, began the gradual displacement
of these conservative elements until there came into the forefront the parrot
ritualist, the Brother with the big Past Master jewel and a love for Masonic
nomenclature to the nth degree. I would not have you believe this true in
every' community, but our readers will recognize such instances. With
leadership gone, a program of charitable, educational and social activity
ceases to exist. Finances exist only for feeds, for show, for jewels. With
lack of a definite program, individual interest wanes and Masonic influence
is gone.
The needs of Masonry today are more effective leadership-a sustained
program of charitable, educational and social activity-more friendliness,
more companionship-more brotherhood.

Pennsylvania (1939):
{Grand Master): A Lodge has no defined territorial Jurisdiction. It may
possibly work out that way, but no Lodge has the property right to any
man who may reside in its community. The only reason inquiry is made
of a Lodge nearest to the residence of a petitioner, is to ascertain whether
Masonic objection exists, so that the Fraternity may be protected from the
admission of those whose standing in society would make them unworthy.
The theory being that those nearest his residence would know him best.

South Dakota (1939):
(Grand Master): Next to the collection of dues in our Lodges, the subject which should be uppermost in our minds, is the Suspension of Members for Non-payment of Dues.
·
If you will examine the rec,:ords of our Lodges you will find in most
cases that the number of members suspended for non-payment of dues has
exceeded the increase from all sources. In other words, we have suspended
more members than we have raised, admitted and reinstated. There is need
for giving serious thought to the question of salvaging lost man power that
was once an asset.
·
Not so many years ago we considered them excellent material for
Masonry and not a dissenting ballot was cast to question that belief. The
responsibility comes right back to our own door. Surely we would not be so
arrogant as to say that "we exposed them to Masonry, but it didn't take."
It apparently· didn't "take," but mig·ht we not well ponder the possibility
of our failure to make it "take." Even so, no one would dare say that the
suspended members, who are now out of the fold, as a class were really
undesirable. Unfortunately some of them are, were, and perhaps always will
be that type, but it is a sad commentary on our judgment if we have such
a high mortality for that reason alone.
Frequently in our social and civic life we meet men from whom we
learn that they were formerly members but allowed themselves to be suspended. When interrogated as to the reason, they have no definite answer.
They usually comment on the virtues of the Order; they have not lost faith;
they are good substantial men, but they have just drifted away. And drifting, my Brethren, is a tragedy. This is so easily ignored, for, with a shrug
of the shoulders, we exclaim, "Well, it's up to him. He allowed himself to
be susQended."
We are all too well aware of the delusion of mere numbers. Membership statistics merely indicate the material trend, but do not necessarilv
reveal spiritual power.
Referring again to the "lost battalion," as I might term the suspended
Brethren who have been out of Masonry less than five years, there is here
a great field for the demonstration of some real brotherly love and friendship.
Some may be unworthy, but a vast number were recently labelled as worthy
and well-qualified and they still are. They have left us for reasons best
known to themselves, for in many instances they were too proud to volunteer the real reason, and we assumed that it was none of our business to
inquire into their private or personal affairs. They were hut recently
interested and if approached in a friendly, brotherly manner, their appreciation o~ that beauty, that dignity, that solemnity, that ideal of Masonry, may
be rekindled. We, as members of a great Fraternity, owe to those Brethren
whose membership has lapsed the most friendly support. It may do them
an inestimable amount of good, and then, too, we will have fulfilled our
obligations. Bear in mind that many Masons whose membership has lapsed
have been ashamed to admit it.
I therefore recommend this procedure to save the "lost battalion":
Make Masonry so attractive that the former ardor will glow! Keep Masonry
so alive and active that it will serve as a great fraternal magnet! And, last
of all, so live Masonry that others! seeing its reflection in you, may be
stimulated to higher deeds and zeal to belong again to the institution,
Masonry!

OFFENSES
The edicts, rules and regulations of Grand Masters and Grand Lodges
prohibiting gambling, lotteries, and liquor seem to have produced some
effect, as there is less criticism along this line than for the past two years
and less legislation. We still believe that effort to regulate the appetites
and desires of men, even under Masonic auspices, will prove ineffectual.
The less legislation that is enacted to govern the appetites and passions of
men and more attention paid to the promotion of good fellowship cultivation of Masonic ideals, and the development of Americanism th~oughout
the Nation, the better the results will be for the Masonic Fraternity.

Connecticut (1940):
(Grand Master): The original structure of American Masonry has during the years undergone a large expansion, not only through the development of additional degrees and ceremonies, but also by means of the establishment of numerous correlative orders, membership in which is dependent
either on membership in a Masonic Lodge or on relationship to a member
of a Masonic Lodge.
.
While this expansion of the Masonic ideals is valuable in that it creates
more fields for. individual work through the variety of rituals and ceremonies, yet it must never be forgotten that any organization. which bases its
membership on Masonic relationship thereby accepts a definite responsibility to avoid any conduct or action which might derogate against the
honor and.integrity of Ancient Craft Masonty. The world at large does
not recognize the distinction that we maintain but criticizes thoughtless
action oil the part of any correlative body as though it were a Masonic
misdemeanor.
For many years the Grand Lodge of Connecticut has ruled that the
conducting of games of chance to raise money for Masonic purposes is improper and un-Masonic. I am happy to report that our constituent Lodges
continue to uphold this rule and that the leaders of correlated organizations
have assured me of their fullest cooperation in its ·support. Moreover the
Grand Lodges of Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, by resolution and edict
have this past year reaffirmed their position against gambling for Masonic
purposes.
Although the playing of Bingo under certain restrictions has been
legalized .in Connecticut, and while a few less careful thinkers inight like to
see our Masonic standards correspondingly liberalized, games of chance for
Masonic purposes are still un-Masonic and I am confident that the members of this Grand Lodge will never permit a lowering of our standards or
a cheapening· of true Masonic ideals by any change in our present rules.
Delaware (1939):
(Grand Master): During the year I have been approached on the question of whether an organization, the prerequisite for membership being
membership in the Masonic Fraternity, could conduct Bingo games as a
means of raising funds. My answer was that they could not. Masonic Law
under Section 30 clearly states that gambling is not permitted and those
participating are guilty tif un-.Ma~onic conduct; I further stated that should
they carry out their plans I had no alternative but to prefer charges against
those responsible for the violation.
The ·principles and purposes of Masonry are too noble to be sacrificed
for the sake of paltry dollars, let alone the fact that in recognizing such
practices we condone disrespect for civil authority.

North Dakota (1938):
(Grand Master): However, after reading our Masonic Code and a digest
of treatment of similar matters in 'other jurisdictions, I have reached the
conclusion that the scheme or device as contemplated to be used by this
organization appeals to the same gambling instinct in an individual and
accomplishes the same purpose as though it were an out and out lottery.
It is the aim and desire of the Masonic institution that no one connected
with it should do any act which should bring the organization into disrepute.
The stand of our Fraternity relative to gambling, liquor, Sunday observance
and the like, has been definitely and clearly defined. It is none of our concern if any other organizations permit any of these devices to further sales
or raise money even though the purpose for which the money is raised may
be charitably mentioned. The general effect of a scheme such as suggested
is identical with that of a lottery and I do not believe that it would be in
keeping with the principles of our Fraternity.

West Australia (1939):
(Reviewer): When reading the Proceedings of the different Grand
Lodges, and especially the denunciations of gambling, I sometimes ask
myself whether Lodge representatives attending Annual Communications
at which those denunciations are delivered ever listen to them or have the

Jurisdictions have repeatedly declared that Lodges must neither sponsor,
originate nor become associated with games of chance or gambling devices,

Masters have repeatedly described at those communications that when such
gambling was initiated or sponsored by organizations like the Shrine or the
Grotto (which predicate their membership on the Masonic qualification),
those distinguished Grand Masters have taken prompt action against the
offenders. For years past Grand Masters have repeatedly issued edicts
against these practices and had them transmitted to the Lodges within their
jurisdiction. Yet these infractions of Masonic law persist.

The Grand Master of Massachusetts, on his visitation, presented
Grand Master Lewis with the Henry Price jewel. Henry Price was the
first Grand Master of the provincial Grand Lodge at Boston which Massachusetts claims as the beginning of things Masonic in this country. Mention
that in Pennsylvania, however, and you can get a fight in a hurry, so this
particular ceremony may, in the next century take. on added meaning.
Doubtless our grandchildren will be told (in Massachusetts) that it indicates that Pennsylvania's Grand Master, in accepting it, conceded the
claims of Massachusetts, while in Pennsylvania they will learn that by coming to Pennsylvania to do the foul deed, the Bay State recognized the
latter's seniority. Just what difference it all makes, we never could quite
fathom, but we doubt not that the controversy will still be raging down
through the centuries.

OFF THE RECORD

As you know, except for one period of thirty years, a member of our
House has occupied the Throne of Grand Master for over a century and a
half. For the past sixty-five years this Throne has been filled first by our
grandfather, King Edward VII, and then by our great uncle, the Duke of
Connaught, who is beloved by men and Masons throughout the world.
During this period, English Freemasonry has prospered in a remarkable
manner. It will be ·no easy task for any Mason to follow in their footsteps
but I have every confidence that you will succeed in the office to which .
you have been elected by your brethren.

stories or quotations from Grand Masters, Grand Orators, Chairmen of
Correspondence Committees and others.

and instructive to the reader and relieve the monotony of our formal report.
. A story is told.of an American sergeant during the battle of Gettysburg.
Under cover of smoke and some protecting woods, he had carried his flag
forward until it was several hundred yards in advance of his regiment. The
<;olonel in command saw, as he thought, that the flag had gotten too far
ahead of the soldiers and he sent orders to the sergeant "Bring the flag
~ack to the. regiment." But the sergeant's only reply was to say to the
messenger, "¥ ou tell the colonel to bring the regim.ent up to the flag."

The matter of the number of Masons who signed the Declaration of
Independence seems to produce as many different opinions as does the
number of "Landmarks." Grand Master Patterson stated that 29 out of 56
signers were Masons. W. L. Boyden in his "Masonic Presidents, VicePresidents and Signers," names 15. Of course in the twelve years that have
passed since the book referred to was published, the additional 14 may have
been discovered.
Some years ago "The Square and Compasses" of New Orleans, quoting
the "Home Journal" of Kentucky listed 23 signers, but in that number
was the name of John Adams, who was not a Mason, according to his son,
John Quincy Adams ("Letters on the Masonic Institution," pp. 10-12).

During this year was celebrated the greatest event in Canadian Masonic
history; the Bicentennial of the founding of the .first Masonic Lodge in
our Dominion at Annapolis, N. S.
The founder of Freemasonry in that Province, of which New Bruns.wick was then a part, was Erasmus James Phillips, a major in a regiment
of British infantry stationed in Nova Scotia. While in Boston in 1737, be
became a Mason. On his return to Nova Scotia he carried with him a Warrant from Henry Price, then Grand Master of Massachusetts, appointing
him Provinci"al Grand Master for Nova Scotia. He formed a Lodge in the
garrison at Annapolis in July, 1738. Thus from this small beginning.
Masonry in Canada has grown to a membership of 171,600.

The Grand Secretary of Arkansas called the attention of Grand Lodge
to a decision of the Supreme Court of Arkansas in the case of Franklin
vs. Parallel Lodge, rendered October 3, 1938, in which it was held that a
provision, such as found in the Constitution of Grand Lodge, to the effect
that upon demise of any subordinate Lodge its property belongs to and
is vested in the Grand Lodge, was contrary to public policy and void as a
confiseation without judicial process.

"In one of the schools in a remote section, -the teacher secured a pair

This story, alone, is worth all of the cost of the entire project.

I took part in a very interesting meeting in London last June, as your ·

180 years old being founded somewhere about 1754 or 1756. They were one
of the Lod~es which helped to found the Grand Lodge which joined
shortly afterward with another Grand Lodge to found the Grand Lodge of
Massachusetts, and they have been active in the Fi~st Battalion of the
Worcestershire Regiment ever since, and are a very active Lodge now.
As you know, the Guards guard the Tower of London. For three weeks
in the year the Guards . go on. maneuvers, and a line regiment is called on
to undertake the duty of mounting guarcj. in that ancient fortress. The
Worcestershire Regiment received that privilege this Summer, and their

POLITICS
it is to be regretted that too often members of the Masonic. Fraternity
use ·their connection with the Craft to promote their political aims and ambitions. This is evidenced in a number of Masonic publications who publish
advertisements of aspirants for public office and print their Masonic affiliations in connection with the same.
While these publications are not recognized as speaking for Masonry
the general public view them· as such.
.
Perhaps the best solution will be to prohibit any publication, under
private management, to us~ the word "Masonry'.' : in connect~~n therewith,
and also make it a Masonic offense for ·an aspirant for political office to
advertise his connection with the Craft.
·

363

Florida (1939):

(Grand Master): One of the sore spots in connection with. Masonry in this
Grand Jurisdiction, and I assume it is no different from others, is the man.ner in which some political candidates attempt to use Masonry to fur.t her
their own political anibitioris. It is not only unseemingly on the part of
any Mason to parade his Masonic affiliation to serve his political ambiti'ons,
but it holds the Order up for ridicule by the non-Mason and the general
public..
It is a standing joke in many parts of the Grand Jurisdiction that you
can always tell when a political campaign year is approaching by the influx
of would-be political officers into Masonic meetings and the very sudden
interest they acquire in Masonic affairs. If they are elected, they are rarely
seen in Lodge until the next campaign. If defeated, they are not seen · in
Lodge, and unless they are going to make a retry for some political office
they want, the chances are that they will drop out for non-payment of dues
only to rush in and pay up back dues and get themselves reinstated if the
political office fever rises again.

Political office seekers have been heard to declaim from the platform
before a public audience that .they were "High Masons," even as high as
the 33rd degree.
These Masonic misfits do not know, as the Masons know ana the
public knows, that they are really doing themselves an injury ~s well as
bringing more or less shame on the Masonic Fraternity.
·
I do not know if it is practicable to frame any law of Masonry that
would put a period on this practice, but I hope the Jurisprudence Committee of this Grand Lodge will take the matter under advisement and if
at all possible, draft a regulation that will at least tend to put the soft
pedal on it.
'
'

148 pages, House document No. 529) and which could not be analyzed by

We all believe in education of our children, but where appropriations
are made by the feleral government for education it should be for taxsupported free public schools only. As good citizens of the United States
of America we should be and are proud of our public school system, that
is, "free public schools open to all children without distinction as to race,
color or religion, or whether citizen or alien"; purely an American institu. tion, founded by our ancestors who fought the war of the revolution ·in
the belief that a democracy, where all have a voice in the government, can
only endure if the citizens are educated sufficiently to study and understand
the constitution and laws by which they live and practice the rights of
citizenship, and to that end should labor to improve, protect and preserve
our tax-supported free public schools.

RITUAL
In a large number of jurisdictions perfection in the Ritual has become
the trademark of a Mason. Perhaps the sooner we get back to the original
idea that Masonry is to unite men who might otherwise have remained at a
"perpetual distance" rather than a strict adherence to form, ritual and ceremonies, the sooner Masonry will become a vital institution. '
Arizona (1939):
'(Grand Master): Although I have seen few of our Lodges confer degrees during the past year, so cannot say how rigidly our ritual is followed
when initiating, passing, and raising candidates, I have listened critically
to the opening and closing ceremonies, and have been struck by the
numerous minor variations used in many Lodges. In very few of them have
the officers been letter-perfect in their parts, and in some instances rather
serious errors were noted.
I am positive that this situation is not in any way the fault of our
Grand Lecturer~ it would be hard to find a more diligent and conscientious
officer than he is. Neither do I blame the Deputy ·Lecturers. It is, I believe,
our system that is at fault. As long as the work must be learned by listening to brothers who must depend almost entirely upon more or less unreliable memories, and the Lodge officers and Deputy Lecturers have a
chance to check their renderings during only a week or two each year,
mistakes are sure t'o be made.
I am not one who believes that complete accuracy in rendering our
ritual is essential; I should much rather hear it given fluently and forcefully, with expression and feeling, even if to some extent inaccurately, than
to. listen to a letter-perfect rendition delivered haltingly or monotonously.
The thing I really deplore is the unnecessarily excessive amount ·of time
that must be devoted to the task of learning their work by most of the
officers under our present system. Many of' us experience extreme difficulty
in memorizing material wholly by ear, and are greatly aided if we can also
use our eyes, especially as we can then go over the work repeatedly whenever we have leisure to do so.
I am convinced that much · of the time now consumed in learning the
ritual could be spent much more constructively in making our stated meetings more enjoyable and instructive, and that the adoption and distribution
of an initial-letter key would not only materially shorten the time now

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GKAND LODGE OF.CALIFORNIA

devoted to memorization, but would result in much more uniform and
correct ritualistic work.
I am aware .of the fact that this Grand Lodge has voted adversely _on
this plan, but those of us who wish to have Lod!Se officers put t~e ?1a1or
part of their time and thoughts upon the. really important an? s1gmficant
things that we should be doing are not discouraged. We .reahze that few
.improvements are adopted when firs.t sug_gest.ed. We ~n~w .th.at the plan
n1entioned is used with complete satisfaction m many 1urisd1cttons, so we
shall surely not be doing anything reprehensible by adopting it.
I strongly recommend, therefore, that our Grand Lectu~er prepare
an initial-letter key of all our ritualistic work, occasionally usmg two or
perhaps three letters for a word when experience ha_s shown that the wrong
one is apt to be used, that this initial-letter key be printed,, that the necessary .
amount to cover printing be budgeted, and that five copies be sent to each
Lodge in the state, to be entrusted to the Mast~r, the Senior Warden, the
Junior Warden, the Senior Deacon, and the Jumor Deacon.
I further recommend, if the preceding resolution is approved, that
the use of the keys be forbidden during the time a Lodge is in session.
They are to be used solely as aids in memorizing the work.

are not easily read by a person who has had any experience with ritualistic
work, and it is begging the question to presume that adequate protection
would be given to such ciphers as to prevent their falling into improper

with such ciphers. They may be found in unlocked drawers of desks in

this seems to be the most effective manner in which to accomplish the
result. Your committee, therefore, recommends that no cipher be adopted
by this Grand Lodge.

West Australia (1939):
(Reviewer) : In Mississippi the Committee on Masonic Law and J urisprudence advises the Grand Master on his rulings, which seems to me a much super.for method to the more usual practice of sitting in judgment on his decisions
after they have been rendered. The following, which summarizes one of
the cases submitted and dealt with, is the only one of outstanding interest
to the Craft in general, and also points to the curious ideas of a certain
type of Mason relating to Lodge ceremonies. A Lodge proposed to hold
a barbecue, which, of course, is the open-air roasting of an animal for
consumption by attendant picnickers. I have witnessed it on our Perth
esplanade in bygone days, and on the ice on the River Thames in London
when I was a child, but on neither of those occasions was the affair styled
a barbeque, as the Lodge appears to have spelled it, although as it is a
Haytian word, the Lodge spelling may be correct. The Lodge seems to
have conceived that there was a certain harmony, if not affinity, between
the Sublime Degree of a Master Mason and the roasting of an animal, provided it could be combined with a Grand Master's dispensation to perform
the cereinony in the open air more or less in the vicinity of the roast, in
the sure and certain hope of the spot being insulated against cowans and
eavesdroppers, and buttressed by the expected presenc of Grand Lodge
officers, and eke a special team from a neighboring city to confer the degree
in the presence of the brethren and t he roasted ox. But the Committee on
Wet Blankets, or rather Jurisprudence, unfeelingly said it did not think the
Grand 'Master had authority to grant such a dispensation, and for its own
part exhibited a thoroughly useful dislike for open-air degree ceremonies.
And then it added the last straw which broke the camel's back by saying,
"We are in favor of encouraging Masons to meet in camps and club houses
in fraternal companionship and hilarity, but we think they should confer
their deg'r ees 'in the Lodge room, and then repair to the· place of festivities."
With which opinion this scribe heartily agrees. It is in tune wtih the eternal
fitness of things, but the degree we call "Sublime" owing to its splendid
lessons (which need not be mentioned here) combined with the odor of
roasted ox ·assailing one's olfactory organs, and in the questionable privacy

(Reviewer) : A matter that frequently astonishes the writer when reviewing the volumes of Proceedings is the emphasis placed by Grand Masters on the work of the Grand Lecturers. This lecturing is imaginary rather
than real, for what is mainly done is to teach the Lodges how to perform
the ritualistic work. It is, of course, proper that the degree work should
be performed correctly and impressively, but the system of lecturers does
not seem to me to make for such efficiency as we obtain by the Master
instructing his brethren at the rehearsals, and our Grand Inspectors passing
on the results. Still, it is North Carolina's affair, and the system seems to
satisfy Grand Lodge, but the same system--one prevalent in most of the
United States-seems to me to negative the oft-repeated explanation of a
Master's duty: "To employ and instruct his brethren in. Freemasonry."

fact. I know brethren in Australia as impressed with their powers of improving the ritual as the Spanish king of several centuries ago was of his
abilities as a demiurge, when he impiously declared that had the Creator
. consulted him at the Creation, he could have saved Him many absurdities.
Loyalty to the ritual as "well as to Masonry, brethren.

Maine (1939):
(Grand Master:) Sec. 137 of the Constitutions of the Grand Lodge ordains:
"No Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons can legally assemble
in this State under a warrant or charter granted by any foreign Masonic
power."
Information has been received that Lodges of other grand jurisdictions
have been invited by Lodges in this State to assemble in Maine Lodge
rooms and there work the degrees upon their candidates under a ritual
of the grand jurisdiction from which each Lodge came. This method, of'
course, is contrary to the provisions of said Section 137, and no Lodge in
this grand jurisdiction should encourage such procedure. The inter-visitations of members and officers of the Lodges of the several states should
be encouraged, as such course tends to promote general interest and enthusiasm, increases attendance and lays the foundations for splendid friendships. There is, however, a right way by which it may be done. The
proper method of proceeding is plainly set forth in the Maine Masonic
·Text Book.
We know that the aforesaid procedure, thoughtlessly done, was intended to have been in the interest of the Cr~ft; we hope, however, that
officers of host Lodges will be more careful in the future.

Montana:
The address of the Grand Master is comparatively brief, as befits a

The Grand Master closes his address under · the caption, "Chief Glory
of California." He paints in eloquent terms a beautiful word picture of the

One activity in California Masonry the value of which is evidenced by
the almost ·unanimous response of the Fraternity is the observance of
"Public Schools Week." From no jurisdiction have we found such glowing
results from this enterprise as in this active Masonic state. Reports from
the press, from the State Department of Education, from teachers and
students, all testify to the interest on the part of the public in this observance and fully justifies .the assertion that the program is worthwhile.
Public Schools \Veek Observance has been carried on under the
auspices of the Grand Lodge for eighteen years and the popularity of the
activity is attested by .the fact that practically every city, town and hamlet
in the State recognizes its value and endorses its aims and purposes. ·

I once heard an American Grand Secretary spoken of as "A Grand
Master's backbone." · I don't think the speaker meant the vertebral column; rather he meant, I think, the Grand Mast-er's mainstay. And, indeed,
everywhere a good Grand Secretary is as valuable "as Solomon's virtuous
woman-"above pearls." At most American annual communications Grand
Masters deliver appreciations of their Grand Secretaries, and these are well
deserved.
Attention has been given, not only to perfection in the wording of the
ritual, but also to expression and emphasis, says the Grand Lecturer's report. " Officers are encouraged to lend themselves whole-heartedly to the
work and attempt to live the part they are exemplifying." Let us hope they
don't exemplify too artistically. The American third is sufficiently strenuous without the super-imposition of realism.
There is a certain hint of irony in the Grand Lecturer's reference to
the well-known Lodge complaint: "We have no work," which Lodge officers regard as synonymous with degrees, and in the absence of the one
and only "work" nothing else counts. But the Grand Lecturer points to
the educative side of the Craft as proof. Yet I verily believe that the average Lodge officer, if asked to spell "work" would reply "D-e-g-r-e-e-s,"
poor fellow!
