Tennessee:
The committee on Twentieth Annual Ob~ervance of Public Schools
Week reported a very successful observance during the last week in September. This Public Schools Week was instituted in 1920 because of the crisis
with which the public school system in America was then confronted. There
was such a scarcity of teachers that more than 18,000 schools had been
closed. Today in California there is probably not another anniversary with
the exception of Independence Day and Thanksgiving and Christmas, which
is so widely observed as is Public Schools ·Week.
Wednesday, October 11th, the second day of the Annual Communication was devoted to Masonic Day at Treasure Island, site of the Golden
Gate International Exposition. Approximately half of the 43,000 people who
attended the Fair on that day were there because it was Masonic Day.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation of the
world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L .), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000-5923.
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology
is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
1.dd 3760 to the common era. Thus : 1923 and 3760-5683. After
September add another year.
'
.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno lnventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the year of discovery."
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the temple of
Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.), "in the year of the
deposit."
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commencc their era with the organization of their
Order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the qrdcr."
·
From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118 from 1923---:-805.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of .the blessing of
Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis (A. B.),
"in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing. Thus 1923 and
1913-3836.

The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the Mark
Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the Royal Arch.
The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred
in a Council of High Priests upon those who have been regularly elected
to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular
because they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meanirtg
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the Royal
Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master. They are
called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are the
Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes
from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the temple at Jerusalem
from the Mohammedans.
'
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd,
inclusive. In the Southern jurisdiction of the United States (which includes
all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River)
the organization of the different Bodies, and the degrees conferred by them,
are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to
18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to 30°; Consistory, 31 ° to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33 °.
In the Northern jurisdiction (which includes all states north of the
Ohio river and east .of the Mississippi river) the degrees conferred are:
Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council Princes of Jerusalem, 15°
and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18° ; Consistory, 19° to 32°: Supreme
Council, 33°.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly speaking,
they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the
one called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United
States.
·
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the Cryptic
and the Templar degree.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the Entered
Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They are called
Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.

Lloyd Earl Wilson
Grand Master 1940 - 1941

Lloyd Earl Wilson was born in Portland, Oregon, August 16, 1895. He
received his elementary education in Portland and graduated from the high
school in Salem, Oregon. He attended Drake University at Des Moines, Iowa,
leaving that institution at the outbreak of the first World War to enlist in the
service of his country. A sergeant in Company "C," 8th Field Signal Battalion,
4th Division, Regular Army, he served practically all of his eighteen months in
France with the 39th Infantry, 4th Division, participating in four major
offensive and one major defensive campaigns. Following the Armistice he
served in the Army of Occupation in Germany.
Our outgoing Grand Master had a very active business career following
his return from Europe. He was employed by the B. F. Goodrich Rubber
Company in San Francisco from November, 1919 to March, 1921, when he
was transferred to San Diego as Service Manager and Sales Representative.
In these capacities he worked for that Company until his resignation in 1922
to accept a position as Membership Secretary and Director of Promotion in the
Y. M. C. A. at San Francisco. Since 1928 he served the "Y" as Public Relations Director.
On September 7, 1933, our 74th Grand Master was happily married to
Elsie McElaney, whose pleasing personality and womanly attainments ideally
equip her as the marital companion of one who has dedicated his life to the
service of his fellow-man. This marriage has been blessed by a most delightful
daughter, Helen Janet, who is the pride and joy of the Wilson home.
He is an orator of distinction; has the courage of his convictions and
has always been a stanch and outstanding champion of good government
and civic righteousness. His popularity among the craft was abundantly attested
by his election as Grand Secretary at the last communication of Grand Lodge.
He brings to that office an experience and ability which vouchsafe for him
a long and successful career in that very important office in California
Masonry. He is a member of the San Francisco Rotary Club; The American
Legion; The San Francisco Advertising Club and various professional organizah:ms.
He has· the unique distinction of having received his Blue Lodge degrees
in three different Grand Jurisdictions. On August 27, 1917 he was initiated
in Pilot Lodge No. 240 of Lyons, Nebraska; on April 5, 1918, was examined
and passed by Excelsior Lodge No. 261, of Charlotte, North Carolina, and
011 May 5, 1920 was raised in Marin Lodge No. 191 at San Rafael, California.
At the organization of Ingleside Lodge No. 630 of San Francisco he
became a charter member and its first Senior Deacon. He is a Past Master
and still a member of that Lodge.

LLOYD EARL WILSON
Grand Master

1940

His unusual ability as a ritualist was recognized and rewarded in January
1931 by the appointment as Inspector of the 40th District. On November 1,
1934, he was appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer, which position he held until
October 14, 1938, when he was elected Junior Grand Warden. On October 13,
1939, he was elected Deputy Grand Master and was elevated to the Grand
Oriental chair on October 11, 1940.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Past Grand Masters

Has any generation of man been called upon to make sense of a world
as chaotic as that which you and I now must face? Would that Almighty
God. might speak to you and to me-right here and now.
Is this a vain hope? In pronouncing this plea are we as naive as a
little English girl who is reported to have prayed as follows: "Please God,
take care of mummy and daddy and take care of Michael and Joan, and
take care of Uncle Arthur and, above all, 0 God, take care of yourself,
01 we shall all be sunk."
In all humility may I suggest: It has been revealed unto · us what the
Lord doth require-revealed in the Holy Bible which is given to us as
the rule and guide of our faith, yes, but revealed also and with painful
clarity by the affairs of the world which we are now witnessing.
Do you recall the words of the "Battle Hymn of the Republic"?
"Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord:
He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of
wrath are stored;
He hath loosed the fateful lightning of his terrible swift sword;
His truth is marching on."
Aias, the fateful lightning of his terrible swift sword has been loosed
upon the face of the earth. Alas, the vintage where the grapes of wrath are
stored is being trampled out. Mankind has sinned against the law of God.
Man has been cruel, vengeful, greedy, intolerant, self-centered. Man has
&corned and ridiculed such virtues as brotherly love, relief and truth. Man
has mocked at temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice. Therefore,
has come the day of judgment. For a time it seemed that man could successfully violate the laws of God. Judgment was slow in coming. However,
"the mills of the Gods grind slowly, yet they grind exceeding small." If punishment be delayed it will come nonetheless. Every physician knows that a
person may be suffering from some ailment of which he is unaware, perhaps
for ten or twenty years before it will make itself known. He is continously
violating the laws of health but because the ultimate breakdown is delayed
he does not change his ways. And then suddenly his misfortune becomes
known to him. A dread disease is upon him; and there is no help. And then
he laments unto himself, "Would that I had known in sufficient time that
this would be my fate, then I would have observed the laws of health."
So it is with the moral conduct of man. With our own eyes we see today the
fulfillment of the words of Holy Writ: "The Lord shall judge the ends of
the earth." With our own eyes we behold the glory of the coming of the
Lord.
Who is there among us who can now doubt the retribution of God.
As there is a law of cause and effect in nature so there is a law of cause
and effect in the dealings of man. Dare we violate the law of gravity and
expect that we shall escape unpunished? Do we plant potatoes and expect
that strawberries will grow up instead? Do we eat toadstools and expect
to enjoy . good health? .Why then does foolish man think that he can
practice injustice and receive justice, that he can exercise hate and receive
love, that he can terrify and enslave and then enjoy peace? Verily, my
brethren, "The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth." Let him who has
ears hear this. Let him who has eyes see this. It is the fundamental
truth of our very existence.
How sublime then are the teachings of our fraternity! If we plant
the seeds of brotherly love we know for a certainty that we shall reap a
harvest of brotherly love. If we pattern our every word and deed to conform with the architectural blueprints set forth by our fraternity, we know

received with Grand Honors, and appropriately welcomed by the Grand

Devotional Services
A very interesting and uplifting devotional service was then
rendered by the Grand Chaplain.
My brethren of Grand Lodge:
We have assembled in the name of the Great Architect of the Universe
whose blessing we have invoked. In the opening prayer we united in uttering
a desire to proceed in all our doings in conformity with the demands of
our Supreme Grand Master. It is fitting and proper that we have done so
for our ancient order of Free and Accepted Masons derives its inspiratio~
and sustenance from a contemplation of divinity. If we could but know
God and what God requires of us we could live the more truly as Masons.
The problem in life is to ascertain for our individual sdves a knowledge
of the will of God. No 01~e may speak with finality upon this subject; it
baffles hum;in comprehension. And yet we must know. We seek to know.
What might we say, what might we plan, what might we do to raise the
le.vel of our Masonry to reflect the order and beauty of the divine throne?
When we convene in Grand Lodge it is no ordinary gathering. We
come here to meditate deeply, to expand the horizon of our vision to intensify our zeal. We must come forth from these sessions with r~newed
vigor and refreshed ardor. How shall we discover that greater vision and
vigor? Would that God might speak to our souls and instruct us in our
assigned duties.
My brethren, if there ever was a time in the history of mankind when
men must derive strength and wisdom for worthy living, is it not now?

for a certainty that there will come to us the divine reward-we know this
with the certainty that we know that there is a law of cause and effect.
Here in this knowledge, here we find renewed incentive to live our lives
as Masons; here we find determination that the din of confusion which
surrounds us on every side will not be permitted to swerve us from the
ideals which we have learned in our degrees of Masonry.
Brethren of Grand Lodge, will you proceed with me to one further
thought? May I now emphasize with the greatest conviction that I can
command that we are not here dealing with the ideals of Masonry in the
abstract but rather with the day-to-day performance of those ideals. Let
us not talk of justice, let us be just; let us not talk of tolerance, let us be
tolerant; let us not talk of charity, "let us be charitable; let us not talk of
truth, let us be truthful; let us not talk of temperance, let us be temperate;
let us not talk of prudence, let us be prudent, let us not talk of fortitude,
let us display fortitude. And, my brethren, in no day and age were there
so many opportunities available at hand to do these things, to show mercy
and brotherly love and justice. And in so doing let each one say to himself:
"I do these things because I am a Mason; I am living my Masonry; I am
doing that which the Lord doth require of me."
The high resolve thus to live cannot be postponed to a future date.
It must be made here and now. Who knows how long the opportunity will
be ours? A year hence it may be too late. Life itself is so tragically brief.
How many years remain for any of us. Five years? Ten years? Twenty
years? Consider if you will the wisdom contained within these words
of verse:
"Life is like a journey
On a railroad train,
With a pair of travelers
Seated at each pane.
I might sit beside you,
Never know you,
Or I might sit elsewhere,
All the journey through.
But, if fate should mark me
Seated at your side,
Let's be pleasant travelers
It's so short a ride."
In conclusion may I refer to an experience which came to me during
this past vacation period. It was my pleasure to spend a few days in
Yosemite National Park, world famous for its majestic setting. As do many
of the visitors to Yosemite, I traveled to the elevation above the park
known as Glacier Point, whence descends the Firefall. I walked to the
edge of the cliff and looked down. The people in the valley below looked
like so many insects, the automobiles like toys, the swimming pool like a
green cardboard. Looking down, terror seized me. I tightened my grip on
the handrail. I felt unsafe in my surroundings. Then I returned to the
floor of the valley and looked up to Glacier Point where I had· been. It
was not at all frightening to look up. The cliffs that surrounded me seemed
to embrace me and my fellow-visitors to the valley in a vast bond of nature
that m:ade us kin. I felt uplifted and my eyes wandered from the tops
of the cliffs to the heavens above. Then there flashed into my consciousness
the realization that when we look down upon life, fellow man is but an
insect and life is terrifying. But when we look up, as we do in Masonry,
up to the heights, the cliffs, the sky of blue, and the Creator of them all,
then life is indeed comforting, brotherly a11d ~ublime.

The membership situation throughout the jurisdiction is somewhat

I can report from personal knowledge that the homes at Decoto and
Covina are well-conducted and well-administered. The Board of Trustees
has met in separate and in joint sessions throughout the year and has given
literally hundreds of hours to the problems presented to them. The welfare

residents is practiced and that everything is being done for those under
our care which you desire to have done.
The situation in our Masonic clubhouses at Berkeley and at Los Angeles
is good, but I cannot bring myself to say that it is excellent. The trustees
in both cases have labored earnestly, and I believe intelligently, in the areas
in which they have operated, but I feel that there are difficulties in the way
oi the successful operation of these clubhouses.
I do not feel that we are getting enough student participation in the
clubhouses, and I do not feel that we are "getting our money's worth." I
do not belong to that group who feel that if even a few students are being
provided with an outlet for sound social activity that it is worth all we are
putting into it.
I have caused to be submitted to me the records of student participation in both clubhouses and while the reports ·are good, I say again that
they are not in my mind what they ought to be. I frankly think this is due in
a major part to our organizational set-up. The Board of Trustees, as now
set up, represent Grand Lodge largely in a legal fashion. They are the
trustees of the property and it is right that they should be. They are the
older group of men and again it is right that they should be, for in the
final analysis they are responsible for these properties and for the good
name of Grand Lodge in their operation. It is not to be expected that these
trustees, most of them removed by many decades from college life, 'will be
very close to student activity. It is not to be expected that they will have
very close touch with student life o r know from actual contact with the
university, what s tudents are thinking and doing. This cannot reasonably
be supposed to be their province. I t is equally unreasonable, I think, to
expect that students can be given a free hand to run the clubhouses to suit
themselves, and particularly to develop and promote whatever programs
they may desire. There needs to be both control and stimulation in this
connection.

or expedient for the welfare of the craft." This serves not only to inform

In pr11senting this message I am aware that I would not have had the

am pleased to report that in my judgment the state of the fraternity

My suggestion would be that the trustees continue to serve in the capacities in which they now serve, but that they give serious consideration
to the formation of an intermediate body between them and the students,
which shall act as the program and promotion stimulating body. I picture
this as being a group of young Masons, university graduates living near
the universities, and between the ages of 25 and 35 years. I suggest these
ages because they should be long enough out of university to have established themselves somewhat and to have gotten away from the purely undergraduate activities, and yet young enough to still keep some hand in

This intermediate board of advisors would be responsible to the Board of

This does not require any legislation, because the trustees already have

Necrology
Death has struck hard and often in our ranks since our last communication. I doubt if there has been any previous year when so many men
who have served so well and so long have been taken from us during such
a brief span.
It is not my intention to eulogize any of those who have gone, for that
will be done under the direction of the Committee on Necrology, by others
more competent than I. I do, however, wish to record the names of a few
outstanding members at this time in order that you may see something of
the great loss which we have suffered. ·
The greatest single blow, and one which every Grand Master has prayed
might not come during his term of office, fell on March 31, 1941, when our
well-beloved Grand Secretary, the Very Worshipful John Whicher, was
taken from us. His loss was to me not only the loss of a true personal
friend, but it was likewise the loss of what would have been to me, as Grand
Master, the most valuable aid which I could possibly have had during my
administration, for every man who has occupied the office of Grand Master
during the past thirty-two years would say without hesitancy that much
of the success of his administration was due to the able, friendly and farsighted counsel of John Whicher.
On April 2 I, with the assistance of nearly all of the Grand Lodge officers, opened Grand Lodge and conducted the funeral service for Brother
Whicher. On the day following the Very Worshipful Walter Leonard,
Grand Lecturer, passed away. This double blow, within the space of a few
days, seemed far more than should have been our lot, but the end was not
yet. We had previously suffered the loss of three of our fine Inspectors in
big, friendly Herbert Walker, the venerable Jacob Hughes and in the young
but extremely competent Harold W. Conklin. There now followed in most
rapid succession Thomas Anderson, third oldest Inspector in point of service in the Grand Lodge; and Foster G. Dyer, fourth oldest Inspector in
point of service and former Grand Lecturer. All of these men were close
personal friends of mine over a long period of years, and in every case where
it was possible to set aside my affairs or to rearrange my schedule, I conducted funeral services for them.

Grand Masters' Conference
In February I attended the Annual Conference of Grand Masters in
Washington, D. C. I was present at every session of the conference, and feel
that while it is a long way to travel for a three-day conference, the time is
well spent. The subjects discussed were pertinent, and in most cases the
presentation of the subject matter was excellent. There have been many matters concerning which I have had to correspond with other Grand Masters
during the year, and the fact that I had met them at Washington seemed
to make the solution of our problems much easier. I recommend attendance

This Grand jurisdiction was honored in having its Grand Master as

In this latter capacity your Grand Master was invited to make the

George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association
I attended the meeting of this association in Alexandria, Virginia, and
was impressed with the great progress which has been made, not only in
the building itself, but in the affairs of the association.
The final form, size and general furnishing of the Memorial seems now
to be finally set, and as a matter of fact it is well on the way to ultimate
completion. I do not believe that any great changes or additions are contemplated in the structure.
A most important . agreement has been reached with the old Lodge in
Alexandria whereby the George Washington relics are to be placed in the
Memorial in a room now under construction, which will be an exact replica
of the old Lodgeroom in which Washington presided as Master. This agreement assures not only the preservation of the relics from fire and theft,
but also assures their permanent maintenance.
This Grand jurisdiction has had a vital connection with this Memorial
from the beginning, for our own Past Grand Master Lawler was one of the
originators of the Memorial, if in fact the idea did not first come from him,
and we have had a member on the Board of Directors, I think, from the
very beginning. Your Grand Master was elected to the board for a threeyear term, succeeding our own P. G. M. Boynton, who resigned due to ill
health.

During these years the plans for the Memorial have been expanded
from time to time, and of necessity the per capita levy has likewise been
enlarged from time to time. On the basis of the original levy of $1.00 per
capita, this Grand Lodge has more than paid its quota, but on the per capita
levy of $1.70 per member adopted some years ago, we have paid approximately 75 per cent.
I am aware that this matter has been before Grand Lodge on previous
occasions and I do not at this time make any recommendation for an appropriation, but I would like to suggest that we do not entirely close our
minds to this matter because the time will come when the Memorial will be
completed and this Grand jurisdiction ought not to allow a relatively few
thousand dollars to forever keep it out of the honored list of those Grand
jurisdictions which have had a full participation in the completion of the
project. The Memorial will stand for hundreds and hundreds of years and
so likewise will the record of participation in its erection.
Pettus Bible
At the last communication of Grand Lodge Worshipful William B.
Pettus, Past Master of International Lodge, Peiping, China; Past District
Grand Warden, China; Massachusetts jurisdiction, presented to Grand
Lodge a copy of the Bible published entirely in the Chinese language, requesting that it be held each year by the Lodge which has rendered the
best service to Masonic charity, and it was accepted in that spirit.
Brother Pettus did not define the word "charity," but I assume that
he did not mean it in the sense of the giving of alms, but that he intended
that the Bible should go to the Lodge which displayed Masonic charity in
the sense of universal benevolence and universal brotherhood.
I have selected as the Lodge most entitled to this honor this year,
Fidelity Lodge No. 120 of San Francisco. This is one of the oldest Lodges
in the city and one which, across the years, has attracted to its membership
large numbers of outstanding citizens of the ] ewish faith. The particular
act of this Lodge which in my judgment merits the presentation of the
Chinese Bible to it, was the election by that Lodge of a Chinese applicant
for the degrees of Masonry. I have witnessed no better example of the
universality of Masonry this year than this one, which I honor today, and
I commend to all of you the witnessing tonight of the conferring of the
third degree of Masonry upon this Fellow Craft of Fidelity Lodge, when
the Pettus Bible is upon the altar.
National Emergency
There is already ample evidence that a period of increased activity in
the Lodges is going to result from the national emergency in which we
find ourselves.
·
The number of requests for emergency degrees has increased many
fold during the past six months. It should be borne in mind that when
these requests are presented to a Lodge through the Grand Lodge office,
the Grand Secretary merely certifies to the regularity of the request. The
decision rests with the Lodge as to whether or not they desire to confer
the degree by courtesy.
I personally feel that wherever we can do so we should confer the
degrees upon those applicants who have been elected in another jurisdiction and who, being in the armed forces of the United States, are not the
masters of their own time or place of residence. They are in no position
to make any choice, but are moved about by the orders of their commanding officers, and therefore I feel that they are entitled to any courtesy
which we can reasonably show them.

1

I

,

i

419

I think that we should, however, guard against being imposed upon
by those individuals not in the service of the armed forces who are legitimate
residents of the State of California or who expect to make their pei:manent
home here, but who decide to petition a Lodge in their own State and then
immediately come to California. They should come to California and wait
until they acquire the qualifications of residence and then petition a California Lodge in the same manner as any other resident.
I should like to issue a warning also against the too-ready acceptance of
applications and applicants during the emergency. During the last World
War there was a great influx of applications and petitions. I do not wish
to cast any discredit upon any of these applicants, but I do want to urge
the greatest care and discretion in the acceptance of applications, and likewise the greatest vigilance by investigating committees. I hope that no
Lodge will look upon the emergency as an <?PPOrtunity for increasing its
membership. I hope that no Lodge will carelessly accept applications or
carelessly investigate them after they are received. It should be borne in
mind that once a man becomes a member of a Lodge he remains a Mason
until his death or until he is otherwise removed from the fraternity, and
that the members of a Mason's family remain the charge of the Lodge and
of the fraternity long after his death. I cannot place too much emphasis
upon this warning to every Lodge in the jurisdiction to guard carefully
the outer door, and to make as certain as is humanly possible that only
good men and true are permitted to pass within.
In those cases where applicants elected in California are transferred to
some other part of the country and desire to have degrees conferred by
courtesy of another jurisdiction, I would like to remind the Lodges that
these courtesy requests must be transmitted through the Grand Lodge
office, receive the approval of the Grand Master if he so desires, and be
forwarded to the proper Grand Lodge by the Grand Secretary. It is not
a matter which originates and is carried through between and by the subordinate Lodges of the Grand jurisdictions.
Emergency Welfare Work
The problem of welfare work for Masons in the armed forces of the
United States in the present emergency is perhaps one of the most difficult
and persistent which we have had to face this year.
The activity of the welfare department of the Masonic Service Association in the United States has served to bring this problem to the front.
Upon the presumption that there are great numbers of Masons in the
armed forces, that association has developed a very extensive plan for
building Masonic service centers in cities adjacent to large concentration
of troops. The building plans roughly call for establishments similar to
those planned by the Government for the United Service Organizations.
The Masonic Service Association proposes to staff these buildings with
adequate personnel and to pay for the entire operation from funds received
solely from Masonic sources. Some of these centers are now in actual
operation in various parts of the country.
Much of this activity has been actuated by the feeling on the part of
some that Masonic organizations did nothing for Masons during the first
World War and that its failure in this respect resulted unfavorably to
the fraternity, both in the eyes of Masons who were not served, and in
the eyes of the public which criticized such failure. Whether or not any
failure to serve in such a capacity in the first World War was a mistake
is a matter for each individual to decide. I P.ersonally do not think that it
was a mistake.
Because of the plan outlined heretofore, the question of this welfare

have no doubt that this Grand Lodge would, by its vote, have endorsed
such action on my part.
The second possibility which confronts us is that in one or two exceptional cases, where there may be concentrations of men, perhaps as
many as 80 000 in one place, and if there is established need for it, we may
need to op~n an office and employ one man whose business it would be
to operate an information center as well as a clearing house for such purely
Masonic services as might be brought to his attention.'
I do not believe that any legislation is necessary at this time to continue
what has been done or to provide for the second contingency if it should
arise, and I am therefore making no recommendation for legislation in this
respect.
I must report to you, for your information, that I have been in constant .touch with the Inspectors and with some of the officers of the
Lodges adjacent to these military posts, as well as with other competent
Masonic leaders, and I have tried to keep myself informed of what was
going on and of the needs, both of the men and of the Lodges. I say to
you, after almost a year of dealing with this problem, that I do not know
of a single case in which the Masonic need of any Mason was not met, nor
do I know of any Lodge which has found it necessary to curtail its planned
program for Masons in the armed forces because of a lack of funds.
I think I should give you the benefit of my judgment for what it may
be worth, as to the sort of emergency in which we find ourselves. I do not
claim to be the seventh son of a seventh son, nor the son of a prophet, but
I think that one need be neither of these to say, that judging from all the
signs and from such information as is available we are in for a long emergency and, in all likelihood, war. If this is true, it .be~ooves us to chart ?ur
course very carefully, to give the best of our th111k111g t? the develop1?g
of a policy for handling this welfare problem, and to consider the financial
implications of a more extensive program with great care before plunging
ourselves into a very extensive and expensive program, covering a long
period of years.
The essential things to be kept in mind in developing our policy are:
that this is a democratic army; that all men should be treated alike, preferably well; that Masons are, after all, American citizens first, with all of
its implications for loyalty and service, and Masons second; ~nd that ai:y
service to which they may be entitled because they are Masons 1s a Masonic
service and should be rendered by Masons in strictly Masonic surroundings,
and guided strictly and solely by the need of the person and the ability
of the responsible Masonic body in and under whose jurisdiction the Mason
may find himself.
As a good example of what can be done in this direction. I present
herewith a copy of a letter addressed to me by the Board of Directors of
the Central California Masonic United States Service Bureau.

I start from the premise that a Mason in the armed forces of the
United States does not need any service different from that of any other
soldier in the army save and except a purely Masonic service. I see no
reason why our members need any different or any more extensive athletic, recreational, social or religious privileges and advantages beyond those
enjoyed by any other soldier. Even if I were persuaded that they needed
·it, I am not certain that I would favor giving it to them, for ours is a democratic army, made up of all kinds and types of people, and what is sufficient for any should be sufficient for all.
When we come to the question of Masonic service it is quite another
matter. By Masonic service in this connection I mean such service as will
provide information to Masons in the armed forces whereby they may
know where the Lodges are, when they meet and when work is being done
by those Lodges.
By Masonic service I also mean service in those cases where a Mason
is sick, or where his loved ones are sick, or where emergency has struck
his family in some way, and in which emergency he needs to have the assistance of the Master or members of a Masonic Lodge. This is a service
which we should and must render, and it is a service which in my judgment
should be rendered only in and by Masonic Lodges. We do not need
recreational buildings, shower baths and social events to render Masonic
service.
In this whole matter I should like to point out that in the matter of
establishing contacts with Masons in the armed forces, whereby they may
know about available Masonic services, it is equally the duty of the Mason
himself to search out his Masonic contacts and to make his desires as well
as his needs known to those who can serve him.
I oppose the building type of service on financial grounds also. I
know, from long experience in this field, that buildings and personnel are
expensive and that they also bring problems even greater in their seriousness than mere problems of money. I can see no justification for spending
thousands of dollars every month for the operation of service centers which
duplicate the work done by recognized welfare organizations.
I am not impressed at all by the record of the volume of work done by
the service centers now in operation because I know, again from long
experience, that when any group, under any name, opens for the use of all,
any building where free services are given, that building can be packed
every hour of the day or night when men are free to be in attendance, but
the mere volume of such work in no wise indicates the actual need for it.
I can see two possibilities which may confront us in the carrying on of
our Masonic service as it has been conducted this year and as I believe
it should be conducted. The first possibility is that the Lodges located near
army posts may find that the demands made upon them for both fraternal
and social services are more costly than they are able to bear. I have said
to such Lodges this year that I would appropriate from the general funds
of Grand Lodge sufficient funds to subsidize their program where such
subsidy was recommended by the Inspector and the Master, after adequate investigation. I had the promise of approval of such action from the
Finance Committee, and had I been called upon to advance such funds, I

Consolidations
I have watched with great interest the progress made by Educator
Lodge No. 554 which is the re.s uit of a consolidation last year of Golden
City Lodge No. 553 with Educator Lodge No. 554. This consolidation has
worked out with great satisfaction to all concerned. The consolidated
Lodge is more active and more able to perform its functions than the
two Lodges were before the consolidation. I call attention to this because·
I have a conviction that there are other consolidations which should be
effected.
There are many cases in the jurisdiction where c;onditions which existed
when Lodges were formed no longer exist and the need for Lodges has
disappeared. The Lodges have however gone on in a rather weak and ineffective manner. In some cases they did not consolidate because they were
not aware that consolidations were possible; in other cases because they
feared the processes of consolidation were too intricate and uncertain of
success; and in other cases because they feared that one or the other of
the Lodges would lose its identity.
The inspectors, generally speaking, know where consolidations would

425

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

be advisable, and I recommend that they discuss, at appropriate times,
with the Masters of the Lodges the possibilities of consolidation. It should
be pointed out by the inspectors that the processes of consolidation are
not too intricate and cumbersome, but that on the contrary they are
rather simple. There is no real reason to lose identity. The new Lpdge
may have the name of one and the number of the other, or it may simply
take both the name and the number of the one. Provision can be made in
the group of officers to make it possible for really capable men to continue
in office; and if the officers of the stronger of the two Lodges exercise care,
diplomacy and consideration for the rights of others, there need be no
strained relationships. It is far better to have one sound, strong Lodge than
two or three ineffective ones, and in the long run the brethren of the resulting strong Lodge will take greater pride in their Masonic membership.

Annual Election Date
During the year I have had a number of requests for approval of an
amendment to the by-laws of a Lodge which would permit the holding of
the annual election in November rather than December.
While it is true that we have legislation which permits such a change
if approved by the Grand Master, I have denied such approval in all but
one or two cases. The purpose of the legislation, as clearly set forth in
the reports accompanying the legislation when it was adopted, was to
provide a way whereby those Lodges which could not comply with the
requirements for December election because of climatic conditions, might
advance the annual election one m onth. Many of our mountain Lodges
are snowed in in December and the members find it impossible to attend.
It is in such cases as these that I have approved the change. The instances
in which I have denied approval have all been in and around Los Angeles,
and I would have been willing to grant the approval in those cases had
the request been accompanied by a certified statement from the United
States Weather Bureau that the snow really does get so deep in Los
Angeles in December that the members cannot get to Lodge.
Investment of Lodge Funds
Many times during the year I have been asked if it was permissible
for a Lodge to invest its funds in defense bonds or other bonds designated
by the inquirer. The answer is so simple that I hesitate to give it, but in
the hope that it may save future inquiries, I will say that I directed the
attention of the inquirer to Section 152, Constitution and Ross Digest, 1940,
with the suggestion that inquiry be made at a local reputable savings bank
as to whether or not the bond in question was legal for savings banks.

Carpinteria Lodge
During th e year Carpinteria Lodge No. 444 suffered damage to its
building due to an earthquake. The Lodge was unable to finance the rebuilding of the Temple and I was asked if Grand Lodge could render any assistance in the matter.
Upon inquiry I was informed by the Inspector that it would require approximately $2,500 to repair the building. There was at that time a mortgage
of $12,000 on the building. I was informed that this mortgage could be
satisfied for the sum of $5,000 and that a new loan in the amount of $7,500
could be negotiated on the rehabilitated building. The $7,500 thus secured
was to be used to retire the present mortgage for $5,000 and to repay the
Grand Lodge th e $2,500 advanced for the purposes of repairing the building.
Under the terms as set forth here, I authorized the advancement of
$2,500 to Carpinteria Lodge No. 444. ·

Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies
It seems that periodically some well-intentioned brethren decide that
there should be some organized public Masonic display, and with this
conviction and with, I presume, excellent motives, they proceed without
authority to organize some great public showing under some Masonic
title chosen because of its publicity value.
Such a public display was organized under the title of "Cavalcade of
Masonic Bodies," which was to make a great public display in the Orange
County Park on Sunday, September 14, 1941. The following letter, signed
by the chairman of the Central Committee went out to the Masters of
Masonic Lodges as well as to the presiding officers of other Masonic bodies
on the letter-head of the "Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies" :
·
"To you, and to the members of the organization over which you
preside, we bring this most important announcement, and appeal
for your cooperation and support.
"At no time in the history of the world has Masonry been so
openly flaunted, its members persecuted, and its principles so successfully attacked by men in high places of power and authority as
is being done today.
"vVe stand challenged by powers that know no justice except such
as may be imposed by power and might. We possess the answer
to that challenge in the membership of over 1000 Masonic and
Affiliated Masonic Bodies in California, with an estimated membership of 300,000 carefully chosen people. We propose to demonstrate that power and might, and to answer that challenge by a
colossal assembly of Masons, their families and friends in the 'Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies' at Orange County Park on September
14, 1941. We propose a gigantic parade to the park, in which every
Lodge and club, augmented by our public officials, will be represented. We propose a full day of first class and elaborate entertainment, and all we ask of you is your whole-hearted support
and attendance.
"By such a demonstration as this we expect to fortify our own
courage in the promotion of our great fraternity. We expect to
impress our friends, and especially our enemies.
"It is a duty you and the members of your organization owe
this fraternity to support the Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies. The

"It has come to my attention that it is proposed to hold a 'Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies' at the Orange County Park, Sunday,
September 14, 1941. It is my understanding that the Committee
sponsoring this affair has no official standing of any sort from any
recognized body of Masons but that on the contrary it is being
planned and arranged by a group of individuals. I do not question the motives of this group nor their earnestness in attempting
to accomplish the ends indicated in a circular letter from them
dated August 9, 1941, and signed by one Henry J. Brankey as
Chairman of the Central Committee. I do however question the
wisdom of such a display as has been arranged.
"The use of the word Masonic in this connection is ill-advised
as well as unauthorized and I feel that if the purposes as set forth
were accomplished under the name of Masonic Bodies it would
ultimately bring the fraternity into disrepute.
"The purpose of this letter is to inform you that the proposed
'Cavalcade of Masonic Bodies' has had no approval of Grand Lodge
or of the Grand Master and that had such approval been requested
the Grand Master would not have granted it. You will therefore
understand that no Master need feel under any compulsion to lend
his cooperation and likewise no Lodge need be subjected to pressure from any source to have its members participate. If individual
Masons, as citizens, desire to attend the picnic and march in the
parade, it is a matter for them to decide, but I hereby direct that
no Lodge participate as a unit and that no banners of any sort be
carried by any Lodge or members of a Lodge of this jurisdiction
in this public display, which would call the attention of the public
to the fact that they are Masons, or a group of members of any
particular Lodge. "
The processions in ~hich it is proper for Masonic Lodges to participate
as Lodges include those for funerals, for the decorating of graves, for the
laying of cornerstones, for the dedication of Temples, and for such affairs
as are purely and strictly the proper functions of Masonic Lodges.
On this whole subject I suggest that you see further the comments of
Past Grand Master Sherman (Proceedings of 1923, pages 461 and 707),
Past Grand Master Boynton (Proceedings of 1926, page 23), and of Past
Grand Master Fischer (Proceedings of 1928, pages 34 and 282) .

I am of the opinion that wherever it is practical and wherever there

430

Decisions
There have been many matters presented to me in which I have felt
the law was perfectly clear and in such sases I have simply directed the
attention of the inquirer to the law or have assisted in the interpretation of it.
Unless some real point has been involved I have felt it unnecessary to
make decisions and therefore I present but a few for action by Grand Lodge.
1. I was asked if a prospective applicant for the degrees of Masonry,
whose sole business was the operation of a retail bottled goods liquor store,
was eligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry and if the Lodge might
receive the application.
I held that under our present law the applicant was eligible and that
the Lodge might receive the application.
2. I was asked if a prospective applicant for the degrees of Masonry,
whose sole business was the wholesale liquor business, was eligible to
apply and if the Lodge might receive the application.
I held that under our present law the applicant was eligible and that
the Lodge might receive the application.
3. A Lodge desiring to recognize and reward an excellent piece of
service to the Lodge by one of its oldest Past Masters, voted to purchase a
Life Membership from the Lodge funds and present it to the retired Past
. Master as a testimonial.
I held that this was not a proper use pf Lodge funds.
4. A Lodge desired to tender a banquet to the local Chapter of the
Eastern Star and asked if they might pay for it out of the refreshment
fund.
I held that this was not a proper use of Lodge funds.
5. A situation developed between a Lodge in San Jose and a Lodge in
San Mateo with reference to the funeral of a deceased brother. The facts,
which no one disputed, are that the deceased, a member in San Jose, died in
San Mateo, and that the Master of the Masonic Lodge in San Mateo
denied the request of the San Jose Master that San Mateo conduct the
funeral. It is also not disputed that thP Master of the San Jose Lodge had
a day off from his work on the Saturday in question when the service was
to be conducted, and that he pressed the San Mateo Lodge on the ground
that since the member had died in San Mateo, it was the duty of the San
Mateo Lodge to bury him.
In my judgment the Master of the San Mateo Lodge ought not to be
censured in the case for having failed to bury a member who died within
the jurisdiction of his Lodge. The fact of the matter is that the deceased
had long been a member of the San Jose Lodge, that he was known to the
officers and members of that Lodge, that he died within approximately·
twenty-five miles of that Lodge, and that he had requested a Masonic
funeral.
The provision in the law which provides that a sojourning brother shalt
be buried by the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he dies, was in my judgment never intended to relieve a Lodge from a duty which it should perform
if the performance of that duty was a reasonable one. The provision of
the law was intended to cover the situation where a brother dies at such a
distance from his home Lodge that it would work an unusual and unnecessary hardship upon the officers and members of that Lodge to journey to the:
place of burial.

Applying Section 218 I held that Palo Alto Lodge No. 346 could
rightfully receive and act' upon the petition of this applicant.
Recommendations
Life Membership: Lodges which have Life Memberships _fr_e~uently
find that the life member moves away, drops out of Lodge activities and
eventually loses all contact with the Lodge. The efforts of the Secretary
to locate the member are without avail and there is no possible way by
which the Lodge may communicate with him. As the _years pass by the
law of probability would indicate that the member ha_d died, but the L odge
continues to pay the per capita tax to Grand Lodge just the same as there
is at present no method by which the member may be re~oved from the
Lodge rolls. This seems to me not only to work a hardship on the Lod!Se
but also to make it impossible to get a real figure of our total membership.
I therefore recommend that appropriate legislation be adopted which
will cure this situation.
Financing Building Projects: The work of the Committee ~n ~inancing
Building Projects has resulted in so much good to the. Fraternity m general
that it seems to me that the scope of work of the committee should be broadened and that proper legislation should be enacted to provide for the additional work of the committee.
I therefore recommend that legislation be enacted which will give this
committee general supervision over the fi nancing of_ new temples, the _refinancing of old temples and the financing of remodelmg and reconstruction
wherever such operations assume major proportions.

The Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary, and the office

Conclusion
I cannot conclude this, my last message to you, without directing your
attention to the very serious times in which we are living. What the future
may hold I would not dare to forecast, but that we stand in the midst of
a great world cataclysm cannot be denied. It is equally apparent that this
is no mere recurrence of an age-old succession of wars but is in fact a world
revolution and a titanic struggle between two opposing philosophies ·of
government. That we are not already engaged in the actual physical
struggle is our good fortune, and it is to be hoped that we may be spared
such participation. That we are~ however, a part of the total struggle and
that we need to guard ourselves against being taken unawares cannot
be denied.
One of the most interesting phases of the present world situation is the
casualness and the almost indifference with which the people of the United
States view this world cataclysm. There seems to be a general feeling that
the war is still a long way removed from us and that we will never become
involved. Perhaps we can't be hurt and perhaps we should mind our own
business and merely provide for our own defense and ignore what has
been happening elsewhere in the world.
I say perhaps, because there is another side to it which deserves more
than passing attention. It ha.s been a tradition in the United States that
"any American Boy" might become President, and that is still true. We
have always, however, pointed out that in only 'one or two other countries
of the world was this true and the very fact that it was true in America
helped make and keep this a democracy. It certainly was not true in Russia,
Italy and Germany. Consider for a moment how things have changed. The
three individuals who are the rulers of these countries would all classify
under the title, "any boy," for certainly none of them was born to rule.
There is, therefore, a parallel between the United States of America and
these other countries where a boy from a non-ruling family has succeeded
to great power, but there the parallel ends.

In the United States that system helps to make and keep a democracy.
In those nations it destroys whatever democracy there was and makes its
revival impossible. In the United States such leadership is possible by the
Bill of Rights. In the other nations of the world it is possible only by the
law of might.
The inevitable results of totalitarian governments are those constantly
portrayed for all the world to see, namely persecution, conquest, destruction
and domination. These are bad enough, but the steps by which they are
achieved are equally bad. Before the results can be obtained, individual
rights must be destroyed, minorities crushed and groups in which there

433

'rhe question immediately before us is, do these rulers have any way by
which to destroy our representative form of government and our democratic processes in this great republic? If we are thinking in terms of
an immediate wholesale destruction, the answer must be no, for it must
be evident to any thinking person that a successful military conquest
of the United States cannot be made at one fel1 swoop. If we however
think, as we should be thinking, of the slow, insidious method of d~struction'
we then have real cause for grave concern; for an attack upon any phas~
of American life which is itself a part of the pattern of a total attack upon
American life, directly affects us.
The methods employed are, after a11, simple. Without elaborating them
they include anything.which causes Americans to lose confidence in this for~
of government, causes los_s of confidence in its leadership, continues to
foment unrest between capital and labor, sets one man against another advocates the superiority of one group over another, despises a grou~ of
people because of their religious faith, and which demands for itself and its
own subversive groups the rights which would be denied to a11 men if they
themselves should accomplish their purposes. These are the simple methods
by which, over a long period of time, it is hoped to render the people of the
United States dissatisfied, impotent, defenseless and disunited.
The task then of Masonic Lodges in these times is a simple one for the
task of a Lodge is nothing more than the task of the individual Mas~n · that
task is to continue to be loyal to the philosophy of government and the' laws
of. the cou?try in ~hich we reside, even though we may rightfully disagree
with certam techmques and work for what we individually feel to be the
welfare of mankind. It means to continue such practices in our relationships
with ?1en as will kee? this a united nation. It means the insistence upon
the rights of others m order that there may be rights for all. It means
~ontiriuing to demand that the freedom of every man shall be respected
m order that there may be freedom for all, and above all it means in these
times that every Mason should, with great intelligence and deliberation
exercise _that steadying influence in his own circle of friends, which is s~
essential if we are to avoid chaotic thinking and precipitous action.
The success of the United States up to this day has been due to a
of government and the willingness of the people to
submit to that government. The best governmental system in the world
will not work if there is not on the part of the governed a spirit of obedience and cooperation. If we want to preserve for ourselves and our posterity
the government under which we have enjoyed the fruits of our labors
under which we have been free to enjoy life, liberty and the pursuit
happiness there must be a rededication of ourselves to the principles of representative government and a willingness to be bound by those things
which mean the greatest good for the greatest number. There must be a
new dedication to obedience to law and an insistence upon the application
of that law to all alike, which implies a willingness to have the law applied
to ourselves.
basic~1ly sound form

of

To the practice of these principles and to the preservation of these
fundamentals of the American form of government, we can, as did those
early Masons pledge, "our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor."
And no:v at the close of this, my final message to you, I want you to
know how smcerely grateful I am for the honor which has been conferred

REPORT OF GRAND SECRET ARY

To the M:. W : . .Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor of presenting herewith my report as Grand Secretary
·during the past six months, together with a report of the transactions of
the office from the last Annual Communication of Grand Lodge to the date
of my assuming the duties of Grand Secretary.
In the passing of our beloved brother, V. W . John Whicher, Masonry
in California has suffered an irreparable loss. His long, efficient service
as Grand Secretary and his delightfu l personality, and his willingness at
all times to be of service, greatly endeared him to the members of the craft,
not only in California, but throughout the entire Masonic world.
·
I greatly appreciated and highly prized his friendship, his assistance
and fatherly advice throughout the many years I served on the History
Committee and particularly during the years I served as a line officer and
as Grand Master. And I assumed the duties and responsibilities of Grand
Secretary fully conscious of that which my subsequent experience has
verified.

It would have been difficu lt for any one to fill the office which John
Whicher's experience and personality had so glorified. This difficulty has
been particularly acute in my case because 6f my realization of the contrast
between his background and experience and my own.

Past Grand Master Adams presented the following resolution on the

and it was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and Committee on
Policy and General Purposes with instruction to report thereon at the next
Annual Communication.
Resolved, That unless otherwise ordered by unanimous consent,
every resolution proposing to amend the Constitution, Regulations,
or the Uniform Code of By-Laws, shall be presented in writing at
a regular Annual Communication and shall be immediately referred
to the appropriate committee, which shall report thereon in writing
at the next Annual Communication; and that the proposed resolution
shall appear in full in the printed Proceedings of the Communication
at which it was presented.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The ruthless hand of unkind Fate and the indulgence of your Most
Worshipful Grand Master qave permitted me, for a few short months, to
serve this Fraternity as Gdnd Lecturer. The price for this privilege has
been greatly excessive, for we all appreciated, loved, and revered our dear
friend and brother, Walter Leonard. It is not my thought here to attempt,
nor within my capacity here properly, to eulogize him, who, before me,
served so well and truly with distinction in this office. The Grand Lodge,
in proper season and in due form, will officially and appropriately · mark
his passing. Rather must I stand before you in his stead, and, within my
limits, ,make this report which otherwise would have been so aptly made
by hinl.
•
In the short period of time since the 15th day of April, 1941, it has been
possible for me to accept but a few of the numerous kind invitations which
the brethren of the various· Lodges have extepded, but permit me here to say
that I am exceedingly appreciative of their thoughtfulness, their offers of
assistance and cooperation, and their expressions of congratulations and
best wishes.
From the very few visitations which I have been able to make, from
my conferences and correspondence with the Assistant Grand Lecturers,
from Brother Leonard's records and files, and from the formal constitutional
reports made by the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts, I am here
able to assure the Grand Lodge of California that the high standard of
ritualistic perfection which for years has prevailed in this Jurisdiction
fa not only being maintained, but is being further extended; that the officers
of the respective Lodges, and all of them, duly regard the importance
of ritualistic precision and each constantly strives to perfect his own work.
I commend to your particular attention the zeal and untiring effort of
all the Inspectors, who, so assiduously, have taught and are teaching the
ritual of Grand Lodge to the ever-changing succession of officers of the
several Masonic Lodges, and otherwise supervising the Masonic activities
within their several districts.
The policy of instruction which emphasizes not only the perfecti'on of
word and expression, but also explains the meaning behind the words, the
historical background, and the reasons for each particular ceremony is,
through their hands, bearing good fruit and producing in California a more
intelligent Masonry and a more complete understanding among the Craft
of its finer meanings. .
"By way of constructive suggestion, which through the written word,
I hope, will reach all members of the Craft, I desire to make four observations :
Fit:st: The ceremonies of the several degrees are not alone for the benefit of the candidate of the particular occasion, but are also intended to contribute to the enlightenment of the members of the Craft in attendance. No
portion of the work should be performed in complete darkness, or in a light
so dim that the brethren cannot see and appreciate the dramatic expression
of movement as well as hear the inflection of the spoken word.
Second: Never, at any time, should the brethren lose sight of the
serious formality of the entire ceremony. A portion of our Third Degree
includes a form which alludes to one of the oldest known initiatory rites
.and also symbolizes a very important event in the history of the human

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

449

race. Any lightness of atmosphere within the Lodge room during that
portion of the degree is sure to defeat the purpose we have in mind, to
detract from the impression which we seek to make upon the candidate,
and to affect adversely his attitude toward the fraternity and the basic
teachings which we seek to inculcate into his very existence.
Third: By resolution of Grand Lodge passed in a season when candidates were unusually numerous, it was made permissible to omit from
the lecture of the First Degree a portion of the Monitorial work. It
seems to be the general practice of Lodges working in and near the larger
cities always to take advantage of this privilege. On the other hand, the
rural Lodges almost universally deliver the whole lecture. I am unwilling
to admit that our city brethren are less capable, less industrious, or less
zealous, than the other members of the Craft. My personal view is that
in the First Degree the candidate receives a deep and lasting impression
of the Craft and its teachings. First impressions are persuasive and tenacious. A · thoughtful candidate can, and does, receive much more to think
about when th e full lecture is delivered. I commend to the Masters of the
several Lodges of this Jurisdiction the thought that only in those cases
where there has been an over-abundance of work during the particular
evening should this privilege of omission be exercised and the candidate
be referred nonchalantly to the Monitor for further instructions.
Fo11rth: Masters of Lodges should insist that the Inspector of the
District, on his official visit to the Lodge, be received with Grand Honors.
We all know that there is a certain inherent modesty in every man-even
in lnspectors--and it is to be expected that if an Inspector is given any
choice in the matter, he will forego the formal reception. We must not,
however, lose sight of the fact that the honors are being paid to the office,
as well as to the office holder, and that, on his official visit, the Inspector
of the District comes as a direct representative of the Grand Master.
Under such circumstances, reception with Grand Honors is not optional.
This is not only the proper procedure, but it will have the further practical
advantage of familiarizing all Lodges with the form of reception so that
when the Grand Master, or some other Grand Lodge Officer coming under
circumstances entitling him to formal reception, does arrive, the ceremony
will then be conducted with the same perfection of word and form as
graces our other work.
L.o oking ahead, let me observe that the Ritual Committee hopes to
provide, at an early date, a check chart for the Inspectors of the' several
Masonic Districts which will serve them as a guide of inspection in supervising the Lodges under their jurisdiction. This chart will relate to those
matters of Lodge business, operation and management, other than the ritual
which properly should receive the particular attention of the Inspector'
and will also ser ve as a basis for the constitutional r eports which th~
Inspectors annually make to the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer.
It is not intended that every matter covered in the chart should be reported
to Grand Lodge. Rather it is contemplated that where an Inspector following the lines indicated in the chart, discovers methods of oper~tion
and management which are particularly meritorious, or faults requiring
specia.l attention, then such matters shall be included in the annual constitutional reports, together with his comments and recommendations in
relation thereto.
In recommending the use of these charts, it is not our purpose to
pry unduly into Lodge affairs, but rather to attain uniform inspection and
to assist each particular Lodge in its operative problems. More particularly, it. is hoped, through the reporting system based thereon, to give the
Fraternity as a whole the benefit of the individual Lodge's experience in

solving special or unusual .problems. Thus; the other Lodges will not be
compelled to pursue a trial and error method when difficult situations
· arise and, at the same time; when required, Grand Lodge experience and
assistance will be immediately available.
Finally, let me report that the Ritual Committee has in ·preparation
a revision of the present Monitor and Officers' Manual. I beg of you, be
not perturbed by this statement, for the items of revision consist only of
minor matters. The changing of' a word to conform to the original text
where a quotation is involved; the crediting of quotation by inclusion of
quotation marks and citation references; the capitalizing of the initial
letter of all words referring to the Deity, and such other minor matters
which are merely perfecting the typographical set-up of the imprinting.
Further, in order to clarify the intended form to be followed, there have
been a few changes of words in the directional and explanatory notations
which are not a part of the ritualistic work. These do not require action
of Grand Lodge, but are here noted for your information.
I do have another matter in relation to the Officers' Manual which
should receive your special attention, but likewise it does not require
formal action of Grand Lodge. By resolution passed in 1927 the Grand
Lodge directed that the flag of the United States shall be presented at
the altar by the Marshal and be received in the manner prescribed by the
Grand Lecturer. The word form of a nationally used "Pledge to Our
Flag" was included as a part of that ceremony. Since that time a civilian
custom of gestures to accompany the pledge has come into arm·o st universal
use ih this country, which custom is somewhat at variance with ciili" form.
This is a day when the enemies of Democracy, by ev~ry device kno:.Vl)
to knaves, are attempting to disrupt a.n d confus.e the peoples of the . world
who believe that the State exists solely to protect the liberties of the
individuals. ·There is properly much honest difference of opinion in a
Democracy,· but there are now entirely too many professionally induced
differences and customs. A slight change in our flag ce'r emony to make
it conform to the now almost universal national civilian form is a step-a
small step, but, nevertheless, an important step, toward that national unity
of thought, purpose ·aria action so essentially necessary to preserve in
these times 1 the liberties of a free people. The extended arm salutation
long used by a national patriotic organization, but which now so closely
resembles, and suggests to the popular mind, a dictator's salute, h'a s been
purposely omitted. This seems to be the latest and presently most accepted form. The Ritual Committee deems the omission to _be more ' in
keeping with democratic ideals, and that the amended form, with this
explanation, will be more acceptable to the Craft.
The language of the ceremony as used by the Marshal at the Altar is
also to be amended to read : "Worshipful Master: I have the honor to
present, etc." .as this wording is a more dignified statement than that now
in use, and, in the interests of uniformity, the same phrase is to be substituted in the 'language of thP. Grand Master's reception. I commend
these amendments directly to the brethren as no Grand Lodge action is
required, neith_e r wording having been ever adopted by action of Gran<!
Lodge. In the absence of the Grand Lodge, at this comm uni~ation,
making forma l objection to this improvement in the two ceremonies as
reported here, the Ritual Committee will order the adoption of the new
Monitor and O_fficers' Manual will be imprinted · accordingly.
