PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ANNUAL ORATION
(by HENRY C. CLAUSEN, Grand Orator)
OCTOBER 14, 1941

"Toward Greater Masonic Action"

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Past Grand Masters,
My Fellow Grand Lodge Officers and Brethren :
Your enthusiastic introduction makes me feel almost as I did when
a nervous tiler in a northern Lodge introduced me as the Grand Architect
of the Universe!
·
About two hundred and twenty years ago, the Mother Grand Lodge
of London adopted a General Regulation which read, "at all annual communications a brother selected by the Grand Master shall harangue the
brethren and give them good advice." I am now supposed to follow that
ancient charge. You may be thankful, though, that Grand Orators are
like fleeting stars. They shine forth officially from the firmanent of
Masonry briefly, and but once a year. So I suggest you sink deeply into
your chairs and relax, for this fleeting star will soon sink over the horizon.
It has been my good fortune this past year to have had the opportunity
of serving you. For this I am indebted to our Grand Master. To you,
Brother Lloyd, I express my very real thanks.
I suppose every Grand Lodge Oration given anywhere this year will
discuss the dictators and this disjointed world. I wish there was a way
oi talking about something else. But, as one wit remarked: "These dictators and their wars : If you take them seriously, they will drive you crazy.
If you don't take them seriously, you are crazy."
Whether we like it or not, we must think about a world gone mad with
bombs, bullets, and bayonets. And as Masons, we must consider some of
the larger aspects.
Similarity of Our Times
Th<;:re is a similarity, almost twin-like, between the times of today and
the times out of which speculative Masonry sprang. Then, as now, the
British Isles were beset by confusion. Then, as now, the press made an
indelible impact upon the mind. Then, as now, intolerance was in the air.
Then, as now, bloody wars were being waged. Truly, the spiritual flame
flickered feebly.
It was out of the travail of these times that speculative Masonry
was born.
On June 24, 1717, four London Lodges met to celebrate the Feast of
Saint John the Baptist. Among the members were those thinkers who
had sought a light for the darkness of their day. They decided to constitute a Grand Lodge of London. From this point they abandoned "operative"
Masonry and organized for the growth of "speculative" Masonry. Thus
was found a nucleus for unity, a focal point, a rallying place which had
been sought for a spiritual upsurge. Masonry was enthusiastically launched
into the world. The world, in turn, seemed ready for the civilizing force
of Masonry.
Civilizing Force of Masonry
A great intellectual and moral revolution was thereby in the making.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

455

While Masonry zealously refrained from interference in politics, still its
basic teachings and idea of human equality so expanded in the minds of men
that reforms were automatically advanced in opposition to the established
order of heredity, the so-called divine rights of Kings, inequality, and a
dogmatic church. Throughout the craft there grew a strong will to liberty.
Men began expressing in words that which before they had even hardly
dared to vision. The human mind, propelled by a new-born desire for
freedom, finally was emerging victorious from a death-like struggle in the
field of ideas. This liberation, as well as the moral regeneration of the .
people, was accomplished throught the social force and directive power
of Masonry.
The alert student of history will also see here a starting point from
which came our American concept of a free mankind. For, as the importance, prestige and power of the Mother Grand Lodge of London
grew, Masonry spread rapidly over the world. And wherever Masonry
penetrated, the new freedom followed. The constant result was a step
forward in mental activity-immense progress toward an emancipation
of the human mind. Hence, when Masonry arrived in America, it was but
natural that she should come clad in the robes of freedom. Then, through
the initiative of our Colonial Masons, the wh,ole world was pointed toward
a liberalistic age. ,
It was no accident, brethren, that one of our greatest American
gains, stemming from a Masonic concept, was the release of man from any
dogmatic, dictatorial church . No matter what religious faith you profess,
you can thank our Colonial brethren that a separation of church and state
was firmly bolted and riveted. down into our Constitution.
Masonry Today
You might now feel like saying to me: "It is all very well and even
inspiring to sing hosannas of praise for what Masonry has done in the
past. We tingle with pride when we hear the heroic names. We thrill with
emotion when we see the many romantic pictures in our gallery of Masonic
memories. But those are old stories. We cannot live in the past. We are
living now in a so-called modern, fast-moving, scientific age. Look to
this world of ours and see the mighty armies of warring nations locked
again in a fight to death. Look to our craft abroad and see our Lodges
that have been brutally blacked out. Look to our craft in America and
see our membership rolls showing that we are numerically on a decline.
Look to the writings of our men of great intellect who tell us there is
danger that our civilization may eventually be killed by our civilization.
Then you tell us, how can Masonry justify its existence in this transformed,
troubled world? Should we streamline and adjust Masonry to the changing
times? What can we do as Masons living in this age?"
I don't profess to have any magic secret nor do I presume to preach.
I am not like the visiting gentleman from Georgia at the colored church,
whom the colored clergyman introduced with these words, "The speaker of
the day knows the unknowable, he can do the undoable, and he will unscrew
the unscrutable."
My most immediate answer to your acute questions, though, would
be that every age is modern to those living in it. Every age also accumulates a useful backlog of lessons. And all ages are the same when we consider that the moral precepts of Masonry ever were and ever will be.
Froude, in his essay on the Science of History put it aptly when he said:
"Opinions alter, manners change, creeds rise and fall, but
the moral law is written upon the tablets of eternity."

456

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our fundamental human problems remain the same in all ages. The
yearning of mankind for happiness, for friendship and fraternalism for
justice, truth and virtue has been constant. It has been repeatedly expr~ssed
in the teachings of men of religion, the speeches of Demosthenes, the letters
of Cicero and Montaigne. Finally, it was crystallized into the sentiments
of Freemasonry.
Of course we should not stand still, on the means of applying Freemasonry. Of course we should be creative, on the means of applying
. Freemasonry. Of course we must move ahead, on the means of applying
Freemasonry. As a celebrated Danish author said, "Life can only be understood backwards, but must be lived forwards."
But the means of Masonry should not be confused with the end of
Masonry. Our compelling function, always, is to resist any innovations
which would be destructive of the end of Masonry. Our Lodges, pins
degrees, buildings, homes and charities are but the roots· Masonry itself
is the fruit.
'
Need for Active Masonry
It was Horace who said wisely, "All virtue is a struggle; life is not
a scene of repose, but of energetic action."
Brethren, a mere passive admiration for the sublimity and inherent
goodness of Masonry will not suffice today. We need an active constructive
a P!actical way of applying Masonry! We need increased, gr~ater Masoni~
action! We need the kind of Masonic action that was exemplified in the
lives of our Colonial Masons. We need the kind of Masonic action that
has been uniformly exemplified in the lives of our Past Grand Masters
and in the life of our Grand Master, they who have given so generously
of their time that we might be the richer through their guidance. We need
the kind of Masonic action which was exemplified in the life of the late
and beloved John Whicher, he of saintly Masonic memory. We need the
kind of action that will result in another living, vibrant, enthusiastic, upsurge of Masonic force!
What we should think about is, "How are we going to do this? What
are we going to do?" A great psychologist said that when we are faced
with a difficult problem, the start is half the solution. We can all start
increased Masonic action in several simple ways.
,Follow the Guide of Grand Lodge
Grand Lodge is the nerve center from which active impulses can
radiate to and from each Lodge and member Mason. You can deaden the
nerve line running to you by the narcotic effects of indifference and apathy;
or you can use it for energizing your manpower into channels of action.
Study . and put into practice the recommendations of your Grand Lodge
committees and of your Grand Master. It would help even if you were
like the young lady of whom the bishop asked whether she followed the
ten commandments. She said,· "I can't say that I follow them but they
do give me a lot of good· ideas." Get some ideas from the annu'al address
of your Grand Master. He is the voice of Grand Lodge. He speaks to
you and for you. With your help he can speak louder and ~ay more.
Make Known the Real Meaning and Mission of Masonry .
Everett B. Clinchy, president. of the conference comprising ] ews,
Protestants and Catholics, a few years ago wrote an extraordinary book
called "All .in the Name of God." He analyzed the recurrent anti-Masonic,
anti-Catholic and anti-racial movements. It all sums up to this-the movements arise from fear. Those who do not know are afraid. They suspect

457

the so-called secrecy and mystery. Quoting from his book, Dr. Clinchy
said:
"The strength of the anti-Masonic society that flourished in
this period lay in the dread among those of native stock of the
mystery and secrecy of· Masonry that was suspected of concealing a
threat to American institutions. Both Masons and Catholics either
lacked the ability, or disdained to take pains to allay these unnecessary suspicions."
You remember we recently laughed at the lengths to which some will
go in fostering this fear. An example in point was Goebbel's ridiculous
"expose" of a photograph showing President Franklin D. Roosevelt with
his sons and Mayor La Guardia, dressed in Masonic regalia, sitting in a
Masonic Lodge. And just a few weeks ago we read again how Petain, the
would-be dictator, laid all the ills of France at the doors of Freemasonry.
The consequent thinking which goes on in the minds of some people
is like the speech of a recent refugee from Europe. He spoke perfect
English but in between his words he whistled and hissed. Someone asked
him why he did this. He replied, "I learned to speak English by listening
on the short wave radio." There is a great deal of "whistling" and "hissing"
in the thinking of some people about Masonry.
Brethren, as Masons, we have a responsibility to safeguard ourselves.
Of course, we should not be driven by a spirit of exasperation to the use
of counteracting methods which would be as foolish as the attacks leveled
against us. We must conduct ourselves with patience, dignity and reserve.
But we. can firmly show that we do have the ability and . will take the
pains to allay unnecessary suspicions. Examples in point of effective and
proper counteracting methods will be found in how the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines jurisdiction stopped anti-Masonic radio broadcasts, and
how the Swiss Masons prevented the passage of anti-Masonic legislation.
Let's make known what is meant by Masonic secrecy; that a few
years ago the Mother Grand Lodge of London issued this statement,
"There is no secret with regard to any of the basic principles of Freen1asonry."
Let's make known that Masonry is non-partisan; that we know any
intrusion by us into the arena of partisan politics would be the eventual
death of our institution, like dying of drinking too deeply of the fountain
of youth.
Let's make known that Masonry is tolerant of all creeds, all races
and all religions; that we say:
"Let pridish priests do battle with creeds,
That church is mine that does most Godlike deeds."
Let's make known that Masonry has no bars because of position in
life; that true equality exists under the square and compass.
Let us make known that Masonry conceals no threat to American
institutions but that on the contrary American institutions owe their very
life to American Masons. We can stand for the free way of life. Do you
remember that inspiring passage in a Greek drama written over 2000
years ago? One of the characters put this question : "Who is the shepherd
over you, and the lord of your host?" The chorus thundered back, "Of
no man are we called the slaves or subjects." That democracy for which
they felt such a passionate devotion was later preached by Christ. Then, like
a river of. gold flowing on through centuries, that ideal has come down to
us as our priceless inheritance.
The fundamentals of Masonry have never prevented individual action

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR="IA

by Masons within the orbit of good citizenship. On the contrary our individualistic concept calls for individual action. Masonic strength lies in
the realm of each individual's action. "The strength of the wolf is in the
pack, and the strength of the pack is in the wolf."
Many, many years ago there also lived a powerful, a cruel and .a doublecrossing dictator, Xerxes, King of the Persians. He sent an emissary to
Athens, seeking an alliance and offering a territorial bribe. That system
of strategy is old as the hills. But the free Athenians replied, "Tell Mardonius that Athens says 'So long as the sun keeps the path where now he
goeth, never shall we make compact with Xerxes; but we shall go forth
to do battle with him, putting our trust in the God who fights for us and
in the mighty dead, whose dwelling places and holy things he hath condemned and burned with fire.'"
In the same spirit say we to all foes of freedom, never shall we make
compact with alien forces of aggression! Never shall we permit the intrusion
of their false philosophies into our way of living! But we shall stand
steady, strong, and united. We shall insist upon a continuance of the
Masonic doctrine of equality and unity. We have no place in these United
States for any man or group who would tear us apart through demonstrations of racial or religious hatreds!
Let's make known why the Masons abroad have been persecuted.
I refer to the Masonry which we recognize. Goebbels, Minister of Propaganda for Germany, gives the reason quickly. In 1933 he declared:
"The conception of spiritual freedom is contrary to the supreme
authority of the leader. There is no other truth .'"
·
Following this declaration, an order was issued on May 11, 1933 for
the destruction of 20,000 books at a public bonfire in Berlin. Significantly,
the first book thrown upon this heap was the Bible.
Masonry and Masons immediately collide with such a concept. Like
oil and water, the two cannot mix. The two ways of life are irreconcilable.
We say that the cosmic importance of man transcends any mere manmade state. We stand for the emergence of man as an individual, for the
emancipation of the human mind, for morality in action throughout ~ur
daily lives. There we blow the bugle and draw the issue.
As a result our European brethren have· suffered a crushing defeat
for their way of life. They have been mistreated, their Lodges closed, their
property confiscated, their leaders killed.
We can say to the world, "Go to that symbolic figure who holds the
scales of justice with equal poise; lay before her the men who have oppressed
our brethren, armoured (IS they are with steel and iron, riding with 11
cavalry of hate over the bodies of their prostrate victims. Show her the
sack of cities, the burning and bombing of innocent men, women and little
ones, the people· made miserable all over the earth. When she is under
the impact of this view, follow these diabolical men into the dark rooms
where they plot their plans, hear them scheme to steal country after country,
to rule by force and fear, to snatch from the faithful every vestige of their
spiritual and temporal freedom. When she has tired of this prospect, show
her the men of Masonry, working without any bloody war, without any
fabulous hero, without any Trojan horse. See plain men who use plain
means for lifting man into a contemplation of his own exalted soul, leading
toward a liberation of the human mind, unfolding a priceless philosophy
of life, keeping in view always the higher meaning of immortality. Then
ask her, 'Which of these do you choose?'" But the answer is easify made.
The same ideas, the same emotions must have passed through the

mind of one who in his day was heralded as a hero-patriot, one who in later
days was universally acclaimed the sage of America, _that Master Ma~on
of deathless fame George Washington. Writing to his brethren of Kmg
David Lodge at Newport in 1790, he was inspired to express his opi.nion
of Masonry in these words:
"Being persuaded that a just application of the principles upon
which the Masonic Fraternity is founded must be promotive of
private virtue and public prosperity, I shall always be happy to
advance the interests of the Society, and to be considered by them
a deserving brother."
Let us stretch forth a helping hand to our oppressed brethren abroad
and say to them with Emerson, "The hour may be against us, but the
centuries are for us." Let us make known to them that we do feel for
them, that we do stand by them, and that while their hands are tied, we
will fight the good battle for them.

Make Our Lives Exemplify Masonic Teachings
Napoleon at one time thought he was a great and lasti?g conqueror.
Later, iii exile at St. Helena, he told the truth when he sa1~: "The only
conquests that are permanent are those we make of ourselves. He should
have known.
Masonry is not a mass gift; it is an individual _conquest. It canno_t be
be conferred; it must be acquired. Merely walkmg through the ritual
never made a Mason. We must regenerate and refresh ourselves each day,
like the. manna the Israelites found in the wilderness. We are rewarded
in direct proportion as we live the Masonic philosophy of life.
The world also judges our institution by the character of its members.
We should so act · that others may say, "Masons revere God, they pay
their bills, they are gentlemen, they are moral, clean-minded and friendly."
Shakespeare wrote the simple rule :
"To thine own self be true,
And it must follow as the night the day.
Thou canst not then be false to any man."
We are told in the holy writings, "Let us hold fast the profe~sio~ of
our faith without wavering.'' Brethren, would you out-distance this mght
of the world despair? Then hold fast to your Masonic faith. Would you unlock a priceless philosophy of life? Then, my brethren, hold fast ,to Y?Ur
Masonic faith. Would you touch a brother's hand, hear a brothers v01ce,
know what is meant by Masonic friendship whenever you go around the
globe? Then, my brethren, hold fast to your Masonic faith.
Make Masonry Live and Grow
Back in the days of Mohammed the Prophet, people had great respe~t
for horses. Those with outstanding intelligence were selecte? for use. m
warfare and were trained to follow the bugle in battle. Havmg occas10n
to acquire some horses for himself, the great prophet went to a famous farm
to make some personal selections. He ordered all the horses pastured
next to a river but fenced off and unwatered for three days. At the end
of three days the bars were let down. The horses rushed i_n a mad body
to quench their thirst. Just as they were about to plunge mto the water
the . war bugle sounded. Of that great number, only ten answered the
call. The ten were then chosen as the beginning of the famous "Prophet
Breed" of Arabian horses.
Masonry also uses a wise and selective process for enrollment of its

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNfA

members. But greater Masonic action will automatically result in an attraction of suitable new material. Thus will follow an ever-increasins:
fl.ow of that social force and directive power so sorely needed today. While
the principles of Masonry are eternal, ever were and ever will be, still
Masonic Lodges require strength and stamina through active members.
Masonic action will result in Masonic growth .

world. We. say with ho.p e and high confidence, that when history shall
have passed her stern sentence on those er~ing men '."ho have oppressed
our brethren and beset this world with stnfe, Masonic Lodges will continue to exemplify the spirit of courage, the brotherhood of man and the
fatherhood of God. V\Te say with hope and high confidence that Ma.sonry
will fulfill mankind's hope for the emergence of leaders of whom, hke of
the leaders of the Renaissance, it will be said : "The dazzling ligqt of
their genius shines on through the centuries, showing future ages what
man can be and what man can do."
Brethren! Now is the time for us to act-act to follow the guide of
Grand Lodge-act to make known the real meaning and mission of Masonry
-act to make our lives exemplify our Masonic teachings-act to make
Masonry live and grow! Thus, we shall enjoy and move toward greater
Masonic action!

What of Our Future?
In the olden days the watchman of the night would walk the watch
towers of the town. In times of danger the people would ask, "Watchman,
what of the night?" Today we ask of those on the higher watch towers
of Masonry, "What of our future?"
Experience has shown that the fundamental and simple reason for the
breakdown of our way of life elsewhere in the world has been a lack of
able, courageous and constructive leadership. There has been a woeful
want of moral as well as political leadership. The whole world literally
cries out for leaders.
Some years ago a party of explorers, driven by a west wind from the
Amazon River far out to sea, were dying .o f thirst. They had been without
water for days. Drifting they suffered the tortures of the damned. At
last a ship came into sight. They signalled frantically for water. 'The
captain of the ship signalled back, "Let down your buckets. There is
fresh water all around you." They did not know that the Amazon River
remains fresh for more than a hundred miles out to sea.
In much the same way, the moral leadership for which the world cries
out is just as available. Surely Masonry has proved itself a fountain source
of" inspiration for leadership. Where else in the world today is there an
organization dedicated to moral uplift which includes every creed, religion,
and race? Who but the Masons have adhered more firmly to the faith of
their fathers and shown more patriotism? Where then, but from the ranks
of Masonry, can there come such leaders?
As Masons have always championed the emergence of man, so from
the ranks of Masonry have there come leaders of mankind. Masons abroad
have been the champions of democracy : Bolivar, South American liberator ;
Goethe, German poet ; Mozart, Austrian composer; Lafayette, French
patriot; Kossuth, Hungarian patriot ; Garibaldi, Italian patriot. They were
not only men in the forefront of movements for freedom, but all were also
Master Masons.
It was no accident that in early America the stirring words, "Give me
liberty or give me death " echoed the thoughts of Master Masons. It was
no accident that when Paul Revere made his historic ride, he was spurred
on by the heart of a Master Mason. It was no accident that most of
the pens from which fl.owed the immortal words of the Declaration of
Independence were those of Master Masons. It was no accident that the
Masonic doctrine of equality of man was indelibly written into our constitution by Masonic hands, directed by Masonic minds.
Down to the present in the United States we have had twelve presidents,
fourteen vice-presidents, outstanding statesmen and soldiers, leaders of
business and science, leaders of labor and letters, leaders of bench and
bar, men of great and important affairs, all of whom also knelt at our shrine
as humble Master Masons.
Looking toward the boundless future, therefore, we lift up our eyes
from the darkness of the day to that letter "G" still shining brightly in
the East and we are then ourselves uplifted. We say with hope and high
confidence, that Masonry will again light the way for an awakening

Experience. of Other Homes
We recently sent a questionnaire to every other Masonic Children's
Horne in th e United States, as to their population trend. We find that they
have all experienced a drop, in most cases greater than ours. Their combined enrollment shows a decrease of 45% from peak figures, which in
various Hornes were reached between 1931 and 1935.

properties in fir st class condition and feel that funds spent for repairs,
painting, etc., as' a good investment. The appearance of our buildings speak
for themselves. ·

Our questionnaire made inquiry as to what were regarded as the
causes for decreasing numbers. Strangely enough the consensus of opinion
seems to be that the largest factor is the recent financial depression. The
depression caused a falling birth rate; school enrollments in the United States
are now two million less than ten years ago. A second result of the depression was a decrease in Masonic membership, those first to drop out
being borderline economic cas ~s whose children would have become wards
of Masonic charity. The third cause connected with the depression is the
· unprecedented expenditure of public funds for charity, part of which went
to relieve families whose children otherwise would have come to us.

Covina: Dishwashing machine, steam cooker, corrected plumbing installations, installed inter-communicating telephone system, installed boiler
feed pumps and installed celotex in ceiling of kitchen.

464

Another cause, not connected with the depression, has undoubtedly
contributed to lessened enrollment in all children's institutions, Masonic'
and others, namely, the increasing tendency to care for dependent children
in foster homes rather than in institutions. Arguments can undoubtedly be
advanced both for and against either the institutional or the foster home
method of child care. Those of us who have hl\d a part in the operation
of the Covina Horne during the past twenty years or more, believe that its
results abundantly justify our faith in it and the efforts of the fraternity
in sustaining it.
Results at Covina
In the office of the Covina Horne hang the group photographs of all the
classes of graduates for the past fifteen years. We have made it our business to know how these boys and girls have turned out in later years, and to
know also how they themselves feel about the Home and its influence
upon them. While not all of them are 100 per cent successful, their average
performance when thrown upon their own· resources compares favorably
not only with children brought up in foster homes, but with those reared
by their own parents. The thing that is significant in this connection is
not the achievements of the best or the failures of the poorest, but rather
the performance of the average; and that performance, in spite of the fact
that many of them emerged from the Home into the severest period of
the depression years, is a good one. They have found jobs and held them;
they have kept off of relief and . out of jail; th.e y have married and are
raising families; they have taken their places as good and representative
American citizens. That is a fair picture of the average product of our
Masonic children's institution.
0

We are glad that the immediate need for this form of Masonic relief
seems to be a ' decreasing one. We cannot predict the future. Some there
are whose opinions should have weight, who foresee conditions following
the present world-wide carnage and destruction, which will make the Covina
Home more necessary than ever before. It is the opinion of your Board
that we should continue to maintain this Horne on its present high plane
of efficiency, and to have it re:>dy to do its share in caring for the distress
which seems certain to follow in the wake of the present emergency.

Death of Superintendent Hartman
On February 3, 1941, Superintendent Frank B. Hartman was stricken
with a heart attack while driving his car in Oakland, he passed away on
February 6. The funeral services were conducted by Grand Master Lloyd
E . Wilson at the Masonic Home, Decoto.
For thirty-one years Brother Hartman served the Home and the Masons
of California as Superintendent, and at all times was more a Brother Mason
than Superintendent in his relations with those who were residents of the
Home. He insisted that Masonry intended it to be truly a Home and all
who lived therein were members of the "Family"; as the Father his job was
to promote happiness. His success was evidenced by the sorrow of the
"Family" at his passing. A true Mason departed when Frank Hartman
joined the great caravan.
The vacancy caused by the death of Superintendent Hartman was filled
by the appointment of James· R. Eubanks, a member and Past Master of
San Mateo Lodge No. 226. Brother Eubanks has had many years' experience in institutional work as Superintendent of the San Mateo Horne for
the Aged.
Minnie B. Richardson who had served the Masonic Home as Matron
for twenty years felt that her health made it imperative that she resign.
She retired on May 1, 1941 and in consideration of her long and faithful
services the Board of Trustees voted her a pension of $50.00 a month.
Mrs. Virginia Lord wno had been for sixteen years assistant in the
Home hospital was appointed Matron.
Although but a few month s have elapsed, we feel that we have made in
both instances a happy choice.
Resident Physician
The proper care of our residents of the Decoto Home who are ill has
long had consideration of your Trustees. For years we have called in a
physician from the neighborhood town of Centerville. This at times has
been unsatisfactory. Early this year we heard that Dr. Val Priestley Osburn
of San Diego, a member of Anaheim Lodge No. 207, a physician who
specializ.ed in diseases of the aged might be available. Arrangements were
made for a resident physician and Dr. Osburn is now at the Home in that
capacity.
We would like to acknowledge our debt to Dr. W. L. McWhirter whom
he succeeded and who served the Horne faithfully and well as a visiting
physician. The number of residents hospitalized as well as the demands
for medical attention due to the ailments of old age compelled the appointment of a resident physician available at all times.

Silver Plates
During the years of existence of the Homes many donations have
come from individuals and lodges, which your Trustees have greatly appreciated. In many cases such gifts have been commemorated by. a silver
plate or bronze tablet indicating the donor and apprising the public of his
generosity.
,
But another thing that has perhaps been overlooked, is that by these
markers also the residents of the Homes are continuously reminded that
they are the objects of charity. This we believe is damaging to their selfrespect, particularly in the case of the children in the Covina Home. The
best ideal for the institutional home is that it -should be as much as possible
like a private home; the display of donor's plates does not fit in with this
ideal.
In this connection it is worthy of remark that we have found that a
donation is much more readily given for an ornamental or monumental
gift, such as an expensive vase or a piece of statuary, than for a merely
useful item such as a floor covering. Yet linoleum for the kitchen floor may
do more than a hall clock to make the place seem like home.
We cannot but commend the spirit of the Southern California Edison
Masonic Club, who have made it their project to maintain the kitchen of our
hospital at Covina since since 1926. Last year after expending several hundred dollars in bringing its equipment up to date, they voluntarily requested
the removal of the silver plate which recited that they were the donors. "We
don't want any credit," they said, "all we want is the satisfaction of knowing
that this need of the Home is being taken care of, and we are glad to do
it for that reason alone." That, we submit, is a spirit truly Masonic.
Having these considerations in mind we have resolved to discourage
the giving of gifts which have as a consideration that they be identified by
markers visible to the public and consequently to the residents of the Homes.
We trust and believe that persons or organizations who may be moved to
contribute to the work of the Homes by their gifts will be willing to forego
the gratification of commemorations in silver and bronze, in the faith that
there is a place where every good deed is recorded imperishably.

suc;h applicants not physically handicapped whose happiness would be promoted by giving financial aid which would enable the aged brother to
continue to live in his home environment and among his friends, provided

among friends and relatives in the community where he has in many instances spent the years of his adult life?

Hospitalization
Under our regulations admission to the Decoto Home is refused to
those who are invalids or otherwise incapacitated and unable to care for
themselves. If we were to admit such who need hospital and nursing care
we would have to greatly increase our capacity. Furthermore, our location
is such that an adequate visiting medical staff is almost impossible.
A check of other Masonic Homes would indicate that with few exceptions all refuse such cases as cannot go to the dining room and care for
themselves.
Hospital costs in those states that admit the incapacitated run from
$2.7 5 to $4.50 daily as against our per capita of $1.11 which includes our
hospital costs.
It is interesting to note that the Grand Lodge of Washington refused a
gift of $200,000 for a hospital after careful study, reporting that the maintenance cost of such an institution would be greater than private nursing
care.

An Irreparable Loss
With the death of John Which er the Trustees of the Masonic Homes
lost more than its secretary. Secretary of the Homes since 1908 he was a
stor~ho1;1se of information regarding the rules, regulations and a~tivities of
the institutions. Age did not impair his faculties and· to the last his reports
of the business transactions and the recording of the minutes truly reflected
the actions of the Trustees.
Beyond all this he had contact with many who were about to become
residents of the Home and in his kindly way gave courage to the applicant
and ma?e the entrance to the Home easier for the aged brother. Incidentally
h_e retained his interest after their admission, never failing to give them a
kindly word in his frequent visits.
His heart was with the children and the letters he wrote to the gradua~e~ on their leaving the Home at Covina will long be treasured by the rec1p1ents.
It will be long before his place is filled.
Entertainment Fund
Last year we called your attention to this fact: for a number of years
the ;esponse of lodges to our Christmas card, which is a polite way of suggesting that you make a contribution for the entertainment of our residents
at Decoto and our children at Covina, has not been as generous as in the
past. The result has been that in order to carry on the activities which lent
pleasure to our aged and children, not only during the holiday period but also
throughout the year, the contributions have not been sufficient to meet our
ex~enditures. In the last several years we have created a deficit of $4233.29.
This year the response was $58.00 more than the amount expended. This
is promising and we hope the response this year will wipe out the deficit.

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home

To the Board of Trustees,
Masonic Homes of California:
The year of 1941 having drawn to a close, it becomes my duty and a
privilege to submit at this time my first report of the management and
operation of the Home.
Previous reports have, from year to year, traced the development of
the Home. Its fundamentals have become stabilized. Its existence has
become a secure fact, and the management will, I assure you, endeavor
to keep pace with every new development in the care of the aged.
At the beginning of the year, there were 322 residents; 34 were admitted during the year, at an average age of 73.06; 50 passed away, the ·
average age being 77.40; there were 6 departures and 1 withdrawal. Of
the 300 in the Home, 143 are women, and 157 are men, including 21 married
couples. There are
4 residents between the ages of 50 to 60,
71 residents between the ages of 60 to 70,
138 residents between the ages of 70 to 80,
83 residents between the ages of 80 to 90,
4 residents between the ages of 90 to 100.
The average age at this time is 75.68 years for nien, and 74.61 for women.
Advancing years bring with them ever increasing demands for greater
service to those who are blind, crippled, infirm, or otherwise unable to care
for themselves.
The hospital department is under the supervision of one registered
nurse, Miss Esther G. Payne, who, with a corps of able assistants, render
kind and faithful serviCe to those who find it necessary to be in the hospital. Dr. P. P. Osburn is in charge of the medical work.

487

At present there are about 50 in the hospital, most of whom are infirm and feeble. The fact that we have so few in this department would
indicate that a large percentage of our guests are enjoying fairly good
health. In an attempt to render better service to our patients, we have
added a Cold Quartz Ultra Violet Ray machine and a Short Wave Generator Lube! Florsheim machine. This department has been renovated and
brightened with a new coat of paint.
The Matron, Mrs. LOfd, is in charge ·of all departments in connection
with the care and comfort of the residents. Assistance is rendered cheerfully and impartially where needed.
The kitchen and dining room are among the more important departments. An attempt is being made to plan better balanced meals.
With the assistance of our steward, I am very hopeful that there will be
a satisfactory imp.rovement very soon. In this department we have had
. all the ice-boxes put in first-class condition, and have a dish-washing machine ordered, which we hope will be installed soon.
The laundry contributes much to the operation of the Home by providing fresh, clean clothing and linen.
The grounds and flower gardens are cared for by one paid gardener
with the assistance of many of the residents, and they present an appearance that is very attractive.
The heating plant operates very efficiently under the supervision of an
engineer. He has a paid fireman and two residents assisting him, and
with this assistance he is able to take care of the plumbing and electrical
work. This department has checked all the fire-fighting equipment and recharged all the chemicals.
The farm land has been leased on a share basis to several people, and
the returns have been fairly good. This arrangement was not entirely
satisfactory; therefore, the Trustees have decided to lease the land on a cash
basis to one responsible party.
The portion of land that is retained for the Home's use supplies quite
a few of the vegetables and berries, and also an abundance of fruit during
the fruit season. The chicken ranch supplies a good portion of our eggs
and an occasional chicken dinner.
We have disposed of three of the old cars which were in use here at
the Home and have replaced them with a new station wagon. This acquisition has enabled us to supply comfortable transportation for our guests.
We are also able to convert it into an ambulance when the occasion requires.
A gasoline pump has been installed to service our own cars.
Our old well-pump, which has been in service for many years, is
being replaced with a new modern one. Inefficient operation on the part of
the old pump and expensive repairs necessitated this installation.
The road leading from the Decoto Highway into the Home's grounds,
which was damaged by the heavy rains last winter, has been put in firstcl'.Lss shape.
During the year many splendid entertainments have been provided by
visiting Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, Job's Daughters, and friends for
the entertainment of the Home folk. Outstanding among them were the
East Bay Past Matrons' Association, who entertained the residents with a
fine program, introduced the present Grand Officers, and then presented
the Home with enough jams, jellies, blankets and other articles to last
a year, and the Sojourner's Ceremony, under the direction of Colonel Jesse
M. Whited. At the conclusion of the Ceremony, which was very impres-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sively exemplified by the officers of that organization, they presented the
Home with a beautiful flag.
Through friends and members of the Fraternity, we have received
many contributions of magazines, books, papers and periodicals. These
were placed on the shelves of our library by our very efficient librarians
and are enjoyed by many of our guests.
Through the courtesy of the San Francisco Film Distributing Companies we are able to entertain our guests with movies every Thursday
evening, for which we tender our grateful thanks and appreciation.
Devotional services are conducted in the Auditorium every Sunday.
Dr. W. A. Pankey of Hayward is in charge of the arrangement. We want
to assure him and the kind gentlemen who conduct these services that we
appreciate very much their interest in our behalf.
I am fully aware of the fact that the responsibilities of the Home will
increase from year to year. It will not be my policy to follow in the footsteps of the past, but to mold the approaching problems of the Home into
policies of the future. I assure you of my willingness to accept suggestions,
and that when changes can be made to make these policies more in keeping
with the best, it i·s my purpose to do so.
May I say that our Matron, our staff and myself are very grateful
for the many courtesies extended to us by the Board of Trustees.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home

To. the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Herewith I am presenting my fifteenth annual report as Superintendent
of the Covina Home. During the past year there were 12 admissions (7
boys and 5 girls); 28 discharges (20 boys and 8 girls).
Of the 28 discharged the causes of discharg~ were:
Graduated from high school.. ...............................................................10
Returned to their parents at their request, account remarriage .... 7
Returned to parents, account improved economic condition ...... 7
Dismissed account unsatisfactory conduct ...............,.................. 4
The present business activity resulting from the Defense program has,

506

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

for the time bein~, made the problem of employment for our graduates an
easy one. Our class of 1940, numbering 14, are now occupied as follows:
In college................................ 2
In the Navy....~....................... 1
Unemployed ............................ 1
In secretarial work. ...........,... 3

Airplane factories .................. 2
Other factory jobs................ 1
Store clerks .......................... 2
Cosmetologists ...................... 2

It is an inspiring procession, these young people going forth year after
year from the doors of the Home into the outside world. During the past
fifteen years 414 have thus gone out; 177 of these have carried with them
high school diplomas; the other 277 have left before graduating, in most
cases be.cause of improved family circumstances which made care by the
Home no longer necessary. A relatively small number of cases were discharged because they were not profiting by their opportunities in the
Home and wer.e standing in the way of "other children making satisfactory
progress.
We are not justified in classifying children as "good" and "bad." Yet,
although no child may t'ightly be called "bad," we must recognize that he
may be very detrimental to other children who are closely associated with
him. Occasionally we must weigh the good we can do a boy against the
harm his presence will do to others.
On the other hand, an important benefit that comes from group living
is the educative influence of the group upon the individual. The general
intention of the Masonic Home group is sound and wholesome, and it
works beneficially upon each individual. The Home child cannot live to
himself alone ; he must give as well as take; there is a strong incentive to
comradeship and team work.
Alumni of the Home-The terms "alma mater" (fostering mother),
and "alumni" (foster children) are usually applied to a college or school
and its pupils; but. are more truly applicable to the relationship that exists
between a Home such as ours and its wards. Our alumni are a factor far
from negligible in the life of the Home.
During the past year ther~ have been three gatherings of Alumni: a
dinner in San Francisco during .Grand Lodge Week; a dinner at Covina in
February; and a reunion picnic in August at Camp Tucker, Balboa Island.
In June was issued the ninth of a series of Alumni Newsletters which have
been issued during the last several years. This issue, consisting of 24 mimeographed pages, contained news of 315 farmer boys and girls of the Home.
Because it helps them to keep in touch with each other, and to preserve
their childhood friendships, we think it is well worth the work and expense
involved in its publication.
I have often said to a Home boy or girl whose conduct had reached a
crisis : "We are not so much concerned with what you think now of our
decisions and our treatment of you, as we are with what you will think of
them five years from now. Come back then and tell us whether we were
unwise or unjust." They do come back frequently, and their characteristic
remark is: "You were too easy with us." Their letters to us and to their
friends in the Home help to convince our boys and girls that we are right
even when we find it neioessary to "bear down."
If They Could Try the World- Boys of' sixteen or seventeen (and
sometimes girls) occasionally get tired of Home routine. They are impatient under the restraints which we think it necessary to impose upon
youngsters of their age. They think they would like to be out in the world,
freed from the requirement to go to school, earning a man's wages and
having a man's freedom.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

507

Frequently we have thought it would be beneficial if such a boy could
have his wish, and then after a few months, when he had had his measure
taken in the world of men, to let him come back into the Home. Recently
one of these discontented boys was discharged to his mother, who had
remarried. During the summer he earned $30.00 a week working on oil
derricks. When our school started he came back to see if there might not
be some way for him to re-enter the Home. He said: "I see the Home
different now. The kids here don't know what they've got. Some of them
said to me this morning that it's like a concentration camp. I told them
that's right, and my advice to you is you'd better concentrate on your
studies and your jobs in the Home while you have the chance; I sure would
like to get back." If that boy came back, his next year would be his best.
Special Events-Many Lodges and individuals have exerted themselves
during the year to bring to the children pleasures and recreations. While
all of these are listed herewith under the head of "Entertainments," it
seems that some should be given special mention.
For the past seventeen years the Lodges of Monrovia have given an
annual Christmas party for the children. They come to the Home and
carry the children to the Lodge Hall at Monrovia in their automobiles,
provide them an entertainment with a Christmas tree and special gift for
each child, followed by refreshments. The children look forward to the
"Monrovia party" for months, which is explainable not only by the character
of the entertainment, but by the unique atmosphere of hospitality which the
Monrovia Masons contrive to put into the event. ·
For the past seven years Huntington Beach Lodge No. 380 has invited the children to take part in its annual picnic in the park at Huntington
Beach. Here are provided games and recreation under skilled leadership,
after which the children sit down with the Lodge members and their
families to a grand picnic dinner.
For several years past the Lodges of Santa Ana have taken a particular
interest in the welfare of the children ·during the summer season when they
are in camp at nearby Balboa. Noteworthy expressions of this interest
this year were the gift of two rowboats; also their entertaining the older
children at some of the DeMolay dances in the Santa Ana Masonic Temple.
Noteworthy Donations--Elsewhere in this report are listed the many
gifts, large and small, which have come to the Home during the past year;
but we wisJ:i to call particular attention to certain ones of these.
The most noteworthy gift during the past year was a complete set of
dental equipment of a value of more than $4,000.00, given by Dr. Walter
Wilcox. Special interest attaches to this donation, owing to the fact that
Dr. Wilcox was the first Masonic orphan cared for by the Grand Lodge of
California, after having lost both of his parents in a yellow fever epidemic
iu New Orleans in 1877.
Good fortune again befell the Home in a bequest to Santa Monica
Lodge No. 307 in the sum of $2,078.50, from the late Tharald Steen, which
was to be expended on some project agreed upon between the officers of
Santa Monica Lodge and those of the Covina Home for the benefit of its
wards. It was determined to use this money in improving the large playground, by the installation of an automatic irrigating system for the maintenance of turf upon this two acre area, the furnishing of a power lawn
mower and renovator, and other items necessary. This will constitute a
real and most welcome addition to the recreational facilities of our Home.
For many years Mount Olive Lodge No. 506 has maintained an enthusiastic interest in the welfare of the. Home's wards. They maintain a

Another noteworthy gift was that of Mrs. A W. Pye from the estate

This was noteworthy not only because of the generous amount, but also
because it is unusual and welcome for a gift of furnishings to be made
without stipulation as to what the furnishings shall be.
Another fine gift was that of Mrs. Fred ]. Ham, whose late husband

Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, having been appraised that a girl, a ward of
their Lodge, who had been in the Home for twelve years, was to be graduated and needed vocational training, advanced $500.00 which has enabled
her to take a course in cosmetology. She has recently finished the course
and passed the California State examination as a beauty operator.
Ada Chapter, 0 . E . S., of Sacramento, made inquiry as to what special

to provide vocal instruction to a girl of the Home who has a really promising voice. During the past Year they have advanced $200.00 for this
purpose.

they could desire-a fine and generous gift of real educational value.
A.s in many seasons past, Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319 has taken special
interest in the supplying of a large quantity of canned fruit, . particularly
peaches; a practical gift that is ever welcome and most useful.

is meant that boy or girl who has been most public spirited, who has done
the most in making the Masonic Home community a better in which to live.
T.he awarding of these prizes is determined by the ·boys and girls

The concept of citizenship is not an easy one for boys and girls to grasp.
These prizes have placed a particular emphasis upon this concept, have
been a valuable means of training our young people toward being better
citizens in a nation which, in coming days, will need good citizenship
above all else.
JOHN M. DOWNEN, Superiatendent.

Past Commanders Association Prizes-The boys and girls of the Home
have been often described as "one big family" ; however, it is perhaps
more accurate to tl)ink of them as a community. The influence of each of
them upon the community is far from negligible, and this is especially
true of . the older ·boys and girls.
The' basis of our national ·life is citizenship; that life can be no better
than its people · as citizens make it. In · the present days of national stress
this fact takes on added significance. Therefore, we can do · no better
thing in training our children than to teach them the meaning of community responsibility.

Past Commanders Association has for the past several years offered two
prizes (gold watches), awarding one to the boy and girl adjudged to have

Annual Report-1941
The entire world today is acutely and vitally concerned with headlines. Whether these headlines be written by free and unrestrained hands
or through the mandates of dictators, they represent the passing scene in
which we all must of necessity take a part-large or small as the case may
be.
The stories recently told in these headlines are on the ancient theme, repeated anew, ~f man's inhumanity to man. They tell of the horrors of
modern warfare, of sly misrepresentation in or-der to gain an end. They
tell of conquests over defenseless peoples and of the murder of ancient
faiths and beliefs. Through the banner lines of world presses we learn of
the ruthlessness, the all-out efforts, of despots to impose their rule of might
and brute force upon a world staggering under the impact of tyranny and
destruction. They tear away the crusts of civilization and reveal the savage
beneath.
D ay and night these headlines assail us, pounding into our minds the
incessant stories of lust and intolerance. There is no escape, no relief,
from the constantly repeated tales of violence on land, on sea, and in the
air. These horrors are actually happening and must be told. We must be
told of the incredible fall of nations, of the rule of organized arrogance
·and military might, of lurking submarines in the waters of the world, of
downtrodden symbols representing peaceable pursuits and endeavors, of
the horrible aftermath of incendiary bombings of populous areas. We
must be told because it is actually happening; of piracy on the high seas;
of pledges broken between nations formerly proud of their national honor;
of the ascendancy into world diplomacy of the qualities of cunning, deceit,
and force instead of the honorable and decent policies of the past; of the
crucifixion of tolerance, kindness, and brotherly love.
These are the headlines of the day-ghastly, unbelievable, yet horribly
true. And because of its fearful truth we must all struggle, must fight and
endure, while the doctrines of force and assumption of power are alive
in the world.
There is, however, another headline, another banner, that streams
0

525

across the lands of the world today and enfolds within its kindly embrace
the hearts of all mankind. It is the headlines of the heart, and it is of those
headlines that the Board would speak today. It is the headlines of simple
kindness, of benevolent care and protection, the unsung, unseen headlines
written by the sacrifice and brotherly love of the humane and charitable.
We of the Jurisdiction have made those headlines, have written by our
faint efforts during the past year, as in years gone by, the lines that
make up the completed paragraphs and chapters. Without fanfare, without ostentation, but with strong determination we have gone forward and
produced, in a world gone mad, the fruits of benevolence and compassion.
While the completed results for the year do not wholly represent the
full potential power of the Jurisdiction, nonetheless the Board is happy
and proud to present its report, realizing the serious need of the times and
the many calls made upon the Brethren by numerous programs, patriotic
and charitable.
Program for Year
Adhering to its stated policy of encouraging purely voluntary contributions, the Board dedicated its services during the past year to the
educational theme rather than to a promotional or quota drive for funds.
We restate and reaffirm our belief in such a program. We believe that
with the growth of knowledge among the Brethren concerning the Homes
project, the dissemination of facts and figures regarding the Homes proper,
the intimate and personal stories emanating from the individuals making
up the Homes, the facts of capable and humane management, and finally,
the utmost security guaranteed by the Permanent Endowment Fund, we
believe all these things not only will cause a birth of interest and concern
among the uninformed brethren, but will cause as well a renewal and rededication of efforts among those who have so generously participated
in the past.
The sum total of the Board's endeavors were this year given to the
task of serving as agents rather than that of an agency. Our stewardship
consisted merely of representing and acting for the Jurisdictional officers, the Masters, Secretaries, Home Endowment Chairmen, and of
those Craftsmen of Constituent Lodges who actively and with great
generosity and sacrifice carried out the vital work of the program through ~
out the year. To .them goes all the credit. To them the Board is greatly
appreciative of the opportunity extended by the program of serving with,
and for them, in the interests of those in our care at Decoto and Covina.•
Ours was merely the ministry, in their name, for the great privilege of constructive and lasting service, and we are des'i rous of recording our deep
gratitude and appreciation to every one who participated in the great
charitable program of the Jurisdiction.
In our capacity as agents for the great endeavor of the Homes, the
Board handled 16,030 pieces of incoming and outgoing correspondence.
In addition to this, 87,690 pieces of literature covering various phases of the
program were sent to the Lodges, which requested printed matter regarding
the Homes. The bulk of the outgoing correspondence consisted of regular
messages forwarded to Masters, Secretaries, and Homes Endowment Chairmen, and contained ideas, methods of procedure, educational items on the
Homes proper, and messages from Grand Lodge officials bearing on the
program. The incoming correspondence dealt mainly with requests for
information, reports of progress within the sender's Lodge, calls for
printed material. and checks to be added to the endowment fund.

526

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Following out the program of economy instituted last year in curtailing expenses of printing new pamphlets, the Board urged Lodge officials
to order from the large supply already on hand. These pamphlets, covering
practically every phase of the program and illustrated with pictures of the
Homes buildings, the adjoining grounds and recreational facilities, and
with photographs of the management and of the Home Guests, were
widely distributed throughout the Jurisdiction and undoubtedly contributed
much to the individual Craftsman's enlightenment regarding the great
vision-made real through characteristic Mason\c generosity.
One new pamphlet was added during the year to the long list already
available to the Craft. This pamphlet found wide distribution and elicited
much favorable comment from whose who took the time to secure and
read it. Published under the title of " Foster-Parentage of California
Masonry," it was written around a letter received by one of the House
Mothers at Covina from a graduate of the Home. It is illuminating and
heart warming, in that it portrays splendidly the heritage with which the
graduates of Covina are endowed as they leave the Home to face the
problems of life. In no finer way could the story of our sacred stewardship of the Homes be told than through the written though ts of one who
actually experienced "the filling of the gap" between bereavement and homelessness and that of security and wantedness. The Board strongly suggests
that all Masons of California secure a copy of this pamphlet from their
respective Secretaries and learn with pride of the glorious part their
contributions take in making their fo ster-parentage a definitely real and
splendid thing.
As a service to Secretaries and Editors of Lodge Bulletins, the Board
forwarded a list of briefs, composed of short sentences and paragraphs
bearing on Homes data for inclusion, throughout the year, in the monthly
'releases of Lodge news. We are gratified to report that these briefs were
widely used and served as a distinct contribution to the work at hand. A
careful check-up on Lodge Bulletins carrying these informative briefs
regularly revealed a greater interest in Home affairs among the Brethren
of that Lodge with a correspondingly high r esponse in contributions. The
Board strongly recommends the continued use of these Bulletin briefs in
the months to come.

Home V isitations
A hospitable and cordial welcome for all Brethren has ever been a
warm reality at both the Decoto and Covina Homes. The portals have
ever been flung wide with gracious friendliness for all who care to e~ter
and mingle with the Home Guests on the ground hallowed by generat10ns
of Masonic benevolence.
Decoto and Covina by virtue of their unique place in the charitable
history of the Jurisdiction should be the Mecca of all California Craftsmen.
They should be included in the itinerary o~ ever:l'. conscious M_ason! ?eca~se
within their halls dwells the physical manifestation ~f Masonic spmt~ahty.
Abiding within their predncts :ire the yields of man's finest and highest
instincts-brotherly love·, kiiidn·e ss, compassion.
It has been for years the B~~rd's constant desire and expressed h~p.e
that every Mason in California would, at some time or another, pay a v1s1t

529

to the institutions symbolizing the precepts and principles of the Craft.
We sincerely believe that a visit would constitute an object lesson in the
fundamental maxims of the Fraternity and be of lifelong value to the
pilgrim in measuring such doctrines of faith and good will.
The great good such a visit would produce would be twofold: first, the
pilgrim himself would be vastly benefited by such contact and would be in
a better position properly to judge the actualities of the Homes Endowment program; secondly, the Home guests would come to realize through
such friendly association that the program was not one based on abstract
principles of charity alone, but one alive with the warmth of human understanding and human comradeship.
The visitor "could see for himself the happiness of the children, the
contentment of the elders. He could see the physical manifestation of
an ideal. He could see many monuments erected by the desire of an
individual, or of a group, to make their living presence felt in practical and
useful things for many years to come-the dining halls, swimming pools,
recreational apparatus, temples, dormitories and hospitals-all erected
by and bearing the name of a gracious donor in perpetuity. He would
realize that here, here in this place consecrated by years of Masonic idealism,
of security:, contentment and peace, where a successive parade of homeless,
orphaned, and bereaved were sheltered, fathered, and made happy, here
indeed was the place where he, as an individual, or acting in concert with
his fellow Craftsmen, could best erect his monument in and for a real and
lasting benefaction.
The portals of the Homes are ever open to welcome those who would
seek and find. May the Board, voicing the cordial invitation of the Grand
Lodge, the management, the Home guests; present again to all Craftsmen
the opportunity an·d privilege of viewing at the Homes the practical application of Masonic solicitude and kindness.

Bequests
Testamentary gifts to the Fund this year totaled $35,850.62. Of this
amount the smallest totaled $1.00, while th e largest reached the figure of
$10,343.50.
The Permanent Endowment Fund will absorb these bequests and will
pay out in the many years to come the financial interest made possible by
the generous hearts of the donors. Needless to say, these bequests have
been placed in sound investments and will be carefully g uarded by the
Board in order that they may never lessen, never cease, their constant flow
of material good to the general program.
·
The Board wishes in this report to accord full credit to attorney members of the Craft, who have made available to their clients fu ll and complete
. information regarding the Homes, and in doing so have presented the
opportunity to such clients for making lasting benefactions. This splendid
work, for and in behalf of the Homes at Decoto and Covina, is fully appreciated by the Grand Lodge and has earned the admiration and deep
gratitude of the Board, ·which has, in many cases, been privileged to cooperate with such attorneys in the preparation of wills and bequests.
It is a matter of great pride to the Board to know that this great work
is still going on, that members of the legal profession are donating their
services in this regard, telling their clients of the permanency of the Fund,
showing the material good that each testamentary gift will bestow; pointing out the utmost safety of the investment in happiness for- others, and
finally preparing the necessary papers for the ultimate disposition of the
bequest.

For all these co-operative efforts in a field ever fertile, ever needful,
and ever appreciated, the Board is indeed grateful; and in extending its
thanks, urges a continuation .of the same splendid spirit of collaboration
for the future.

a building, never wholly completed, but one to which each generation may
devote his share of toil by hand and heart; that each generation, in erecting
its wings and roofs, may place, in common with those of the past, their
mark of care and consideration.
We believe, sincerely believe, that no mechanical basis is needed for
the erection of our building of charity. We ask for no government help;
we neither ask nor would accept it if offered. Ours is a unique benevolenceone predicated on the Masonic doctrine of unity, one grounded in the solid
soil of kindness and compassion.
We believe, sincerely believe, in the words of a fellow Craftsman who
recently penned these glowing words to the Board:
"Truly, I wonder if Masons anywhere need more than a request for the
aid of so fine a Masonic object."

530

Work of Grand Master and Officials
In line also for the considered praise of the entire Jurisdiction is the
outstanding work of Most Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Master,
Masters and Secretaries· of Constituent Lodges, and of the many Endowment Fund Chairmen who performed ably and creditably during the past
year. The Grand Master, by virtue of his able proclamation designating
the month of May as Homes Endowment Month, by his qualified and
sincere addresses on the subject of the Permanent Endowment Fund, and
by his gifted and capable efforts throughout the entire year, earned the
lasting appreciation and commendation of every Craftsman in California.
To our Grand Master go the thanks of every Home guest and of those
who experienced the great privilege of working with him during the past
months.
Assisting greatly in the program were the Masters and Secretaries of
Constituent Lodges. Their efforts were constant and resultful. Secretaries,·
as in the past, were on call throughout the year passing out information,
pointing out the needs of the Homes, writing and personally contacting the
Brethren, and otherwise rendering signal service to the general program.
The Board cannot too highly praise the splendid efforts of the various
Lodge Secretaries, and can but say in deep appreciation that without them
the program would decline in direct proportion to their decline in cooperative effort.
Another group of sincere and capable workers were the Homes Endowment Chairmen appointed for work within their respective Lodges.
Of this sincere and able group the Board is especially proud. Their work
was of the highest order and contributed much to the completed program
for the year. Our sincerest compliment is the .request to incoming Masters
that their services, wherever possible, be again utilized by early re-appointment in order that they may again move forward in the interest of the
Jurisdiction's major charity.
In keeping with the Board's established policy of welcoming suggestions
as to methods and procedure in carrying out the program, a letter requesting possible proposals was forwarded to Inspectors and Masters in July.
Many and varied were the answers received. Many fine suggestions were
offered, and the Board will see to it that these plans, which have proved
successful in the writer's Lodge, will receive the widest possible circulation
for the benefit of others. A small percentage of those answering favored
a per capita tax to be levied for the Endowment Fund and some suggested
a program based on a quota drive; but to the Board's 'gratification, the
great majority of the answers contained approval of the present method.
It has been your Board's sincere belief throughout the trying years
behind us, and we still believe for the uncertain future ahead, that the
plan based on a purely volunteer structure is the one most desired, and,
in the long run, the one most likely to prove successful.
We believe, sincerely believe, that Masonry needs no force, no must;
that neither of these qualities, represented by quotas or taxes, can equal
the output of conscious Craftsmen motivated by the basic liberality of Freemasonry. We believe that the free and entirely voluntary gifts of those
whose hearts are attuned . to the rare privilege of giving will far transcend
those exacted by drkres and .taxations. We believe that an endowment is

The Board recommends the following resolution and moves its
adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of six thousand dollars be appropriated for
the use of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board.
Fraternally submitted,
