REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
TWENTY-SECOND ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
"If the man bites the dog," that's news. And so, in beginning this
report of the Twenty-second Annual Observance of Public Schools Week,
instead of referring to its great success (which of course is nothing new,
except perhaps in extent) we make mention of the fact that this year
there were apparently more Lodges than there should have been, even
though few in number, which made absolutely no contribution to it.
That's news.
There were observances (and successful ones too) in which the local
'Lodge should have been the motivating factor, but took no part whatsoever.
Now it was fortunate, of course, that an observance was held in that the
purpose of Public Schools Week was thus subserved; but it was extremely
unfortunate (as it was where there was no observance at all) in that the
defection of the local Lodge was a reflection on California Masonry generally, as well as on the particular Lodge and the Masons of that community.
As a result of the effort made by the fraternity, the observance of
Public Schools Week has become a community affair; but as should be
well known by this time, this does not mean that any Lodge anywhere should
now do less than was expected of it by Grand Lodge when the only outside assistance that was received came from school people who _sensed the
importance of the movement that had been instituted in the interests of
our public schools.
Indeed now that the annual observance has become a community affair,
it is perhaps more important than ever before that there shall not be lacking
that Masonic support and influence which was, if not entirely;-certainly
very largely, responsible for its growth and development; because its
Masonic origin is well known and very generally referred to at every
annual observance-not only by Mason~, but also by speakers at public
meetings and over the radio, and by writers of newspaper articles, who have
no connection with the Masonic fraternity.
This is true even in those communities in which the Committee of
Arrangements studiously avoids any reference in its literature to Masonry,
and is especially careful to do nothing that could possibly warrant a suspicion that the observance is not in every sense a community affair in which
Masons merely participate with other .friends of the public schools. And
there 'are communities (large as well as small) where Masonry is so identified with the observance, and the connection with the fraternity so emphasized by advertised Lodge sponsor.ship of meetings to which the public
is invited, that the community aspect is not as apparent as it might well be.
With Masonry thus publicly credited with the responsibility for the
observance of Public Schools Week, it must be obvious that if we do not
play the part we should, indeed take the lead, in every observance, those
who are not ol our number may believe, and they will have a right to believe,
that our protestations of regard for our public schools are "as sounding
brass or a tinkling cymbal."
We trust that nothing we have said will be taken as even an intimation
that there was any lack of Masonic endeavor this year (except in the few

555

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

instances to which reference was made); because nothing could be further
from the fact. The reports indicate that never before were the arrangements for an observance made by the Masters of our Lodges and by their
officers and committees with more loyalty, zeal and intelligence. And the
natural result was an unprecedented success.
The care and attention with which the arrangements for an observance
were made are often evidenced by the type of report submitted. Some of
them not only furnish all the information called for by the questionnaire
sent to the Master, but also include a typed summary, frequently in narrative form; with such detail as would enable one to visualize the entire observance from the appointment of the committee through all the arrangements to its close. The newspaper clippings are neatly pasted on sheets
of paper of the same size as the questionnaire and also attached to the ·
report are copies of programs and of notices, instructions to sub-committees,
bulletins from the principals to the teachers, instructions for the reception
of visitors to the schools and of practically all the literature incident to the
observance, including letters written after its close by teachers and appointed
"observers" giving their impressions, and in some instances making recom·mendations for the following year.
Because of its importance, we deem it advisable to here again rep.eat
what has been said from time to time in the reports of this Committee to
Grand Lodge with respect to the report the Master of each Lodge is
expected to make. We believe the repetition necessary, because there are
Masters who have no knowledge of any report made by our Committee
other than the one presented at the communication at which they are in
attendance; and some of the Masters, we regret to say, apparently do not
appreciate the value of the reports they are expected to make of the observances for which they are responsible.
The~e reports are a factor in what we have termed the "mechanics" of
an observance of Public Schools Week in so far as it is fostered and guided
by Grand Lodge; and in this connection we think that even as Masons
we may not unbecomingly say that although the observance has become
a community affair, nevertheless the growth, development and success
of the movement are undoubtedly due to the fact that it a highly organized
activity of Grand Lodge, and that it is through our Masonic Lodges that
the cooperating agencies are coordinated.
As is of course known, each year there is sent to the Master of every
Lodge in the jurisdiction a form on · which his report is to be made, and
which contains a series of questions he is expected to answer. The request
for this report comes from the Grand Master; and of course is not deliberately disobeyed nor ignored. But it occasionally happens that the kind of
report furnished would seem to indicate little more than a perfunctory
compliance with the Grand Master's request; and there are too many instances in which no report at all is made until after repeated, and urgent
requests.
We are not unmindful of the fact that it sometimes happens that a
Master is so situated that it is difficult, if not impossible for him to make
his report in the form we, and undoubtedly he also, would like to have it.
But there would appear to be no good reason why the form sent out for
the purpose should not be promptly returned with every question answered;
and there can be no doubt that most failures are due to simple carelessness.
We believe that if the value of these reports were fully realized, a special
effort would be made by those from whom they are expected to forward
them as promptly, and with as much detail, as possible.
Although our committee maintains contact with city and county super-

1ntendents of schools and with the State Department of E ducatio? and
also with the parent bodies of the organizations which cooperate m the
observance of Public Schools Week, it is largely through the rep«?rts from
the Lodges that . information is obtained with respect to the details of the
local observances. It is from these reports also that there come the suggestions which emanate from our committee. But in some instances they
serve a still more valuable purpose.
Every Lodge has a file of its own in our records. If we find, as we
·o ccasionally do, that some particular observance has not been as successful
in every particular as we believe it should have been, the report from that
community is carefully analyzed. And if we find, as we usually do, that the
procedure recommended as a result of past experience has not been fol~owe.d,
w e immediately write the Master of the Lodge while the matter ~s. ~till
fresh in his mind; not, as we are careful to explain, b.y way o.f cnbc1sm
of anything done or left undone, but solely with the desire of bemg helpful
and with the hope that any mistake which possibly may have been made
will be thereafter avoided; and we always ask that our letter b~ handed
to the one who will be in charge of the observance the followmg year.
And it is gratifying to be able to report that we have evidence of the
fact that this has proved well worth w hile.
In our report last year we quoted an excerpt from a newspape~ ~lipping
accompanying a report from one of our Lodges as well. as descnbmg the
general observance. Following that precedent, ~e .ag.am. q~ote a ne~s­
paper account of a local observance this year which 1s md1cattve of a situation very general throughout the State, both as to weather and attendance.
" Despite the fact that rain had fallen all day and that the
weather was still threatening at curtain time and that two ~ther
major attractions were being held in the town on the sa.me mght,
the biggest crowd in the history of the observance of Pubhc Schools
Week in .................. was present. Every seat in the higfh scho o 1
.. 1ctitorium the largest in .................., was filled long be ore 8 :00
o'clock A'n chairs available were brought in and many stood .in
the aisles and doorways while many were unable to secure even
standing room."
In this connection it seems to us worth while noting that the 'report
from a city in which the week's attendance is meticulously recorded shows
that the attendance at the evening programs increased from 15,922 last
year to 22,398 this year.
.
More than once attention has been called to the fact t hat without the
slightest depreciation of the fine cooperation of the California Chambers .
of Commerce ( Senior and Junior), California Cor:gress o~ Paren~s ai:d
Teachers, The California Department of the American Leg10n, Cahfor?1a
Federation of Women's Clubs, California League of Women Voters, Native
Sons of the Golden West, Native Daughters of the Golde~ ~est and State
Farm Bureau and of the various service clubs and other c1v1c and fr:iter~al
organizations which join in the observance, there are two factors pnmanly
responsible for the growth and development of Public Schools ~eek
One is the active cooperation of the school people, and the other is ~he
hearty and cordial support received from t~e newspapers and broadcastmg
stations.
Notwithstanding extraordinary demands on th~ new~pa~rs ~nd b;oadcasting
stations due to the war in Europe and the resultmg situation m this countqr,
they were no less liberal in their contributions this year t?an they have been m
the past. Indeed due to a situation t o which reference will. be hereafter made,
not only did the programs of the local observances receive very generous

556

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

newspaper notice, but there was probably more editorial reference to Public
Schools Week than otherwise there might have been. In this connection,
and in spite of our determination to make no reference to any particular observance, however well deserved, we cannot forbear mentioning that in
an extremely interesting report from a little Lodge serving an area of
about 8,500 square miles, there is a "challenge to any weekly newspaper
in the State of California to show more space devoted to Public Schools
Week in 1941" than was given that observance, which, by the way, covered
every school in the area. lncidently there were five hundred and twenty
column inches of newspaper articles with mention of Public Schools Week
by thirty-two merchants in their display advertising.
In c'onnection with our acknowlegment of the cooperation received
from the press generally, both urban and rural, we feel that we should
make mention of the fact that there were several communities, this year,
where there was an issue during Public Schools Week of a local newspaper which was entirely the work of the class in journalism in the high
school.
Except, in the larger communities, the public meeting with a guest
speaker is no longer the important feature it once was. But there has
been a material increase in the number of "radio talks." This is due, of
course, to the cooperation and courtesy of the broadcasting stations which
also make very generous "spot .announcements" of the observance. and
of the programs to be given.
Not only are public addresses broadcast, but time is also given for
the presentation of playlets and student programs. On one station this
year the time allotted to a Parent-Teacher Association was devoted to a
novel program presented by a Chapter of the Future Farmers of America
depicting a phase of the course offered by the high school in vocational
agriculture. Very interesting in itself, it must have been also fine publicity
for the local observance.
Some of the Lodges which did not join in the observance made no
report of any sort; and from the Masters of others came explanations
which were more ingenious than convincing. In one instance, however,
the faifore of the Lodge to join in the observance was fully justified; because
it was in consonance with the inhibition against taking part in any controversy between individuals or groups in a community even though it be
' in connection with, or grow out of, public school matters. The facts as
reported by the Master are substantially as follows :
In a certain community there was a bond election to be held one week
prior to the date set for the observance of Public Schools Week. The School
Board fixed that week as the date for holding the local observance; and
it was obviously for the purpose of affecting the bond election over which
there had been a bitter battle between two factiotis. Both factions were
represented in the membership of the Lodge. If the Lodge joined in the
observance to be held at the time fixed by the school board it might be
deemed an endorsement of the bond issue. On the other hand, if the Lodge
refused to join in that observance and held one at the time fixed for the
general observance of Public Schools Week, it might be assumed that the
Lodge was opposed to the bond issue.· The Master, therefore, very wisely
decided that the Lodge should not join in any observance of P ublic Schools
Week this year.
In a report such as this it is not feasible, of course, to do more than
refer to · the programs in general without making especial mention of the
many which well deserve it. Again this year there was an increased number
evidently designed to convey information as to just what the schools are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

557

doing, rather than to merely furnish entertainment. T hey included demonstrations of classroom procedure in cultural, vocational and homemaking
activities with exhibits of school wor k of every sort and kind, and of the
,tools and equipment with which students are trained for occupational
and defense industries. And there was an increase this year in the number
of "panels" and "forums" for the discussion of questions affecting the
schools. " Back to School" night was featured in many observances as
were "Father and Son" meetings held in the schools and also in some of the
service clubs participating in the observance. Among the most interesting
meetings were some held by the service clubs, or in which they participated
either as hosts or guests. There were m any instances reported in which
the regular luncheon meeting of a service club was held in a school cafeteria with a program presented by pupils of the school and which was
followed or in some instances preceded, by a visit to the classrooms.
Many of the . observances were . built around "themes" or "motifs"
and among these were "Builders of America," "The American Way of
Life," " Educated Citizenship," " Free People in Free Schools," " Foundations
of Democracy" and "The Part the School Plays in National Defense." It
is interesting to note that in sonie communities the announcement of a
program in which the schools and national defense were associated undoubtedly accounted for an increase in attendance ; while in at least one
other in which there was held an otherwise especially successful observance,
a forum for ' the discussion of the situation of the local schools as a result
of the national defense program was very poorly atten ded.
In view of the nature of the programs generally, it is fair to assume
that the incr.ease in the number of visitors to the schools, and in the
attendance at the public meetings, was due to an increased desire upon the
part of the parents of school childrP.n, and of the public generally, to find
out for themselves whether or not what they had been hearing and reading
about the public schools of the 11ation were true.
The people everywhere apparently wanted to know whether or not
their schools were permeated with " Communism," or "Fascism " or any
.other "ism." They wanted to find out the truth, if they could, about such
magazine articles as "Are D emocratic Principles Disappearing From Our
School Books" and "Propaganda In Our Schools . .. Treason to the
Spirit of America" ; and whether Dartmouth College or the American
Federation of Advertisers had correctly appraised certain high school
textbooks. Some of them had perhaps read the attack on progressive education by the author of "Lpllypdps v. Learning" ; and in one community
they probably want ed to know if it were true as had been said, or rather
intimated, by a newsp aper columnist that the children were not being taught
how to compute interest because the time which should have been thus
employed· was spent in the gymnasium learning the tango. And those
who could availed themselves of the opportunity afforded by Public Schools
Week. And, by the way, if that. columnist had done likewise that "anything but complimentary attitude towar d the public schools system" (his
own words) might have been changed.
To learn just w hat is being taught in the public schools generally,
and how, and why, and the real character of those by whom, it is being
taught is in itself no easy task for any particular individual parent or
.group of parents. And it is rendered · still more difficult by reason of
. certain conditions which here can be only indicated.
· There never has bee.n a time since Horace Mann initiated the movement
for free tax supported, non-sectarian public schools that they were not
being criticized for something :they were either doing or leaving undone;

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and we have with us today one of those periodic recrudescences of the
battle he waged. So bitter was this contest, by the way, that the late
Professor Cubberly said of it that with the exception of the struggle for the
abolition of slavery there had never been a question before the American
people which caused so much . feeling and aroused such bitter antagonism.
The criticism being voiced by some parents today is not unlike that
which their parents made of their schools. It is honest and sincere, but
seldom thoroughly informed. And there is criticism of a different sort
from other sources which also is sometimes, but not always unfortunately,
.honest and sincere. But there can be no doubt that honest and sincere
and even well-informed criticism has been capitalized and publicized by
certain individuals and groups with nothing but ulterior motives.
The public school system is too firmly entrenched in the minds and
hearts of the American people to be in any great peril as an Institution;
but no person familiar with the facts can doubt that there is a determined
effort being made in certain quarters to curtail and limit the scope of
public education.
There is today a contest being waged in which in addition to individuals
and certain comparatively small groups, there are arraigned against each
other large and· influential organizations such as the National Education
Association, The Progressive Education Association, American Federation
of Teachers, National Association of Manufacturers, United States Chamber
of Commerce and New York State Economic Council. And then, of course,
there are also among the school people State Teacher Associations; and
among the lay groups State Taxpayers Associations. The result has been
a flood of propaganda with which the earnest seeker for truth must
struggle; and which too often leaves one not personally familiar with the
facts baffled and confused.
In connection with the reference to certain lay organizations which
may be assumed to be the representatives of large business interests, it
should be pointed out that no more loyal, enthusiastic, unselfish protagonists of our public schools, and of modern education can be found than
some of the members of these organizations. To them the encouragement
of a sound critical faculty in high school students does not constitute a
threat to the safety or perpetuity of our democracy. One of them in an
address before the National Education Association said:

is no other group of American citizens more devoted to the ideals of our
Democracy and of our American way of life than are those fi ne men and
women to whom those of us w ho believe in our public schools willingly
and confidently entrust our children.
Of course criticism of our schools is inevitable, and desirable too·, in
so far as it is honest and sincere and made with that knowledge of the facts
on which it should be based. Such criticism should be welcomed; and not
considered as hostile, nor be deemed "propaganda" in the opptobrious
sense in which that word is used by those against whom it is directed.
As we once confessed, yes boasted (in answering a charge that the
Masonic fraternity in sponsoring Public Schools Week was engaged in
propaganda) " Yes, accepting the definition of propaganda as a plan for
the propagation of a doctrine or system of principles, we are, of course
propagandists for our system of public education." And so, too, are those
thousands in the Parent-Teacher Associations and in the service clubs
and in the American Legion and in the other social and civic organizations
who so eagerly and cordially join each year in the undertaking in which
we are engaged. And no less so are those owners, publishers and editors
of newspapers and the directors and managers of broadcasting systems
and radio stations without whose sympathetic aid and whole-hearted cooperation that undertaking would not have assumed its present proportions.
We are propagandists for our public schools because of our belief in the
contribution they are making to that enlightened citizenship upon which
depends the hope for the future of this nation of ours-perhaps the hope
oi civilization itself.
All of which is respectfully submitted,

558

"Teaching our children what "to think cannqt possibly fit them
for life in these changing times. We do not know what they should
think; for they must deal with things which we know nothing about.·
We must teach them how to think-how to find out about these
things, so that they may apply this new knowledge to the new problems with which they will inevitably be faced."
The unkindest criticism to which the schools have been subjected, and
particularly because so undeserved, is that which reflects on the loyalty
and patriotism of the school people.

perhaps the social science studies are being over-emphasized; possibly the
taxpayers' burden for the support of our public schools should be lightened;
it may be that some of the money is being wasted. Indeed even the fundamental idea of providing at public expense for every child an opportunity
for an education beginning with the kindergarten and ending only with the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCING
BUILDING ·PROJECTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the year ending September 30, 194( your Committee has
reviewed the following projects in accordance with the prov1s10ns contained in Sections 87 and 152 of the Constitution and Ordinances.
John Mashall Lodge No. 636, F. & A. M., situated at Los Angeles:
This Lodge through its Inspector, Brother Roy C. Bryan, has discussed
with your Committee a plan whereby it was sought to purchase the property in which the Lodge now meets. Your Committee made a thorough
study of the affairs of this Lodge, including its membership and financial
standing, and also the plan for the purchase of this building.
Your Committee feels that the desire to secure a permanent home for
this Lodge is a commendable one, but is of the opinion that considering
the size of the Lodge, the number of years it has been in existence, and
that the amount of cash in the treasury of the L odge is not more than
sufficient to place the Lodge in a comfortable financial condition; that
therefore, the purchase of this building wou ld be very apt to prove a very
heavy financial burden on the Lodge and its members, and because of this
it might result in hampering the future growth of the Lodge, and might
also be the source of creating discord therein.
For the above reasons, your Committee disapproved the plan.
Alhambra Lodge No. 322, F. & A. M., situated in Alhambra :
Your Committee approved a request· in which Alhambra Lodge desired to deed a strip of the property it owns to the City of Alhambra for
street purposes. Your Committee was of the opinion that by giving its
approval the lots now owned by the Lodge will materially increase in value.
Beverly Hills Masonic Building Association, situated at Beverly Hills :
It has long been the desire of the brethren of Beverly Hills Lodge
No. 528 to have a Masonic Temple in the Beverly Hills area. A plan of
finance was presented to your Committee whereby sufficient funds to
defray the cost of a new building are to be raised by a "life insurance
plan" and the solicitation of gifts. The plan of finance did not contemplate
the investment of any Lodge funds.
Your Committee was unwilling to approve the so-called "insurance
plan" ·for the reason that this method of raising money · has met with considerable criticism in the past. The Master of the Lodge was notified
that the question of the practicability of the "insurance plan" as a means
for raising the necessary funds is a matter for the Lodge itself to determine.
Your Committee suggested that the Lodge and the Building Association
should proceed with the greatest caution that no embarrassing complications
may develop in the future.
Your Committee examined the plans for this new building project
and approved them subject to the following conditions : First, that no
Lodge funds shall be solicited or invested by Beverly H ills Lodge; secondly,
that all building ordinances are to be strictly complied with . .

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee regrets to report the death of W. Brother A. Heber
Winder, who for several years was chairman of the Committee on Masonic
Education. Brother Winder was an indefatigable worker; under his direction
the Committee was very active and Masonic education was stimulated
throughout the jurisdiction. He was a sincere and devoted Mason, one
who lived his Masonry, and the craft in California will miss his progressive
leadership, his wise counsel and his splendid example. The Committee is
glad to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the memory of Brother
\\Tinder and to express appreciation of the service he rendered Grand
Lodge in particular and the fraternity in general.
The passing of Brother Winder made it impossible for the Committee
to formulate an effective program for the current Masonic year. We did,
howe~er, send a questionnaire to all Masters of Lodges for the purpose
oi (1) determining what was being done along the lines of Masonic education, and (2) to obtain from the Masters suggestions for the future.
There were 275 replies received and the recommendations made in this
report are the result of a careful analysis of the answers.
There seems to be no consistent or generai program of Masonic education in the Lodges. Some Lodges have a fairly comprehensive and
effective method of education, either through the coaches to the candidates
receiving the degrees, or by means of programs, speakers, quizzes and
discussions for the enlightenment of the older brethren. But most of the
Lodges have no regular and systematic program throughout the year. At
the same time, a great majority of the Masters iridicated that they were
of the opinion that the brethren would welcome Masonic information if
it were given in brief, interesting form.
The Manual of Masonic Education, as prepared and published a few
years ago, is not in general use, although some Lodges use it as a reference
work. The booklet has been withdrawn from circulation by action of
Grand Lodge, and no more copies are being sent out.
The little pamphlet, Masonic Law and Custom, continues in demand
and there is ample supply on hand to meet the requirements for the coming
year.
The term "Masonic Education" is unfortunate. There seems to be a
decided and enduring prejudice against the phrase. Many brethren resent
the implication that they are ignorant and need education, and they also
object to other brethren being set up as instructors and mentors. This
feeling seems to be widespread. Brethren welcome "information" on Masonic
subjects, but do not want "education." In the popular mind, education
carries the thought of high-brow stuff, dry-as-dust and difficult to understand. We think the time has come to change the name of the committee.
In these days of digests and short cuts, Masonic information must
be put out in concise, interesting and challenging form. Brethren do not
like profound, long-winded dissertations on abstract and abstruse themes.
They ask for facts; not philosophy. They want capsules of pre-digested
data that can be shot at them with the rapidity, clearness and vividness of
a radio announcement. The day of the ponderous sermonic lecture is past.
Methods of Masonic education must be revised to fit the rapid-fire procedures of the quiz programs. Many Lodges arrange their own prog·rams

on the question and answer system and find them attractive and satisfactory.
Most of the Lodges from time to time invite speakers to address them
and this has been found a most efficient way of promoting attendance and
stimulating interest. Complaint is made, however, that Masters do not
know what speakers are available or upon what subjects they are prepared
to speak. The committee should be of help to the Masters by supplying
information regarding speakers.
At the last communication of Grand Lodge the sum of $300 was appropriated for the use of the Committee. Only $20.49 was disbursed.
This Committee recommends:
I. ·That the name of the Committee be changed to "Committee
on Masonic Information."
2. That the Lodge system of instruction be continued.
3. That the Committee be authorized to prepare and print a monthly
four-page bulletin giving ten questions and answers each month
on Masonic subjects, to be mailed to the Masters and to be used
by the Lodge to make up quizz programs.
4. That the Committee be instructed to prepare a roster of available speakers for the benefit of Masters who may desire lectures
on Masonic topics.
5. That the Committee prepare, in consultation with the Grand

Wednesday, October 15, 1941.
Grand Lodge was called from refreshment to labor at the
hour of 10:00 o'clock A. M., the Grand Master presiding.
Devotions were led by the Very Rev. Grand Chaplain.
The Most Worshipful John A. Emigh, Grand Master of
Masons in Washington, was received with Grand Honors, and
after being welcomed by the Grand Master, was escorted to a
seat in the East. Grand Master Emigh responded to the welcome
of our Grand Master and expressed the greetings of his Grand
Jurisdiction.

during Tuesday's sessions he had used the gavel presented to him
at the commencement of his term by his own Lodge, Ingleside
No. 630; and that he was now using, for today's session, the gavel
made and presented to him by the Secretary of Georgetown
Lodge No. 25.

Grand Master of Masons in the Province of Ontario, Canada.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC PUBLICATIONS
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee appointed to consider the recommendation of the
Grand Master in his Annual Message to the last annual communication
of Grand Lodge concerning the so-called "Masonic" magazines and publications has had the same under consideration pursuant to resolution of
Grand Lodge and begs leave to report:
The members of the Committee and others have offered suggestions
ranging from a total prohibition of the use of the word "Masonic" or any
kindred term implying a connection with Masonry to other and milder
forms of limitation upon the conduct of the business of these publications.
We have considered these suggestions, together with the recommendation of the Grand Master, from legal as well as ethical grounds and have
come to the · conclusion that the recommendation of the Grand Master irt his

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Annual Message to the last communication of Grand Lodge to be the most
effective available method of meeting what at times has been a troublesome situation.

un-Masonic, ·unethical, fraudulent, misleading or questionable acts
or practices in connection therewith.
Respectfully submitted,
'vVILLIAM B. OGDEN,
]oHN STEWART Ross,
J. W. DAVEY,
Committee.

572

If these publications are to be permitted to hold themselves out to the
public and to our institution and its members as Masonic in character,
then they should be compelled to meet the high ethical and moral standards
bf our Order or cease their activities.

Representations made to secure advertising, and even the class of
advertising, should be subject ~o the scrutiny of the Grand Master or other
authority appointed for the purpose. 'vVe are of the opinion that in a publication allegedly devoted to the interests of Masonry that, through its
advertising space, the patronage of Masons should not be solicited for
liquor stores, cocktail parlors and other similar businessses, in which, under
the Masonic law of California, our members can have no interest. We also
think that advertising solicitors should not be permitted to solicit advertising on the representation that it is the Masonic duty of our members to
buy space, or upon the representation that the purchase of space will
assist Masonry, or upon the representation that the purchase of space
will insure the patronage of the craft, or that such publication in an
"officiaP' publication or that, in fact, it has any connection whatso~ver
with this Grand Lodge.
Many of our members have been fearful that in effecting a remedy
for a magazine evil that we might thereby give some sort of recognition
or official standing to this appendage to Masonry, and this; we believe,
the craft is loathe to do. The legislation hereinafter proposed can in nowise
be said to give such recognition, nor, perhaps, need it ever be applied to
them if the necessary reforms be made before it becomes necessary to
exercise the power granted.
While it may seem that the wording of the proposed legislation departs
from the purpose for which this committee was appointed, and is perhaps
broader and could cover more subjects than merely publications, a situation
might arise, where such power in the hands o'f the Grand Master might
be the only and much needed remed"y, while, at the same time, in our
·opinion, it will meet any situation that may arise in connection with the
subject of our report.
\Ve therefore approve the recommendation of the Grand Master in
his Annual Message to the last communication of Grand Lodge concerning "Masonic" magazines and publications and recommend that the
following legislation be adopted:
That Article II, Section 34, of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge be
amended by adding thereto a clause to follow the clause thereof numbered
"12th" to be worded as follows:
"13th. To issue interdictions requiring the officers and members of constituent Lodges to refrain from traffic with and to cease
and desist from giving aid or support to any business, project,
scheme, plan, individual or concern asserted to be Masonic in character, or using any term, name or words implying a connection
with Masonry, whenever facts presented to the Grand Master prove
to his satisfaction (a) that any such business, project, scheme or
plan is un-Masonic, unethical, fraudulent, misleading or questionable, or (b) that the individual, group, or concern in charge of
or employed in the prosecution, promotion, operation or conduct
of any such business, project, scheme,, or plan has indulged in

REPORT OF HISTORY COMMITTEE
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:

Your Committee on Masonic History submits the following report:
Although there have been no discovies of unusual historical material
during· the past year, a considerable amount of detail work has been accomplished. This has included a thorough check of our files to properly
classify material for easy reference. Listings have also been made where
·e ssentiaf data are missing to assist the committee in future efforts to make
·our historical records as complete as possible.
Most of our information is filed under the name and number of t he
particular Lodge 'with which it is associated. In addition there is rµuch
of a general or specific nature which properly can not be thus filed. Such
material is placed in separate files bearing distinctive titles. There are now
278 of these special files besides one for each of the 683 active and extinct
Lodges of the California jurisdiction.
An attempt has been made to learn more of a number of "phantom"
Lodges which are associated with California's early histor y. Meager
records or tradition indicate that possibly there were fourteen of such
Lodges, as follow:
(1) A Lodge at Honolulu, Sandwich Islands for which a Dispensation
was issued by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts o n September
13, 1848. Nothing further has been learned of . this L odge.
(2) In the same year, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts issued a Dispensation to Robert F . Parker which authorized him to form a
Lodge at San Francisco. No local accounts of this L odge have been
found. Early records of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts were
destroyed by fire and they have no evidence that either of these
two Lodges ever reported to them after the issuance of the dispensations.
(3) Another Dispensation for a Lodge in San Francisco was granted in
1849 by the Grand Lodge of Indiana. It has not yet been shown that
this Lodge ever functioned.
{4) In May, 1849, the Grand Lodge of Indiana also issued a Dispensation
for: Sierra Nevada Lodge to be located at Centreville, th e present
site of Grass Valley. One report shows that the Lodge had ten
members in 1849, which increased to seventeen members in 1850.
In 1851, after the formation of our own Grand Lodge, the members
of Sierra Nevada Lodge sought to exchange their Indiana· Dispensa-

574

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tion for California authority. The request was denied by Deputy
Grand Master Hyam. Later the Lodge disbanded without ceremony,
and members joined in a petition to form what is now Madison Lodge
No. 23, at Grass Valley.
(5) A forerunner of San Joaquin Lodge No. 19 was Yale Lodge, meeting
at Stockton under a Dispensation issued by the Grand Lodge of
Florida in 1849. Authority had been vested in Gregory Yale, a
member of Solomon Lqdge No. 20, of Jacksonville, East Florida,
and empowered him "to establish a Lodge in California." After
starting the Lodge at Stockton, Brother Yale moved away, the
Lodge seems to have disbanded, and the brethren assisted in the
formation of the present San Joaquin Lodge No. 19.
(6) On March 5, 1849, the Grand Lodge of Ohio issued a Dispensation
for a Lodge "to be located in the mining district of California." With
such an indefinite location it has been difficult to trace the outcome
of this dispensation. Actual formation seems doubtful for the records
of the Grand Lodge of Ohio reveal no reports of work.
(7) Another Lodge of doubtful existence and vague location was "Richmond Traveling Lodge,'' for which a Dispensation was granted by
the Grand Lodge of Virginia, on December 11, 1849. It would have
been possible for such a Lodge to have met at sundry places and to
have made Masons, but this is questioned since the brethren who carried the Dispensation could hardly have arrived in this State before
the formation of our own Grand Lodge. Virginia Grand Lodge
records shed no further light on this traveling Lodge.
(8) California jurisdiction was unintentionally violated by the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin when the latter granted a Charter dated April
20, 1850, for La Fayette Lodge No. 29, located at Nevada City. The
infringement was without knowledge that the Grand Lodge of California had been formed one day previously. The Lodge opened and
conferred degrees in ignorance of the trespass of territory. On May
7, 1851. Deputy Grand Master Tutt reported that the Lodge "was
working under a Charter from the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin until
. the destruction of Nevada City by fire in March last, when the Charter
was lost, leaving a great deal of unfinished work on hand, which was
considered a good and sufficient reason for granting a Dispensation."
Under that dispensation the Lodge became Nevada Lodge No. 13,
which we still have on our roster.
(9) The Grand Lodge of Illinoislissued a · Dispensation in March, 1849,
which authorized a Lodge "to be opened in any State or Territory
where no Grand Lodge existed." Under that authority, and acting
as DeplitY Grand Master of Illinois, Dr. j. R. Crandall reported the
opened .. a Lodge in Marysville, California, "in the spring of 1850."
On May 4, 1852, Brother Crandall reported that "the Lodge had
continued work until the organization of this Grand Lodge; at which
time the Lodge ceased its labors under such Dispensation, and applied to this Grand Lodge for and was granted a Charter to constitute
and open a Lodge at Marysville, California, under the name of Marysville Lodge No. 9. There is some doubt about the name of this early
Lodge. Sherman in his "Fifty Years of Masonry" says it was known
as "Saville" Lodge. Brother John Whicher, in his "Masonic Beginnings in California and Hawaii," gave the name of "Lavely" to an
early Lodge at Marysville and fixed a different date for the Dispensation, namely, October, 1849. It does not seem probable that these
names referred to different Lodges. It is more likely that the names

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

575

of "Saville" and "Lavely" are erratic interpretations of the name of
Grand Master Lavalle of Illinois who signed the Dispensation for
the Lodge formed by Dr. Crandall at Marysville.
(10) In October, 1849, the Grand Lodge of Illinois is also reported to ·
have issued a Dispensation for Pacific· Lodge to be located at Long's
Bar, with a Brother Morse as Master.. In 1852 a report was made to
our Grand. Lodge that the Lodge had operated .. under the Illinois
' authority, but had closed and dissolved before communication could
be held with it.
(11) Two Lodges which were formed in California prior to ;the establish(12) ment of our Grand Lodge were by authority of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient York Masons of Louisiana. The latter body had been
formed in conflict with the older Grand Lodge of Louisiana and was
therefore considered to be irregular at that time. One of the Lodges
was known as P acific Lodge, located at Benicia; the other was Davy
Crockett Lodge at San Francisco. Pacific Lodge became Benicia
Lodge No. 5 under our jurisdiction. It still has the original Louisiana Dispensation , dated June 5, 1849. The minute book showing that
the Lodge was meeting prior to the formation of the Grand Lodge
of California seems to be the oldest existing record of Masonic meetings in California, and bears a notation, "there is a book before this
one." We would like to locate that older record.
Davy Crockett Lodge became No. 7 when it received its Charter
from the Grand Lodge of California. All of its records seem to have
been destroyed, and those of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana and of
the irregular Grand Lodge of Ancient York Masons of Louisiana
shed no further light on the history of these two Lodges.
(13 ) There is ii tradition, without evidence, that the Grand Lodge of
Texas granted authority for the formation of a California Lodge in
1849. The Dispensation is supposed to have named Charles W .
Creamer, William Robinson and Harry Nott as officers. Robinson and
Nott are known to have been members of Victoria Lodge No. 40
of Texas from which they withdrew at about the time the Dispensation is said to have been granted. Further light would be welcomed
concerning this supposed Lodge.
·
(14) Older members of La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17 claimed that
their Lodge held meetings under French authority prior to the formation of the Grand Lodge of California. We have never been able
to substantiate this tradition. The early beginnings of this Lodge
are shrouded in deep mystery and it is suspected that enthusiastic
French brethren were probably meeting without any authority. It is
a tempting bit of research for some French Masonic scholar.
(15) Finally, there is the ever recurring story of an early San Francisco
Lodge which met in a tent which was being used as a saloon. Some
years ago we interviewed an old brother who told of having sat in such
a Lodge with a whiskey barrel for an altar, and . with gin bottles
for candlesticks. He gave it as his opinion that th.e, Lodge in which
he sat later became California Lodge No. 1. However, we have
recently established that the ship upon which the brother came to .
California did not sail through the Golden Gate until after California
Lodge No. 1 had been duly const_ituted and organized. No San Francisco Lodge has yet stepped forth to claim the honor of having been
born iri a saloon.
It would be interesting to have more information on these "phantom"

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodges of early California and your committee will greatly appreciate
assistance that can be given to clear up the mysteries of their existence.
Last December when Brother John Downen was in Honolulu, he
found that Hawajian Lodge No. 21 possessed a copy of "The Masonic
Record," a hitherto unknown San Francisco publication. The Lodge
kindly loaned the same to us. This particular copy was printed in 1886
and fully described the first official visit of a California Grand Master to
the Hawaiian Islands. It cleared traditional information concerning the
reception of Grand Master Atkinson by the King of the Islands. We have
found that this journal was published monthly and semi-monthly over a
peri9d of. three or four years. In our search for other copies we found one
number of the issues of 1885. In its news columns it tells that 2,000 Masons
of Sonoma County had observed St. John's Day with a picnic at Hassett's
Grove; while at Los Angeles 400 or 500 Masons had held a similar picnic
at Arroyo Seco. At Santa Cruz it is noted that Lodge No. 38 had adopted
a flag to be hung out on the day of meeting. At night a blue lantern
denoted a meeting of the Third Degree, while a red lantern was hung
out for gatherings of the Royal Arch. When the Cogswell Polytechnic
School was recently razed in this city, the cornerstone was found to contain
a copy of "The Ma sonic Record" bearing the same date as the one owned
by Hawaiian Lodge No. 21. This second copy was presented to Grand
Lodge and is now in our files. \Vhile we do not advise that buildings
be torn down in order to examine the contents of their cornerstones, we
urge all brethren to be on the alert for additional copies of such old publications.
In checking the records of Past Grand Masters we find that one brother
had been suspended for non-payment of dues fourteen years prior to his
election as Grand Master, and that there is no rec.ord of his re-instatement.
It is noted that during a period of ninety-one years there is a total of
fifty-one elective Grand Lodge officers who failed to advance to the Grand
Master's chair. There have been two years in which three of the elective
officers were dropped from the line, and thirteen different years when two
officers were not advanced or re-elected. In contrast three of our Grand
Masters have served for four years, two served for three years, and four
were re-elected for a second term. Thus, we have had seventy-four Grand
Masters in ninety-one years.
"Pacific" has been the most popular name for a Lodge in California.
It was proposed as the name of five other Lodges before its adoption by
the present Pacific Lodge No. 136. Three of our Lodges have borne the
name of "Franklin," and also of "LaFayette." Two have been known by
the name of "George Washington," and two have been named "San
Francisco."
While on the subject of names it may be noted that Martinez Lodge
No. 41 in one year conferred the degrees upon two "Bruins" and a "Baer."
Carquinez Lodge No. 337 observed the family spirit recently when the
candidate's father acted as Master, assisted by two other sons as Wardens.
Henry Clay Lodge No. 95 had a candidate who was unusually proficient in his work. When the new brother was ready to take his Third
Degree he was postponed because the Lodge was then "in mourning" on
account of the death of a member. The Lodge was badly in need of a
Senior Deacon, so the waiting brother was taught the work of that officer,
and exemplified the Deacon's work the same evening that he was examined
as to his proficiency in the Fellowcraft degree.
Such interesting stories as these provide diversion for researchers

who are looking for more serious material, or give entertainment to those
who are interested only in the lighter side of our history.
Throughout the years we have received much help from brethren who
were not members of our committee. The Inspectors have been particularly
helpful and we are deeply grateful to them. Special thanks should be expressed to Inspector Lawrence C. Kelley for his extended research and
history of the development of the uniform ritual in California ; and to
Inspector Roy C. Bryan for his continued additions concerning the history
of the Los Angeles area. To Mr. Louis Roesch of San Francisco we are
indebted for the gift of a rare booklet which was printed by his father
as a program of the Masonic Festival which was held in 1898 to raise
funds for the Widow.'s and Orphan's Home. Through Mr. H. L. Thomas
of the Pacific Coast Borax Company we were also presented with the
script of a radio cframa which gave interesting facts in . the life of Brother
Justin Gates.
. In addition to the fitting eulog·y which will be given in special services
for our dearly beloved late Grand Secretary, this committee wishes to
pay a special tribute to the memory of Brother John Whicher. Studious
by nature, discerning in the value of information, sympathetic in temperament, and a true friend, Brother Whicher was ever helpful to us. Added
to his many rare qualities was a retentive memory, enriched with the
advantages that came with years of experience. Our file was located near
his desk and it was a privilege to have been able to work beside him and
there gain valuable information and .goodly counsel. Outside of his own
family, Brother Whicher will be missed by none more than those of our
committee who had the rare opportunity of such close association over a
period of many years. Earth was made better by him and heaven will be
brighter by the presence of Brother John Which er.
An appropriation of $250.00 was made by Grand Lodge for use of this
committee during the past year. Of this we have used $114.09, for which
proper vouchers have been furnished. We recommend that a Committee on
Masonic History be continued, and request an appropriation of $250.00 for
the coming year.
Respectfully submitted,

Our net loss in membership is again on the decline, the first time in

We again call your attention to the loss of membership by non-payment
of dues which averaged 1961 for the past five years, compared to the
average gain by restoration, 524, or about twenty-five percent reclaiiped.

Our death loss is gradually increasing as our membership arrives

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:
The ravages of death, the dread destroyer of that which is mortal, has
again thinned the ranks of our brethren and taken from us many whose
places of usefulness w ill be very hard to fill. Since Grand Lodge convenecl
a year ago, two hundred and fifteen of our brethren have gone to their
Eternal Home. Fifteen of this number have at some time in the past held
responsible positions. Our greatest loss was in the passing of our beloved
brother, the Very Worshipful John Whicher, Grand Secretary of this Grand
Lodge. A special eulogy will be given Brother Whicher by Past Grand
Master Dana R. 'Weller. I shall give all the time assigned to me in brief
eulogies for the other departed brethren.
Again we look with the eyes of faith to that good old Book, finding
there sustaining grace and peace. "O death, where is thy sting, 0 grave,
where is thy victory. The sting of death is sin and the strength of sin is
the law, but thanks be to God who giveth us the victory through our
Lord Jesus Christ."
To me Masonry and victorious living are synonymous. This is not a
time of sadness to us but rather a time of deep and sincere gratitude for
the assurance that our brethren are now happy in their Father's house.
"Ye believe in God, believe also in Me. I11 My Father's House are many
mansions." God has given us these words for our comfort at such a time
as this and we are assured that our brethren are now in that spiritual
building, that house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. "I will
not leave you comfortless, I will come to you. Because I live ye shall live
also. Peace I leave with you. My peace I give unto you. Let not your
heart be trouble'd ; neither let it be afraid."
We frequently speak of time as an eternal thing, and why not? Surely
we know there is neither beginning nor ending of days. T hose who have
gone on before us have just been translated from what we here call time
to what we speak of as eternity. Whatever our faith, whatever we may
individually believe in the future of our departed, let us for a short time
medita(e and contemplate upon this one thought : Wherever our departed
brethren are this morning they are supremely happy.
There is something about Masonry that when rightfully understood
controls to a large extent the thinking of the individual Mason. Yes, it
does more than this, it directs and motivates his every action. No man
can think seriously about his raising in the third degree without forever
after being a different man. \Vhy can we not fix our thinking for a few
minutes on victorious living! Life lived in all the beauty and glory
of peace and perfect trust. Surely every man who has affirmed his trust
ia God is ready to cross over to be with that innumerable host and sing
as ne'er before "the songs of Moses and the Lamb."
Today we are looking out into the great unknown, not with anxious
hearts and minds but with a spirit ·of confidence. We could not meet
for this service in a spirit of joy but we are meeting in the victorious
spirit of peace and gratitude. \Vhat does N:~nry mean ? It should and

"Today the journey is ended,
I have worked out the mandates of fate;
Naked, alone, undefended,
I knock at the Uttermost Gate.
"Lo, the gate swings wide at my knocking;
Across endless reaches I see
Lost friends, with laughter, come flocking
To give a glad welcome to me.
" Farewell, t he maze has been threaded,
This is the ending of strife;
Say not that death should be dreaded'Tis only the beginning of life."
ALBERT BRADFORD WEBSTER, Past Grand Master
Not entirely unexpected was the passing of Past Grand M aster, Brother
Albert Bradford Webster, June 4, 1941. He was born in Genoa, Ohio,
December 14, 1869. He was married July 6, 1897 and three children and his ·
wife survive him. He received his education in the University of California
and Hastings Law Schoo). He was a m ember and Past Master of Live
Oak Lodge No. 61, F. & A. M. He was initiated March 20, 1896, passed
March 27, 1896 and raised April 10, 1896. He was a member of Oakland
Chapter No. 36, R. A. M ., Oakland Commandery No. 11, K . T., and the
Oakland Bodies, A . A. S. R . He received the honorary degree of K. C. C. H .
October 1919 and the 33rd degree, Inspector General Honorarv December
1921. He was a member of Aahmes Temple, A. A. 0 . .
'M. S. He
!ierved this Grand Lodge as Grand Master in the year 1919, having been
elected to the highest honor in Masonry in California in 1918. His life was
characterized chiefly by service, a never-ending service. In reading his
message to Grand Lodge in 1919 I was amazed at his year's accomplishments. He visited every district excepting two and proved h imself a real
leader among his brethren at that time. In conclusion may I quote from
his address at Grand Lodge in 1919 : "If we can once get the great mass
of the brotherhood to realize that there is nothing more important than
the recognition of the commo11 bonds of humanity, that th e doctrine of
brotherhood means in very fact just what it says, that we are all descendants of one Almighty Father, that we are linked together in fact as well
as in name, by an indissoluble tie of sincere affection, I venture the prediction that we will see th e Masonic Order take its rightfu l place as a.
dynamic force in the Nation, and in the life of the people, an d th at it will
command recognition not alone for its profe ssions, not alone for the beauty
of its doctrine, but deservedly for its solid practical accomplishment in
all constructive policies and endeavors for the uplift and unity of Humanity." This is the voice of one speaking again to us from the pages of the
past and I am< hoping that as we bid him a fond farewell that Masons
and Masonry m California are measuring up to the high standards he
has set forth in the closing words of his address.

N:

WALTER LEONARD, Grand Lecturer
Brother Walter Leonard was born in San Francisco November 10,
1878, and passed April 3, 1941. He received his first appointment as
Inspector of the 42nd District in 1923, serving in that capacity until

592

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

October 1938 when he was appointed Grand Lecturer. In 1939 he was
elected Grand Lecturer and this position of responsibility he still filled
at the time of his death. He was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason
in Oriental Lodge No. 144, June 8, 1915, passed to the Degree of Fellowcraft' June 22, 1915 and raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason
July 13, 1915. So many outstanding characteristics were noticeable in his
daily life which revealed the beauty of his character. He was loving, kind,
considerate, gracious, and charitable to all his friends and brethren. I think
that good old Book which graces every Masonic Lodge must have been his
constant companion and inspiration. I like to think of him as of Enoch of
old in that record where it says "He walked with God and God took him and
he was not." God help us all to be as faithful to the ideals of Masonry as he
was.
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent of Decoto Masonic Mome
Masons and friends of the "Home Family" were grieved to hear of
the passing of Brother Frank B. Hartman, the Superintendent of the
Masonic H ome at Decoto, February 5, 1941. Returning from a Masonic
funeral which he conducted February 3 in Oakland for Brother Herman
Cramer he was taken fatally ill and passed on at the age of 74 after having
had charge of the Decoto Home for 32 years. The life and work of this
great man speak for themselves. What a tribute to his great heart is
found in his loyalty to "his Family." His deeds of kindness and loving ministrations, unnumbered, are recorded in that Supreme Grand Lodge record
and even now he is receiving the reward for his faithfulness, having been
summoned to a higher and greater usefulness. I think he was one of those
kindly, gracious spirits, one of those of our brethren of whom it could
be truly said "He went about doing good. He came not to be ministered
unto but to minister to others."
REV. JOHN SNAPE, D. D., Past Grand Chaplain
Brother Snape was born at Odessa, Delaware, December 13, 1870,
and passed ·to his reward September 5, 1941, having been an active Baptist
Minister for more than fifty years. He was a member of Sequoia Lodge
No. 349. He was appointed Grand Chaplain of Grand Lodge in 1931 by
Past Grand Master Robert B. Gaylord and again in 1932 by Past Grand
Master Frank W. Mixter. His was a life full of active Christian Service.
May we say of him in the words of Kipling, "Scarce had he need to cast
his pride or slough the dross of earth, E'en as he walked that day to God,
so walked he from his birth-In simpleness and gentleness and clean mirth."
FOSTER G. DYER, Inspector and Past Grand Lecturer
Brother Dyer was born December 16, 1879 in Gilroy, California, and
passed July 28, 1941, having been Inspector of the 45th District continuously for more than twenty-five years. He was a member of Park Lodge
No. 449, serving as Master in 1920. Brother Dyer was very widely and
favorably known because of having served as Grand Lecturer for the balance
of the year 1934 at the time of the passing of Brother Tom Baker. Brother
Conway in his eulogy to Brother Dyer says, "He was a marvelous Master
of the ritual; he gave all possible assistance to the young officers who were
coming up the line. His kindliness was well known"; and may I add his
ritualistic knowledge and work were second to none. May his efforts
bring an eternal benediction upon Park Lodge and his brethren of Grand
Lodge.
JACOB ERRATT HUGHES, Inspector
Brother Hughes was born March 19, 1862 at Winchester, Canada and

GRAND LODr.E OF CALIFORNIA

593

passed December 26, 1940, having been Inspector of the 30th District for
twenty-five years. He was 82 years of age. He was Master of Carquinez
Lodge No. 337 in 1910 and 1914. His was such a long faithfu l service to the
ideals of Masonry that eternity alone can reveal its value. Surely these
words are true of Brother Hughes: "Thou hast been faithful over a few
things, I will make thee ruler over many things : enter thou into the joy
of thy Lord."
HERBERT W. WALKER, Inspector
Brother Walker was born October 30, 1895 in Warsaw, Illinois and
passed November 1, 1940, having been Inspector of the 89th District for
six years. He was Master of Van Nuys Lodge No. 450 in 1927. He leaves
his wife, Melba J oh nson Walker, and two children. May I digress: Bert
as we familiarly called him, was at Grand Lodge School of Instruction las~
year and I had a very fine visit with him. When I inquired regarding his
health he said, "I have been in bad shape but I am now improving and
hope soon to be as well as ever." He has now been translated to his
Eternal Home where there is "no more pain or death neither sorrow nor
crying, for the former things are passed away."
'
THOMAS ANDERSON, Inspector
Brother Anderson was born at Aberdeen, Scotland, September 7, 1865
and passed July 4, 1941 at the age of 75 years, having been Jnspector of the
44th. District for twenty-four :irears. He was Master of Pacific Lodge No.
136 in 1916. Brother Tom, as he was fami liarly ca lled, was dearly loved by
all who knew him. Quoting from a eulogy which I received "At the break
of dawn in the morning of July 4 a final summons was i~sued, a kindly
messenger whispered the tidings and the spirit of your friend and my frienr\
departed for that Temple not built by hands to receive h is reward for a
just and upright life. We should not mourn the passing but rather give
thanks that Pacific Lodge was fortunate in having had Thomas Anderson's
advice and service over a long period of years, and while his presence will
certainly be missed, his ideals and teachings will not be forgotten." I am
sure the benediction of his loving service will be felt in his L odge and in his
District for all time to come.
HAROLD WILBUR CONKLIN, Inspector
Brother Conklin was born in Kansas October 6, 1900 and passed
November 15, 1940, having been Inspector of the 33rd District for nearly
three years. He was a member and Past Master of Heary Morse Stephens
Lodge No. 541 and for many years had been active in Grand Lodge activities. He was Senior Grand Steward in 1936; a member of the Jurisprudence
Committee in 1935 ; and a member of the Masonic Education Committee in
1936. So little can be said of this fine upstanding Mason in a report limited
especially as to time. It may be possible to print in full a eulogy delivered at
his funeral by Brother Vaughan McCaughey from which I shall quote
briefly: "Life has few sadder privileges that that of presenting a eulogy of
a beloved friend. Nevertheless it is a solemn privilege to do honor to one
taken so suddei:ty from our midst at the untimely age of 40, one whose life
and deeds so richly deserve all the honor we can give. In 1928 Harold
Conklin and Marian E. Rowe were married. Two lovely children blessed
this happy union, a daughter Joyce Roanne, born in 1934, and a son Warren
CraiE?-, born in 1937." Here, all too briefly, are a few statements 'touching
the hfe of our Brother Conklin. Today I am hoping for him and all those
wh~ have p~ssed, that having laid aside all that is mortal and having put
on 1mmortahty, that they are now permitted to listen in on these services
rendered in their behalf. Theirs is now a blissful eternity w here "Eye hath

not seen, ear hath not heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man
the things which God hath prepared for them that love Him."

. !hen again we drop the curtain which separates time a n d eternity,
bidding our brethren a fond and loving farewell, resting confident in th e
hope that some day "Almighty God in His infinite mercy wi ll grant that w e
may meet to part no more." Often, very often, will memor y recall again to
us our beloved brethren but let us be comforted by these w ords: "He that
believeth in M e, th ough he were dead, yet shall he live."

PAUL G. WELLER, former Inspector
Brother Weller was born in Rialto, California, January 26, 189S and was
taken to his Eternal Home September 29, 1941, aged 46 years. He was raised
June 17, 1924. He served as Inspector of the lOSth District from 19.37 to
1941. He was Master of Rialto Lodge No. S82 in 1929, and a member of
Long Beach Consistory. I quote briefly from a eulogy given at his funeral
service October 1, 1941, by Albert Jess Erichsen, "He was a man of sterling
qualities, fine principle and fine character." As long as Masonry lives his.
memory will be cherished in the lOSth District.
CHARLES B. JONES, former. Inspector
Brother Jones was born September 2, 1882 and passed to his reward
September 21, 1941, aged S9 years. He was raised February 20, 1914 in
Buena Park Lodge No. 3S7 and .became a charter member of Coachella
Lodge No. 476 in 1919 and served this Lodge as Master in 1922, 1923 and
1934. He served this Grand Lodge as Inspector of the 107th District from
1927 to 1932. His funeral furnished evidence of the high esteem of his
neighbors and his friends, for the chapel could not accommodate all who.
came. Brother Charles was a very fine ritualist and gave liberally of his
time to the brotherhood, though not an active Inspector. M ay his work
continue through the endless days of time.
RICHARD WILLIAM O'BANNION, former Inspector
Brother O'Bannion went to his eternal rest November 27, 1940. I wish
it were possible for me to properly honor this former Inspector whom I
have never known. The Press in Hollister gave him due recognition of his
Masonic service, his life's history and especially the large place he filled in
that community, having been a practicing physician there for forty-three
years. He was a member of San Benito Lodge No. 211. Quoting from a
letter from the Grand Secretary: "Dr. O ' Bannion w as for many years Inspector of District No. SS. He w as a physicia n and surgeon; one of the m ost
beloved men in Hollister, wher e he practiced for m any year s. He w as the
personal physician of the late Brother Dan McDonald, to whom I presented a 7S-year veteran button while I was Grand Master." His was a
long life of real service in the community in which he lived and to the
brethren of his Masonic Lodge and District.

Across the mourn fu l m arbles play!

That Life is ever lord of Death,
And L ove can never lose its own.

Eulogy b)' DANA R.

WELLER,

Past Grand Mastrr

Abou Ben Adhem (may his tribe increase!)
Awoke one night from a deep dream of peace,
And saw, within the moonlight in his room,
Making it rich, and like a lily in bloom,
An Angel writing in a book of gold :
Exceeding peace had made Ben Adhem bold,
And to the Presence in the room he said,
"What writest thou?" The Vision raised its head,
And with a look made of all sweet accord
Answered, " The names of those who love the Lord."
"And is mine one?" said .Abou. "Nay, not so,"
Replied the Angel. Abou spoke more low,
But cheerily still; and said, " I pray thee, then,
Write me as one that loves his fellow-men."
The Angel wrote, and vanished. The next night
It came again with a great wakening light,
And showed the names whom love of God had blessed,
And, lo! Ben Adhem's name led all the rest.
These lines, so often used in eulogy of others by him whose memory
we now revere, so aptly portray his nobility of character and his own love
of humanity, as to lead to the conclusion that his life and conduct were
fashioned in accordance with the sentiment therein expressed. He would
have chosen no other epitaph for himself, if in his modesty he felt that he
deserved them. We, and thousands of o thers, can bear witness that he
richly merited all that and even more.
The tendrils of his great heart spread out through the aura of his
presence, and entwined themselves tenaciously with the heartstrings of all
his associates, and will so cling with sweet and tender memories until the
last surviving heart shall cease to beat.
May the Supreme Grand Master so direct our footsteps that when
we shall reach that beautiful shore we may be found worthy of a place
beside him who in our fond recollection led all the rest in his love of
human kind, there again to live in the joy of his affection, and fore vermore
to bask in the radiance of his presence.
JOHN WHICH ER, the son of Isaac Which er and Rachel Jordan
Whicher, was born July 4th, 1855, at U rbana, Ohio. In 1857 his family
moved to Des Moines, Iowa, where John learned the art and trade of
printing. In 1879 he moved to Colorado, engaged in newspaper work, and
remained there unti l 1887, when he located in San Luis Obispo, California,
being editor of the San Luis Obispo Tribune until elected County Clerk of
San Luis Obispo Cou nty in 1895, serving in that office until 1903, when he
was appointed Deputy Superintendent o f State Printing at Sacramento,
Californi~. which position he resigned August 25th, 1908, to accept appointment as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California. H e was first
e lected Grand Secretary in October, 1908, and re-elected each succeeding
year, including the Communication of October, 1940, and served until the
day of his death, on March .31st, 1940.
John Whicher was raised in Pioneer Lodge No. 22, Des Moines, Iowa,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

October 4th, 1879; affiiliated with King David's Lodge No. 209, at San Luis
. Obispo, California, February 26th, 1S96, and held all offices except that of
Treasurer. He served as Master from December 1900 to December 1902.
He was exalted in Leadville Chapter No. 10; at Leadville, Colorado, on
October 16th, 1882. He was knighted December 5th, 1890, in San Luis
Obispo Commandery No. 27, being Commander in 1900-1901. He was a
member of San Francisco Consistory No. 1, Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite, receiving the 32nd degree on June 24th, 1911, and crowned with the
33rd degree on January 25th, 1918. For many years he was a member of
Islam Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S. He was also a member of St. Francis
Conclave, Order of Constantine.
Gifted by inheritance from a line of sturdy ancestors with honesty,
courage, and zeal, enriched with experience in the fields of his endeavor, he
brought to the office of Grand Secretary all of those fine qualities which
made it possible- for him to perform the functions of that office with
peculiar distinction and satisfaction. He was known and respected throughout the world of Masonry, and by his diplomacy the prestige of the Grand
Lodge of California is maintained everywhere. He was meticulous in the
performance of the duties of his office, never presuming to volunteer
advice to the Grand Master, but always more than pleased to contribute
from his vast store of knowledge and experienc,e when requested so to do.
Thirty-two Grand Masters with whom he served have attested to his
uniform courtesy, his dependable loyalty, and his constant regard for the
amenities of the relations existing between the two offices, and all of the
survivors of that group of men have continued through the years to regard
John among their dearest and closest friends,
Among his choicest contributions to the cause of Masonry were his
letters to the children at Covina and the elders at Decoto. Gems of literature and pearls of wisdom, fashioned by his facile hand, are numbered
among the priceless poss·e ssions of many recipients.
As an example of his keen knowledge of the essentials of a successful
life, a quotation from a letter written to a boy leaving Covina to enter the
world and make his way, is typical of many others of like import.

house of memory and reminiscense. Trials and troubles and vexations of spirit assailed us in the days of our youth and inexperience; grim old Fate too often was wayward and adverse as to
worldly fortune; we may say that 'all the ills that flesh is heir to'
have been our lot. Yet I know, and you know, that this old
world is indeed filled with worthwhile life and love and laughter.
As the wrinkles come, and the hair grows thin and 'those that
look out of the windows be darkened,' the blessed memories of
old days, old joys, old friends, grow keener and sweeter, forgetting the days when the clouds hung low, retaining in mind
only the splendor of our few successes and the wonderful men and
women whom we have known and loved. We would not swap
those memories and the friendships enjoyed during a long life
for any elixir of youth . Father time, our dear old companion,
can and will carry his enthusiasm for the things of today and his
love of life and gratitude for blessings past with a jaunty air, thankful-even as you and I-that he has been permitted to participate
for so many years in the affairs of this good old world. "

606

"You will have many problems to solve. When in doubt, try
to find out what is the right thing to do, then have the moral
courage to do it. Seek advice, and after getting it, use your own
judgment. Courage is always rewarded, I don't mean physical
courage, which is common, but moral courage, which is rare.
The boy or girl, the man or woman, who has the moral courage
to defend his own judgment, will usually succeed. Don't, I beg of
you, depend on luck Life of course is necessarily an uncertain
venture. Some of you may not have all your dreams come true;
but whatever Fate may decree, hold fast to your good name, which
is your most precious possession. 'A good name is rather to be
chosen than great riches.' "
His own philosophy which he so successfully followed is best expressed
in his own words in a letter· to a resident of the Home at Decoto, thus:
"I am glad you have had the courage and the good sense to
grow old gracefully. One of the glories of old age is that we can
retrospectively view the trials and troubles and vexations of youth's
salad days as having been so puerile, and now know that the annoyances and . griefs of earlier days were really petty things. Like
you, I have lived way beyond the Biblical three score and ten,
and the experiences of those years are now lodged in the store-

607

Though in the later years his steps faltered, his eyes dimmed and his
heart weakened, not once did he falter in his devotion to his work, his
keenness of mind, or his affection for friends.
And finally he closed his mortal life, as he desired to do, at his desk,
his post of duty.
This po9r tribute delivered by one who is proud to have been numbered
among John's friends, is but a feeble expression of the great love we all
bear for John Which er, our Grand Secretary, and our very dear friend and
brother.
·
Inscribed upon our hearts is a precious memory which cannot be
translated into spoken or printed words, but will linger with us as a benediction for the remainder of our days.
"There is no death! The stars go down
To ·rise upon some fairer shore, ·
And, bright in heaven's jeweled crown,
They shine forever more.
And ever near us, though unseen,
The dear immortal spirits tread;
For all the boundless universe
Is life; there are no dead."
