PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"TRELLISES"
Eulogy by G. ELLSWORTH

MEYER

In the year which has lapsed since our last communication, a goodly
number of our brethren have answered the summons to that higher Grand
Lodge which must come to every man in turn. In memory of those departed
we pause in our deliberations today. We do not pause to lament or say,
Woe unto those rather, we lay aside for the time the thoughts and cares
of our finite world to contemplate the infinite; to join ourselves in a true
fraternal spirit, a spirit marked by faith in the Supreme Grand Master
and his beneficence to these our brethren; a spirit marked by hope that
after we too have joined the innumerable caravan we shall be reunited
with them; a spirit marked by affectionate remembrance of their smiles,
friendly words and kindly deeds. So, within these services abide these
three, faith, hope and charity and may these quiet moments be to us like
trellises, trellises for our climbing thoughts.
To these services one can bring no word that is wholly new for poets
have given words wings, scientists explored the farthest reaches, philosophers speculated through countless tomes and yet life and death remain
the enigma of the ages. We cannot capture the infinite plan in earth-born
words, we cannot circumscribe eternity with man-made tools or examine
it beneath a microscope. We can ·only say:
A breath of joy, an hour of pain,
Dark paths to tread, white heights to g·ain,
A little love, a little strife,
And this is Life.
A little rest, a swift new birth,
A snapping of the bonds of earth,
A joyous stride, · a tingling breath,
And this is Death.
For Life and Death walk hand 111 hand,
With never a span between,
And our path leads to that Other Land,
Where the sunlit fields are green.
Seeing then that we cannot reduce life and death to a mathematical
equation, that we cannot make a round trip to that other land, how necessary it is that we should possess faith; faith in the wisdom and power of
Him, who created the heavens and the earth, faith in the beauty of that
other shore. Such faith is not a mark of weakness but rather the mark of
a'Man and a Mason. Such faith gives purpose and value to life and without
it life would have neither purpose nor value.
The ways of men and nations are hard to accept without faith. It is
difficult for a father to comprehend why his infant son who had but arrived
in this world should be taken ere he took his first tottering steps. It is
almost incomprehensible why a brother should be gathered up in the first
bloom of manhood. As yet unanswerable questions are raised by the life
of toil without comfort which some endure while others possess worldly
goods they have never earned. \tVithout faith these burdens would be unbearable. Without faith that somewhere, sometime, there shall be just compensation, men would not be able to go on carrying their loads; without
such faith men would have no reason to practice temperance in thought
and deed; there would be no reason for courage and justice would be as.
sounding brass. But faith whispers:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

609

There the tears of earth are dried,
There its hidden things are clear,
There the work of life is tried
By a juster Judge than here.
Though we do not possess proof by word of mouth of any traveler
returned from yonder, the circumstantial evidence at every hand is sufficient
to warrant our declaration of faith in God and life hereafter. While science
has uncovered but the smallest fraction of the wonders we may yet behold,
it has found that from the invisible electron to the galaxies of the Milky
Way there .is unerring response to law inscribed by some omnipotent
hand; it has discovered that all matter is composed of energy and that
while energy may be transformed, it is never, never lost. Is man then an
exception? A germ of wheat entombed with the mummy of a Pharaoh
will yet spring to life when given soil and water. Would Infinite Wisdom
forget man whilst he remembered the kernel of grain?
Charles Darwin, about whose head have been loosed ecclesiastical
lightnings, gave faith voice when de declared, "Believing as I do that man
in the distant future will be a far more perfect creature than he now is, it
is an intolerable thought that he and other sentient beings are doomed
to complete annihilation after such long continued slow process."
Socrates as he held the cup of hemlock is reported to have said, "Having
an end with the foolishness of this body, we shall now become pure and
converse with the pure."
So too, you an<l I, in those hours when we are intellectually and spiritually at our best, cannot, without violence to our profoundest instincts,
conceive of a world which would lose all its gains, a world in which
all that we have willed and hoped and dreamed was to no avail. We adhe~e
therefore to belief in God and immortality not in the sense in which we
accept the demonstrable truths of science, but as a supreme act of faith
in the reasonableness of creation, as the necessary crown to a creative
work marvelous and beautiful in all its myriad stages; though we can express ourselves only in myth and symbol as ever we must express our
deepest perceptions.
'
Death may be a great. adventure but may we face it as Columbus
faced his first voyage from the shores of Spain. What lies across the sea
we cannot tell, all our special expectations may be mistaken, but our insight
into present facts persuades that the sea has another shore and that we
shall be rewarded by the .vision of a new continent. Here abideth faith.
The hope of immortality is the heart of every religion, and the purpose,
to serve as the avenue and vestibule to the attainment of that life. In that
regard Masonry may be classed with the religions for by myth and symbol
we give expression to that hope. But whence came it? Who put it in the
human mind?
Wherever consciousness ripens this audacious hope appears; as soon
as thought is exercised it is expressed; as soon as virtue glows it is impressed in the structure of minds. It is not through sight that this hope is
born, for "hope may end in fruition"; rather it is as elemental as a father's
hope for his child yet unborn. May it not have been impressed by our
Father as part and parcel of his everlasting plan, as the summary and
completion of man?
Our hope is not sentimental but is grounded in the necessities and
forces about us. Here eternal law prevails and at that point, far, far beyond ·
our ken eternal law must still hold its sway. On this human sphere inequality, intolerance and error at times prevail in spite of all our efforts.

610

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We y~arn for perfect justice though we realize it may prev:i-il only in
"that house not made by hands."
Our hope of immortality-the poets have sung it, the seers have told it,
and our hearts, in their deepest pulses, throb responsive. Here on our trellis abideth hope.
There is yet one final lesson to be gathered from these moments of
meditation. Our paths may have seldom crossed those of some whose days
of toil are now o'er, but of all we know that they were good men and true,
seekers of the greater light else they would not have knocked at the Masonic door, or having knocked, would not have found time to serve the
order well. Those whom we were privileged to know more intimately, we
remember, not for the worldly goods they possessed, but for their manifold nobilities. We remember them, not for their clothes, but the smiles
they wore. We remember them, not for their large purses, but for their
large hearts. We remember them, not for the speed of their motor cars,
but for the speed with which they reached our sides in time of need. We
remember them, not for the number of rooms in their houses, but for the
many noble thoughts in which they dwelt.
If then these matters of character are the remembrance which these
brethren have left behind them, how obvious it is that these must be attributes of prime import. With these same attributes Masonry is concerned
and with those only.
It is not mere fraternal pride to declare that we believe .these brethren
were better men because they walked the Masonic path. We freely admit
we are the richer-because they walked a while with us.
Someone has said, "To live in the hearts we leave behind, is not to die."
Of our brethren we then declare, "They yet live in our hearts." Here on our
trellis blooms that love which is charity and which "extends beyond the
grave through the boundless realms of eternity."
A memorial song: "Taps" (Custance).
Benediction: Grand Chaplain.

Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance reports:
While the report of this committee is not listed on the printed program,
the Grand Master assures us that an opportunity for its presentation will
be afforded. We assume that its omission was an inadvertence, and was
due to the fact that this is only the second year of appointment of this
committee.
The Constitution of the United States and perpetuation of the rights
which it guarantees, and the spirit of individual liberty which it represents
are probably the most important questions confronting not only the
citizens of the United States, but also the world at large, and the civilization
of which that Constitution is the fruit. Equally, we believe that the opportunity of Masonry to make its traditional contribution to the perpetuation
of those institutions is one of the most important problems, if not the most
important, which today confronts Masonic organizations. Wherever dictatorship has flourished, Masonry and religion have, hand in hand, been
ostracized.
The fact that the Masons of this jurisdiction realize the importance
of the situation is exemplified by the reports which have been returned t.o
the Committee.
If the Committee is continued for the ensuing year; many of the statistics which appear in the reports will be of value for guidance of future
activities. We also suggest that the information from these report"s is
of value to Grand Officers as an illuminating exemplification of the Lodges
which are inactive and the districts in which Inspectors have neglected the
activities of Grand Lodge.
·
We emphasize the fact that a form for report was sent to every Lodge
and to every Inspector in the jurisdiction. The form specifically stated the
person to whom responsibility attached for its return, the importance of
its return, and the person to whom it was to be forwarded, being to the
Regional Chairman in North and South respectively. Apparently, many of
these forms were either consigned to the waste basket or were not read.
Some of the districts have not reported. A substantial number of Lodges
have failed to report. In several instances a general letter report has been
returned, and in several instances the reports have come to either the Grand
Secretary's office or to the General Chairman. While this specification may
seem rather technical, it is presented because of the value of the reports
each year for reference in succeeding years, and because of the difficulty in
compiling statistics in the absence of uniform reports of all meetings.
Both the Grand Master and the Committee emphasize the desirability
of public meetings wherever practical. Reverence for the Constitution and
the fostering of its ideals are the purposes of the movement which is represented by this Committee. It should be a safe assumption that any good
Mason is already familiar with those purposes and desires to play his part
as a citizen of the United States. Accordingly, it was the recommendation
of the Grand Master, and it is, and has been, the recommendation of this
Committee that so far as possible the meetings during Constitution Month
be open to the public, and that every effort be made to promote the attendance of the community in general and the sponsorship of service clubs
and other patriotic organizations. This practice has been so successful in

the observance of Public Schools Week that relatively few citizens realize
that this observance is primarily a Masonic activity. It may well be that in
the case of Constitution Month the fostering of the movement by Masonry
shall not be kept too much in the background-both for emphasis on the
patriotic ideals of Masonry, and because of the emphasis which may be
placed throughout the community upon constitutional institutions by reason
of the efforts of our Masonic organizations to maintain them.
However, our appeal is to citizens in general; and every effort should be
made to procure participation and endorsement by civically-minded organizations of every type, whether Jewish or Gentile, Protestant or Catholic,
secular or religious. To obtain such participation, public meetings are
essential, and undue stress need not be placed upon the fact that the movement is fostered by Masonic organizations.
While reports throughout the jurisdiction are not complete, the Committee is able to give a general cross section of .the meetings. As evidenced
by returns to date, approximately 175 meetings were held under the auspices
of individual Lodges, of which 105 were open to the public, and 70 were
closed meetings. Closed meetings usually were held in conjunction with a
stated meeting or with degree work. Approximately 70 joint meetings were
held, of which 50 were open to the public, and 20 of which were closed.
The best estimate which the Committee can make from the attendance
reports is· that there was an attendance of approximately 14,000 at the
meetings conducted under the auspices of individual Lodges, and an attendance of approximately 16,000 at the meetings conducted under joint
auspices, being a total of 30,DOO. This attendance represents both public
and closed meetings·and is estimated in part because of the fact in a number
of instances attendance is reported as " good," "average" and similar expressions .. Although larger and more representative attendance is an ideal,
nevertheless, the presentation of constitutional objectives to a total of 30,000
people in California is worthwhile, particularly when we realize that the
persons in attendance undoubtedly were of sufficient intelligence and were
sufficiently civic-minded to assure continued effort on · their part to promote
the purposes of American civilization.
Your Committee feels that appreciation should be expressed to Grand
Lodge for the very general manner in which support was given to Constitution Observance by both the Inspectors and the Lodges of the jurisdiction.
It is a tribute to citizenship and an exemplification of loyalty to the efforts
of Grand Lodge which cannot be overlooked. In a few instances, the reports
indicate a lack of cooperation upon the part of inspectors, but these instances are exceptional. There are also a few reports in which complaint
is made that the inspectors failed to cooperate in the condu'tt of the joint
meetings; it is to be noted in this connection that the meetings were held
notwithstanding lack of cooperation by the Inspectors, and that the results
were satisfactory. Your Committee recommends that in the absence of
exceptional circumstances, joint meetings be held whenever there are
several Lodges in the community.
In general, the average attendance at joint meetings, even though
conducted by three or four Lodges, was six times the attendance at meetings conducted by an individual Lodge. The Committee realized that there
are many. instances in which it is impractical to successfully hold a joint
meeting. On the other hand, a joint meeting where Lodges are in the same
community has greater attractive power, particularly for a public meeting.
Also, it is easier to obtain a first-class speaker for a large meeting than for
one where a limited number is in attendance.
In the majority of instances the reports favor open meetings, and

favor joint meeting in urban sections. The Committee concurs in this view.
Whether a meeting is conducted by a single Lodge, or is held under the
joint auspices of several Loages, it is practical to invite the general public,
and we stress the fact that the primary purpose of this movement is an appeal
to the general public. A meeting at which families and friends of the members of a single Lodge participate is more effective than a closed meeting.
Reasonable entertainment can be provided in any locality however small,
·and necessarily contributes to the attractiveness of the meeting and the
promotion of larger attendance.
There have been several suggestions that notice to Lodges for Constitution Month meetings be issued at an earlier date. In the first year of
its activity, the date of its appointment prohibited the issuance of an earlier
notice by the committee. The notice for the past year was issued at what
was hoped to be an appropriate date : the Committee feared that too early
a notice would escape attention, and that too late a notice would prevent
proper observance. Apparently, the guess for an appropriate date was not
well timed. The concurrence of opinion indicates that a notice should be
issued in May in order to afford adequate time for preparation. If this procedure is followed, we recommend that a secondary notice be issued in
August emphasizing the importance of the event and confirming the May
notice.
In some instances, particularly in the warmer sections of California, it
has been found difficult to hold meetings in September because of the
heat and the vacation season, and the suggestion has been made that permission be granted to hold the meetings in October. The only objection
to an October meeting is that it would be impossible to incorporate the
result of the meeting in the Committee's report to the Grand Lodge. However, the importance of this observance is the fact that meetings are held
rather than the presentation of a categorical report to Grand Lodge. We,
therefore, recommend that September be designated as Constitution Month,
but that in those instances in which this month is undesirable, permission
be granted to hold the meeting in October.
The Committee would be unappreciative if it failed to acknow\edege
the generosity of speakers at meetingS'. So far as we know, no re-imbursement has been given to any speaker for even his own expenses. In no
instance has any requested speaker refused to permit his name upon the
panel, except in one or two cases in which absence from the State or similar exigencies prevented acceptance. The enthusiasm with which Lodges
have supported the movement, and the courtesy which has been extended
by speakers is a tribute to both Masonry and American citizenship.
Tribute also should be paid to the cooperation of the press throughout
the State. Lodge after Lodge reports the publidty which has been given to
its meetings. This, also, is a source of satisfaction in the general level of
citizenship in this country.
By way of illustration, we quote from the reports of two or three
Lodges:
One Lodge suggests that substantial efforts were made by the Master
to conduct a successful meeting, that efforts were made to obtain the cooperation of other civically-minded bodies, and that only "the faithful few"
were in attendance, a'nd that they were there from a sense of duty. When
inquiry was made of some who were absent as to the cause of their absence,
they stated that they already were fully conscious of the Constitution, patriotism and the duties of citizenship ; therefore, that they had no interest
in attending "a lecture on the subject." The criticism may be well merited
in this particular case. However, it exemplifies the suggestion made by

your committee that a meeting is not primarily maintained for Masons
who are good citizens, but should be developed to promote general public
interest and general public attendance. The same criticism was leveled in
the early days of Public Schools Week, but Public Schools Week is a
subject of enthusiastic support throughout the State, and unquestionably
has developed interest in, and support for, our public school system. However, we feel that the writer of this report may have been unduly pessimistic.
The criticism was made that the meeting was held in an auditorium which
will accommodate 800 persons, and that 150 were in attendance. We contrast this with the fact that the membership of the Lodge which conducted
the meeting is less than 100, and that the listed population of the town in
which the meeting was held is approximately 2,000. Under these circumstances, we believe that notwithstanding the meager attendance which resulted from sincere efforts to promote the meeting, it should not prove too
depressing; we must creep before we walk, and it is to be hoped that continued efforts from year to year will develop that spirit of civic consciousness
which is well worthwhile.
In another letter, it is suggested that forty inches of news space in three
cities resulted in an attendance of three persons per inch; that a troop of
Boy Scouts was in attendance as ushers; but were not needed because of
the meager attendance, and that "Masons turned out just as badly as
others, if not worse." In such instances, the only suggestion your Committee can offer is that we should not be unduly discouraged by a limited
interest at the outset of the movement.
By comparison, and for such encouragement as may be derived from
it, we quote a report from Honolulu, in which it is stated that a splendid
meeting was held jointly by the Lodges in Oahu, and that it was "the
largest gathering I have seen in any public assembly under the Masonic
Lodges of the Island." Obviously, there are two sides to the picture, and
if there is perseverance in the movement, results cannot fail to follow:
Your Committee recommends:
1. That a Constitution Mon th Observance Committee be continued
for the ensuing year
2. That September be designated as Constitution Month, but that
Lodges in areas where September is inadvisable, be permitted to hold meetings in October;
3. That the Committee be organized in its present form, to-wit, with a
General Chairman for the State, and regional committee for the North
and South portions of the State;
4. That expenses be allowed to the Committee in the discretion of the
Grand Master. The expenses of the Committee have been nominal, being
confined to stationery, multigraphing and postage. We see no occasion for
increased expenses during the coming year, but we believe that any members
who may be appointed to this particular committee will be glad to bear the
expenses themselves if Grand Lodge feels that the expenditure is not
justified by the purposes sought to be accomplished.
We have compiled a list of Lodges and districts which have failed to
report, and, therefore, presumptively, have failed to hold meetings. It will
unnecessarily consume the time of Grand Lodge to· read the list in connection with the oral report. However, we request permission to attach
this list to our report, and recommend that it be published in the proceedings in order that there may be adequate information for future reference
as to Lodges and· districts which did not deem the observance of Constitution Month of sufficient importance to justify a report or to warrant a

your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 987, reports as follows :
Accused, an entered apprentice Mason, was charged with un-Masonic
conduct in one specification, that, in his petition for the Degree~ of .Masonry, which was presented about Apri~ 23, 1940, h~ made c7rtam willful
misrepresentations in that he answered m the neg~tlv~, questions 8 and .9
of the petition-have you ever presented an apphcat10n t? any Masonic
Lodge and, have you ever been rejected by an~ Masonic L?dge; that
in his said petition he answered in the affirmatrv:e the q~es~tons-have
you read all the questions contained in the f_o;egomg application, are all
of your answers thereto in your own handwntmg and do you, upon your
honor, declare your foregoing statements to be true. However, the reco~ds
of the office of the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of New Mexico
show that, on September 3, 1931, accused petitioned Temple Lodge No. 6,
Albuquerque, New Mexico, and he was rejected.
In answer to the charge, accused stated that he ha.d petitioned to
become a Mason and contacted the Secretary of a Lodge m Albuquerque,
New Mexico. "I' didn't make out a petition and didn't know if the Secretary did. I told some gentlemen (giving names of thr.ee perso~s), I would
like to put my petition into McKinley Lodge and smce I dtd not know
my status, they said I should put " No" on the petition.
The three persons referred to in the testimony of the accused we~e
called as witnesses at his trial. All three of them were members of Masonic
Lodges but none of them was a member of McKinley Lodge.
The first to give his testimony stated that he did not. assi~t accused
to make out his petition. The other two, members of California Lodges,
testified as follows :
The first, after stating that he was a member of Bay View Lodge
No. 401, thus testified:
Q. " Is it true that you assisted accused to fill out his petition?"
A. " Yes."
Q. "Is it true that you told accused to answer these two questions,
that is Nos. 8 and 9, by No?"
A. "Yes."
Q. "Is it true that accused told you he did not know he had ~een
rejected, and that you said it would be proper to answer these two questions
by putting No?"
A. "Yes-under certain circumstances."
Q. "What do you mean by under certain circumstances ?"
A. "At the time he made his petition out, he stated he did not know
whether or not he had been rejected. I told him to answer No, and leave

622

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

it up to the Investigating Committee of the Lodge to ascertain the facts."
Q. "What gave you the idea that the Investigating Committee would
ascertain the facts?"
A. "My understanding has been that each petition is investigated
through all Grand Lodges throughout the country."
The other witness, after stating that he was a member of Sun Garden
Lodge No. 530, stated in part as follows:
Q. "Did you assist in filling out accused's petition?"
A. "Yes."
Q. "Did you know that accused had petitioned a Lodge in New
Mexico?"
A. "I didn't know where he had, but he read the question to me and
said 'Bill, I don't know what to answer.' As he was filling out the application, and said he didn't know what to answer, as he didn't know if he
was r.ejected or not, I asked him if he knew the name of the Lodge, and
he said no. I told him not to fill it out, as the Investigating Comm.ittee
would then find it out. I thought by doing this the Grand Lodge would
be able to furnish or get this information. I remember very clearly that
it should be left to the committee to find out whether he had been rejected
or not. I also asked him if he ever got a notice from the Lodge he
petitioned before and he said no. Also asked him if he received ttis money
back and he answered that he didn't know whether he got it or not."
Q. "Then your answer is that you knew he had petitioned a Lodge
before?"
A. "Yes, but didn't know if he had been rejected or not."
Q. "Did you tell him to write 'No' to these questions?"
A . "No. I told him not to fill.it out until he found out."
The portion of the testimony just quoted does not justify accused
in answering the questions falsely nor does it excuse him from adequate
punishment at the hands of the Trial Committee. The circumstances
surrounding its signing, in the judgment of this committee makes it inequitable for accused to be expelled and suffer, what might be termed, the
extreme punishment.
This committee has almost uniformly recommended to Grand Lodge
in cases such as this where there have been misstatements in applications
for Degrees that the punishment should be fixed at suspension, rather
than expulsion and in the instant case we believe that we are fully justified
in recommending reduction of the penalty and fixing it at suspension.
We cannot refrain from commenting upon the action of the two
brothers who presumed to give accused advice relative in the preparation
and signing of his petition. The testimony of both displays a woeful lack
of understanding not only of the English language but also the duties
of a Mason relative to petition for degrees. Although this statement of
the committee may do little practical good we hope it is not amiss.
to make these comments.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved, That the action of McKinley Lodge No. 347, in finding the
accused guilty of the charge and of un-Masonic conduct be and the same
is hereby approved and affirmed but the sentence imposed by the Trial
Commission be reduced from expulsion to suspension

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 993, begs leave to report as follows:
On November 6, 1940, the Junior Warden of Crockett Lodge No. 139,
by direction of the Master thereof, charged Brother A. ] . S., a Past
Master of said Lodge, with un-Masonic conduct on two specifications,
to-wit:
First: That in. April, .1930, he accepted from the daughter of a deceased fon;ner Secretary of said Lodge, the sum of $1,100 or thereabouts,
for the purpose of investing said money for her account in shares of the
capital stock of the Pacific Gas & Electric Company and to hold the said
sum of money, or the shares of stock in trust for the use and benefit of
said inmate of the Masonic Home at Decoto. That in violation of his
trust, said accused brother had dissipated said money and appropriated
the same to his own use and contrary to the wishes and desires and
instructions of the aforesaid inmate of the Masonic Home at Decoto.
Second: That the accused had conspired with said inmate and connived at the retention by her, contrary to the rules of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, by accepting the money in
specification No. 1 and not advising the Board of Trustees of said
Masonic Homes of California, which resulted m depriving the Board of
Trustees of the said sum of money.
It should be here added that the inmate in question had been admitted to the Masonic Home while the accused was Master of the Lodge.
In view of the fact that the charge involved a Past Master of Crockett
Lodge, the officers thereof were somewhat embarrassed at the prospect of
trying one of their own Past Masters and thereupon requested our Most
Worshipful Grand Master to designate some other Lodge for the purpose
of hearing the charges. The Most Worshipful Grand Master thereupon
requested Bethlehem Lodge No. 453 to hear and determine the charges.
Your committee has examined the minutes of the meeting for election
of Commissioners, the record of the trial proceedings, issuance and service
of Summons, and the regularity of the trial, with all of which your committee is in full accord.
The accused appeared before the Commissioners and admitted that
he had taken the money in question and contrary to the rules and
regulations concerning inmates of the Masonic Home at Decoto, but
endeavored to excuse his actions upon a plea of lack of intention to
commit a fraud upon the inmate of the Home, or the Fraternity in general.
The Trial Commissioners were evidently not ·impressed ·with that explanation and thereupon found the accused guilty as charged, recommended
suspension, and thereafter and on April 1, 1941, he was ordered suspended.
With this latter portion of the proceedings your committee cannot
agree, as this committee has invariably recommended expulsion on account
of embezzlement of funds and has generally been sustained by Grand
Lodge. For the foregoing reason your committee believes that the
penalty should have been fixed at expulsion rather than suspension.
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption:
In the matter of trial record No. 993, wherein one A. J. S. of Crockett
Lodge No. 139 is the accused, your committee recommends that all steps.
and proceedings in the trial of said accused be ratified and confirmed, save
and except that the penalty be raised from suspension to expulsion.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances begs leave to report as follows on
Case No. 997 :
The accused was found guilty of living and cohabiting with a woman
not his wife. Because of the separation of the accused and his wife this.
conduct on his part continued over a considerable period of time.
In legal proceedings between the accused and his wife in the Superior
Court the above-mentioned facts were admitted and the case resulted in
a great deal of notoriety.
The Trial Commission found the accused guilty of several specifications of adultery, and fixed the penalty at suspension.
We are in entire agreement with the findings of guilty. One could
hardly imagine a case in which the conduct of a man was more brazen,
open, and notorious than was the admitted conduct of the accused in this
case. There can be no justification or excuse for adultery on the part of
any Master Mason. Open and notorious adultery on the part of any of
our members must inevitably bring reproach upon our Fraternity. Such
conduct cannot be excused or condoned or justified.
Therefore we cannot agree with the penalty of suspension, as fixed
by the Trial Commission. We are all of the opinion that this penalty must
and should be raised to expulsion. Your committee therefore recommends
the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, That the action of Marin Lodge No. 191 in finding the
accused guilty of the charge of un-Masonic conduct be, and the same is
hereby approved and confirmed, but that the sentence imposed by the
Trial Commission be modified by changing the same to expulsion from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Accused was fond of accuser's two children and apparently they of him.
All parties seemed to have enjoyed the existing friendship. Accused's wife
developed a nervous disorder. A doctor advised against keeping a boarder
in the house. Accused offered to leave but the husband dissuaded him
and sought his help in working out a recovery from the wife's "illness.
The wife desired to .take a trip to visit her parents in the East. The
accused was going to visit his parents in Oklahoma City. The wife and
the accused traveled East to Omaha by accused's auto. She then went
on by train and accused went to Oklahoma. They met and came back
together. This trip was with the entire knowledge and consent of the
husband, he paying part of the gas and oil charges, as otherwise accused
would have gone by train. On their return some trouble seems to have
developed. Accused moved out of the home but later returned at the
husband's insistance and with the approval of the Master of the Lodge
to whose attention the matter had been brought. A few days later he
again left at the wife's order.
While in Oklahoma, the accused wrote some letters to the wife dealing
in part with arrangements fo,r the return trip. In them were some expressions of affectipn which would have been better left unwritten. They are
susceptible of different interpretations. Accused categorically denied any
effort to alienate the wife's affections or to disturb accuser's family relation.
He does not seem to have done either. In fact, he is not so charged but
only with the attempt. Aside from the letters there appears to have been
nothing in the relations of accused and accuser's wife of which the accuser
did not have full knowledge. No clandestine meetings were shown nor
any other acts of affection other than mere association.
The Trial Commissioners, nine in number, heard the evidence, saw
the parties, read the letters, listened to the explanations made and found
accused not guilty on the six specifications in questiQll. Had a contrary
finding been made, we would be loath to sustain it.
We are unwilling to recommend that the Trial Commission be overruled.
We, therefore, offer the fo.llowing resolution and move its adoption:
Be It Resolved, That the finding of the Trial Commission and the fixing
of the penalty at reprimand in trial record No. 1001 be and the same
hereby is ratified and affirmed.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 1001, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused, one L. E. G., was charged with un-Masonic conduct
as set forth in seven specifications. The first six of these specifications,
in substance allege that the accused attempted to win the affections of
the accuser's wife, attempted to alienate her affections and attempted to
disrupt accuser's home. Of these the accused was found not guilty.
The seventh specification charged accused, in substance, with having
lied to the accuser by asserting that he had never written accuser's wife
more than one letter. By a divided vote the accused was found guilty
of this specification. By a vote of five to four he was found guilty of
Un-Masonic conduct and by a unanimous vote of the Trial Commission
the penalty was fixed at reprimand. The accuser has appealed and
accuser's counsel urges in his brief that the accused should be found guilty
of the first six specifications and expelled.
Your committee has carefully studied this record of over one hundred
pages. We nnd ourselves in entire accord with the findings of the Trial
Com"mission and · feel that the penalty of reprimand is ample for the
single specification of which the accused was found guilty.
It would be impossible with any due regard for time to review in
detail all the evidence in the case. However, we will set forth a very
brief summary thereof. Accuser and accused are members of the same
Lodge. Accused was a roomer in the home of accuser and also boarded
there to the extent of the morning and evening meal. The three parties
involved became· close friends. They spent considerable time of evenings
together in the home, played cards and attended social functions. Accuser's

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Control is pleased to submit a report of the activities
coming under its supervision during the past Masonic year.
Before doing so, however, it desires to call to the attention of our
brethren the great loss that has been sustained by Masonry due to the
passing of our beloved Brother Frank Tade.
In all things of life, he was earnest and sincere, he was loyal and
kindly, he was charitable, and he was a good Mason. He was an outstanding member of the Board of Control. We shall greatly miss the value
of his strong personality and sage advice for many years to come.
Our appreciation is expressed to the Grand Master, also to the Grand
Secretary and his assistants for the information and assistance given to
us. The splendid co-operation between the Board of Control, and the
Boards of Relief and individual Lodges continues with gratifying results.
While all justified relief has been freely extended; nevertheless, due to the
proper handling of such cases, the Grand Lodge is called upon to make
reimbursements in the very small amounts mentioned below.
Meetings
'The Board held one meeting on February 1, 1941, in Los Angeles.
It had several conferences by mail during the year and a special meeting
with Secretaries of Boards of Relief and Managers of Employment
Bureaus, October 15, 1941 (during Grand Lodge).
Members of the Board of Control also attended Annual Board of
Relief and Employment Bureau Breakfasts at Long Beach, San Diego,.
Los Angeles, Fres.no, Sacramento, and Oakl~nd.
Reimbursements
We have recommended to the Finance Committee that the following
requests for reimbursements be granted:
Los Angeles Board of RelieL .........;.............................................$ 67.00
Sacramento Board of Relief... ...~ ..................................................... 100.00
San Bernardino Board of Relief........................,........................... 51.00
East Bay Masonic Board of Relief.............................................. 180.00
Total ..........................._. .....................................................".........$398.00
Employment Service
The upswing in many lines of business and industry occasioned by the
Preparedness Progra111 has had great influence in reducing unemployment
and our seven employment services have taken full advantage of the
·s ituatimi, not only to place our brethren in jobs, but to assist them in
securing better jobs.
Necessary Priority Orders from our Government have also · affected
many businesses, causing a shifting of jobs. Our Employment Bureaus
have been very active in assisting our brethren under these circumstances.
There is nothing which brings more. happiness to anyone than to be
able to provide the necessities of life and some of the luxuries for those
dear to him, as evidenced by the many letters of appreciation received by
' all employment managers.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

627

That employers also value our services is evidenced by the many
letters of appreciation on file.
The number of applications received from our unemployed brethren
this fiscal year was 23,826,. and the number of jobs secured totaled 18,368,
a 35% increase in applications and a 51 % increase in jobs over last year.
As expected, employers' requests for help likewise increased-24,194
as compared to 14,836 the previous y ear.
The expense for the year was $32,642.46, of which Grand L odge
appropriated $15,400.00 or 47%, the other 53% being provided by the
Lodges and other Masonic bodies served.
The average cost per job hit a mark so low that it may never be
equaled, $1.78 as compared to $2.53 last year .
Had these jobs been secured through .private fee-charging agencies,
our needy brethren wou ld have paid out more t han a quarter of a m illion
dollars. We spent only $32,642.46 in producing these outstanding results
an d t he investment made by Grand Lodge was 84 cent s per placement.
We feel that the men and women employees in this work merit and
need every assistance the brethren of the jurisdiction can give them.
Remember that it is the little things that count, words of good will a nd
encouragement regarding this great Masonic work are of considerable
help. This job of spreading happiness through employment is one th at
every member can participate in and it pays big dividends.
Gratifying Words from the Philippine Islands
Antonio Gonzales, P.G.M ., Grand Secretary of Grand ·Lodge, F . &
A. M., Philippine Islands, writes: " I read about the great success of your
Masonic Employment Service. Inasmuch as we would like to institute
the same service in our Grand Jurisdiction under p lans carried out by your
Grand Lodge, would you be kind enough to please give us all the infor matio n about the work." Information was furnished to him and a very
appreciative reply was received.

GENERAL REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to submit the following report:
Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the
firm of Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, certified public accountants, to
· examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, the Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The
·reports of Brother Webb's examination of these records have been filed
with your committee and have had its consideration. These reports are
now on file with the records of G~and Lodge. They indicate that all
records are correct and in proper shape and all receipts properly accounted
for · and all expendi~ures properly made.
Your committee is again mindful of the debt it owes Brother Webb
for the personal interest he has shown in making the various audits because
of hi·s membership in the Fraternity and his interest is more than usual
in this work. He has given the Fraternity an unusual service for the
fee allowed.
The total amount paid for the audit this year is $700.00 of which
sum the Homes has paid $550.00 and the balance of $150.00 has been
paid out of Grand Lodge funds.
Grand Lodge Week Activities
Your committee has had a discussion with the chairman of the Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities, who has furnished us an estimate
of the cost of entertainment which this committee has provided for the
members who are attending this session of Grand Lodge. Necessarily, the
best that the Activities Committee can do at this time is to furnish an
estimate of the costs, as it is impossible to determine the actual amount
of expenditure until all activities are over and all bills are actually presented.
As has been stated in previous reports, the Finance Committee is in
entire accord with the pl~n of providing the representatives attending
Grand Lodge some entertainment. It is. also to be noted that a part of
the duties which had been assigned to this committee are the arrangements
for the transportation for the trip to the Decoto Home.
. That there should be extensive visitations 'to the home is earnestly
desirable, according to our opinion. We are, t.h erefore, very much in
accord with the expenses incurred in providing for these visitations. The
Committee on Grand Lodge Week Activities has a difficult duty to perform. It is our opinion that this committee has fulfilled its obligations in
a most creditable manner. You who partook of the entertainment last
night already know that it was entirely developed by the Committee on
Activities and presented by members of the Craft. The chairman of the
committee, Brother A lfred F. Breslauer, is entitled to particular commendation for the preparation and development of this entertainment.
There was appropriated at the last session for the p urpose of defraying
the expenses o'f . this entertainment, as well as a trip to the Homes, the
sum of $2,500.00. According to the best estimates the Activities Committee
is able to furnish at this time, it is believed that this sum will not be
exceeded, and if so only slightly. If there should be any amount expended

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

635

above the amount of the appropriation we ~pprove this additional expenditure and recommend that the Grand Secretary pay the same.
We are of the opinion that the same amount which was appropriated
last year .s hould again be . appropriated. We therefore offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved That the sum of $2,500, or as much thereof as may be necessary to pay' the expenses incurred by the Grand Lodge Week Activities
Committee, be, and the same is hereby appropriated out of the funds of
Grand Lodge, and that the same be allocated to the payment of ~he
expenses incurred in the entertainment ·of officers and members attending
the next annual communication of Grand Lodge.
Masonic History
Your committee has had a discussion with Brother Mark Sawrie, a
member of the Masonic·• History Committee, concerning the work this
committee is planning on doing this coming year, as well as the amount
that it will need to perform the work it has in anticipation. It is to be
noted that while the committee has continued its activities for the past
year and has done considerable valuable work in collecting historical data
of the fraternity, but that only $114.09 of the appropriation of $250.00 made
last year has been expended by the committee. This is in keeping with
the record which this committee has made in the past, and that is, that
much has been accomplished in seeking out and ·w riting up the early
history of Masonry in California, and that the cost to Grand Lodge of
this work has been modest indeed.
The History Committee is to be commended for its constant an.d
painstaking efforts in carefully digging up the real facts on Masonic
History and also for the moderate demands it has made f~r fund~ in
seeking and compiling this history. As has been expressed in previous
reports, the Finance Committee is still in favor of encouraging the History
Committee and its work. Vv" e are also in accord with the modest amount
which the committee is asking from Grand Lodge this year and therefore
offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved That the sum of. $250.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodg~ to defray expenses which may be incurred by the com1?1ittee
in compiling and preparing additional information gathered on the history
of Masonry in California.
Masonic Education
The chairman, Brother Reynold E . Blight of the Committee on
Masonic Education, appeared before this committee and gave a ~omplete
outline of his plans for the activities of the committee for the coming 3'.ear.
Brother Blight expressed a wish that the designation of the com.m1ttee
should be to Masonic Information· instead of as it now reads. While the
approval of this change is, no doubt, the province of the C?mmittee on
Policy and General Purpose, and yet the members of the ~inance Committee feel that it will not be out of order to express their approval o.f
this change.
.
The committee was also impressed with the plan of this committee
for the coming year. It is recognized by. ali, however, that the plan is on
trial. It is therefore thought that the Masters of the several Lodges sh?uld
avail themselves of the information being furnished . by this committee
and make an effort to determine how effective the new plan seems to be
so that it may be determined whether it shall be followed in future years
or some other one worked out. We commend this recommendation to the
Masters present.

The chairman of the committee expressed the hope that he would be
able to accomplish the purposes he has in mind with an appropriation of
$500.00, and your Committee on Finance is in accord with this recommendation.
We therefore recommend that the sum of $500.00 be appropriated out
of the funds of Grand Lodge to defray the expenses of the Education
Committee in further promoting its educational plan.

theme rather than to a promotional or quota drive for fu nds. This is a
practical application of the principal, that information precedes inspiration.
Despite all of the pamphlets which have been issued and all of the
personal work which has been done, apparently too many of us are
unaware of the value and importance of the Fund. This is emphasized
by a glance at last year's " Report of Contributions to E ndowment F un d."
Lodges, generally, with four, five and six residents in. the Homes gave
small amounts regardless . of good sized memberships. On the whole,
only 5.25% of the Craft responded. Surely we have not yet caught the
vision. Perhaps some of us have hesitated about contributing because
we were unable to give as much as we should have liked. Shall we remember the lesson of the widow's mite? Small amounts make surprising
totals and are always helpful. We should all help according to our abi lities.
A broad base of support assures a stronger and more permanent foundation
and structure.
The character, integrity and consecration of the personnel of this
Board gives us great hope and confidence in the future. We commend
the zeal and devotion of each . member of the Board, and especially its
chairman, Frank M. Smith, in attaining such satisfactory results and
recommend that the Grand Lodge continue its investment in this going
enterprise.

funds of Grand Lodge for the use of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board during this fiscal Masonic year.

University of California Clubhouses
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the reports of the Trustees
of our Masonic Clubhouses, giving a resume of the activities for the past
year. We have also studied the financial statements prepared by public
accountant.
It is the opinion of your committee that the business affairs and the
expenditure of funds at the clubhouses have the constant and careful
supervision of the Trustees. We are further convinced the Trustees are
conscious of the fact that only through the continued active use of the
clubhouses to their fullest extent by students attending these universities
can they fulfill the purpose for which they were brought into being. ·
We commend the attention of the clubhouses to the officers and
representatives assembled at this Grand Lodge, with the request that they
go back to their Lodges and inform their membership of these two fine
institutions. We urge you to recommend to your -members when they
have a son or daughter entering either the U niversity at Berkeley or Los
Angeles, their first point of contact on the campus should be the Masonic
Clubhouse.
The budgets covering operating expenses for the coming year submitted by the Trustees have been considered by your Committee on
Finance, and we, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend
its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $15,000 be appropriated from the funds of
the Grand Lodge for the maintenance of the Masonic Clubhouses $7,500
to be paid to the Trustees of the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley and
$7,500 to be paid to the Trustees of the Masonic Clubhouse at Los Angeles.
Masonic Homes Endowment Board
Your attention is directed to the "Report of Masonic Homes Endowment Board"-a report which contains good news, inspiration and a story
of accomplishments that is gratifying.
. Each Master and delegate present is urged to study the well written,
interesting and carefully prepared report with the. purpose pf bringing it
to the attention of the brethren of his own Lodge.
·
Did you know that in 1941 this Fund earned $42,047.76, which, together
with other accrued income, was transferred to the Masonic Homes General
Fund? Otherwise a 35-cent per capita gift would have been required for
each Master Mason: This substantial financial amount, in itself, is worth
while aside from the spiritual satisfaction experienced in maintaining the
·splendid service of the Homes.
$89,131.10 in addition was added to the Endowment Fund principal
through gifts and profitable disposal of securities. We are greatly indebted
to our beloved Grand Treasurer, Wm. P. Filmer, for a net profit of
$18,001.19, due to his ability and diligence in handling the securities.
The Board, this year, "adhered to its stated policy of encouraging
purely voluntary contributions and dedicated its services to the educational

Masonic Homes
Your Committee on Finance to which was referred that portion o f

finances of our Homes, begs leave to report as follows:
We have reviewed the report of the certified p ublic accountants and
are of the opinion that the financial affairs of our Homes are fully and
correctly reported by the Trustees.
The report submitted by your Board of Trustees and the review of
the acco.untants is, of course, submitted in printed form and we do not

only to the best interest of those housed therein, but also to the interest

Report of the Committee on Finance on the Committee of Correspondence
The Committee on Correspondence for the last several years has reviewed many of the reports of the proceedings of Grand Lodges throughout
the world. Reviews of these reports are printed in the proceedings of
Grand Lodge and are, therefore, made available to all Masons in the jurisdiction.
·
After all, what Masonry is doing, wherever it may exist, is something
in which we are all interested. Such information is made available through
the good work of this committee and should be continued.

Your Committee on Finance has reviewed with care the report of the

various Trust Funds, including a list of securities held and of securities

report again indicates the ' great care given and the efficiency displayed by
our Grand Treasurer in handling the financial affairs of Grand Lodge. The
responsibility which the Grand Treasurer has is very great. The praise
and appreciation of this committee is unbounded for the work which this
worthy officer is performing for Grand Lodge.
As has already been reported on the Audit of Accounts, all items of
Receipts and Disbursements have been properly accounted for · and all
records are in perfect shape.
I
Our Grand Treasurer has performed his duties this year under real
difficulties, as in March he was taken down with bronchial pneumonia.
Due to the severity of the attack our Grand Treasurer has been confined
to his home most of the time and in bed much of the time since the attack
in March. It, therefore, has been necessary for him to carry the great responsibilities which rest upon him as Grand Treasurer, while at home,
and yet in no ways have the duties of the office been neglected. In fact it
is to be noted by' the report that in the transactions in Federal and other
bonds, a profit of $18,001.19 has accrued to the Endowment Fund and this
without any decrease in the income received therefrom.
Vv' e are sure this Grand Lodge is desirous of expressing to Brother
Filmer its appreciation of the services which he has performed, and by this
means your Committee on Finance is tendering to Brother Filmer the
thanks of Grand Lodge. We are also sure that you want to hope for our
Most Worshipful Brother a speedy and complete recovery and that we
may have his wise counsel in Grand Lodge for many years to come. We
also express this wish for you.
Report of Grand Secretary
This is the first time in thirty-three years that the report of this officer
of Grand Lodge has been presented by other than John Which er, and the
presenter of this report asks the ·personal privilege from Grand Lodge to
pay a few words of tribute to a friend of thirty-four years, for it has been
that length of time that I had known John, and in all those years my life
has been the better because I knew him. It was his privilege to do that
work in life which pleased him most and that was to serve Masonry. He
lived as he most liked to live, and died the way he often expressed a wish
to die, and that was still in the harness and laboring for Masonry. He was
always considerate, always courteous, always just and his life more nearly
approached the noble than any man that it has been my privilege to know.
His life was truly a benediction to all those who knew him, and he achieved
success in the truest sense: in that this world and Masonry and the lives of
those who knew him were the better that he passed by this way.

Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
At the annual communication of this Grand Lodge two years ago
there appeared before this committee a committee selected by the Inspectors
for the purpose of conveying to this committee a wish that the manner of
returning the expenses of Inspectors in performance of their very official
duties, should be changed and that instead of receiving the expenses from
the individual Lodges of their district that the same be paid by Grand Lodge,
This committee was in accord with the suggested change and requested
that a study be made of the requirements as well as the necessary change
of laws and the same be presented at .next communication of Grand Lodge.
This was done and at our last annual communication the Grand Lecturer
recommended the appropriation of $3,000.00 for the purpose of covering
these expenses. The Grand Lecturer's recommendation was accepted and
an appropriation made of the amount recommended.
It is particularly pleasing to note that while the money was available
to return to the Inspectors, the expenses incurred in the performance of
their duties only $224.23 of the $3,000.00 has been paid out, or in other
words, the great body of Inspectors of this State are performing their
duties fully and efficiently and that most of this work entails expenses
that could in all propriety be requested returned, yet this most important
work is being done for the pure joy of the services rendered without the
willingness to accept any return for any money out. This is the spirit
which 111akes Masonry what it is and which will always keep the banner of
Masonry high. It is obvious that this fine group of officers of Grand Lodge ·
are enjoying one of the greatest satisfactions in life, and that is, the rendering
of unselfish service. Masonry is indeed fortunate to have such a body of men.
As was expressed in the previous reports of this committee, it is of the
opinion that the Grand Lecturer should promulgate certain rules governing
the reimbursements of these expenses, such rules to first have the approval
of the Grand Master. This procedure was followed by our deceased Grand
Lecturer, Worshipful Brother Walter Leonard. It is suggested that the
rules adopted for last year be studied by our incoming Grand · Lecturer

Grand Lodge Per Capita
The Constitution provides for the levying of a per capita of SO cents
to provide for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various activities. In
addition to the sum provided for by this per capita levy, there is additional
revenue accruing to Grand Lodge from degrees conferred and income
on investments and from some other sources of approximately $24,000.00.
There is also some other revenue derived from the sale of supplies and
from surety bonds covering Lodge officers. This revenue, however, cannot
be taken into consideration in the budget because it is offset by corresponding items of disbursement, which are also eliminated from the budget. The
income derived from these sources is not sufficient to pay the operating
expenses of Grand Lodge during this coming year and the various appropriations being recommended in this report. It also should be borne in
mind that there are always some expenses which cannot be estimated,

to make any estimate as to the amount which may be required.
This committee has always taken the position that while there was

COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE MASONRY
To the M.". w.·. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
This committee was first appointed in 1928 by Grand Master Hutaff
upon the recommendation of Grand Master Fischer and has already made
twelve annual reports. It seems proper, therefore, to summarize the work
of the committee and check our sights.
A thorough review of the prev.ious reports of the committee discloses
no statement of the history of previous Grand Lodge action upon the
subject. The craft in general, and Masters and Secretaries in particular,
are entitled to this for their guidance when occasion requires. With this
in mind, a complete check of Grand Lodge reports from 1850 to date
has been made by the committee. A summary of that research is here
presented.
Policy Concerning Clandestine Masonry
. Prior to the organization of the present Constitutional Committee on
Clandestine Masonry, the subject arose in Grand Lodge twenty-eight times
at twenty different sessions. It prompted the Grand Master to appoint a
committee in 1853, and from that committee's action in 1854 is traced the
thread of a consistent policy founded upon a doctrine of nonintercourse
with those who are not regular Masons ·or not regular Lodges. The principles thus established may be briefly summarized as follows:
That every man, be he white, black, yellow or red, and whatever his
belief in God, is eligible to be a Mason, provided he is qualified and found
worthy. That no organization of clandestine or irregular origin can ever,
as such, become Masonic. That the only way to be healed Masonically
is for the individuals comprising that organization to repudiate it, and
to petition for the degrees of Masonry in the regular way. That it is
inadvisable to legislate against clandestine Masonry.
From this summary it is apparent that a regular Mason has no more
business to visit a clandestine Lodge than he has to admit a clandestine
Mason to his Lodge or to vouch for him. Any such act is a Masonic
offense. This should be known and remembered by all members of the
craft. The principle was established at the Grand Lodge session of 186J
when the charter of one of our own Lodges was "perpetually arrested"
and that Lodge "declared extinct" for admitting to its meeting members
of clandestine Lodges. It is hoped that this brief review will be noted
by Masters, Wardens and Secretaries, and that they will in turn educate
the craft upon the subject.
Previous Reports of This Committee
Your committee has in previous years reported upon the existence,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE O .F CALIFORNIA

personnel and numbers of eleven Clandestine Grand Lodges with the
names of their constituent Lodges. A summary of the status of this
activity or non-activity is desirable at this time. The committee is unanimous in the view that these should not be given any further existence or
recognition even by naming them in the reports of Grand Lodge. It
recognizes that that which is unnamed soon languishes uncoffined and
unknelle9.
There are two colored Grand Lodges. The first one was last reported
upon in 1934 as having nine Lodges but none of them active. There is no
material change up to the present except that it seems to be chartering
Filipino Lodges to perpetuate its struggling existence. The second, while
· quite thoroughly organized after the pattern of our own Grand Lodge,
has according to the most recent report, had a considerable decrease in the
number of its constituent Lodges. It seems to be doing a worthy service
for its race.
The four Co-Masonic Groups previously reported as existent in
California have split off from the parent organization of "International
Order of Co-Masonry" with headquarters in London, England.. This
movement in California is now a sort of American federation of human
rights whose existence is waning and is not of any present concern to us.
Of the numerous Grand Lodges working in Spanish, the first one
reported upon suspended all of its charters in 1934 and its Lodges have
since dissolved. The second one was last reported upon in 1938 as having
almost ceased activity but maintaining some social communication. The
third, while mentioned in the 1930 report has not been heard from since.
The fourth had at most but five subordinate Lodges and these have since
been lost to our investigation.
Among "the four Filipino Grand Lodges, the first one was reported
upon as allegedly Masonic but with no ceremonies resembling Masonry.
The word Masonic does not appear in its name. We, therefore, are not
concerned with it. The second was reported in 1932 as existent but has
not been heard from since. The third has been previously reported as
having labor, economic, political and social ideals and as being intensely
patriotic. The eight points of its creed as printed in its convention magazine in February, 1941, are none of them strictly Masonic. It does not
have Masonry in its name and should therefore not concern us. The
fourth, while existent since 1916, had a split in its organization in 1940,
and while three of those Lodges splitting off formed a new Grand Lodge
in 1941, at present neither of these Grand Lodges seems to e_..xist any more
than in name.
Thus is the clandestine Masonry previously reported upon by this
committee summarized with what your committee deems proper emphasis.
It is to be here stressed that at no time during the past thirteen years
has any of this Clandestine activity concerned itself with the white race
in which this Grand Lodge is rooted. It is to be further noted that, so
far as this committee has been able to ascertain, the movement has not
deprived any worthy person of regular Masonic membership nor has
lolicitation been made of any such material, with one exception. In that
one exception, your committee was able to point out to the applicant the
OpJ?ortunity of being recommended to Masonry by a regular brother who
stood ready to do so, or joining in a social welfare movement among his
race, if tha't was the applicant's desire. The committee has not since
been informed of the decision.

of this committee and such recommendations as are proper. A majority
of your committee has met in conference upon this question and is
unanimous in presenting the following :
As noted from the foregoing, this so-called Masonry has been confined
to three races, viz.: the Negroes, the Filipinos and the Mexican·s . In the
first two the movement may be properly classed as that of social welfare
or patriotic, with such Masonry a s they claim· used as a cement to bind
them together. With such movements, confined to their own classes,
regular Masonry has no quarrel, but may well God-speed them on their
way. Only in the Spanish language groups has there been the tendency
to racketeering. As summarized above, this group is the nearest to being
extinct-as justice itself would dictate. At least the termite has not
spread to our Masonic timber.
The committee believes that its ac~ivity in the past has served to curb
the spread of clandestine Masonry into the field of regular Masonry and
to deprive it of any semblance of recognition in the eyes of the law.
Today there · is on the statute books a law placed there in 1933, providing
for prosecution even for the wearing of any Masonic pin or emblem to
which the wearer is not entitled. Prosecution may also be made of anyone
selling spurious degrees for money. The committee is in favor of such
prosecution handled through the regular law enforcement agencies and in
such way that regular Masonry does not appear as the prosecutor, much
less a persecutor.
As to the scope of the future activity of the committee it is thought
that it should continue to gather the data concerning all movements of
clandestine character and furnish the information to the Grand Secretary's
office so that it is available upon inquiry by those concerned in the areas
affected, or furnish it to Lodge officers direct upon request. This relieves
the· Grand Master of all burden in this regard. In t)le gathering of such
information the officers and members of our constituent Lodges can be
of the greatest service and it is hoped that they will heed this and co-operate
with the committee in passing along the information they obtain.
The second line of activity would be, in the event of a prosecution,
to function as an investigator and furnish information and counsel to those
charged with the prosecution as to the policy and attitude of regular
Masonry. This activity should be under the supervision of the Grand
Master whenever the committee's action affects the public.
The third and last line of activity should be to counsel with local
Lodge officers as to the means and methods to be employed to suppress
any spread of spurious Masonry to our own ranks, to track down
racketeers and to prevent wherever possible any impositions upon good
men who may have a sincere desire to become Masons.
With such purposes in mind and specifically defined we trust the
committee may be of greater service to the craft. Our one request is that
this report be read in each Lodge for the purpose of giving information
and making known to the membership how they can be of service in
promoting this work of the committee.
Respectfu1ly submitted,

I have obtained from the President of the Masonic Clubhouse Council,
the President of the Boys' Masonic Club, and the President of the Girls'
Masonic Club letters hereinafter set out in full. I know of no better way
to present to the Grand Lodge the reaction and activities of our girls
and boys than to present to you in their own language their appraisal of
the benefits and advantages they enjoy by reason of their membership in
the Clubs.
The first of these letters is from Harold Neeland, President of the
Clubhouse Council. He says:
"The Masonic Clubhouse was built with the objec~ive of
providing a place for the students of the University of California
having Masonic affiliation to meet one another, to make acquaintances, and to form worthwhile and lasting friendships.
"Just as the expectations of those who originally saw the need
and · the opportunity for such a common meeting place were

653

fulfilled, and exceeded, due to the erection of this beautiful structure, so much and far more has been the fulfillment of the original
objective.
"
"This semester alone, the clubhouse facilities are being enjoyed by approximately five hundred members. Through such
events as luncheons, evening fireside programs, social dancing,
and many others, the clubhouse serves a multi-purpose function.
Primarily it is a common meeting place, not only for the organized
clubs within, but mainly for the individual members who look upon
the clubhouse as a friendly campus home. As a center of activity,
interest, and college spirit the clubhouse provides an essential
part of student education. Alone, as a source of loyal friendships
and kindly interest to the new student and the old, the clubhouse
serves a value more than justifying its maintenance."
Jerome L. Kush nick expresses his reaction in the following language:
"As this semester at the University reaches its prime, and as
social event after event unfolds itself at the Masonic Club to the
delight of the members, they have asked me in behalf of the
Men's Masonic Club to express their gratitude to you and to all
the Masons of California for assisting in making their days in
college happy ones.
"It is difficult to relate to you the emotions of joy and
satisfaction that are written on the faces of freshmen jls they
express their approval of the clubhouse after their first visitation.
And when they become more active, partaking of our dances,
luncheons, firesides, picnics, bridge parties, banquets, and other
social functions, their approval is not only by their smiling faces
but by the very words they speak.
"To me the Club has given many opportunities. I find it a
place where I might come to relax and forget for a while my, at
times, monotonous college routine. It is a place where I might
meet young men and women; men and women to whom I might
speak and share mutual interests; men and women who I may
look forward to as having as lifelong friends; and lastly, but above
all, men and women who are worth knowing. Without any hesitation I say that the Masonic Club is the only place on the
University campus that has all this to offer.
"To relate my thoughts and opinions is to relate the thoughts
of all the members of the Masonic Club, for they coincide precisely.
So once more I express our thanks in appreciation of your kindness and generosity and trust that the opportunities you are giving
us may continue, that those to follow us may also sip from the
cup of happiness."
Finally, Doris K. Wilton, President of the Women's Masonic Club,
gives us her ideas as to what our Clubhouse life is and amounts to in
the University of California:
"I deem it an honor and a privilege to express for the members, as well as myself, the deep felt gratitude to the Board of
Trustees for the Masonic Clubhouse they have provided for us.
"In creating this building for us, some of the advantages must
have been realized. I say 'some' as only the members themselves
can experience its full value. The Clubhouse is more than a beautiful building just off campus for the association of students with
Masonic affiliation. It is more than a wonderful social organization
where people can meet and enjoy various types of entertainment.

It is a place' where enduring friendships are formed. I believe
this fact is most important, for life wouldn't be half so rich and
full without ·friends to help share the joys therein.
"With friendship as the basis of club life, the various social
activities may progress successfully. Luncheons, dances, barbeques,
and firesi.d es, ar e but a few of the functions that help weld the
Club into a more compact unit.
"In carrying out this program we hope that we are fulfilling
the purpose for which this Clubhouse was founded."

Masonry is at work, ,my brethren, in many ways and in many places,

members of our Board, they being Brother Charles H . Dodds, Past
Master of Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677, and Brother C. H . Robison, a
member of the same Lodge. During the year, because of ill health, both
of these brethren resigned a fter a number of years of fine service, and
we here record our appreciation. Our Most Worshipful Grand Master filled
these vacancies by appointing Brother D. K . Bjork, Professor of History,
and Brother D. G. Madise, Business Manager of the University. Both of
these brethren have long been interested in Clubhouse activities and
will be of great assistance in carrying on the work.

One of the serious problems that confronts the Trustees · the membership of the Club and our very capable and loyal Hostess, i~ to determine
the most satisfactory and legitimate means of approach to the young men
and women of the University who are Masonically affiliated. Many such
young men and women who enter the University know nothing of the
existence of the Masonic Club. Our thought is that the best method of
approach wou ld be to educate the parents of these young people by
putting in their hands information regarding the Club, that they might
in turn communicate to their sons and daughters.
·

and place these photographs, together with suitable information as fo
the advantages offered by the Club, in the hands of the Secretaries of

Lodges. In order to make this rea lly effective it should be supplemented
by having the attention of the several Lodges called to the subject matter .
through a circular letter by the Grand Master to all the Lodges in the St~te.
