REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M.'. W:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Charters, to which was referred the petition for
Charter of Trona Lodge, U . D.; submits herewith for your consideration
the following report:
Trona- Lodge, Trona, San Bernardino County, was granted a· formal
dispensation on September 10, 1940, by Grand Master William B. Ogden.
At the last Annual Communication this committee recommended your
approval of the request for a continuance of the dispensation and the
recommendation was adopted by· Grand Lodge.
Your committee has heretofore examined in detail the records and
exhibits accompanying the petition, as a result of ~hich we are prompted.
to recommend the same, in their entirety, as a pattern worthy .of imitation.
We also feel that we would be remiss in our duty if we did not offer a
word of praise to the .Master and ~'ardens of Trona L odge and to Brother
Sam Levin, Secretary, whose combined efforts are responsible for the
painstaking preparation of this excellent and illuminating report on the
history of Trona Lodge during the thirteen-month period under dispensation. Despite the fact that virtue is its own reward, any personal commendation herein contained would be incomplete without a reference to
Brother William L. Davis, Inspector of the 60th District. Your committee
is informed that Brother Davis has taken an active and friendly interest
in the affairs of Trona Lodge from the date of the second organization
meeting a nd has, by his kindly, patient and sympathetic understanding of
the many problems ~ttendant upon the birth of a new Lodge, completely
endeared himself to the membership and fully merits the applause of his
brethren.
Ordinarily, your committee would not presume upon the time of this
Grand Lodge to offer statistieal information; however, in the present
instance it is believed that a brief allusion to facts and figures may be
interesting as well as significant, in tha t they may reflect something of the
character and type of men who now seek your favorable consideration.
The record discloses: 13 stated meetings and 28 special meetings; a
Charter membership of 23 and a present membership of 35, which includes
only one affiliation. Of the 23 Charter. members, it is noted that all paid
$12.00 dues in advance and that 13 made voluntary contributions to the
Organization Committee in amounts varying from ten to fifty dollars.
That the example thus offered ho.re fruit is evidenced by the further fact
that of the eleven men raised seven also made additional contributfons.
The total voluntary contributions of $1 ,225.00 also included $155.00 donated
by five non-mt!mbers of Trona Lodge. The problem of securing suitable
quarters was very quickly simplified by the praiseworthy action of the
officials ·o f the American Potash & Chemical Company who, 'through
generous financial and amortization arrangements, made possible the
Masonic Temple, which is now the home of Trona Lodge, entirely freed
of all indebtedness· and confronted, for the time being, at least, with only
one financial obligation'-the payment of an annual rental of $60.00.
Much might be written concerning Trona as a community and what
we, as Masons, may have a rlght to expect from the members of Tron a
Lodge. However, this re;,.ie:W of the past thirteen months gives every
assurance ·.of a--;p11amising future quite in keeping with the best traditions

George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association
The Grand Master referred in his message to the payments. heretofore
made by this Grand Lodge to the George . Washington Masonic National
Memorial Association, directing attention to the fact that the full ·quota
of $1.70 per capita had not yet been fully paid by us. He asked that \ve
do not close our minds to the possibility of making future appropriatioils
for this outstanding effort by American Grand Lodges to complete an
undertaking which has been well begun. He did not say in words, but it
doubtless is a fact, that during the present national emergency it would
be inexpedient and extravagant to expend large sums for building operations which could be deferred· until a propitious time.
Your committee recommends tha.t the subject be postponed for further
consideration by Grand Lodge.

The recommendation was adopted.
Courtesy Degrees
The Grand Master in his message has expounded a sound policy with
reference to courtesy degrees and has given a timely warning of the dangers
and abuses of a too-ready acceptance of applications and petitions. during
the present emergency. Much can be forgiven that is motivated by a
patriotic fervor, but carelessness in accepting petitions and in investigating
candidates should not be condoned. If our Lodges are vigilant, the mistakes made in 1917-1918 will not be repeated during these critical times.
A wise Lodge is not one that never makes a mistake but is one that does
not make the same mistake a second time.

Adopted.

timely report on the subject of Emergency Welfare Work. He co~­
clusively convinces your committee that it would be unwise to build and
staff Masonic service centers adjacent' to tl).e army camps and naval
stations and that no Masonk duty requires such an activity. His expositiort
of the obligations of Grand Lodge, the Lodges and members with reference
to 'Masonic service during the emergency is worthy of careful study and
in our opinion i-s a lucid -and practical statement which conforms to 'good
sense 'is well as Masonic principles and practice. He is right in belie.v ing
that 'Masonic:: service centers do not afford the proper approach to' a
difficult and pressing problem.
As ·he· :reported to you, he is persuaded that the ·wiser course. is to
leave the matter ·of Masonic ministrations and courtesies to th,e ·Lodges
near army posts, and in the case of extraordinary concentrations of men,

by services given m arms, . should by reason of such fact be relieved of a

·our law now prohibits the remission of dues in advance and it prohibits
the remission of dues for any stated period, but it gives to the Lodge the

Masonic Homes Endowment Fund
Thomas F. Lewis of El Dorado Lodge No. 26 has proposed an
amendment to the Constitution to pr~vide for an increase in the per
capita tax of an amount not exceeding ten cents per member to be paid
into the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund until the fund is self-sustaining.
Lodge Maui No. 472, at the 442nd stated meeting thereof; by resolution
has proposed a similar amendment but has not fixed the desired amount
of increase in the per capita tax.
The reasons advanced by the proponents are that the present method
of raising endowment funds is not satisfactory: that there is a lack of
co-operation and participation 'on the part of the majority of the membership; that the cost of present methods is greater than the receipts; that
the work of the Lodges in connection with the funds is burdensome; tliat
uniform contributions should be made by all Masons without solicitationand they want a change.
There seems to be much misunderstanding of this widely publicized
and , important activity of Grand Lodge. All contributions an: voluntarily
made by members and not by Lodges. The work of the Board and of the
Lodge Committees is solely to acquaint the members with the Homes,
the need of a safeguarding and protective fund of ample proportions, and
to afford an opportunity for voluntary participation by gift or bequest.
Instead of drives for money, the effort is educational. A full understanding
of the needs of our Homes, which are a great, tangible expression of a
Mason's devotion to the principle of Relief and the care of Masons in
distress, widows and orphans, must neces.s arily persuade every Mason
to give something out of his store for the good of his Homes and the
proper ·subjects of his Masonic bounty.
The lack of full participation in the task of increasing the endowment
fund is due to our failure to fully acquaint the membership with their
opportunities to be helpful. The annual cost of the work of the Board
thus far has· never ·e xceeded $6,000 and the entire expense has been paid
out of Grartd Lodge funds and no expense money has ever been taken
from the endowment fund. The fund this year paid over to the Board of
Trustees of the Homes for maintenance $42,047.76. This was all jncome
from investm.ents. From gifts an<l bequests and capital gains the fund
was inci:eased $89,131.10 this year. Six thousand dollars is well spent
w~en it produces. such .splendid results.
While the members of your committee had varying views relative to
the endowment. fund, they are agreed that contributions .thereto should

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

663

be voluntarily made by Masons as individual gifts to a noble benevolence
and they deem it unwise to require contributions to be made by the
Lodges. A tax on the Lodges would shift what should be an act of grace
and benevolence on the part of a Mason to an act of compulsion imposed
upon Lodges that already are taxed to maintain and support the Homes.
The tax on the Lodges for the fiscal year just ended was $194,179.10.
A tax in any form is not a valid substitute for a generous heart.
For the foregoing reasons your committee recommends that the
resolutions be not adopted.

The recommendation of the committee was adopted.
Life Member Whose Address Is Unknown
The Grand Master recommends legislation to provide for those cases
in which the whereabouts of a life member is unknown for a period of
years. In some instances the discovery of the fact of the death of a life
member is not made until years after his demise. The rolls of the Lodge
continue to carry such a life member and annual per capita taxes to the
Grand Lodge are paid on his membership.
Your committee recognizes the need for the proposed legislation and
recommends that the Ordinances of Grand Lodge be amended by adding
a new section thereto, to be numbered 253 (a) and to read as follows:
The Secretary of a Lodge which has life members shall send, by first
class mail, annually to each life , member at his last known address, a
membership card. In the event such card is returned by the post office
for six consecutive years because unclaimed or the addressee is unknown,
the Secretary shall on the seventh year send such card by registered mail
to the last known address of the life member. If such registered mail is
returned to the Secretary by the post office, then the Secretary shall
report the fact to the Lodge at a stated meeting and make a note thereof
in the Minutes, and shall remove such member from the Roll Book of the
Lodge and shall transmit to the Grand Secretary, with his annual report,
a notice that such life member had been removed from the Lodge Roll
and the reason therefor.
·
In the event that such life member be found at any time subsequent
to his removal from the Lodge Roll, he shall immediately be restored
thereto and the fact shall be notified to the Grand Secretary with the
annual report and the Lodge shall pay all per capita taxes accrued on
such life member from the date of his removal from the Lodge Roll to
the date of restoration thereto.

The recommendation, having been approved as to form by
the Jurisprudence Committee, was adopted.

Financing Building Projects
The Grand Master recommends that legislation be enacted which would
give the Committee on Financing Building Projects general supervision

<Jver the financing of new temples, the refinancing of old temples, and the
financing of remodeling and reconstruction wherever such operations
assume major proportions.
The Ordina_n ces of Grand Lodge provide that a special committee shall
be appointed on financing building projects but it does not specify the scope
<Jf the duties, powers and limitations of such committee.
The Ordinances also provide, with respect to the investment of funds
of Lodges, that no such funds shall be invested in the shares of a corporation
owning or proposing to erect a Masonic hall, or in the land and building of
a Masonic hall owned or proposed to be erected by a Lodge. In this particular section of the law is to be found the only authority directly given
to the Committee on Financing B uilding Prqjects.
We are of the opinion that the law should be amen ded to broaden the
scope of action by said committee and to specify c learly the power and
duties of the committee. At the present moment there appear to be divergencies of opinion among members of committees having this matter under
consideration, and until some definite action and certain conclusion has been
reached regarding the proper legislation to be adopted, we respectfully
recommend that this subject matter . be postponed and considered as unfinished business at the next annual communication of this Grand Lodge.

Salary of Grand Secretary
Our old and good friend Brother C. E. Mallochowitz, Past Master of
Caledonia Lodge No. 486, proposes a resolution that the salary of the
Grand Secretary be fixed at $5,000.
·
The . Grand Lodge is a sovereign body and from time to time· can and
does fix the amount of compensation to be paid to officers and employees.
A restriction endeavored to be imposed upon Grand Lodge with respect
to its payroll could be binding only until such ti.m e as Grand Lodge, in the
exercise of its rightful power, rescinded it. Annualfy the Finance Committee reports to Grand Lodge a recommendation of salaries to be paid,
and upon such reports being -made, Grand Lodge determines for itself,
unrestrained and without limitation, the proper amounts to be paid. Therefo_re your Committee recommends that the resolu.tion be not adopted.

The recommendation of the committee . was adopted.
Organist
Brother Harold Morrison, Inspector of the 89th District, has introduced a resolution proposing that Section 1 of Article 2 of the Uniform
Code of By-Laws (Section 133 of the Ordinances) be amended to provide
that any Master Mason in good standing, whether or not a member oi the
Lodge, may be appointed organist.
There is no reason why any suitable person may not be appointed
organist by a Lodge although he may be a member of another Lodge . .
Expediency may make it desirable that some person other than a member
of a Lodge should be its organist. If appointed organist by the Master of
the Lodge, the person so appointed should be installed as organist.
Your committee therefor~ ~ecommends that Section 133 of the Ordinances be amended to read as. follows :
"Section 1. The Master, the Senior and Junior Wardens, the
Treasurer and the Secretaty, shall be elected in conformity with
Section 180 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge. The other officers
shall be appointed by the Master, except the Junior Deacon, who

may be appointed by the Senior Warden. Any Master Mason in
good standing, whether or not a member of the Lodge, may be
appointed Tiler, or Organist."

Having received the approval of the Jurisprudence Committee
the proposed amendment was adopted by unanimous vote.

Time of Annual Meeting of Grand Lodge

M:. W:. Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Master, recommends that Article
.1. Section 31, of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge be amended by striking
out the word "Tu.e sday" and substituting therefor t.he word "Monday."
If this resolution is adopted, Grand Lodge will meet on the second Monday of October in each year at ten a. m .
·
The .reason for the change, as stated by the Grand Master, is the
lack of tline for .the careful transaction of the business of Grand Lodge
during the time of the Communications as now provided by' the Ordinances;
that an increase of one day in the length of the. session will give gr'eater
opportunity for fraternal fellowship between the officers and committee-me·n
of Grand Lodge and the brethren in attendance thereat; and that a len'gthened session would add to the pleasure. of Grand Lodge week.
Your committee is in accord with the recommendation of the Grand
Master and is of the opinion that the business of Grand Lodge is of
sufficient volume to require more time for its deliberate consideration.
Therefore we re~ommend the adoption of the proposed amendment to the
Ordinances of Grand Lodge.
The committee also recommended that Section. 12 of the Constitution
be amended by deleting the word "fourth" therein and substituting the
word "fifth" therefor.

Report was adopted with the instructions to the incoming
Grand Master fo place this matter before the Jurisprudnece Committee for report at the next Annual Communication.

REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the M~'. W:. ' Grand Lodge of California:

.
This committee has functioned since it was appointed by M.". W." ..Leon
Q. Whitsell, pursuant to the resolution of the 89th Annual Communication
·of Grand Lodge in 1938. The last annual report of the committee is to be
found in the 1940 Proceedings of .Grand Lodge, page 246.
The members of the committee for the current year have been:
R. P. Wisecarver, chairman, Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478.
James E.' Hammond, Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568.
Walter Perry Johnson, California Lodge No. 1.
In the last annual report the committee advised that Lodges make ' a
full report to the various collectors for both old age security and · unemployment taxes, pay the taxes assessed, and then file a claim for
refund, which should not be pressed until later, pending decisions on test
cases. ·
· As of June 15,, 1941, the committee made a special report, which was
printed by Gr.and Lodge and distributed to the subordinate Lodges. A
copy of that communication follows this report. In this report we
recommended that returns for old age security be filed with the Federal
Government on any employee whose wages exceed $45.00 per calendar
quarter and, second, that returns be made for unemployment' taxes to the
Federal Government if the Lodge has eight or more employees (and to the
State of California if there are four or more employees), each of whom
receives ' over $45.00 per calendar quarter. This report of the committee
was based on the following decisions that have been rendered subsequent
to the last Annual Communication:
·
.'
1. A decision by the Deunty Commissioner, U. S: Treasury Departinent, November 18, 1940, that both the Grand Lodge · and subordinate
Lodges are exempt from the income tax under Section 101 (3), \Vhit;h
section exempts certain fraternal beneficiary societies. The sam~ d.etisio,n
refused to exempt the fraternity under Section 101 (6) of the Irtcoi:ne
Tax Act, which section exempts religious, charitable, · scientific, literary
or educational societies. The importance of 'this decision lies· in the fact
that Section' 101 (6) of the Income Tax Act is· given as a ground for'
exemptiori under the federal old age and security tax and the ' federal
employment tax, but Se.ction 101 (3), while it constitutes an exemption
under the i Income Tax Act, does not constitute an exemption under .. the
social'. security and unemployment acts.

GRAND LODGE OF · CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE '

670

The· same decision also exempts both Grand Lodge and the subordinate
Lodges from all capital stock tax.
'
2. A similar decision by the Deputy Commissioner holds. specifically
that neither Grand. Lodge nor the subordinate Lodges are exempt from
the old age secudty tax (federal insurance contributions act) or the
unemployment tax (federal unemployment tax act) and therefore that
returns must be made and taxes paid under both laws.
The plan followed by Congress in the federal revenue acts is to state
the exemptions under: the Jnq~me Tax Act and the taxpayer is classified
as to exemption by the specific exemption given him under the Income
Tax Act. Some of the .exemptiqns, but not all of them, are carried into
the other revenue acts. The one with reference to fraternal beneficiary

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Your committee has held many conferences during the year and has
been in close touch with your Grand officers, particularly the office of
the Grand Secretary. We have answered many communications from
individual Lodges, in addition to filing the special report referred to above.
The committee had thought it would be able to recommend its discontinuance at this Communication, but unfortunately many of the questions
in issue have not yet been decided by a court of competent jurisdiction.
In addition, new revenue laws have been enacted both by Congress and
by the State Legislature which will reqµire careful scrutiny and interpretation to determine their applicability to Masonic Lodges. We believe
there will be urgent and technical .questions which will require the attention
of a special committee, and therefore we recommend the continuation of
the . committee for the ensuing Masonic year.
Respectfully submitted,

R. P. WISECARVER.
]AMES
HAMMOND,

E.

WALTER PERRY JOHNSON,

Committee.

The report was adopted.
To all Lodges in the Jurisdiction:
Re·: Special Report of Taxation Committee as of June 15, 1941.
Reference is made to previous reports of this committee and especially
the Annual Report for 1940, a printed copy of which was sent to each
Lodge and which is also to be found in the 1940 Proceedings o·f Grand
Lodge, page _246.
Both Grand Lodge and the subordinate Lodges of California have
been held to be exempt from income tax but not exempt from the taxes
of the Old Age Security Act or the Unemployment Reserves Act by the
Commissioner of Internal Revenue at Washington. No decision has been
rendered by a higher court.
The organist and soloist of Masonic. Lodges have been held to be
purely ritualistic officers and not employees, and no return need be made
for them. A claim for refund for any taxes paid on account of their
inclusion in previous returns may be filed or a credit may be taken for
such overpayment by applying such overpayment to the payment of the
current taxes.
The committee therefore still recommends : ( 1) That returns for old
age security be filed with the Federal Government on any employee whose
wages exceed $45.00 per quarter, and (2) that returns be made for unemployment taxes to the Federal Government if there are eight or more
employees (and to the State of California if there are four or more
employees) each of whom receives over $45.00 per calendar quarter.
·. We recommend that claim for refund or credit of taxes improperly
paid for organist and soloist be made immediately. As to other taxes
paid, we have come to the conclusion that no useful purpose will be
served: by the filing of a claim for refund at this time. There is a period
of four years from the date tax became due within which claim for refund
may be made for payment on the Old Age Security Act, and a period
of three yea.rs from date tax became due for payments of unemployment
taxes, and such claims can be made if and when a decision by a court
justifies it.

Respectfully submitted,
Approved by
LLOYD

E. WILSON, Grand Master.

R. P. WISECARVER,

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
In presenting its report for the 1941 your Correspondence Committee
desires to express its condolence with our chairman, Brother Jesse Whited,
in his recent bereavement by the loss of his wife, his helpmate and companion for nearly forty ·years; and also our sincere best wishes for his speedy
recovery from his own serious illness.
Practically all the subject material for the committee's report had been
gathered, but remained to be classified and edited when Brother Whited
became too ill to continue. If, therefore, the report lacks its usual final
polish and finish it is because of his indisposition, for who of us could hope
to replace, at a moment's notice, the benefit of Brother Whited's consummate skill and twenty years' of experience.

APRONS
Queensland, 1940:
When a brother is initiated into the Craft he is invested with the distinguishing badge of a Freemason, and is informed that it "is more ancient
than the Golden Fleece or the Roman Eagle; more honorable than the
Garter or any other order in existence"; and it follows that the right to
wear this badge should be regarded as a great privilege and it should be

745

treated with becoming respect. It has been observed and reported to the
Board of General Purposes· that many brethren--even Past Masters-have
been seen passing from the Lodge room and even. appearing in public
streets with this badge in the reverse position, under the coat tail, where it
will probably be sat upon, and thus suffer what may be regarded as most
contemptuous treatment. The Board of General Purposes hopes that, having
called attention to a practice which may have had an origin in thoughtlessness, all loyal brethren will treat this badge with the respect due to a
sacred symbol. Attention is drawn to the last paragraph of·Article No. 192,
Book of Constitutions, which reads as follows: "Brethren are strictly forbidden to wear emblems of Freemasonry outside a Masonic Lodge."
Western Australia, 1940, (Chairman Correspondence Committee):
Customs vary among us, but we are told that our ancient brethren wore
their aprons "to protect their clothing, whereas o·ur brethren of Western Au-·
stalia evidently we;tr a portion of their clothing to protect their aprons. This
friendly observation is made only because we think it a shame to allow a
coat to hide so generous a portion of so beautiful an apron. Well, "thereby
hangs a tale." There was a time, and not so long ago, when those of us who
wear dinner -dress with our regalia were threatened with the possibility of
being obliged to wear our regalia belted outside and over the dinner jacket.
Such a possibility was horrible to even think of, as we knew that our Australian summer has an unpleasant influence upon the theremometer up to 110°
' (it has exerted it during the past few hours iri. which I wrote this l-eview),.
and a jacket with its front covered with regalia fastened theret~ and therefore to the body with a tightly fitting belt would be about as exhilarating
as St. Lawrence's gridiron, and we would be roasted a deep, rich brown,
which would not be for the good of Freemasonry in general or the Western
Australian section of it in particular. This was the view that this scribe
held, and he persuaded Grand Lodge to help him hold it. And since then
we, including R. W. Brother Russell, have been enabled to wear our aprons
in a style which, although it conceals a portion of our regalia, saves us
from sizzling or being fried in Grand Lodge assembled.

seem to be possessed w"ith a mad craze for pleasure that apparently cannot

Florida, 1941 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
We think the committee ·was right. This scribe is going to join any
organization he pleases to join, and he has sense enough not to get into
•anything subversive, immoral or in violation of the spirit of Freemasonry.
The Grand Lodge steps outside its legitimate sphere when it presumes
to tell me what I may or may not join. The tendency is for Grand Lodges
to do entirely too much legislating. . They stick their noses into things
beyond the legitimate functions of a Grand Lodge of Masons, and what
ought to be happy Freemasonry gets itself into a state of unnecessary
agitation as a result.

1940 (Anonymous Bulletin):
How frequently the old adage, "A chain is no stronger than its weakest
link," may be applied in human affairs. While the maxim, because of
peculiar human equations, is not strictly applicable to bodies of men, the
principle involved should never be lost sight of when forming a Masonic
Lodge or in passing upon petitions of candidates for membership.
·
The importance of careful selection of charter members of a Lodge
is at once obvious; likewise the investigation of candidates. However,
if the latter is done with that caution and prudence so necessary to carry
forward those sublime truths "instituted by virtuous men" in the moral order
of Freemasonry, the former will take care of itself.
It stands to reason that our great system of morality calls for not
only the proper administration of its business affairs and its various
1 ceremonies, but for devotees whose rectitude is above reproach. How
very important, then, it is that the Master of a Masonic Lodge · should
exercise great care in appointing committees to investigate the petitioners
for the degrees in his Lodge.
A committee of inv~stigation should fully appreciate not only its
responsibilities to the Lodge, but to the fraternity, in determining the
moral character and other qualities including his religious views, particularly his belief ih God, habits, associates, how he spends his leisure time,
his physical condition, whether he meets his obligations, whether he is
financially able to become a Mason, whether, if married, his ambition to
join the fraternity meets with the approval of his wife, and other details.
In other words, investigation of a candidate for Masonic degrees should
not be perfunctory as is sometimes the case.
The sources of investigating a candidate are many and varied, and no
favorable report should be made until those sources are exhausted. They
include the petitioner's church affiliations, other lodge connections, home
environment, employer, fellow employes, his charities, acquaintances, associates, social life, business concerns with whom
deals, clubs if any,
and last but . not least, the candidate's motive for becoming a Mason.
That is, does he understand the gravity and . seriou.sness of Masonry;
that the fraternity in which he seeks membership was not instituted to
afford amusement and entertainment centers for its members; nor to
provide insurance ·for them,- bu~ to inculcate and perpetuate among men
the sublime truths, principles and teachings which are the basis of Freemasonry and whiCh our brethren saw reason to adopt in forming an
exclusive system to pass through the world unconnected with the religion
and politics of all times and every people among whom it should flourish
and increase.
Each member of the committee, having exhausted his sources of
investigation; should present his findings iri a purely objective mannerthe cold facts of the inquiry. The report should be unanimously positive
and free from sentimental considerations. A report tending to qualify the
petitioner on the grounds that nothing of a particular nature was found

he

Maine, 1941 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Alhambra Temple (Shrine) in Chattanooga has been permitting "Sa_turday Night Public Dances," much to the discredit of the Masonic name

Imperial Potentate (Bro. Miles T. Gilbert) who promised that "Saturday
night dances will be discontinued." But this was, according to the Grand
Master's .conviction, merely an "evasion" for it was immediately announced
"that the dances would continue as before at Alhambra Mosque, sponsored

Master who "pulled no punches" when confronted by this evasive action.

may speak of our high ideals and sublime principles, but if our members
disregard them, yea even resent them, Masonry will die of moral and
spiritual decay."

Utah, 1939 (Grand Lodge):
Beginnings are ever of true interest. The imagination is kindled with
the commencement of the new. Perchance there are so many failures
of completion that the race has turned to initiating ideals rather than
to concluding attainment. Of old, the ceremonies of building have centered
about the cornerstone. Anciently it was garlanded, jeweled, berobed,
and of superior workmanship. Shoutings accompanied its setting. All
the elements of holy consecration blessed it. Of utmost care was the
task of aligning it. Ages ago when compasses were unknown no pains
were too great to have it laid true to the true north. In fact, archeologists
find in the trueness of direction of primitive . cornerstones one of the
surest indications of the education of those of the time and place where
the stone was placed. We Occidentals think we have outgrown all that,
and many of our cities do not square with the compass, to say nothing
of regarding the true north. Consequently we give little care to exactitude
of direction, and it is doubted if there is a true stone in the west. The
Indians of Central America, however, laid the cornerstones of their temples
with exactitude for the true north.
The olden tools of the Craft have been placed upon the Craftsmen's
work not as vain show, but as indicative of the teachings that the ages
have found helpful. Times like this were selected, because of general
attendance and deep interest, as fitting to impress on serf and leader the
basic foundations of con~inued government. The level indicated the time
element. The unlevel stone if continued would result in a leaning building
as it did with the tower of Pisa. If care was not taken at the foundation, serious trouble and ruin were the only pos~ible iesult. Honesty,
carefulness and exactitude of justice were the properties on which to
build. The square indicated the breadth angle. If true it would be none
less than brotherhood of all the citizenry with bonds of sympathetic
justice. The plumb, in their estimation, told of uprightness. If these seem
far-fetched and duplicating', remember in other days the printed page
instructed not. Populaces learned much from public ceremonials.
There is another interesting line of thought for us today. We are
gathered ·here as integral parts of a city. It was with the cify that most of
our life impelled upward from the tribe and clan. ·Republic commenced
with cities. The history of the early city states of Greece, Rome, and
later northern Europe and Italy, is filled with interest. Representative government commenced there. What we know as ,commercial corporations,
combinations of interest in guild or industry, art, sanitation, education, and
cultural virtues arose within city confines . People learne'i to live together,
legislate for common ends, work together for united goals not in the rural
areas, but in cities and towns. We.meet as citizens of a city, and that thought
alone is pregnant with interest and historical thought: We overlap many
centuries in that we plan here that the finest structure of this city shall be
the city building: It should be so. Pride in our city should tone and lead
upward eoming movements. Most fitting is it that the oldest of all building
organizations should have full part in the placing of the first stone, and of
supreme honor is it that tools of kin-1.red form and words of like meaning
should be used here that another Grand Master used and voiced when
George Washington laid the cornerstone of the National Capitol so many
years ago. Upon · that stone, so laid, arose the structure and dome of the
home · of our nation. These same tools and words have officiated for the·

, Alberta, 1939 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
We note with regret that the interest taken by the members of this
Grand Lodge in the report on Foreign Correspondence has so diminished
as to raise the question of the advisability of its future publication. In the
committee's report the subject is djscussed purely on a basis of costs. It is
most surprising that a report that has for years received such · generous
approval throughout the other English-speaking jurisdictions, a report that
is always referred to as one of the most outstanding .of any Grand Jurisdiction, should be regarded with such indifference by the membership of
its own Grand Lodge.
Arizona, 1939 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
The Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence presents (without
benefit of personal appearance) his sixth report under the plan of reporting
and reviewing the proceedings of sister Grand jurisdictions as has been in
vogue since 1934. This, briefly, is that of having reviews prepared by the
Grand Representatives, or others where the Grand Representatives cannot
perform. These review's are edited, prepared and retyped for the printer
by the Chairman.
The disadvantage.s are that several jurisdictions are missing each year,
because those few to · whom the work was assigned could not prepare a
review-not because they did not wish to, but pres·sure of their own affairs.
On the other hand the reviews present a wider and more varied series
of reviews than is the case where one brother does the whole task, no matter
how capable he may be or the time at his disposal. The brother privileged
to submit a review certainly has a pleasant and instructive duty and receives
the greatest benefit. Thus forty to fifty brethren are annually given an
opportunity to labor among the circle of foreign correspondents, both by
reading and doing.
This year several new names appear (each reviewer is given due credit
for his efforts) and have contributed splendid reviews, comparing favorably
with the efforts of the "Old Guard" Grand Representatives, who have performed so nobly these six years.
Your chairman still insists these reviews are not ~orth the expense of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

printing as far as reader interest is concerned. Who reads them besides the
fraternal correspondents of other jurisdictions and our own contributors?
The answer is probably "no one."

If you want to know what and how other Grand Lodges do things, simply
take time off (not much required), and read the booklet, prepared, published, and presented to you for your personal use and information.

Iowa, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Past Senior Grand Warden A. E. Jensen, now Grand Secretary, submitted a short report on Foreign Correspondence. He paid a modest compliment to their fraternal correspondent and to his reviews. Then he
suggests that as these. reviews are not widely read, or read 'scarcely at all,
the small good accomplished does not justify the cost of the printing and
distribution, and for economic reasons they might well be discontinued.
The record does not show official approval of the suggestion. Will it be
proper to say that should such action be taken there will be deep regret
among reviewers atid other Masonic students all over the Masonic world
who hold the work of Brother Archdeacon in the highest regard and
admiration.

New York, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
The Committee has read the Proceedings of all the Granci Lodges
which have been received. Herein is presented a digest of the principal
events and decisions of those Grand Lodges. No attempt has been made
this year to present each Grand Lodge separately, because very often
much of what happens is largely of temporary or local interest. The number
and names of visitors in attendance, the number of visitations made by
Grand Masters, are of some value for the historian of that particular Grand
Lodge, but not of general usefulness to the Craft at large.
The request is often made by the Committee on Foreign Correspondence
that its report be read in the Lodges for the information of the brethren.

of course, not to be recommended, for among those suspended are many
of whom the fraternity is well rid. But the worthy brother, unable to pay
his dues, but earnest in his love for Masonry and in his attachment to
the Lodge, is deserving of fraternal consideration.
Each case must be determined on its own merits and it is a task
requiring careful investigation and unprejudiced study. Every member of
a Lodge can be interested in th"is work and can perform valuable service by
contact with personal friends who· may be delinquent, ascertaining 'the facts
and reporting them to the Master of the Lodge.
Discussion of these cases in open Lodge is not to be recommended.
The principal officers of the Lodge, being informed of conditions surrounding a delinquent brother, can determine the right thing to do and
the unfortunate brother should not be embarrassed by knowledge that
his circumstances are discussed among the brethren in open Lodge. The
problem is one that requires tact, confidence in the officers of the Lodge
and realization of our Masonic duty to the unfortunate brother.

The reviewer of the District of Colu.mbia is gratified to notice ari

Oregon, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
The Committee on Masonic Research and Education in Alberta made
an experiment to find out just how many Lodges or individuals were
interested in Masonic lore to the extent that they would take the trouble
to seek information. They were quite disappointed over the results as
only four inquiries were received.
It is the same old story over again of inviting men to come and
partake of something, the assimilation of which will require some effort
on their part. When
Masonry learn that it is dealing with humans?
When will it learn that the human is an animal that, in 99 per cent of
the time, does' nothing that r equires effort unless it is driven to do so
either by its own needs or by an edict laid down by authority. Men
work in the majority of instances not because Of the love for work but
rather because of pride and station, their own need for food and the
need of their dependents. Even the latter at times are not sufficient of
an incentive and families are deserted and left in want rather than to
put forth an effort to provide for their needs.
So, too, we find them in their relation to Masonic education if the
acquisiti9n requires effort on their part. Even if another spend the time
to prepare a paper on a subject, many find the effort of attending Lodge
to hear it too great.
It is the contention of this writer that efforts made to educate those
who are members at the present time is in the majority of instances a
waste of energy. Education should begin the moment an initiate enters
the Lodge for the first time and continue with mounting force through
the three degrees. By the time he has finished his degree work there will

will

have been aroused in him a desire for further knowledge that will in itself
drive him on or he will be one of those content to re11t where he is in
which case nothing but compulsion will cause him to go forward.
'
~an as a whole desires either to be led or driven. This is not only
true m fraternal but in other activities. For instance look at his reaction
to religion. Over 50 per cent of the chur ch members o~ the North American
continent prefer to be told, thus and so you shall approach your God-in
these words you shall ofl;er up your prayers and here and so you shall
bend your knee. Man does not worship God because he loves him
although we like to assure ourselves that such is the case, but rather fo;
fear that when he steps from the known into the unknown he will be
numbered among the goats on the left.
This writer contends that Masonry should demand more of its members and request less. This holds true particularly in the matter of attendance on communications. Masonry in its kind and benevolent manner
has gone on its wa-y persistently losing members and a decline in interest
o n the part of those remaining on its rolls while the service clubs with
far l_ess to offer have continued to grow. A r e the meetings of the various
service clubs less stereotyped than his Masonic meetings? We think not,
al~hou~h what. he hears there is of a far lighter vein and interspersed
with hg.ht stones. T hey'. too, become burdensome and trying to him, yet
he continues to attend simply because non-attendance brings a monetary
, · fine and af~er so many non-attendances he is dropped from the roll. They
rule that either you attend the meetings or out you go.
W,e possibly have wandered far from the original subject of Masonic
education and on second thought we admit that we have, yet we cont~8:d tha.t for Masonry to succ'eed in any of. its activities under present cond.1t10ns 1t must. take ii:ito· consideration the changes tha t h ave occurred

Oregon, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
As the law now stands the fifty year or the Grand Lodge Veterans

"medal" either to their Grand Master who as a rule has had sufficient
recognition or to the Grand Master of another Jurisdiction equally honored.
Our contention is, and even though it is .none of our affairs vet we
voice the opinion that among the various Lodges of a Jurisdictlo~ there
are men who have given their entire life in the interest of the local Lodge
without thought of reward or honor and that it is these men who have
rendered meritorious service rather than those who through circumstances have sat in the Grand East.

Missouri,. 1940 (Grand Lodge):
All • Lodges in Alaska Territory are under the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge at Washington. The first Lodge in the territory was established at Sitka, June 3, 1880, but its charter was later revoked. Lodges
were also established at Anchorage, Nome, Douglas, Ketchikan, Juneau,
Cordova\ Petersburg, Seward, Fairbanks, Valdez, and Skagway. The
total membership of the eleven Lodges is 1,495.
. The Grand Lodge Swiss Alpina is becoming quite generally recogn~zed by American jurisdictions. During the past year it has been recognized by Arkansas, Colorado, Nevada, West Virginia, Wyoming, Manitoba
and South Australia.
The Masonry of Switzerland is of high character and in origin it
traces back to .the Grand Lodge of England. As a Grand Lodge it has
done pioneer work in the handling of refugees from belligerent nations
and, through necessity, has become the clearing house for all donations
from American Grand Lodges.
·
South Australia recognized Alpina "guided by the decision that the
United Grand Lodge of England had granted recognition an~d in c,onformity with a resolution arising out of a discussion at the Fourth
Australasian Conference that the procedure of the Grand Lodge of
England be the practice of the Grand Lodges of Australia."
.. It is possible that the Grand Lodg'e. of Argentina should be more
generally recognized than it is, for Masonry seems to have been introduced into the Republic by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania in 1825,
with the establishment of Southern Star Lodge No. 205 in the City of
Buenos Aires. The Grand Orient of France and the Grand' Lodge of
England later established Lodges, and by 1856 an attempt was made to
establish a Grand Lodge. In July, 1857, six Lodges organized by the
Grand Orient of Brazil, established the Grand Or:ient of Argentina.
There is little i,nformation· concerning this Grand Lodge in any of the
proceedings we have read.

New Hampshire, 1940, (Chairman, Foreign Correspondence Committee):
· The Republic of Mexico has seventeen Grand L odges working in
the Spanish language, which apparently conform in all respects to our
Code of Standards. None of them are recognized by us, a lthough repeated

the late Kernel Ataturk, and no Masonic organization exists there of which
we have any knowledge.
In Italy, both the Grand Orient of Italy and the Grand Lodge of
Italy were dissolved by Mussolini, with ruthlessness. A number of distinguished brethren were murdered in cold blood for no reason e·xcept
their .connection with the Order. The Grand Master of the Grand 'Lodge
was exiled, became blind and later died in prison. ·
In the recently seized kingdom of Albania, Masonry has never been
organized, and of course, does not now exist under Italian rule.
In Spain also Freemasonry has be~n suppressed by .Dictator Franco.
During the civil war there was much testimony to the effect that whenever the insurgents occupied a town they shot or murdered in the most
· diabolical way, all Masons whom they could identify and even those
related to them.
On March 2, 1940, the Dictator of Spain issued an edict against Freemasonry and all other seqet societies in that country, on the ground
that membership in these bodies is considered by the Nationalists as indication that the accused is opposed to the government. Masonry was
classed along with communism and all its. property confiscated by the
decree. Any person carrying on Masonic activities was made liable to
imprisonment for six years. The law was made retroactive and all persons who had been members of the Order· were required fo file a statement with the government within two ' months, explaining why they joined
the Order and why they left it. If their excuse was not acceptable to the
government, they were made liable to six years imprisonment, or twelve ·
years if they had received higher degrees, or held a position of special trust,
or attended international meetings. Apparently Spain needs to make much
more progress towards the light before she can find a place as a decent
member of the family of nations.
·
When the Great War of 1914 started, Britain's great foreign minister,
Sir Edward Grey made the historic statement that "The lights are going
out all over Europe." Just such a statement can be made today respecting
the prese,nt Masonic situation in Europe.
In Germany, where Masonry once flourished under seven Grand
Lodges, Hitler ordered the dissolution of all Masonic Lodges shortly
after he came into power in 1934. Some of these bodies tried to continue
their existence under other names, but · they were compelled · to dissolve
and all properties were confiscated by the Huns.
In all these dictator ·countries Masonry has entirely disappeared.

Before closing this report, reference should be made to a resolution
recently adopted by the Grand Lodge of England, dealing with the
status of Masons of enemy nationality during the period of hostilities.
In the interest of peace and harmony, the resolution asks Masons
of enemy nationality to abstain from attending any Masonic meetings
for the duration of the war, and would give the Master of any Lodge the
privilege of asking any member of enemy birth, o.r any other person
whose presence might create .d iscord, to abstain from attendance.
During this period, such Masons are absolved from the payment of
subscriptions to their private Lod.ges, to the Grarid Lodge, and to Provincial or District Grand Lodges. The resolution further provides that
these members shall not be counted as in arrears and will be again raised
to full membership when hostilities have ceased and the Grand Lodge
believes that the attendance of members of any enemy nationality would
not cause trouble in the Craft.

British Columbia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):

Idaho, 1940 (Grand Master) :
I can easily overlook mistakes a Master may make in ritualistic
work when filling his station · in the East. I cannot overlook bungling
and inexcusable mistakes made at a Masonic funeral. This is the only
occasion when our fraternity is on trial or appears before the public.
If the funeral service is worth anything at all it is worth learning, I
recommend that the funeral ritual be included in the Master's examination
required before his proficiency certificate is issued to him.

Michigan, 1940 (Grand Lodge) :
Grand Lodge provided for the formation of "Memorial Lodges"
where two or more lodges have concurrent jurisdiction. The social
fun ction of the Memorial Lodges is to be the conducting of funerals
for deceased sojourners. Officers are to be the same as in a -regular
Lodge. The Master and Wardens of such a Lodge shall have attainep
that rank in a regular Lodge. There are to be no fees charged and
membership shall be plural membership. Such Lodges are to_ work under
dispensation of the Grand Master and under his supervision. Expenses
of such Lodges shall be paid by the Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction.

Michigan, 1940 (Grand Lodge):
Where two or more Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction have concur-·
rent jurisdiction, there may be formed in each of such jurisdictions a
Memorial Lodge to conduct Masonic funerals of deceased sojourners only.
Upon proper applications approved by two-thirds of the Worshipful
Masters of the jurisdiction, made to the Grand Master, he may issue a
dispensation to the constitutional number of Master Masons of such jurisdiction to form a Memorial Lodge. Such Memorial Lodge shall remain
under the dispensation and until revocation by the Grand Master. They
shall have the same officers as have other Lodges; provided, that the
Worshipful Master and Wardens thereof shall have attained the same
rank in a chartered . Lodge. They shall pay no fees or dues to Grand
Lodge and shall not collect fees or dues. Their expenses shall be
met -by voluntary contributions of the Lodges in their jurisdictions, or
by their local Board of Relief. Membership in such Memorial Lodge
shall be by plural membership only. Any member of a Memorial Lodge
may terminate his membership ·at will, upon written notice to the ·secretary thereof. Regular Communications of Memorial Lodges shall be
held quarterly with an annual meeting for the election and installation
of officers.
We realize this is an experiment, that experience shows that there
are some things lacking, other things that may not be worthy, but we
think this is a worthy proposition as a whole, and that the only way we
can find out is to try it out; we think it is worth a trial, and we recommend the adoption of the report.

Missouri, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee)!
The Grand Lecturer in California calls · attention to the failure of
brethren to appear at Masonic funerals. He does not believe the present
attendance 1s representative of Masonry and that we, as Masons, must
live· up to our reputation. Such showing impresses relatives with the
thought that Masonry must be either indifferent or fails to practice its.
fine spirit of brotherly love. Masonic funerals should not be distasteful
duties imposed upon Lodges, but should be sincere tributes paid to departed brethren. We should not create the thought that we are merely
reciting a ritual because it is our duty to do so. Under the heading of
"The End of the Trail," reviewer Whited says that practically all funeral
rituals adopted have proved to be unsatisfactory. Our ceremonies have
been influenced by the evolution performed in the last decade. The
general criticism he thinks is the iriability of a Master to produce a
favorable impression on the public. What used to be a public event has
become a personal proposition.

North Carolina, 1941 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
We could wish that Masonic funerals such as we have seen in the
past might be discontinued-and they are being discontinued to a large
extent. We do not like the traditional funeral ritual of Masonry. We
have prl!pared, and have tried, another which is not the traditional one
or like it, which seems to us better in the light of present day funeral
psychology. Because of the old one, the cities had trouble in getting
sojourners buried Masonically. Hence the Memorial Lodges. It was
frankly stated that they might be a failure, but the experiment is worth
trying.
Ohio, 1940 (Grand Master):
The Grand Master stated that the Burial Service contained in the
Constitutions was intended only for a guide and could be used in whole
or part, which often resulted in Masonry earning for itself an unfavorable
impression on the part of those who attended Masonic funerals, whereas,
"this ritual should be one of dignity, impressiveness and helpfulness."
He therefore recommended that the Committee on Ritual be instructed
to see that some suitable service be prepared and submitted to the
Grand Lodge in 1941, and that the use of which ritual, .when adopted,
be made obligatory upon the constituent lodges. The Committee on
Ritual was, later in the session, instructed so to do.

West Australia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
In re funerals, Masonic law in Indiana does QOt-in fact, it could
not-say a brother must not die. It permits him to be buried Masonically
if his dues are paid up, but if they are not-well, then, no funeral. There
is very much to be said both for and against this phase of Masonic
law, a phase noticeable in many jurisdictions. I don't like it, although
I admit that it is logically just, and that Masons should have it impresse d upon them that the privileges and advantages of Masonry cannot
attach to membership if the payment of dues is carelessly or wilfully
disregarded. Most Worthshipful Brother Morrison's experience of many
sad cases of Masonic funerals being refused owing to delinquency in
dues is, fortunately, not greatly shared in Western Australia: Masonic
funerals are rare in this state. The brethren attend the funeral of a
brother, but without regalia, and the orrly service is that of the "church
to which the deecased belonged in his lifetime. We have an abbrevia:ted
form of funeral service," but I don't think it has been used more than
a dozen times since I compiled it in 1919, when it . was · approved by
Grand Lodge. The researches of the late ·Brother Henry Sadler, SubLibrarian of the United Grand Lodge of England, fully a quarter of a
century ago, all tended to show that early Masonry only gave a Masonic
funeral to a brother who was a stranger to the country in which he di·ed,
and without relatives or friends to attend to the arrangements for his
burial. That seems to have been the raison d'etre of Masonic funerals
in olden ti!Iles, and in British Empire Masonry the later vogue is not
so greatly favored as it was generations ago.

Massachusetts, 1940 (Grand Master)·:
I invite the serious consideration of the Craft to the advisability of
organizing a Masonic Senate of North America to consist of the strongest
available representatives from each Grand Lodge in North America to
meet at least annually, and more frequently by committees, to consider
all matters affecting Freemasonry, but without power to take any action
binding upon any Masonic body. If each Grand Lodge were to select
-4.!S its Senators, say two of its wisest, strongest Masonic statesmen to
serve for a reasonably long term, with or without the right to stand for

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

reelection for successive ' terms, there would be a continuing body of
men whose considered judgments could do much to mould and direct
Masonic thought. This would supplement, but not supplant, the present
conferences of Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries, the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, and the Masonic Service
Association.
Such a body could do much to win the battle for existence . that
M:lsonry may well be facing here as it has already had to do elsewhere.
It might help to solve some of the problems arising out of the relationships between Symbolic Freemasonry and the collateral bodies. Perhaps
only such an organization could solve some of the pro~lems .arising. out
of the Masonic publications, both official and commercial, so we might
profit by their admitted benefits without sustaining their occasional detriments.
Such a body might eliminate some of the misunderstandings between
Freemasonry and other agencies which likewise seek to benefit mankind.
Perhaps, in spite of the bitter· and unjust attacks on Masonry that are
prompted, or at least tolerated, by some members of the Roman Catholic
hierarchy, such a Senate might make it clear that Masonry seeks no
controversy with that or any other church, but that, on the contrary,
we have a great many objectives in common with each other.
Many questions of interjurisdictional comity and interests and of
general ideals and policies could profit from statesmanlike study .bY a
body of men broad in outlook, wise in experience, lofty in vision, and
sound in judgment, commanding respect but not exerting any official
authority. Such a body would be a unifying force between geographical
interests, between the fifty-eight Grand Lodges of North America, between
the several branches of Freemasonry, and between Freemasonry and
all other institutions of good will. It should do much to hold aloft the
torch of Freemasonry and of civilization in their years of supreme testing.
If the immediate creation of such a Senate seems too costly or
· elaborate for a first step, a less pr'etentious experiment, to be expanded
or abandoned in the light of subsequent experience, might be the creation
of a Masonic Cabinet for North America, composed of a smaller number
of members from regional districts, or even a series of Regional Cabinets.
The more technical aspects of the matter-size, basis of representation,
tenure of office and all similar matters, should be determined not by
the proposer of the plan but by some genuinely representative body.
The chief concern is that by this, or some better means, there should
be a workable instrumentality for mobilizing and unifying our Masonic
contribution toward the welfare of mankind in these critical days.

New York, 1940 (Grand Master):
In my 1939 address to Grand Lodge, I described the character and
function of my Council, and I shall not repeat. The same brethren
met regularly with me again during my second year, reporting conditions and activities in their various departments, discussing matters
which I presented for their consideration and giving me the advantage
, of their ideas. They willingly expressed their opinions, whether coincid- ·
ing or at variance with my own, with unrestrained candor, not to say
fervor, and much ,could be said for the quality and vitality of any idea
which successfully ran the gauntlet of their inspection ·and dissection.

and I shall. always recall them with the warmest fondness ..
Oregon, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Formerly it was customary to spend $1,500.00 for a jewel for the
retiring Grand Master. Of late years, however, this sum has been cut
to a mere $1,000.00. This ·reduction in the amount paid plus the rise
in the cost of gold during the New Deal era should make the present
recipients loathe to exhibit their jewel in the presence of those who
possess the more costly ones. To our way of thinking the expenditure
of such a sum of money for a ·mere bauble, the intrinsic value of which
is but a fraction of its cost, is an extravagant waste of money that
could be used for the purpose of relieving human suffering and want.

that have plagued humanity in all ages: liberty against democracyindividual rights against centralized authority and right against wrong.

liberty and justice. He is of the opinion that the battle will be neither
lost or won, that it will be continuing struggle and that our responsibility
is to pass on to the next generation a strong vigorous Masonry capable
of maintaining its sector of the battle line.

We like that Grand Master. In these days when men who want the
honors, but not the labor and responsibility of Masonic official service
are as numerous · as jack rabbits in the sagebrush flats, the Doctrine
preached and practiced by the Grand Master Rose is most refreshing.

Oregon, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
"Contumacy" means stubborness, inflexibility, haughtiness, perseverance, or obstinateness. In other words, pure cussedness. Under this
heading the Grand Master calls attention to the lack of cooperation on
the part of Lodges and individuals with the Grand Lodge officers. The
ignoring of communications and, at times, if answered, done so in an
insolent, fault-finding and defiant manner. The Grand Master states

Lodge regulations and requirements should be referred to the incoming
Grand Master and proper disciplining measures taken, to the end that
the requirements and regulations of the Grand Lodge may not be set
aside or 'flouted."
No doubt the incoming Grand Master was elated over the beautiful
legacy left him by the present incumbent. The thing that puzzles this
writer is that if these violations were so flagrant, why did ncit the Grand
Master pin the offende,s' ears back himsel~ and not leave it to his
successor. No new regulations were incorporated in the law to enable
his successor to handle this situation, so no doubt they already exist in
sufficient force to have enabled him to demonstrate to the offenders the
supremacy of the Grand Lodge. Evading an issue or simply "passing
the buck" to those · who follow, does not, in our opinion constitute true
leadership.

This isolated statement does not reflect the unanimity of fundamental purpose that has always actuated the Grand Masters' Conference in Washington, D. C. Often difference of opinions arise, but
every question is met frankly with open, friendly discussion and never
has there appeared bitterness or evidence of intolerance.

Wisconsin, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):

Colorado, 1940 (Grand Master):
Consider the wail, rightfully woeful, issuing from the Committee on
History pointing out that for "the past three years" it had been ready
to go to press with a history approximating 350 pages, but had been
annually fubbed off with the peter-grievous cry that funds were lacking.
The committee felt that the approximation could be printed and published at the cost of $3,000, and that most if not all of this trifle would
be returned by th,e sale of the approximation in five years. The committee seemed to feel that Othello's occupation was gone, with the manuscript of the volume suspended, like Mohammed's coffin, jl.nd therefore
asked that it-to wit, the committee-be discharged.. The Committee on
Finance, to which the report was referred, pointed out that the original
appropriation asked for was only two-thirds the size of the later one,
and in view of the times being out of joint and the re-articulation of the
times at present doubtful, and that there' was no pressing urgency for
immediate publication; etc., recommended that the appropriation sought
be disapproved, and the committee discharged with the gratitude and
thanks of Grand Lodge. And it was so. It is curious how most of us
yearn for Masonic histories, and squelch the yearn when the ghost is
required to walk.

Ohio, 1940 (Grand Master):
All who are familiar with the three-volume history of our Grand
Lodge must realize its worth. Each year Grand Lodge history is being
made, and while we have our proceedings from year to year, yet it seems
to me that we should have our history in perhaps a more concise form.
Our present history brings the development of our · Grand Lodge up to
and including the year 1912. This leaves .an interval of twenty-eight
years, and I do not believe more time than this should .elapse in order
to properly record the many historical important events that ·have transpired during that length of time. I am, therefore, recommending that
our Historian be authorized and instructed to prepare a fourth volume,
and that after it is rea,dy for distribution, one copy be sent to each of
our subordinate Lodges. I am further recommending that an appropriation ·o f such funds as are necessary, but not to exceed $2,500, be
made for the preparing of this history, printing, and distribution.

West Australia. 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
As a rule Grand Orators who enable their Grand Masters to observe
vicariously the ancient custom of delivering what was called in accordance
with that custom a "harangue,'' take themselves very seriously, and their
discourses, as Scots folk would style them, are frequently most fascinating.
At the Annual · Communication under review, the Grand Orator, Brother
A. G. Gainey, tried what is often a double fascination of brevity and humorous stories in addition to thought. There were almost three pages of stories,
after which the speaker indulged in statistics relating to taxation, work,
and so forth, and the announcement that "we," namely, America (which
was named) , have "the highest standard of living of any civilized people
that history has ever known.': This the speaker seemed to diagnose as a
disease, as he announced "there is a remedy. We are the richest people
in the world. We are the most intelligent people in the world. We are the
brains of the world." Possibly, allusion was there made to what one 'can
hear any day in any city in any State in the Union. That remedy lay with
the voters in the Union, the most intelligent, 'patriotic and devoted of whom
were in the Masonic Lodges. He urged the brethren to study the problems
relating to the country, and to do so in such a way as to benefit it. In its
way, the oration was a good one, if somewhat unusual.

"Then came some decisions or official opinions; Number Two of these
was i\itended to help a much-puzzled Iowa City Master. There came to
him a Mason who had been made a Mason at sight in another Grand Jurisdiction, and who wanted to be affiliated with an Iowa City Lodge. Iowa
does not have any truck with any 'at sight' business; so what? He rules
that the Lodge has not any worry about that : if he is a Master Mason
duly certified as such from a Grand Lodge recognized as regular by Iowa,
and presents the proper papers, they can affiliate him and have nothing
to do with how he got raised."

Western Australia, 1940:
Among various matters dealt with by the Committee on General
Policy was that of joint installations. These, the committee felt, were proper
in some localities and served some useful purpose. Grand Lodge agreed that
they be not discontinued. When it came to the other form of Masonic
nightmare, namely, the public installation, the committee was "agin it;"
and said so in Masonic language, Grand Lodge, however, was not disposed
to tell the Nightmare to seek fresh fields and pastures new, with the result
that she is about, whenever wanted. There is an old Manx proverb which
says that "Custom must be indulged with custom, lest custom should weep.''
Apparently, Arizona has no desire to witness that conservative old dame,
Custom, dissolving, Niobe-like, in a fountain of tears.

Rhode Island, 1940 (Grand Master):
On November 3, 1939, your Grand. Master received a petition signed
by eight prominent members of this Grand Lodge requesting him to exercise
his prerogative and make a Mason "At Sight." Your Grand Master gave
much time and thought to this request before refusing to grant the petition.
There was never any doubt in hi,s mind as to the genuine worthiness of the
nationally known candidate proposed, hence attention was especially directed
to· the controversial point at issue-the . wisdom of exercising the right of a
Grand Master to make a Mason "At Sight.''
When eighty-four predecessors in the office of Gran~ Master have been
unanimous in their failure to exercise a right which was definitely theirs,
the wisdom of its exercise by the eighty-fifth Grand Master in this Grand
Jurisdiction becomes all the more controversial. This controversial feature
is further magnified if the candidate proposed, as in the request which was
presented to me, is not a resident of this Grand Jurisdiction, never has been
a resident, and has expressed no intention of becoming a resident in the
immediate or even the distant future.
Extensive study of the question convinced me that the practice of
making a Mason "At . Sight" never has been common in any of the 49
Grand Jurisdictions of these United States. Moreover, the practice seems
to be growing still less and less common as time goes on. Doubtless there
is less and less necessity for it. The very fact that so . few "Makings At
Sigh~ have been found necessary in so many years of American Masonry
· is conclusive evidence that there is seldom any need for it which cannot be
overcome. In denying the request, I did not feel justified in starting a
practice in this Grand Jurisdiction which is either positively prohibited
or is definitely controversial in all other Grand Jurisdictions-a practice
in growing disfavor-a practice which in effect denies to the member of a
Lodge the privilege of exercising one of the inalienable rights of Masonrythe right to ballot upon the worthiness of a petitioner.
West Australia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
In accordance with his announced intention, the Grand Master of

Mr. Ralph Dorn Hetzel, Professor of Pennsylvania State College, upon ·
whom the three degrees were conferred.
I remember when the great outcry was heard at the proposal in an
American Grand Lodge to make President Taft, of the United States,
a Mason at sight, it was stated in one of the dissentient Masonic magazines that the "prerogative" was a mere piece of "official hocus-pocusconjilrocus," adopting the comic speel of the "pea-under-the-thimble"
man to express his horrified feelings . As a Mason who went through
all the trials and probations of the three degrees in three different unpleasant atmospheres of three different stuffy nights, I prefer to see my newlyinitiated brethren made to undergo similar experiences. But there was
no " hocus-pocus" etc., about the three degrees conferred upon Professor
Hetzel. The degrees were conferred each in its own Lodge, the acting
Worshipful Master in the First being the Senior Grand Warden; in the
Second, the Assistant Instructor of the Work; and in the Third by a
District Deputy Grand Master. And in each degree the acting Masters
were assis ted by a full team of officers such as would take part in ·a ny
ordinary degree ceremonial. Probably, the ceremonies were to some
extent abbreviated, as to subject a candidate to the full three ceremonies,
representing a much greater consumption of time than ours do, would
be an ordeal which should call for the intervention of a Society for the
Prevention of Cruelty to Intending Masons.

MISCELLANEOUS
Arizona, 1940 (Grand Master):
"There is no denying the fact that our fraternity is ·at a low ebb,
and it must be our task to find out what is . wrong and correct the situation. We cannot justly blame the depression, since men will do and pay
for the things they enjoy and find profitable, and no Mason need lose
his membership because of financial embarrassment.
"I have emphasized in my Lodge addresses my conviction that the
only remedy is to make Masonic membership so enjoyable, stimulating,
instructive, and profitable that membership will be valued. I believe that
we must direct our efforts largely toward that end if our Order is again
to become as great, influential, and powerful as it once was and should be."

Nebraska, 1939 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Nebraska opens with a splendid photograph of that distinguished
soldier and Mason, General John J. Pershing, who, on January 5, 1939,
in the quiet seclusion of his hotel in Tucson, Arizona, was presented a
badge indicative of his fifty years of membership in the Masonic fraternity.
The presentation was made by Past Grand Master Henry H. Wilson,
himself a holder of a like decoration, and who, in December, 1888, as
Worshipful Master of Lincoln Lodge, No. 19, raised Brother Pershing
to the Sublime Degree. Truly a marvelous experience : making a man
a Mason, seeing him through the years achieve the distinction which has
come to this outstanding soldier, and, fifty years later, to crown the
Masonic experience with such a ceremony.

Utah, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
The property of a constituent Lodge was ·assessed and taxes collected.
The Lodge sued to recover. The Circuit Court rendered an adverse
decision and the Lodge appealed to the State Supreme Court which reversed the decision of the lower court, holding that Masonic property
m Alabama is not subject to taxation. Following is this decision and it
is given place here as showing. the grounds on which it was based and
not because of any general application-another reason may also appear ·
"By virtue of the acts of 1859 and 1875, referred to; a contract exists
between the Masonic Lodges of Alabama and the State, entered into
under constitutional provisions then in effect, it was held, and that contract cannot be abrogated without their consent. In the case under
consideration, it was ruled, the right of exemption is a vested one on
contractual nature, and is protected from impairment by both State and
Federal constitutions."
.
What a contract something besides a mere· "piece of paper" that
may be ignored at will by one party to the agreement? Why! 'Why!
Why! Are we on thin ice here? If so, so be it! In any event, we are grateful to th e Craft in Alabama fvr reminding us in this instance of what once
was referred to, and regarded, "as the sacredness of a contract !"

Victoria, 1938 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee) :
Another contentious matter which took up considerable time was a
proposition to permit the Grand Master to issue a dispensation to any
person, even though he were totally blind, to receive the degrees. In the
course of the discussion it was brought out that there is a Lodge in
England called "Lux in Tenebris," the membership of which is composed
entirely of persons who are blind. Incidentally the name means "light
in darkness." The measure before the Grand Lodge of Victoria was
.passed. It is difficult to understand how a person who is totally blind
can conform to and impart the essentials of Masonry.

British Columbia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee ):
The Committee on the Condition of Masonry in Canada referred
to a tendency in some Lodges to omit the customary respectful manner
in which a br9ther should be addressed. This is, we think, an importation,
and an undesirable one, which should be checked at once. The paragraph
is rather long but is worth attention, so we copy it:
"We may belong to the old school of thought, but we d·e plore the
modern tendency, already creeping into some of our Lodges, of the officers
dispensing with the proper Masonic title~ and addressing each other as
'Bill' or 'Brother Bill' or 'Worshipful Broth·e r Bill.' Your committee are
not slaves to formality but we submit that such terms are not in keeping
with the clignity of our institution. Then, too, such expressions as 'Okay,'
'Church parades,' 'degree teams,' 'side benchers,' are rather jarring to
one's sensibilities and might well be omitted from our Masonic vocabulary.
When or where the term 'Ruling Master' originated, we do not know.
At any rate we do not find it in the Constitution, but surely the climax
in this regard has been reachi;d when we hear the Worshipful Master
referred to as the 'Sitting Master.' Perhaps the only justification for ·this
latter term lies in the fact that some W ·o rs.h.i pful Master'!: remain 'sitting'
when the Lodges have been raised to received distinguished visitors."

Illinois, 1940 ( Grand Master):
On behalf of the Grand Lodge of Illinois it is my desire to clarify
the erroneous impression existent among the brethren of our jurisdiction,
relative to picnics, golf, bowling, baseball, and other modes of amusement, held under the auspices of a Masonic Lodge on Sunday.
'
Be it hereby known to all Lodges under the j urisdiction of The Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Illinois that such procedure, as herein above
stated, is in violation of the by-laws of the Grand Lodge, in that the bylaws specifically prohibit the convening of a Lodge on Sunday, unless
convened for the purpose of a Masonic funeral, and any artifice or subterfuge resorted to thereof, or fraudulent practice, will bring the Lodge
into serious controversy with the office of Grand Master.
Incidentally, the holding of athletic contests -in the form of boxing
bouts and· wrestling matc~s within the premises of a meeting place of
a Masonic Lodge is also prohibited.
