Kansas, 1940 ( Grand Master ) :
Under the heading "Trials and Punishmen.ts," Grand Master Claud
F. Young says:
Our system of handling matters of discipline has certainly gotten
out o( bounds. Civil procedure has nearly superseded the former process
of fact finding. Cases are not being presented because Lodges fear red
tape and expense. It is tiine to call a halt. In 1926 we took the handling
of these matters from the Lodges and p laced them with a Grand Lodge
committee. The reasons behind the change were good, but advantage

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

has been taken of our simple code to introduce improper, if not unfair
tactics.
During the ·year I received a transcript of a minor case in which
three lawyers built up two hundred pages of manuscript, when it appears
to me that only ten were needed to cover all pertinent facts. The Lodge
had to pay for this transcript and the attorney whom we advised them
to secure. We must no longer tolerate such a condition. Mackey says
of Masonic Trials, "It is the duty of a judge, says the great Roman
orator, in every cause to seek for truth. This is the great, the only
object of. a Masonic trial, and hence, in such a trial, no advantage is ever
permitted to be taken of those legal and verbal technicalities, the use
of which, in profane courts, so often e.bles the guilty to escape. This
great principle of Masonic law must never be forgotten in the management of a trial. Every part of the investigation is to be directed with
a single view to the acquisition of truth. Masonic trials are therefore
to be conducted in the simplest and least technical method, that will
preserve at once the rights of the Order and of the accused, and which
will enable the Lodge to obtain a thorough knowledge of all the facts
in the case."

Masons owing allegiance ta this Grand Lodge are enjoined, to respect
the purpose of this resolution."
The Grand Master then said in case the Grand Lodge · should not
adopt this or a similar resolution he would rule that "it is inconsistent
with the purposes and professions of our fraternity and dangerous to its
welfare to permit any form of so-called door prize or game or other
device promoted by a Lodge for financial gain whereby a participant may
by an element of chance or luck stand to win something of value in
excess of the stake invested by him. Such a ruling would no doubt bar
many things not inherently harmful in themselves but potentially dangerous as analogies or precedents.
·
"There are many who believe that the predominant drift of our
times is toward a desire to get something for nothing, to rely on others
rather than on one's own efforts. This disintegrating influence reveals
itself not only in a craving for collective forms of government to promote getting rather than giving but in a myriad of other forms even including 'religious and charitable organizations that are hypocritical enough
to rely on the gambling spirit rather than on the giving spirit. Even at
the risk of being deemed narrow and old-fashioned, Freemasonry must
stand firm against this dangerous tendency. There is probably no Lodge
in the country, certainly not in this jurisdiction, that could not be financially
independent if its memb~rs wished to contribute only a portion of what
'they spend in personal indulgences. Reliance on the public's gambling
instinct is not a necessary way to finance ourselves. It is only the easiest
way. In the long run it is . also a disastrous way. Fortunately the overwhelming proportion of our Lodges have always refrained from such
activities."

"To All Lodges and District Deputy Grand Masters:
"On a number of occasions Lodges have been cautioned about action

"Last year
speaker with some ability and knowledge. wove in some
international propaganda which provoked unfavorable comment.
"A report has come in recently of an address delivered by a nationally

which was couched in vulgar and occasional profane language. We want
no more of this.

to disregard all circulars, sales efforts, ·or offers to lecture. No Lodge
shall permit the delivery of any such unauthorized address, lecture or
talk before its membership."
This is in accord with the spirit of By-Law 78 and· not to be construed as affecting the ordinary discussions of our Lodge communications.

Missouri, 1940 (Grand Master):
Again the cowardly hand of anonymity has made its appearance in
our Grand jurisdiction. My attention has been c·alled to an anonymous
circular received by the Worshipful Master or Secretary of Lodges in
at least five widely scattered cities in the state. All five were addressed
in the same handwriting, mailed from the same post office in Kansas City
and were the same in content; and it seems probable that the circular
was sent generally to the Lodges throughout the state.
The circular, signed only "So Mote It Be," seeks, on political and
religious grounds, to prevent both the advancement in our Grand Lodge
line of our Deputy Grand Master and his re-electioll' as United States
Senator. The man or group responsible therefor are evidently afraid or
ashamed to bestow their names on this illegitimate brain-child which was
sired in iniquity and hat.red, and foaled in cowardice..
.
As Most Worshipful Brother R. R. .Kreeger said under similar cir-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

cumstances in 1909, we do not consider this matter from the standpoin·t
whether any particular officer of the present Grand body shall or sha!I
not be advanced. That question should and must be left to the sober and
unbiased judgment of the representatives in Annual Communication now
assembled. But we feel that in justice to the Craft and in the fulfillment
of our duty we must unconditionally condemn the publication and circulation of this communication, for the reason that it is un-Masonic in the
extreme and a flagrant violation of our laws and traditions with reference to electioneering for office, bringing politics and religion into the
Grand Lodge and violating the common principles of justice, decency
and fair play.
He or they who are responsible for the circular are not worthy of
being called Freemasons. They may be members of Masonic Lodges.
but they are not Freemasons at heart.
Shortly before our Annual Communication last year, anonymous letters.
were sent out. They were vigorously condemned by Most Worshipful
Brother Henry C. Chiles, but his denunciation apparently has not prevented a repetition.
We trust all the brethren in Missouri will heed this warning and
thereby make further action on the part of the Grand Lodge unnecessary. To the honor of the Craft, there have been few such offel}ses in
the past, and there must be none in the future.

. Pennsylvania, 1939:
In order to further clarify and emphasize an edict heretofore issued
the Grand Master on June 8, 1939, issued the following edict:
'
"Whereas, on ..January 18, 1937, an Edict was issued declaratory of
the Masonic Law w hich prohibits Masons from using lotter ies and games
of chance for money raising purposes; and
"Whereas, it now appears that the law may not be fully understood
and its meaning comprehended, wherefore a further declaration is deemed
necessary.
"Now, therefore, I, Robert R. Lewis, Right Worshipful Grand Master
of Free and Accepted Masons in Pennsylvania and Masonic Jurisdiction
Thereunto Belonging, by virtue of the authority in me vested, do hereby
order that no member of the Masonic Fraternity in this Jurisdiction shall
alone or ':"ith others, promote, assist in, or be a party to, any lottery,
game, device of chance, or other activity, whereby or wherein any individual participating may be able, through the element of luck or chance
to win, be awarded or receive a greater value than any other like par~
ticipant, arranged, devised or intended to raise money which shall, either
direc~ly. or indirectly,. in':1re to the benefit of any Masonic Lodge, body,
assoc1ahon, or orgamzat10n, or to any body, club, committee, or other
organization in Pennsylvania whose m embers are required to have membership in the Masonic Fraternity.
"This Edict must be read at the next, and the subsequent stated
meeting of the Lodge. It need not be copied in full in the minutes, but
I direct that the same shall be printed in full in the notice of your next
stated meeting, in order that the contents thereof may be known to each
and every member of your Lodge."
· This is still another emphatic statement of a Masonic principle which
is practically universal in the United States and it might well be observed
by certain non-secular organizations which not only frequently disregard
and ignore the moral principles hlVolved but the state laws as well.

Queensland, 1940:
Most Worshipful Grand Master: There have been several instances
in which brethren, who are not members-of the Craft, have come to our
Masonic gatherings and have been at the festive board. In one instance,
which I know very well indeed, a gentleman (the term is used for courtesy sake) came to one Lodge gathering here. He told a series of stories
he had not right to tell at the festive board, of a character that I would
call disgraceful. The Worshipful Master called him to order. It is a dreadful thing for such a man to come to our festive board-a man who does
not know our ways or customs or tenets. We cannot tolerate that sort
of thing. For this clause I am very grateful ·to the Board of General
Purposes. I now propose to put it for adoption. Carried unanimously.

West Australia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
As if recalcitrant organizations were not more than sufficient for an
unfortunate chief executive, Brother Fish was presented by the goddess
Ate with a new source of trouble in the form of a Lodge and its building
ambitions. 'Twas a small Lodge, my Masters, with a membership of
forty, only thirty-six of whom paid their annual dues, but the Lodge
wanted to embark upon a Lodge building scheme of the kind which tenderly strokes Sister Wild Cat. Feline schemes were disapproved of by
the Grand Master, notwithstanding a Lodge committee tried in vain to
persuade him to stroke pussy, and greatly disappointed one of its members "bluntly informed" the Grand Master that the Lodge would not
abandon its efforts. It did not. Defied the Grand Master's refusal to
approve. Raised funds on debentures sold to Masons and profanes.
Negotiated with the postal authorities to take a lease of the ground floor.
The Grand Master arrested the Lodge's Charter for disobeying the
Masonic law requiring the approval of the Grand Master before proceeding with the building. A large committee sought to procure its restoration,
but the Grand Master was adamant in his refusal, and when reporting
the matter to Grand Lodge recommended that the Charter be not restored owing to the illegality of the Lodge's proceedings, the worthlessness of the bonds in the absence of the Grand Master's approval and
endorsement; also because Masonry in several sections of the state had
been greatly discredited by wild-cat temple-building schemes. He also
recommended the sale of the property, the proceeds to be administered
in the interests of the Craft and the bondholders. So far, so good. But,
alas and alack! the Jurisprudence Committee was so full of the milk of
human kindness that it flowed in streams over all concerned. It approved
the Grand Master's arrest of the Lodge Charter arid his firm handling
of the case. It conveyed the principal officers' disavowal of any intention
to disregard the authority of Grand Lodge and the Grand Master, to
both of whom they tendered fraternal apologies for any laxity or neglect.
The committee was of opinion that the Lodge had been substantially disciplined. The rest of the milk was poured over the bone of contention,
namely, ·the Lodge building which seemed to the committee to be adequately and safely financed.

Ohio, 1940 (Grand Master):
In connection with the conferring of the Past Master's Degree, some
question has arisen as to whether the Master-elect who had received the
Past Master's Degree in a Chapter of Royal Arch Masojls, could be installed before he had attended the Convocation of Past Masters provided by this Grand Lodge.
It is my interpretation of our Code Section 94 that a Master-elect
who has filed his Past Master's Degree Certificate from a Chapter of
Royal Arch Masons,, may be installed any time within the sixty days
allowed by the Grand Lodge, but that he must attend the Convocation of
Past Masters as required by the Grand Lodge either before or following
his installation as Master.
Washington, 1939:
To clarify the Code, the Grand Master recommended that Section
1610 be repealed. This .section was passed as a By-Law and in the minds
of some, this section limits the right of membership in Grand Lodge of
those Past Masters who have taken the so-called "Secrets of the Chair."
As the Constitution prescribes the qualifications for membership in Grand
Lodge, and no change in those qualifications can be made except by
amending the Constitution, the section was obsolete and without authority.
h was repealed.
Also Section 2909 came under scrutiny. It, too, was enacted as a
By-Law, and attempts to add the Past Master's Degree to the Standard
Work. ·
The Grand Masters contended that inasmuch as the Past Master's
Degree can only be given' to · Past Masters and that its ritualistic work
could not be disclosed in Grand Lodge as the Wardens of the constituent
Lodges were members of Grand Lodge, therefore it would either be
necessary to repeal Section 2909 or dispense with the Wardens as members of Grand Lodge. He rather favored keeping Craft Masonry to its
original three degrees, as did all others presc;:nt.

Chairman of the Committee on Ritual, District of Columbia, did not

ritualistic proficiency of a Worshipful Master-eiect. He particularly finds
fault with the statement that: "When the presidirtg officer of a Lodge
has gone through the ceremony of conferring a degree his nerves and ·
his physical energy are sufficiently exhausted so that another brother
can usually deliver a lecture in a more creditable manner than could be
done by the officer." We agree with our Grand Master that if the Degree
is conferred with earnestness and sincerity there is a tax on the nerves,
but the true test by which a Worshipful Master is measured lies not
alone in ritualistic proficiency. In fact, an officer may be a doubtful
ritualist and yet because of his exemplary life, his .sincerity, his practice
of · the three great tenets of our fraternity and his leadership, render
great service for his Lodge. We agree that every Master should be able
to confer all the Degrees and to deliver all the lectures, but agree with

impressed with the lessons taught. To sound the depths of Masonry one

POLITICS
Missouri, 1940 (Grand Master):
It would seem that it should not be necessary to remind officers and
members of the Fraternity that partisan politics should never be brought
within the Lodge, or the Lodge drawn into politics; yet several experiences
of the year lea~ me to believe that such a reminder is both ncessary
and timely. In one city my attention was called to the fact that at the
meeting of a quasi-Masonic group, candidates for political office . were
presented and introduced as such. In another city, at a Lodge dinner
at which I was present, a brother who was called upon to speak was
introduced as a candidate for a named political office. In both instances
I told the brethren o~ the impropriety of which they had been guilty
and explained that while we as Freemasons ate charged to be patrotically
loyal to the country in which we live, and while we 3hould, as individuals,
carry the tenets of Freemasonry with us in our daily lives and apply
them in all our acts-even in our individual political thinking and acting
partisan politics should not be brought into the Lodge or the Lodge
drawn into politics for by so doing the peace and harmony of the Lodge
would ultimately be destroyed.
·
·
A third violation of the above policy was called to my attention
when a Past Master of one of our Lodges filed a complaint with me,
charging the Worshipful Master of another Lodge with un,Masonic conduct in sending to a number of Masonic voters a note, signed by him
as Worshipful Master of the Lodge and reading as follows :·
"Dear Brother:
"Mrs.
, the wife of our Senior Warden, is a candidate for
Republican committeewoman of the ................ Ward. Any assistance you
can give her will be personally appreciated by me.
Fraternally,
----,W.M.

District of Columbia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee) :
On another subject, · however, which the Grand Master freely admits is
a policy criticized by some, we are in agreement with the views of M. W.
Brother Finseth . He says:
"To advocate publicity of Lodge affairs will very likely be considered
.an innovation by some and undoubtedly will bring criticism from others.
However, I am a believer in such publicity. Well directed newspaper
publicity of fraternal events is of interest to nearly everyone, and most
newspapers are more than willing to print newsy articles of this character.
"Men take pride in belonging to an organization whose affairs are
important enough to attract the attention of others, and I would suggest that
every Lodge appoint a committee whose duty it is to see that mention
of special meetings and Masonic events is made in the local newspapers."
We believe it absolutely necessary that such announcements be passed
upon by a competent Maso!J.iC editor before release to the press.

Ohio, 1940 (Grand Master):
In his remarks the Grand Master stated:
"Today there is strong competition for one's time. We are b~sieged
on all sides to join this or that club, society or organization. In addition
to these things a great number of people seem to be possessed with a mad
craze for pleasure that apparently cannot be satisfied. Despite this competition for time, Masonry continues on its silent yet impressive manner
of doing good . . We must not be misled into making our Lodge rooms any
the less sacred places than they have been in ages past. We realize we are
living in a changing world, but as a matter of fact the world has been
changing since time immemorial."
Oregon, 1940 (Grand Master):
To advocate publicity of Lodge affairs will very likely be considered
an innovation by some and undoubtedly will bring criticism from others.
However, I am a believer in such publicity. Well directed newspaper publicity of fraternal events is of interest to nearly everyone, and most newspapers are more than willing to print newsy articles of this character.
Men take pride in belonging to an organization whose affairs are
important enough to attract the attention of others, ·and I would suggest
that every Lodge appoint a committee whose duty it is to see that mention
of special meetings and Masonic .events is made in the local newspapers.
The time has arrived when Masonry should no longer "hide its light
under a bushel."
Speaking of "publicity" the Grand .Master urged a wider use of the
press arid suggested a committee of publicity for each constituent Lodge
to have the matter in charge. In short he believed the time has come
when Freemasonry should no longer "hide its light under a bushel." An
opinion with which many Grand Lodges would cordially disagree.

Whereas : It has been brought to the attention of Sewanee Lodge No.

Whereas: A non-political, non-religious and non-partisan organization
known as the Grundy County Crusaders has been formed in Grundy

Whereas: The Masonic Order was founded on the principles of observance of the duly constituted law, religious freedom, obedience to and
the support of the principles of freedom within the law, morality and

principles;

of the Grundy County Crusaders for my approval. This resolution was
studied by M. W . Chas. Barham, P. G. M. and myself, and we could see
nothing in it contrary to the principles of Masonry, since lawful means
were to be used to eliminate subversive elements and Un-American teaching from Grundy County. The Grand Master feels that as Masons, we
must b.e awake in these difficult days if we are to be "true to our government and just to our country." We have a responsibility to our government, which cannot be discharged by a passive and indifferent attitude,
toward those forces that seek to destroy the rights and liberties guaranteed
by the Constitution. May every Mason loyally support our beloved country.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
Georgia, 1939:
When first originated, Grand Lodges adopted the idea of declaring a
single "Public Schools Week." Georgia now raises the term to one month
and changes its designation to "Good Citizenship and Education Month."
As an initiation of this activity; Grand Master et al. met with the State
Superintendent of Schools in Atlanta, "where a broadcast was given over
WSB announcing Good Citize11ship and Education Month.
From the report of the. Committee on Citizenship and Public Schools
we learn that between 140 and 150 Lodges have taken part in these
programs, with over 34,000 in attendance. The program is further aided
by the Masonic Messenger, the official publication of Grand Lodge. These
educational programs are always of vital importance, but especially now
when our very liberties are at .stake.
Georgia, 1940 (Grand Master):
In accordance with the resolution passed at the .1935 session a proclarbation was issued setting apart the period September 16 through October
15 for the observance of a Citizenship and Free Public School Program.
Worshipful and Rev. Firley Baum again consented to head this committee and he has been tireless in his efforts to make the program everything the Grand Lodge could wish. The observance was inugurated with
a radio program over Station WSB on September 14. Dr. M. D. Collins,
State School Superintendent, favored. us with an ;iddress on this program. We are grateful to the State Department of Education for their
endorsement of and cooperation with this movement. .
The response this year has been exceedingly gratifying; practically
everyone who was asked by this committee to assist, did so, and rendered yeoman service. This year a larger committee was constituted so
that the entire state could be more nearly covered.
· During the year three bulletins were sent out to this committee.
Our Most Worshipful Grand Master; Brother J. Wilson Parker, has
given unfailing and unfaltering support to this program during the yea'r
and frequently addressed the brethren, in the summer conventions and
in the Lodges, on this question. He also spoke over the radio, with Brother
Dr. M. D. Collins, our state school superintendent, and myself. We are
deeply indebted to him and to Brother Dr. Collins.
Lodges .in South Carolina are active in the interest . of the public
schools, assisting attendance teachers in maintaining enrollments and in
some cases Lodges, by small assessments upon their members, are furnishing clothing, books, glasses, etc., for needy pupils.

RITUAL
New Jersey, 1940:
The Grand Master recommended that a change in the · ritual be made
whereby the impreccations used in the degrees would be explained as
being symbolic only, and that the only penalties imposed by Masonry
are reprimand, suspension, and expulsion. Committee on the ritual frawned
on the proposed change but said that the explanation might be made to

of the ritual. Grand Lodge adopted the committee's report.
Tennessee, 1941 (Grand Master):
It is evident that our knowledge of ritual has out-stripped by far our
understanding and appreciation of the noble meaning and high destiny of
Masonry. Our ability to recite ritual with exactness has .surpassed our
zeal for its higher values and dulled our comprehension of the truths presented. Whether we would have it so or not, we are faced with the fact
that only about ten per cent of our membership has any real interest in
learning our ritual or time to become proficient in its performance. This
leaves nearly ninety per ce.nt of our membership with the feeling, although
it may never be articulated, .that the investment by the Grand Lodge
through its. Lecture System does not touch their lives and has nothing of
vital interest to offer them. We owe something to this large group of
intelligent and serious minded brethren, and we must endeavor to challenge
them for the future of Masonry and rouse them to a sacred sense of its
many values. Some of this group may be interested in the beauty of its
symbolism, some in the depth of its philosophy, some in its romantic
history, and still others may become especially interested in the charitable
undertakings of the fraternity. The Grand Master is definitely of the opinion
that the Lecture System can help us and must help us to emerge from our
indifference and lack of understanding and bring us into a day of larger
usefulness.
West Australia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
There seems to have been the desire to curtail the Master Mason
Degree without impairing its structure, in order to save time. The idea
that this was a strong reason is found in the result of inquiries by the
committee addressed to other jurisdictions as to the length of time it
took to "put on" (as it was said) the Master Mason Degree. The degree,
as I have seen it worked in America-and it was claimed to be based on
the York Rite-was certainly a very tedious performance, notwithstanding the skill of the performers, especially when its three sections were
given, even if there was only one candidate. When I witnessed it, it took

796

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

three and a half hours, which was also the time it took in Alberta when
the committee conducted its inquiry. In other jurisdictions, owing to the
absence of so much prolixity, the time was given variously, being from
seventy minutes to three hours. It will be seen, therefore, that the task
before the committee was a somewhat formidable one, and the utmost
the revisers were able to report was that · the reductions proposed, "would
not reduce the time to less than two hours, two hours and forty-five
minutes being nearer the mark." The committee also reported that it
had endeavored to keep in mind that the beauty and dignity of the degrees,
especially the dramatization in the Third Degree, should be preserved;
also that the present form and wording should not be changed except
where necessary; the avoidance of unnecessary repetitions; lectures to be
kept within due bounds; and optional parts to be kept to a minimum.
After discussion the committee's revision was adopted, and the use of
the revised ritual made operative on January I, 1940.
This writer, while readily admitting that the choice of ritual and the
determining of its wording and length is entirely the affair of any Grand
jurisdiction, has often wondered what Western Australian brethren would
think if they had to work degrees that took three hours to put on. Of
course, it could not happen with the rituals we have, because we in Australia rely on symbolism, whilst in America dramatization, especially in
the Third Degree, is preferred. It is very spectacular, and when in the
Third Degree, Pope's ode, "Vital spark of heavenly flame," is sung by a
specially selected choir at the time when iri our symbolic rendering we
have either Handel's "Dead March," or "Chopin's "Marche Furiebre," the
bizarre dramatization is entirely forgotten in the thrill of the immortal
ode, which, we can repoice to remember, was composed .by a brother Freemason-one who was as devoted a Craftsman as he was a Roman Catholic.
Still, to the writer, the less spectacular symbolic performance of the degree
i3 more appealing than the dramatic form.

STUDENT LOANS
Georgia, 1940 (Grand Master):
Prompted by high ideals and pure m.otivt:s for a desire to be of service
to the youth of our state, the Grand Lodge in 1921 created the Student
Loan Fund. While it has been administered as efficiently as possible
and now amounts to approximately $30,000.00, much difficulty has been
encounter·ed on the collection of these notes. It has been necessary on
several occasions to resort to the courts in an effort to recover funds
loaned. This is not wholesome advertising for our fraternity. The commission is quite often confronted with the plea that the recipient thought
the funds were donated instead of loaned. If we withdrew from this field
of activity the cause of education will not suffer, as other organizations
can provide sufficient funds for all worthy applicants.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

797

Maine, 1941 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
The difficulties of any "Student Loan Fund" in Nevada is seen in
the report that there are nine unpaid loans and several students that have
ignored the letters of the committee. Many. students give the matter of
re-payment little consideration and only too often look upon the obligation lightly, and gradually look upon it as philanthropy.
North Carolina, 1941 (Grand Master)l'
For many years the Grand Lodge has maintained a student loan fund
of approximately $85,000, allocated in amounts of from $1,000 to $5,000
or more in some twenty-four colleges throughout the state.. This loan
fund has been operated with a reasonable degree of satisfaction to the committee of the Grand Lodge which has from time to time made reports
to the Grand Lodge. Under the plan originally adopted, when a portion
of this fund was allocated to a college and turned over to the college,
the matter of its administration was left entirely to the college authorities,
with the understanding that it would be loaned preferably to juniors and
seniors who had made a good record during their first two years in
college, and who could not finish without aid of this kind. The colleges
from time to time would make reports to the Grand Lodge Student Loan
Fund Committee. For many years the fund operated very successfully,
and through it a large number of wor•hy students, wPlo . otherwise could
not have finished their ~ducation , were enabled to graduate and take their
places out in the world.
In recent years, however, there has been a very decided falling off in
demands of students upon student loan funds. This situation is attributable to the policy of the Federal government in extending student aid in
generous amounts to all classes of higher schools and colleges. At the
present time, approximately $25,000 of the Grand Lodge fund are not
being used by the colleges in which they are allocated, and the trend
would .seem to indicate very definitely that from year to year the demand
for these loan funds will continue to grow less. In the light of this situation, I recommend that the Grand Lodge direct the Loan Fund Committee or the Finance Committee of . the Grand Lodge to withdraw the
amount of the fund and any accretion thereto, from any college in which
the fund is not needed or has fallen into disuse, and in such withdrawals
there will .be a full and complete accounting between the college and the
Grand Lodge with respect to the fund.

TEMPLES
District of Columbia, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Indiana has one very desirable regulation, which is strictly enforced:
that no emblems other than Masonic may be displayed in a Lodge room
during Lodge meetings. In our own jurisdiction a number of our Lodge
r.ooms present to the candidate, and to members, an East which is dominated by an Eastern Star, in some instances larger and overshadowing
the great symbol which should be in simple dignity alone. It has long
been the firm belief of this writer that all such emblems should be easily
removable and should be removed wHen the organization they represent
is not in session. We believe it is a matter which should have the attention of our own Grand Lodge, and that the example of Indiana is a fine
one to follow.

Oregon, 1940 (Chairman, Correspondence Committee):
Port Saint Joe Lodge No. 111, with a membership of 40 and annual
dues of $4.00, owning a downtown lot in . addition to a small amount of
cash in its treasury, wished to erect a temple costing between eight and
nine thousand dollars, all of which was to be borrowed. They claimed that
the Post Office would be located on the ground floor, along with other
renters of space for business purposes. The Grand Master could not see
it as a good sound business proposition and refused to sanction the scheme.
His disapproval, however, meant nothing in the )'Oung lives. of the forty
dauntless members of No. 111, so they went blithely on their way without
further discussion and built the building. They printed bonds bearing six·
per cent interest and sold approximately $4,500.00 to Masons and profanes.
They also entered into a lease with the Post Office Department for floor
space.
The Grand Master acted in no uncertain manner. He arrested their
Charter, refused the supplications of a committee composed of Lodge
members to rescind his actions, and recommended that the building and
all matters pertaining thereto be turned over to the Grand Lodge Properties Committee to be sold in the interest of the Craft, and the bond
holders be classed as preferred creditors.
Now here comes the comedy: The Jurisprudence Committee in
passing on the matter, did not hold with the Grand Master in his recommendation. They held that the brethren had suffered sufficient punishment and that their Charter should be restored and they be ·a llowed to
go merrily on their way. They only stipulated that they in no way, that
is, the Grand Lodge, could be held responsible for t~e bonds· issued.
To our way of thinking, that was about as lame a solution of a question that we have ever witnessed. They speak of the members having
been sufficiently disciplined. Who, we ask, has suffered anything, except
the dignity of Grand Lodge and the Grand Master. The boys flaunted
the ruling of the Grand Master based on Grand Lodge law; .they now
have th~ir building just as they wished irrespective of what the Grand
Master ruled. Had the ringleaders of this affair been brought up for trial
and deprived of their membership, an example would have been made
that wouJd have had a salutary effect that would have been lasting.

The Masonic Homes of California are their especial pride and rightfully so.
The second big enterprise and service of California Masons is their
observance of Public Schools Week. For twenty years they have been
bringing the schools to the homes and the homes to the schools. They
permit no resolutions to be made, no endorsements or disapprovals of
legislation, but are primarily interested in making all classes in California
acquainted with the operation, development and success of the Public:
Schools. California has lead the way in this splendid field of endeavor.

An interesting account was furnished by the Grand Master of his different visitations to Lodges. One of the meetings was tl)at unique gathering
known as the Strawberry Festival, an annual affair held by one of t~e
Lodges at a place called Elk Grove, whose district is deservedly held m
high repute for its strawberries. The brethre? of that Lodge in:'ite ~asons
in the valleys of Sacramento and San Joaqum to partake of this delightful
fruit io the excellence of which this writer can testify from personal
experience. Whether it excels the best Australian strawberries, our own
included, may be just a matter of opinion, but it can be justly claii:ied f~r
California that its fruit growers are greater adepts than Austrahans m
bringing the high quality of their different fruits under notice. Nor do
Californian growers neglect the more fleshy products. "Beef Steak Feed~"

activities into a vigorous propaganda of their products. I verily believe
there must have been California blood in the veins of the man who wrote,

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation of the
world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000--5923.
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology
is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
/.dd 3760 to the common era. Thus~ 1923 and 3760--5683. After
September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno lnventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the year of discovery."
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus : 1923 ·and 530--2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the temple of
Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.), "in the year of the
deposit._"
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization of their
Order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
From the Christian era take 1118. , Thus: 1118 from 1923-805.
Order of High Priesthood...:....Dates from the year of the blessing of
Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis (A. B.),
"in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing. Thus 1923 and
' 1913-3836.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly speaking,
they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the
one called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United
States.
·
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the Cryptic
and the Templar degree.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the Entered
Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They are called
Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the Mark
Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the Royal Arch.
The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred
in a Council of High Priests upon those who have been regularly elected
to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular
because they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the Royal
Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master. They are
called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" meai:is a secret vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are the
Red Cross, the Temple· and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes
from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the temple at Jerusalem
from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd,
inclusive. In the Southern jurisdiction of the .United States (which includes
all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River)
the organization of the different Bodies, and the degrees conferred by them,
are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to
18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to 30°; Consistory; 31° to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33°.
In the Northern jurisdiction (which includes all states north of the
Ohio river and east of the Mississippi river) the degrees conferred are :
Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council Princes of Jerusalem, 15°
and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18.0 ; Consistory,19° to 32°; Supreme
Council, 33 °.
